# Nava-vraja-mahima. Vol. Eight

## Dedication

Although I have written Nava-vraja-mahima for the pleasure of all Vaisnavas who either physically or mentally reside in Vrndavana, I dedicate this book to those whose hearts are devoted to Radha-Syamasundara and New Vraja-dhama. It is my hope that they will pass their time in this way:

*iha vatsan samacarayad*  
*iha nah svami jagau vamsim*  
*iti sasram gadato me*  
*yamuna-tire dinam yayat*

**“Here our Lord herded the calves, and here He played the flute. I pray that I may pass my days shedding tears as I speak these words on the Yamuna's shore.” (Sri Raghupati Upadhyaya)**

## Preface

The title of the book you are now reading, Nava-vraja-mahima, when rendered in English becomes “The Glories of New Vraja-dhama.” I originally conceived of it as a booklet, meant to guide devotees visiting the holy places of New Vraja-dhama, ISKON’s rural community in Hungary.

As you must have noticed, the book has grown in size since its inception and would now likely require a small handcart for eager pilgrims to be able to transport it from one pastime place to another! Nonetheless, it still serves its original purpose of extolling New Vraja- dhama by praising its presiding Deities, Radha-Syamasundara, and by narrating the Supreme Lord Krsna’s pastimes in His eternal abode, Sri Vrndavana-dhama.

Texts that glorify the holy abodes (dhamas) of the Lord are called dhama-mahatmyas. Two prime examples of this genre of devotional literature are Rupa Gosvami’s Sri Mathura-mahatmya and Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya. Both of these books establish the sanctity of the dhamas they depict — Vrndavana and Navadvipa respectively — by citing Puranic praise of the dhamas themselves as well as the pastime places within their boundaries. There is, however, an interesting difference between the two. Sri Mathura-mahatmya is an unordered compendium of scriptural references to the pastime places it describes, while Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya chronicles the Lord’s pastimes and the places at which they occurred by following the sequence in which pilgrims visit those places as they circumambulate the dhama. Thakura Bhaktivinodaalso recounts the personal spiritual reflections he gleans from circumambulating Navadvipa in an appendix to Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya that he calls Sri Navadvipa-bhava-taranga.

Despite their stylistic differences, the transcendental benefit readers derive from these two types of mahatmyas is the same. They act as practical guidebooks to the dhama, and at the same time they aid pilgrims in immersing their thoughts in the Lord’s glories. For that reason, devotees who do not travel to the dhama can also derive transcendental benefit by circumambulating the holy places in their minds as they meditate on both the Lord’s pastimes and the dhama's glories as they are recounted in sacred texts of this nature.

Nava-vraja-mahimd is a mahatmya in the style of Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya in that it includes an account of my own personal circumambulation, or parikrama, of New Vraja-dhama and the realisations that came to me as a result. In fact, as I visit the pastime places in New Vraja-dhama — more commonly known to the people of Hungary as Krsna Valley — I sometimes reflect on similar parikramas I have undertaken in Bhauma Vrndavana, recount histories of how New Vraja-dhama was established and developed, or express my own devotional aspirations. This personal approach is primarily an attempt to please the devotees of New Vraja-dhama, who requested me to describe the parikrama not as a passive observer but as a participant who shares his adventure with the reader.

Amongst many possible readers, this personal adventure is especially intended to be shared with the residents of and visitors to New Vraja-dhama, for whom this book will naturally be of greatest interest. Those readers who are not a part of that particular audience may rightly question what New Vraja-dhama is and how its glorification can be relevant to persons who live outside Hungary or who may never visit.

As its name suggests, New Vraja-dhama is modelled after the original Vraja-dhama, Bhauma Vrndavana, Krsna’s eternal home as it appears on earth. The inspiration to establish New Vraja-dhama came from my spiritual master, His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acarya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. In the 1960s in America, Srila Prabhupada established New Vrndavana and envisioned it to be a self-sufficient community, dependent upon agriculture and cow protection, as well as a place of pilgrimage in the West. New Vraja-dhama is therefore our humble attempt to fulfil the desire of His Divine Grace that such places of pilgrimage be established throughout the world.

In the introduction to this book and in the essay entitled “The Truths of the Dhama,” the reader will find a detailed history of how and why New Vraja-dhama came to be, along with a philosophical study of the spiritual principles that make it a holy place. I cannot overstate how important it is for the reader to carefully go through these parts of the book in order to clearly understand the spiritual foundations upon which New Vraja-dhama and Nava-vraja-mahimd rest.

What benefit will those who do not visit New Vraja-dhama gain from reading this book? The answer is threefold.

Nava-vraja-mahima contains extensive and very detailed narrations of Krsna’s pastimes at all the major places in Vrndavana, as well as at many lesser-known places. Extensive research went into compiling — from the Vedas, Upanisads, Puranas, Samhitas, and other Vedic histories, as well as from the commentaries of our previous acaryas and other sources — the information it contains. Altogether, the text and the accompanying references offer the reader a unique opportunity to delve deeply into Krsna’s pastimes in Bhauma and Goloka Vrndavana and better get to know the Supreme Lord and His loving associates.

Second, although the topographical orientation, distances, and occasionally the sequence of New Vraja-dhama’s parikrama differ from the same in Bhauma Vrndavana, the book also serves as an in-depth guide for pilgrims to use in visiting the pastime places of Sri Krsna’s original earthly abode.

Third, through the glorification of New Vraja-dhama, this book testifies to the greatness of Srila Prabhupada’s achievement in spreading the potency of Vrndavana throughout the world.

Now, allow me to clarify a few points about certain expressions and literary devices used in the text, about the structure of the volumes, and about the actual parikrama route of New Vraja-dhama.

The expression “Krsna’s pastimes in New Vraja-dhama” is not meant to imply that Krsna manifests His eternal pastimes here in the way that He does, creation after creation, in Bhauma Vrndavana. Rather it means that the pastime places in New Vraja-dhama correspond to the original places in Bhauma Vrndavana or Goloka Vrndavana. Largely due to the uncommon format of the text (which I will discuss elsewhere in this preface) and because of the correspondence between the pastime places in both dhamas, it was sometimes necessary to refer to the pastimes associated with those places in a way that may make it sound as if they happened in New Vraja-dhama.

If I say, for example, “At this place, called Aghavana, Krsna killed Aghasura,” it means “Krsna killed Aghasura in the Aghavana of Bhauma Vrndavana, which is commemorated by the place of the same name here in New Vraja-dhama.” Similarly, phrases such as “At this place Radha and Krsna enact Their rasa dance” should be taken to mean “At the Rasa-sthali of Goloka Vrndavana, the divine couple enact Their eternal rasa dance. The place called Rasa-sthali in New Vraja-dhama commemorates that original place.”

The reason I use such expressions, aside from literary necessity, is to emphasise the importance of New Vraja-dhama and its stature as a place of pilgrimage. Again, the reader will find the philosophical and spiritual reasoning and supporting scriptural evidence for employing this convention in the introduction and the essay on dhama-tattva that follow this preface.

Another literary device found in this book — as well as in other books describing the holy dhama — is that I sometimes speak about New Vraja-dhama as if I were directly seeing the unmanifest (aprakata) abode and pastimes of the Lord. These expressions are not declarations of my existential position; rather, they are poetic expressions of my deep feelings for the subject matter and the places themselves. I qualify such statements here to avoid causing misunderstandings that might blur the line between the manifest and unmanifest features of the dhama, merging them in a way that could be taken as contrary to authorised dhama-tattva.

When, in describing the dhama, authors weave between manifest and unmanifest realities in this way, it often causes the features of the aprakata realm or the pastimes Krsna is relishing there to seem as if they are part of the world visible to conditioned souls. But devotees well versed in the principles of dhama-tattva will have no difficulty following these transitions between the manifest and unmanifest realms, whereas others may either not notice them or find them confusing.

Our great acaryas may express themselves in such ways due to the overwhelming bliss they feel at seeing the aprakata-dhama and the eternal pastimes going on there. Or, in the case of those who are not on the fully realised platform of our great acaryas, authors may be making a conscious endeavour to emphasise the divinity that underlies the features of the dhama that conditioned souls are able to perceive.

In writing Nava-vraja-mahima, poetic inspiration would sometimes impel me to describe the features of the dhama not in terms of what I was seeing with my eyes — for I cannot see that which is unmanifest — but in terms of the aprakata counter-whole as I have heard about it from scripture and as I contemplate it in relation to New Vraja-dhama. Readers who notice such expressions in the pages of this book should take them in this light, not as my personal realisation of the unmanifest dhama in the way of the great acaryas.

**\* \* \* \***

Parikrama is the traditional way of visiting Vrndavana. When Krsna sent Uddhava to Nandagrama with messages for the Vraja-vasis, He directed His cousin along a specific route and pointed out places to note along the journey. Thus Uddhava relished parikrama by travelling from Mathura to Nandagrama, as did Krsna by describing the journey to him.

On His only visit to Vrndavana, Caitanya Mahaprabhu spent the first month of His two-month stay touring through Vraja’s twelve forests. And even though Lord Caitanya is Krsna Himself, He requested the help of a guide and followed the established route of His time. English translations within a single stanza, or having longer verses straddle more than one stanza. However, we feel confident that the book’s format will enable yon to relish the topic all the more.

From the outset I wanted Nava-vraja-mahima to be well illustrated to give windows into Krsna’s pastimes and to contribute to the overall purpose of the work — to increase the reader’s attachment to the Lord. I hope this has been achieved to your satisfaction. In Sri Krsna-samhita (9.16), Bhaktivinoda Thakura writes,

**“By seeing pictures of Krsna or by repeatedly hearing descriptions of Krsna from persons who have seen Him, one’s greed for attaining Krsna increases unlimitedly.”**

To assist you in navigating through the unfamiliar names of pastime places and the variances in the locations of these places in New Vraja-dhama and Bhauma Vrndavana, each chapter also includes a map or maps of the area it describes.

Altogether there are eight volumes of text. The set is complete with a ninth volume solely dedicated to maps of the various holy places of both New Vraja-dhama and Bhauma Vrndavana, along with short descriptions of each pastime place. Devotees can take this map book with them to follow the parikrama routes in both dhamas and have a reminder of Krsna’s activities there.

Nava-vraja-mahima is meant to serve as a companion for devotees who want to take full advantage of the presence of Vrndavana in Hungary and to develop their relationship with its presiding Deities, Radha-Syamasundara. Furthermore, it is meant to encourage devotees anywhere in the world to worship their local Deities with devotion and recognise the Vaikuntha nature of those Deities’ abodes. It is my hope as the author that this work will serve these purposes in some small way and thus bring pleasure to devotees, for my own access to the dhama will be possible only hy the good wishes of the Vaisnavas.

In conclusion, I request the reader, wherever he or she may reside, to consider that in its essence this book praises the same dhama and the same Krsna that are there in their own hearts, and which are thus very near and dear to them. It is in this way that our journey around New Vraja-dhama through the pages of this book is synonymous with our own inner journey back to Godhead.

The journey through Nava-vraja-mahima is a long one. The book spans over five thousand pages and took five years to write. Therein I have tried my best to portray the truths of Vrndavana as they are recorded in scriptures and narrated by perfect devotees like Srila Prabhupada. Sadly, I remain a conditioned soul and thus am prone to make mistakes. If my readers find mistakes within the pages of this book, I ask them to tolerate such faults in the way they do the pebbles or thorns that prick their feet while on parikrama of the dhama.

Hare Krsna.  
Sivarama Swami  
New Vraja-dhama  
Gopastami, 2 November 2011

## Chapter 36 - Introduction to the Maha-mantra

These last six chapters praise Radha-Syamasundara’s most merciful feature, the Hare Krsna maha-mantra: the divine couple’s sound incarnation and the saviour of the world, including this common soul.

This chapter directly extols the maha-mantra along with the process of worship known as nama-sankirtana, by which any offenceless devotee can attain the divine couple’s shelter in Goloka Vrndavana.

The second chapter describes the offences that obstruct us from reaping tangible benefits from our chanting. The last four chapters explore the mantra’s meanings by studying its individual words.

Dear friends! Please come to New Vraja-dhama and chant the holiest of mantras, the maha-mantra You’ll be immersed in an ocean of bliss as you see the names on your lips as one with the forms on the altar.

Although any place is suitable for worshipping the names of the Lord, New Vraja-dhama is special, for here the sweetly smiling faces of Radha-Syamasundara wash away our offensive mentalities.

How can you know that what I am saying is true? Come chant with us! Their Lordships’ special mercy will be evident by the joy in your heart, the tears in your eyes, and the shivering of your body.

Those who have discovered this unique marvel for themselves call it the “Radhe-Syama experience.” At times it feels like a light drizzle of nectar, at others like a torrential downpour of ecstatic bliss.

And why not! Syama is a hovering monsoon cloud of mellows, and Radha is a lightning strike of bliss, continually enticing the cloud to join Her in unleashing one shower of ecstatic mellow after another.

When the clouds let loose a deluge and we’re stranded out in the open, what else can we do but surrender? Let us raise our arms to the sky, laugh, cry, and dance exuberantly in that inevitable cloudburst.

But friends! Do not impatiently demand that the divine couple deliver Their grace. Remain meek and humble in Their presence, pray to Them for Their mercy, and surely the experience will come.

Sometimes I stand for hours waiting for divine grace. At other times that mercy appears to have been waiting for me, making its powers known through a magical embrace from the very first name I chant.

At such times I plunge headlong into an unprecedented land of joy and mirth, where the syllables of the holy name are everything and where Radha, Syama, and Their servants dance in bliss.

In that realm of sankirtana, bliss seems to make mountains quiver, rivers turn solid, the sun and moon leave their orbits, cows liberally give milk, and men, women, and children sing and dance in abandon.

That bliss seems to transform the temple: the floors become cintamani, the walls blossoming trees, the altar a majestic grove with chirping birds, and the name — like the ether — pervades everything.

Words can’t describe it, and so again I say, “Come to New Vraja- dhama. Chant with us.” When you do, at the end of the kirtana you will tell your friends the same thing I do — when it rains it pours.

**\* \* \* \***

Now let me describe one small wave in the great ocean of sankirtana nectar. I pray to the water of that wave and the aquatics that play there to bless me with the power to record the holy name’s glories.

Of these glories, an unknown Vaisnava poet writes,

**“Sri Krsna’s holy name is a reservoir of all transcendental happiness, the destroyer of the sins of Kali-yuga, and the most purifying of all purifying things.**

**“It is the food of the saints who traverse the path from this domain of sorrow to the spiritual world, and the pleasure garden where the voices of the greatest saints, philosophers, and poets play.**

**“It is the life and soul of the righteous, and the seed of the tree of religion. May this holy name, whose glories I have barely touched, bring transcendental auspiciousness to you all.”**

Lord Siva once instructed his dear wife in the secrets of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra by saying,

**“O devi! Please know that in Kali-yuga the most effective way to be freed of sins is by Sri Hari-nama.**

**“For this reason Krsna’s holy names should be widely distributed to everyone, everywhere. By nama-sankirtana the people of this age will be freed of the inevitable fate of going to hell for their sins.”**

Eager to hear the mantra of which her husband spoke, Durga-devi enquired from him about the words of the mantra. Lord Siva replied,

**“To chant the maha-mantra, first chant ‘Hare Krsna’ twice.**

**“Then chant ‘Krsna’ twice, and after that, repeat ‘Hare’ twice. This is half of the mantra. Chant the second half of the mantra in the same sequence, but with the components ‘Hare Rama,’ ‘Rama,’ and ‘Hare.’**

**“By chanting this maha-mantra of Sri Krsna one is freed from all sins and, as a result, is qualified to enter the realm of perfection, wherein no one but the eternal companions of Sri Krsna reside.”**

By the grace of my readers and Krsna’s holy names I will now touch upon some of the endless glories of chanting the maha-mantra, which is identical to Radha and Syama down to the smallest spiritual detail.

Sometimes, as I perform nama-sankirtana in the presence of Radha-Syama, whether alone or with others, it is as if I am witnessing Them displaying two features—Their forms and Their names.

This phenomenon is like a majestic natural force wherein the sankirtana is a waterfall and the Deities are a lake into which those surging names cascade. At other times these roles are reversed.

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami confirms the eternal principle that just as Krsna is His name, Krsna’s name is equally Him:

**“Simply by chanting the holy name, one associates with the Lord directly.”**

Let us now hear about Krsna’s holy name and in so doing directly associate with Radha and Syamasundara, becoming more intimately linked with Them. Who would neglect such an opportunity?

In glorifying Their Lordships, I have left the study of Their holy names until the end, for praise of Their names is the best praise of all. As the common saying goes, one should save the best for last.

Dear readers! Bear in mind that first we receive the maha-mantra from the guru. Only later do we receive from him the diksa-mantras, beginning with the Brahma-gayatri and ending in the Kama-gayatri.

Were we to reverse this progression, our offence to the maha-mantra, the sovereign ruler of all mantras, would nullify the effects of the diksa-mantras, *hari-nama vina putra diksa ca vi-phala bhavet.*

Just as we worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna (svayam-bhagavan) before all other forms of Godhead, we must receive the Hare Krsna maha-mantra before all other mantras.

Moreover, the sacred words of Vaisnava Gayatri mantras (vidmahe, dhimahi, and pracodayat) direct us to thoroughly understand, carefully cultivate, and lovingly chant the maha-mantra.

The Brhan-naradiya Purana stresses that in Kali-yuga, chanting Krsna’s names (harer nama) is the only way to advance from devotion in practice to devotion in ecstasy; there is no other way (nasty eva).

And by repeating the same phrases, the same verse points out that chanting Krsna’s names (harer nama) is the only way to advance from ecstatic devotion to love; there is no other way (nasty eva).

The third iteration of that phrase underscores that chanting Krsna’s names (harer nama) is the only way to advance from love to the shelter of Krsna’s lotus feet; there is no other way (nasty eva).

We may well wonder how to balance these unequivocal words from the Naradiya Purana with Lord Caitanya’s instruction that practising any one of pure devotion’s nine limbs can lead to perfection.

The Lord says to Sanatana Gosvami,

**“When one is firmly fixed in devotional service, whether he executes one or many processes of devotional service, the waves of love of Godhead will awaken.”**

Jiva Gosvami reconciles these two statements by clarifying that in Kali-yuga all activities of devotional service should be performed alongside nama-sankirtana. That is how they bestow full results.

In this regard, Srila Prabhupada quotes the Bhakti-sandarbha,

**“Therefore whatever one does in executing devotional service must he accompanied by the chanting of the holy name of the Lord.”**

Sanatana Gosvami gives further insight into why scripture and Vaisnava acaryas place special emphasis on nama-sankirtana, and why it accompanies all other limhs of bhakti, such as Deity worship.

The Gosvami explains that not only is chanting Krsna’s names the best and most powerful way to attain love for Him, but barer nama itself is also the fruit of devotional practice (bhakteh phalam).

We may object to the idea that nama-sankirtana is the fruit of devotional service by asking, “Isn’t love for Krsna the fruit of bhakti-yoga? Isn’t nama-sankirtana simply a means to attain love of God?”

Surely love for Krsna is the fruit of devotional service. But because the ripening of prem is accompanied by loud glorification of the Lord, prem and nama-sankirtana are said to appear simultaneously.

Moreover, because sankirtana is itself like a mystic mantra that attracts and thus gives rise to the treasure of prem, the two are inseparable and are both considered the fruits of devotion.

Years after first instructing Sanatana Gosvami in pure devotional service, Caitanya Mahaprabhu gave further instructions to the Gosvami and again stressed the pre-eminence of nama-sankirtana:

**“Of the nine processes of devotional service, the most important is nama-sankirtana. If one does this, avoiding the ten kinds of offences, one very easily obtains the most valuable love of Krsna.”**

Once love for Krsna has awakened, we cry out like cakora birds on a moonless night, calling out the names of Radha and Krsna in the agony of separation, and thus further nourish our love.

When Krsna appears in order to relieve our anxiety and engages with us in loving pastimes, we glorify our beloved by loudly singing His glorious names like cakoras on a full-moon night.

Because love for Krsna and nama-sankirtana are so inextricably intertwined, Vaisnavas not only say that one causes the other, and vice versa, but also that the two are not different from each other.

In this way, chanting the maha-mantra is the only way to effortlessly pass through the stages of practice, ecstasy, and love, and at last enter Goloka, the eternal abode of pastimes, which resounds with the name.

As the great Vyasa says,

**“Lord Visnu's holy name removes sin, establishes piety, and makes one disinterested in the attempt to gain an exalted post like that of Lord Brahma. Moreover, the holy name —**

**“Grants devotion for the guru’s lotus feet, brings transcendental knowledge of Lord Visnu, burns the seed of repeated birth and death, and establishes the saintly in complete awareness of perfect bliss.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Despite its pre-eminence, questions often arise about the maha-mantra. So that my readers may hear the glories of the mantra with complete faith, let me first answer six of the most common questions.

First: Why is the Hare Krsna mantra the maha-mantra? Why not some other mantra, like the Kama-gayatri, for example, which is rich with the kama-bija and the three stages of spiritual attainment?

The Ananta-samhita points out that of the Lord’s many names, the name Hari most easily drives away sins, ignorance, and misfortune; Krsna alone delivers divine love, and Rama grants full liberation.

Moreover, the sixteen-name sequence of this mantra is an invocation in and of itself, requiring no further elements such as a seed (bija), the offering of respect (namah), or a declaration of surrender (svaha).

The incomparable cintamani names Hari, Krsna, and Rama are easily accessible to everyone, and their combination, which requires neither Vedic nor pancaratrika elements, is second to none.

The truth of the matter is that, from the transcendental perspective, the Hare Krsna mantra is not actually a mantra at all. It is the ultimate treasure of love, prema-dhana, of the residents of Goloka.

That ultimate treasure of love descended on its own volition in order to benefit those of us who have no other hope, even though people of this world, practitioners (sadhakas) included, would offend it.

To make it easier for Vedic scholars to accept, this sublime form of Radha and Krsna descended through the tongues of Their eternal associates and took its place amongst the other Vedic mantras.

Materialists, neophytes, and smartas, however, could not appreciate it as the treasure house of pure love. Self-realised devotees therefore added the adjective maha (“greatest”) to exalt it above other mantras.

However, to call the Hare Krsna mantra “the maha-mantra” docs not add to its glory, for this transcendental sound is much more than merely a “great mantra.” It is Radha and Krsna Themselves.

But if calling it the “great mantra” makes those who hear its name even one bit more faithful or more inclined to chant it, then that tender-hearted storehouse of love kindly says, “So be it.”

My godbrother Indradyumna Swami frequently reminds us of this ecstatic truth about the maha-mantra by repeatedly calling out during his kirtanas, “Golokera prea-dhana, hari-nama-sankirtana!”

The second question: Where in scripture is the maha-mantra mentioned? And if it is so important, then why is it not mentioned in such essential texts as the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam?

We need first recall that spiritual masters generally disseminate mantras to their disciples by aural reception. But in the matter of presenting mantras on the page, Vedic texts are purposefully indirect.

This intentional obscurity is meant to discourage immature persons from trying to acquire and chant mantras in any but the authorised way — to hear them in disciplic succession from a bona fide guru.

Be that as it may, the following scriptures do record the maha-mantra in its entirety: the Kali-santarana Upanisad, the Brahmanda Purana, the Radha-tantra, and the Sanat-kumara- and Ananta-samhita.

The Brahma-yamala also gives the names in the mantra and spells out the order in which they are to be said, while the Caitanya Upanisad and Padma Purana refer to it as “the Krsna mantra of sixteen names.”

The Padma Purana specifically calls this combination of names *the* maha-mantra*,*

*barer nama maha-mantrair nasyet papa pisacakam*  
*barer agra svarair uccair nrtyam stan-namakrin-narah*

**“The evil witches of an unlimited host of sins are completely vanquished for persons who dance before \[the Deity of\] Lord Sri Hari and loudly chant His holy names with the maha-mantra.”**

Other scriptures mention the chanting of Krsna’s names in general terms. These glorifications also indirectly refer to the maha-mantra because it is the best of mantras composed of Krsna’s names.

Amongst these general references, the most commonly cited is from theBrhan-naradiya Purana,

*harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam*  
*kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha*

**“In this age of quarrel and hypocrisy the only means of deliverance is chanting the holy name of the Lord. There is no other way. There is no other way. There is no other way.”**

Isvara Puri taught this verse to Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who then inaugurated the sankirtana movement that is now spreading through-out the world in fulfilment of the Lord’s will.

In the Bhagavad-gita, Bhagavan Sri Krsna specifies kirtana as the eternal activity of great souls (satatam kirtayanto mam) and japa as the best of all kinds of sacrifices (yajnanam japa-yajno 'smi).

Krsna is the Absolute Truth, and His internal energy, Radha, is the shelter of all devotees. Is it any wonder, then, that to chant Hare Krsna is the best way to realise these verses about kirtana and japa?

Srimad-Bhagavatam is even more explicit in its emphasis on chanting Lord Krsna’s names, which it enjoins throughout every Canto — especially the Sixth — from its outset to its very last verse.

By assimilating two essential messages of the Bhagavatam — *krsnas tu bhagavan svayam and anayaradhito nunam*—its readers know that a third message (nama-sankirtanam yasya) means “chant Hare Krsna.”

In conclusion, both direct and indirect references to the maha-mantra in sruti, smrti, pancaratrika, and Puranic texts give irrefutable evidence tbat the mantra is surely mentioned in revealed scripture.

Sri Isvara Puri teaches us how to be unconcerned about the non devotional students of the Vedas and to be fixed in infallible faith in the chanting of Krsna’s names, the hidden glory of all scriptures:

**“Let the twice-born enter the fearless kingdom of yoga, Vedic study, and solitary meditation in the forest. Let them become liberated in that way. As for us, we will spend hundreds of thousands of births —**

**“Chanting the holy name of Lord Krsna, whose splendid dark complexion and yellow garments are like a host of blue lotus flowers blooming in a grove of yellow-flower-bearing kadamba trees.”**

A third question, more frequently asked: Why doesn’t Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, the most authentic biography of Lord Caitanya, directly mention the maha-mantra? Didn’t the Lord chant it.

We accept the authenticity of the maha-mantra and that the Lord appeared to distribute it. Considering the mantra’s pivotal role in the Lord’s mission, why doesn’t His biographer explicitly mention it?

Although Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami does not record the maha-mantra in its entirety, it is incorrect to say that he makes no direct reference to it. Consider the Lord’s talk with Prakasananda Sarasvati.

In those talks with the Mayavadis, Lord Caitanya disclosed how He had asked His initiating guru, Isvara Puri, about His diksa-mantra. The Lord thought that the mantra had caused Him to go mad.

Lord Caitanya said,

**“My dear lord! What kind of mantra have you given Me? I think I have become mad, because by chanting it I immediately feel an ecstasy that makes Me dance, laugh, and cry.”**

At this, Isvara Puri replied, *krsna-nama-maha-mantrera ei ta svabhava*: “It is the nature of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra that anyone who chants it immediately develops loving ecstasy for Krsna.”

Two things can be gleaned from the phrase krsna-nama-maha-mantrera . The first is that the maha-mantra is directly mentioned in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta and that Lord Caitanya was initiated with it.

The second is that the phrases krsna-nama and maha-mantra are equivalent, and therefore further references in the text to krsna-nama, or just nama, may also be references to the maha-mantra.

Indeed, we find that Srila Prabhupada generally translates krsna-nama and nama as “the Hare Krsna maha-mantra a convention that finds full support in the krsna-nama verse quoted above.

Further scriptural evidence confirms this convention, a convention that some sceptics and scholars have attempted to dismiss, labeling it Srila Prabhupada’s “preaching style” of translation. Not so.

For example, the Pippalada branch of the Atharva Veda says,

**“The name is the root of all mantras, the splendid one that brings joy to all. This root-mantra is chanted with Hari, Krsna, and Rama.”**

This verse from sruti reflects a scriptural convention, not a preaching convention. In mantras comprised of the Lord’s names, the word nama refers to the root-mantra, the maha-mantra.

This authentication of Srila Prabhupada’s translations also reinforces the spiritual principle that we can understand scriptures and the statements of previous acaryas only through self-realised Vaisnavas.

In that light, through the writings of other acaryas contemporary to the Gosvami, we can also view Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami’s statements regarding which mantras Caitanya Mahaprabhu chanted.

Caitanya-bhagavata, another biography of Lord Caitanya nearly as important as the Caitanya-caritamrta, explicitly refers to the maha-mantra three times.First, the Lord says to Tapana Misra:

**“Everything is accomplished by hari-nama sankirtana, including the goal of life and the means for its attainment. In this Age of Kali, the only means for deliverance is the chanting of the names of Hari.**

**“There is no other way, there is no other way, there is no other way. Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. This verse is called the maha-mantra.**

**“It contains sixteen names of the Lord made of thirty-two syllables. Repeatedly chanting this mantra will awaken the sprout of prem in the heart, as well as the goal of life and the means to attain it.”**

The maha-mantra is mentioned a second time, when Lord Caitanya orders the residents of Navadvipa to chant it. In bliss the Lord said,

**“Listen to the krsna-nama, maha-mantra: Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna —**

**“Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Perform japa of this mantra a prescribed number of times and you will attain all perfection. There is no other rule.”**

In a third reference we hear how one day, as Caitanya Mahaprabhu arrived at the home of Advaita Acarya, the Lord’s beautiful face was aglow with ecstatic love from chanting, “Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna.”

Other acaryas also directly mention the maha-mantra in their works. Kavi-karnapura narrates how Lord Caitanya ordered the barber to chant Hare Krsna as he shaved the Lord’s head.

Locana Dasa Thakura, in his Caitanya-mangala, tells how Lord Caitanya once turned the house of a brahmana into Vrndavana by chanting the maha-mantra, which the author quotes in its entirety.

Other references to the Lord chanting the maha-mantra are from the personal testimonies of Kavi-karnapura, Rupa Gosvami, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, and Prabodhananda Sarasvati Thakura.

In summary, the direct and indirect statements of Sri Caitanya-caritamrta and the explicit declarations of acaryas contemporary to Caitanya Mahaprabhu prove that He chanted the maha-mantra.

**\* \* \* \***

The fourth question stems from a long-standing controversy. Some pseudo-Vaisnavas assert that Lord Caitanya did not chant the maha-mantra in sankirtana because it is only meant for japa meditation.

While Bhaktivinoda Thakura was residing in Jagannatha Puri, one Carana Dasa Babaji invented this philosophy along with a new mantra he considered authorised for loud sankirtana.

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura was incensed by these speculations. In fact, his arguments with the babaji became so intense that Bhaktivinoda Thakura sent his son away to avoid conflict.

Both arguments — that the maha-mantra is not for sankirtana and that Lord Caitanya did not chant it aloud — are fallacious. There is no evidence to support them. Rather, all evidence is to the contrary.

In our study of the diksa-mantras, it was found that the structure of mantras meant for chanting in japa must begin with a bija and include words like dhimahi or svaha, which appear in the dative case.

The maha-mantra has no such components, and it is in the vocative case. From the perspective of mantra-tattva, then, there is no reason to conclude that the maha-mantra should be exclusively for japa.

Moreover, revealed scriptures state that the maha-mantra is to he chanted both aloud in kirtana as well as silently in japa. We have already quoted a part of this verse from the Padma Purana:

**“The evil witches of an unlimited host of sins are all completely vanquished for persons who dance before \[the Deity of\] Lord Sri Hari and loudly chant His holy names in the maha-mantra.**

**“Just as the sacred waters of the Ganges purify the universe, persons who circumambulate Hari and with sweet voices loudly sing the sixteen- word maha-mantra and clap their hands also purify the universe.’’**

This verse makes clear that the maha-mantra may be chanted loudly (uccaih). Since dancing and clapping one’s hands makes counting impossible, chanting it silently in japa must not be compulsory.

Another verse, already cited from Caitanya-bhagavata, states that after publicly pronouncing the maha-mantra in its entirety, Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructed people in the two ways of chanting it.

The Lord said, *iha japa giya sabe koriya nirbandha*: “Chant japa of this mantra according to regulation.” He then added, sarva ksana bob ithe vidhi nahi ara: “Chant it all the time. There is no other rule.”

The way to reconcile the Lord’s two instructions — chant with rules and chant without rules — is to understand that japa is done according to rules and sankirtana is done without any rules.

Kavi-karnapura’s account of the Lord’s hair-cutting ceremony is also an example of loud chanting, wherein Lord Caitanya repeatedly told the barber, hare krsnety uccair: “Chant Hare Krsna out loud!”

Furthermore, the maha-mantra can be chanted loudly in japa. Rupa Gosvami writes,

**“He chants the Hare Krsna mantra in a loud voice... keeping count on a series of knots with His effulgent hand.”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami also confirms that the Lord instructed His followers to chant japa of the maha-mantra with these words: “Please chant the Hare Krsna mantra a fixed number of times.

Did Caitanya Mahaprabhu chant the maha-mantra in loud sankirtana? The answer is an emphatic yes. And did He ask His followers to do the same? Again, the answer is an emphatic yes.

In this regard, Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya wrote,

*visanna cittan kali-papa bhitan samviksya gauro harinama-mantram*  
*svayam dadau bhakta-janan samadiset kurusva sankirtatia-nrtya vadyan*

**“Seeing the people dejected from fear of the sins in Kali-yuga, Gauranga gave them the hari-nama mantra and also ordered them to do sankirtana of it while dancing and playing musical instruments.”**

I often hear a question about the two ways of chanting: Which is better, japa or kirtana? The answer is that kirtana is more powerful, but if we are to follow the Lord’s order, both must be done.

Indeed, when we speak of kirtana we speak not only of loud chanting with musical accompaniment and dancing, but also of chanting japa out loud, as opposed to chanting japa softly or chanting in the mind.

Why is loud chanting preferable to soft or silent chanting? Loud chanting benefits not only the chanter but anyone else who can hear it as well. It is also the best way to fix one’s mind on the holy name.

Haridasa Thakura’s teachings to an impious brahmana are especially pertinent in this regard. A presumptuous brahmana once publicly assailed Haridasa for loudly chanting Krsna’s names.

In front of a group of scholars, the brahmana challenged, “Scriptures say that one should chant japa in one’s mind. On what authority are you loudly chanting the names of Hari, Krsna, and Rama?”

In response, Haridasa Thakura told the story of how Nanda Maharaja was caught in the coils of a great snake at Ambikavana. Having no other shelter, Nandaraja loudly cried out to his son, “Krsna! Krsna!”

As soon as Krsna heard His father’s call He appeared on the scene to save him. The mere touch of Krsna’s foot transformed the snake into an effulgent being, who immediately glorified nama-sankirtana.

That Vidyadhara named Sudarsana said, yan-nama grhnann akhilan srotrn atmanam eva ca sadyah punati: “Anyone who chants Your name purifies all who hear his chanting, as well as himself.”

Haridasa Thakura then cited a verse, spoken by Prahlada Maharaja, to demarcate the relative merits of loud and soft chanting: “One who loudly chants the holy names of the Lord Hari —

“Is a hundred times greater than one who silently chants because those who chant silently purify only themselves, while those who chant loudly, purify themselves as well as those who hear them.”

The namacarya also gave the purport of the verse:

**“Although all living entities have a tongue, only human beings are able to chant the name of Krsna. One who chants softly liberates only himself.**

**“But one who loudly chants Krsna’s names liberates himself and all living entities who hear him. What then can be wrong with an activity that liberates living entities who have taken a useless birth?”**

Haridasa Thakura concluded, “A person may feed himself, whereas another person may feed a thousand people. Of the two, who is better? This is the superior characteristic of loud chanting.”

Whenever I dress Radha-Syamasundara I have the good fortune of being able to hear, from the other side of the altar curtain, the soothing and melodic japa-kirtana of Their devotees in the temple.

Apart from those who are mispronouncing or sleepily chanting the mantra, the combined nama-sankirtana sounds like the gentle lapping of the Yamuna’s waves as they flow by the Deities’ altar-grove.

It is a sound vibration not only completely harmonious with dressing and decorating Their Lordships but also visibly pleasing to Them. Surely, Radha and Syama enjoy hearing Their own names.

**\* \* \* \***

Devotees sometimes raise a fifth question: Why don’t we avoid the confusion of the multiple interpretations of the maha-mantra and simply chant the mantra that directly addresses Radha and Syama?

That mantra is often referred to as the Radhe-Syama mantra. It follows the same structure as the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, but replaces Hare with Radha then Radhe, and Rama with Syama.

The first and most obvious answer to this question is that neither Srila Prabhupada nor any of our previous acaryas have corroborated the authenticity, or even acknowledged the existence, of this mantra.

I have not found mention of it in any Vedic or Gaudiya literature, nor is there evidence in the Gaudiya Vaisnava oral tradition that Caitanya Mahaprabhu or any of His associates sang or recited it.

In short, guru, sadhu, and sastra do not mention this mantra, so it remains unendorsed, leaving no reason for chanting it, let alone replacing the maha-mantra with it. It should be avoided at all costs.

Another reason we should avoid chanting this concocted mantra is that its voice is too direct to be pleasing to Krsna. It approaches the names of the most intimate forms of the divine couple too explicitly.

Just as a beautiful woman looks more alluring when her face and body are thinly veiled rather than fully exposed, mantras describing Krsna are more attractive when they are in concealed or esoteric terms.

Moreover, because it has been sung by so many great souls like Caitanya Mahaprabhu, Rupa Gosvami, and Srila Prabhupada, the maha-mantra has an added sweetness that is lacking in other mantras.

Srila Vyasadeva explains this principle in his glorification of Srimad-Bhagavatam. He says that the Bhagavatam, though already nectarean, became even more ambrosial by the touch of Sukadeva’s lips.

For these reasons Gaudiya Vaisnavas prefer the maha-mantra to all others, especially those of questionable origin. To those who chant with faith, the maha-mantra discloses its mysteries and sweetness.

In response to the notion that we should avoid varied interpretations of the maha-mantra: such interpretations are congenial for attracting devotees of diverse dispositions to the lotus feet of Radha and Krsna.

Whether we worship Krsna and Balarama, Lord Rama, or any other form of Hari, the maha-mantra can fulfil our aspirations or transform them into an earnest desire to serve Radha and Syama.

When Govinda Swami and I first moved into our house in Bhauma Vrndavana, our neighbour would chant the Radhe-Syama mantra exclusively — and over loudspeakers, as is the custom.

After some pleasant discussion regarding the mantras preferred hy authorised Vrndavana acaryas, our sadhu friend switched to chanting the maha-mantra, though he still does so through loudspeakers.

The sixth and final question raised about the maha-mantra has to do with the sequence in which the words are chanted. Some say that the two halves of the mantra should be switched — Rama before Krsna.

These scholars base their claim on one edition of the Kali-santarana Upanisad. They also reason that because, chronologically, Rama appeared before Krsna, Their names in the mantra should follow suit.

In reply to the first claim, while one popular deviant edition of the Kali-santarana Upanisad has printed the mantra in an altered sequence, all the other editions follow the generally accepted order.

The version of the Kali-santarana ana Upanisad that contains the standard sequence of the maha-mantra is the one that Gaudiya Vaisnavas have passed down in disciplic succession to this day.

Furthermore, scriptures like the Brahma-yamala, Rddha-tantra, Brahmanda Purana, Ananta- and Sanat-kumara-samhita, and Caitanya Upanisad record the standard sequence: Krsna before Rama.

Since sadhu, guru, and sastra all consistently present one version of the maha-mantra, it is insolent to accept a deviant version on the authority of a single publication that also lacks parampara authority.

The other argument — that Rama appeared before Krsna — is simply offensive. It tries to make relative the absolute nature of the maha-mantra, making it dependent on the currents of material time.

In summary, the arguments in favour of an alternate sequence to the names of the maha-mantra are weak. They are neither guided by scriptural evidence nor received through disciplic succession.

We must be careful to protect the treasure of Goloka from fools who would pervert its eternal form — Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

Following our acaryas, let us aspire to perfect our chanting,

*hare krsna krsneti krsneti mukhyan mahascarya-namavali-siddha-mantran*  
*krpa-murti-caitanyadevopagitan kadabhyasya vrndavane syam krtarthah*

**“When, chanting the siddha-mantra of wonderful names beginning ‘Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna!’ and flowing from the lips of compassion personified, Caitanyadeva, will I become perfect in Vrndavana?”**

This concludes the responses to certain questions we might hear or perhaps confront within ourselves. Now let us return to glorifying the chanting of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, especially in sankirtana.

**\* \* \* \***

Before Lord Caitanya revealed His identity as Radha and Krsna to Ramananda Raya, Ramananda disclosed the two purposes for which the Lord descended with His associates to engage in nama-sankirtana.

Ramananda Raya said, “My dear Lord! You have come to taste Your own spiritual bliss, and at the same time You are transforming the whole world by spreading the ecstasy of love of Godhead.”

This verse implies that the mellows of nama-sankirtana make both the Lord and the living entities dance in love, and when the universe is lost in a festival of bliss, then love of God itself dances as well.

Lord Caitanya introduced hari-nama-sankirtana to India, and Srila Prabhupada introduced it to the world. Now the rising tide of that oceanic sankirtana movement is gradually washing over everyone.

The first verse of Lord Caitanya’s Siksastaka glorifies seven exceblences of sankirtana. By studying these one can sec clearly that the chanting of Krsna’s names is the essence of all religion.

The remainder of this chapter will analyse each of these seven exceblences of Sri Krsna sankirtana, culminating in sankirtana’s ultimate goal, the goal of life: going back home, back to Godhead.

Since the maha-mantra is not different from the absolute form of Radha and Syama, the perfection attained from chanting the mantra is nothing less than stages of personal service to the divine couple.

And as merciful as Radha-Syama are — and have no doubt that I am a sold-out advocate of Their mercy — I must admit that Their holy names are more merciful still, for those names follow me everywhere.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu teaches how to properly cherish the treasure trove of sankirtana, and in so doing points out the bejewelled bracelets, rings, crowns, anklets, and necklaces lying therein.

My unfulfilled desire is to dress Radha'Syamasundara with ornaments made only of gold set with diamonds, rubies, and sapphires. But, alas, we have not yet been afforded such opulence in New Vraja'dhama.

In the meantime, I will worship the nonpareil excellences of krsna-sankirtana. Like priceless cintamani they transform the Deities’ ornaments into jewellery even the Lord of Vaikuntha cannot afford.

Such are the holy names we worship; such arc the forms of the holy name we serve. These transcendental realities join together in the form of Lord Gauranga, who gives Himself freely to all.

The first of eight verses comprising Lord Caitanya’s only written work says,

**“Let there be all victory for the chanting of the holy name of Lord Krsna, which can cleanse the mirror of the heart and stop —**

**“The miseries of the blazing fire of material existence. That chanting is the waxing moon that spreads moonlight on the white lotus of good fortune for all living entities. It is the life and soul of all education.**

**“The chanting of the holy name of Krsna expands the blissful ocean of transcendental life. It gives a cooling effect to everyone and enables one to taste full nectar at every step.”**

This verse lists the seven excellences of sankirtana: (1) It cleanses the mirror of the heart, (2) it protects one from material existence, (3) it dispenses all-auspiciousness, (4) it is the source of all knowledge —

(5) It expands the ocean of bliss, (6) it gives one the taste of divine nectar at every step, and (7) it completely cleanses one’s body, mind, and soul, awakening one to the mellows of love for Krsna.

Let us first glorify nama-sankirtana, the great emperor that rules over the kingdom of spiritual practice and perfection. Then we will hear about the seven wise ministers who serve his majesty’s desires.

The word sankirtana means “complete kirtana.” It has external and internal meanings. The external meaning consists of the physical activities and conditions that comprise the performance of kirtana.

Sri Jiva defines these external meanings as *bahubhir militva kirtanam sankirtanam ity ucyate*: “When many people come together and loudly glorify the Supreme Lord, Krsna, it is known as sankirtana."

We have already heard how loud chanting is superior to quiet chanting. When loud chanting is done congregationally, however, it is “superlative because it awakens a sense of wonder in the heart."

Srila Prabhupada also includes preaching, book distribution, and discussing topics of Krsna as sankirtana. When done alone, these acts arc called kirtana, but with others “that is called sankirtana."

The other meaning of “complete kirtana," the internal meaning, comprises fixed mental discipline, or full attentiveness, and mature attraction for both the process of chanting and for Krsna Himself.

Krsna speaks of this internal mood in the Gita: “Always chanting My glories, endeavouring with great determination, bowing down before Me, these great souls perpetually worship Me with devotion.”

With these words Krsna personally notes those things that constitute worship of Him through constant kirtana: full endeavour, determination, reverence, and — above all —pure devotion.

By definition, then, mechanical chanting, inattentive chanting, and chanting devoid of love disqualify our kirtana from being considered complete, despite the presence of external elements like dancing.

Devotees who chant without offence but lack affection for Krsna may take birth on the same planet as Krsna, but only those devotees who chant with love attain the Lord’s direct company.

Only loving service attracts Krsna. At the stage of prṛma we can perceive that Krsna is not different from His name, and only then can our chanting be called sankirtana in the full sense of the word.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says,

*nama-kara bahir haya*  
*nama nahi haya*

**“Merely reciting the external syllables of the holy name does not mean that one is actually chanting the holy name.”**

Krsna’s immortal words during His meeting with the gopis at Kuruksetra distinguish devotional service with love from devotional service without it, describing how the results of each are different:

“Rendering devotional service to Me qualifies any living being for eternal life. But by your good fortune —

“You have developed a special loving attitude towards Me, by which you have obtained Me. ”Again, immature devotion qualifies one for loving devotion, which then qualifies one for Krsna’s company.

Lord Caitanya and His followers, most notably Srila Prabhupada, taught us both the mood and the activities that constitute sankirtana. Embracing their example, we too can qualify ourselves to meet Krsna.

Lord Caitanya describes one who chants pure nama-sankirtana in this way:

**“One can chant the holy name of the Lord in a humble state of mind, thinking oneself lower than the straw in the street.**

**“One should be more tolerant than the tree, devoid of all sense of false prestige and ready to offer all respects to others. In such a state of mind one can chant the holy name of the Lord constantly.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Of the seven excellences listed in the first verse of Lord Caitanya’s Siksastaka, the first excellence is ceto-darbana-marjanam: the chanting of Lord Krsna’s names cleanses the mirror of the heart.

Due to an endless history of sinful activities, the mirror of the mind is covered by dust — sinful reactions in the form of unwanted habits and offences, plus the cause of it all, ignorance, or forgetfulness of Krsna.

This dust Krsna calls lust. Both He and Lord Caitanya use the exam-pie of a dusty mirror to illustrate the degree of conditioning that characterises animal life. How degraded we have become in this age!

But regardless of how much dust has accumulated upon the mirror of our hearts from lifetimes of committing every conceivable type and severity of sin, the sound of Krsna’s name washes it completely away.

No spiritual activity can compare to chanting Hare Krsna in its ability to cleanse the heart of impurities. In Ajamila’s hour of need the Visnudutas came to correct the Yamadutas’ misconduct and said:

**“By following the Vedic ritualistic ceremonies or by undergoing atonement \[prescribed by sages like Manu\], sinful men do not become as purified as by chanting once the holy name of Lord Hari.”**

Another example is that of the ksatra-bandhu who begged a brahmana to free him from his wicked nature and the sinful reactions awaiting him. The brahmana recommended a process of atonement.

The ksatra-bandhu, a ksatriya in name only, protested, “Sir! I cannot follow your instructions because my mind is too restless. Please tell me if there is something I can do through my body or speech.”

At this the brahmana smiled and said, “My son! Whatever you do —while standing, sleeping, or moving about, in hunger, thirst, or even if falling down — always sing the name Govinda.”

The effects of nama-sankirtana far surpass the inferior effects of Vedic ritualistic atonement. One of the effects of chanting the maha-mantra is to evoke in the heart a wonderful kind of faith.

Even by meditating in Satya-yuga one cannot attain as deep a faith in the Lord. After instilling such special faith, another effect of nama-sankirtana is that it awakens devotion within the heart.

In other words, the natural effect of chanting Krsna’s names is remembrance of His fame, qualities, attributes, pastimes, and paraphernalia, which ultimately brings one to love of Krsna.

As soon as the devotees taught me how to chant Hare Krsna, I felt such faith in Krsna’s divinity and such a strong inclination to serve the Lord that my wife and parents were startled, as was I.

My mind was too cluttered to make sense of the devotees’ preaching, but whenever I took part in kirtana at the temple or chanted japa at home, the sublime effect of the holy name was palpable.

We generally refer to the initial stages of chanting when we describe the cleansing of the heart, but a deeper cleansing goes on even in the more advanced stages of chanting, culminating in love for Krsna.

In later stages, we are elevated beyond the touch of matter. The mirrors of our purified hearts then reflect our eternal spiritual identity(svarupa), giving us a glimpse of our relationship with Krsna.

As spiritual illumination increases, the specific aspects of that spiritual form become increasingly visible, and we are then better equipped to learn of our eternal service in our constitutional position.

In this way the mirror of the heart reflects our advancement in Krsna consciousness, showing us where we stand in our progress, from the initial stages of spiritual development to the final stages of perfection.

The cleansing of the heart (ceto-darpana-marjanam) is thus an ongoing process that continues to the stages of perfection, at which further polishing of the heart invokes ever-fresh pastimes of Krsna.

**“O Krsna-nama! O playful embodiment of intense bliss! O festival of happiness for the residents of Goloka! You destroy the sufferings of those who take shelter of You. I offer my obeisances to You.”**

**\* \* \* \***

The second excellence of nama-sankirtana is its ability to extiguish the miseries caused by the blazing fire of material existence, referred to by Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu as bhava-maha-davagni-nirvapanam.

The word bhava means “worldly existence,” which is comprised of three kinds of suffering: those miseries inflicted upon us by our own bodies and minds, by other living entities, and by the demigods.

The Lord compares this material existence to a forest fire, implying that our suffering is an inherent part of our sojourn in the material world, our own existential condition. In short, the fire is our karma.

Although not readily visible, the fire of karma is within us like the fire of digestion. Just as the fire of digestion consumes our food, with time we can see that the fire of karma consumes our bodies.

Narottama Dasa Thakura says that material existence, also called the cycle of birth and death (samsara), is like a poisonous fire that burns (visanale). Its toxic fumes scald and asphyxiate us day and night.

For those who doubt that karma is the fire in which living entities burn, the Upanisads tell the story of a hoy who followed his guru’s offhand instruction to fetch fire from hell to use in a sacrifice.

The boy did as he was told. In the kingdom of death he saw many living entities suffering in endless hellfire, but when he asked Yamaraja to spare him some flames, he was shocked hy the reply.

The king of death said, “My dear boy! You cannot take any fire from here. The infernos you see are made up of the flames these souls have brought with them. There were formerly no fires in my kingdom.

“These flames, the fires of karma, arc inseparable from these sinners. Sometimes the souls carry the fires with them and at other times the fires carry the souls, just as these souls have been brought here.”

Scriptures give the example of a great forest fire to impress upon us the fact that conditioned souls arc constantly burning in the reactions to their own pious and impious deeds.

In a great forest fire, moving creatures like hears and deer face the same fate as immobile bushes and trees, for wherever they turn they confront infernal flames; without exception, everything perishes.

There is no escape. The souls trapped in this material world can’t extinguish the fire of material existence themselves because the reactions to everything they do cause the fire to burn hotter.

Living entities cannot free themselves from material bondage by material means, even pious atonement, speculative knowledge, or mystic meditation. Why? Sukadeva Gosvami explains the reason:

**“Because even after following such methods one takes to fruitive activities again, unable to control his mind, which is contaminated by the base qualities of nature, namely passion and ignorance.”**

The only way a forest fire can be extinguished is by the grace of an external agent like Indra, who can dispatch banks of storm clouds to mercifully shower torrents of rain on the blaze. There is no other way.

Similarly, the only way living entities can be freed from all-devouring karma is to solicit the grace of the transcendent Supreme Lord, who then sends a shower of His sweet names to deliver them.

Lord Brahma explains this truth with the words karmani nirdahati kintu ca bhakti-bhajam: “All fruitive activities and their reactions are quickly destroyed by engagement in pure devotional service.”

Here bhakti-bhajam includes chanting and glorifying Krsna’s name, fame, form, and pastimes, which arc the only practices capable of totally extinguishing the blazing fire of material existence.

As the welcome showers of Krsna’s sublime names fall upon the fires of fruitive reactions, the flames of material suffering are at first contained and, through continued chanting, gradually extinguished.

One symptom of practising pure devotional service is the cessation of material suffering (klesaghni), which we perceive alongside the systematic removal of unwanted things in the heart (anartha-nivrtti).

We are often impatient for the arrival of such ultimate relief, wondering how long we can remain determined through what seems to be an endless journey from conditioned to spiritual existence.

The astute reader will now reply, “There is no other way!” And scripture agrees: “One who has uttered the name of Hari even once, easily achieves firm determination to attain liberation.”

O Srimati Radharani! O Sriman Syamasundara! The shower of nectar from Your holy names soothes my burning limbs, pacifies my unruly mind, and quenches my thirsty soul. And so I chant, “Hare Krsna!”

Long ago I boarded the boat of Your holy names and set out across the ocean of material existence for the shores of a celebrated realm where You are said to play eternally with Your loving companions.

Since then I have been plying the ocean of material existence, sometimes over rough waters, sometimes against unfavourable winds, sometimes in the face of dangerous pirates or vicious aquatics.

Yet I remain patient and steadfast in my vow to one day adorn You with a garland of Your own ambrosial names, names that like a strong current mystically carry me to the treasure chest of Your lotus feet.

Sometimes, in the mounting excitement of my zeal, that distant land seems to come into view. I think I hear the voices of that realm’s joyous residents and smell the scent of aromatic pleasure gardens.

The happiness aroused by chanting Your names at times sublimely confuses me. At those times I think I have set foot upon the - shores of Your home to seek Your footprints in the sand.

I hear the reassuring voice of my captain, Srila Prabhupada, feel favourable breezes caress my soul, and know that You, the treasured goal of my journey, have made the trials of that journey insignificant.

After some time the lapping of ocean waves breaks my reverie, and I call out to You. Your names then appear as two indescribable forms, forms that bring tears to my eyes and cause my throat to choke up.

By fixing my mind on Your enchanting forms, I can turn my back on the painful past that lured me with false promises. Thinking and speaking only of You, I no longer look back—any future is with You.

O Syama! When I call out to You with affection, Your smile wipes away my sorrows, Your glance ignites a cooling fire in my heart, and Your threefold-bending form destroys the threefold miseries of life.

O Radha! Just writing Your name compels me to run to Your side to dress and ornament You in a way that brings the greatest pleasure to Syama. May pronouncing Your name fulfil that aspiration.

O sacred names! O sacraments of sound! By Your grace I left the past far behind me, and I never look back. If there is such bliss in wanting to serve Your forms, I cannot imagine the bliss in the service itself.

O great mantra of deliverance! Please fill the sails of my heart with favourable winds and quickly guide me to the divine couple. That is my humble entreaty in the sparkling diamond-dust of Your feet.

**\* \* \* \***

The third excellence of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s nama-sankirtana is that it spreads soothing moonshine upon the night-blooming white lotus of good fortune (sreyah-kairava- candrika-vitaranam).

In this beautiful metaphor the maha-mantra is the waxing moon that illuminates the darkness with its rays, making the white lily of good fortune open and spread its auspicious fragrance everywhere.

The kairava is a white lotus — or more accurately, a white lily — that opens at night to the caress of cooling moon rays when all other lotuses stay tightly closed waiting for the warmth of the sunshine.

Let us try to understand the meaning of ultimate good fortune or auspiciousness (sreyah). Then we may comprehend why this lotus opens at night, rather than during the daytime as most lotuses do.

Speaking to Naciketa, the boy who had come for fire, Yamaraja said,

*sreyas ca preyas ca manusyam etas tau samparitya vivinakti dhirah*  
*sreyo hi dhiro ’bhipreyaso vrnite preyo mando yogaksemad vrnite*

**“We can accept either that which is immediately appealing or that which is permanently beneficial. The wise covet enduring happiness, whereas the foolish prefer fleeting pleasure.”**

Sreyah is always beneficial for the soul but not always instantly pleasant for the senses, and so it is as unpalatable to the foolish materialists as sense gratification (preyah) is to the spiritualists.

In Kali-yuga people are inclined to temporary pleasures, and the reactions to their sins cast a night-like darkness over the whole world, forcing closed the lotuses of all spiritual paths but that of the kairava.

What is that white lily of auspiciousness? It is pure devotional service. Lord Brahma says, *sreyah-srtim bhaktim*: “My dear Lord, devotional service unto You is the most auspicious path for self-realisation.”

Bhakti means the progression of devotional service from practice to ecstasy to love, and on through the stages of loving devotion to mahabhava, the greatest auspiciousness for living entities everywhere.

Srila Prabhupada translates the phrase *sreyah-kairava-candrika-vitaranam* as “the prime benediction for humanity at large because it spreads the rays of the benediction moon.” We may logically wonder:

How is it that the moon, not the lotus, has become the source of benediction? The answer is that the moon is the friend of the white lotus (kairava-bandhu). As friends, they share each other’s qualities.

This truth has already been revealed in the section that told how pure love (the white lotus) and sankirtana (the waxing moon) are mutual causes of one another, identical, and equally benedictory.

In this way the moon of nama-sankirtana from above and the white lotus of loving devotion from below together enact their pastime of distributing blessings to all souls lost in the dark night of Kali-yuga.

We should also note that the term “waxing moon” refers to the expansion of Lord Caitanya’s sankirtana movement, which takes five thousand years to become full before again starting to wane.

While the second excellence of sankirtana removes all material miseries (klesaghni), this third excellence bestows auspiciousness (subhada). These are the two attributes of sadhana-bhakti.

One whose life has become auspicious naturally develops the good qualities of a Vaisnava. Situated in a state of ideal happiness, such a person is the object of affection for others, just as others are for him.

As both the source and cause of auspiciousness, sankirtana is praised as madhura-madhuram etan mangalam mangalanam: “The sweetest of sweet things and the most auspicious of auspicious things.”

Fortunate souls who have come in contact with pure devotional service reverently contemplate the moonshine (candrika) of the Lord’s holy names, the cause of their sublime transformation.

From where did they come, these rays of life-giving moonshine that awakened our hearts’ dormant devotional life? Who gave the Hare Krsna maha-mantra to the whole world? Our Srila Prabhupada!

Those who follow in Srila Prabhupada’s footsteps by distributing the holy name are also transformed into cooling beams of moonlight— enlightened souls as praiseworthy as their predecessors.

All moon-ray devotees, great and small, are emanations of the Deities who preside over the benediction moon, Gaura-Nitai, the fathers of the sankirtana movement, and the original moon gods.

Where is that white lotus unfolding? As we have already heard, this kairava is synonymous with pure devotion. Kaviraja Gosvami tells us that devotion culminating in love is found in everyone’s heart.

He says, “When the heart is purified hy hearing and chanting, this love naturally awakens.” Sukadeva Gosvami also says that the hearts of great mystics are like blossoming lotuses (unnidra-hrt-pahkaja).

As that lotus unfolds, mystic yogis see the Supersoul, Lord Krsna’s devotees see Syamasundara, bent in three places and holding the flute, and Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s followers behold the divine couple.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura says that the divine couple never leave Their eternal abode, and so the followers of Lord Caitanya always meditate on the holy land of Sri Vrndavana-dhama.

I follow Cakravarti Thakura’s advice and while chanting try to look within my heart of hearts for that most charmingly beautiful dhama, which is enclosed by the sparkling, blackish river Yamuna.

Daughter of the Kalinda mountain, Yamuna-devi naturally flows around Vrndavana on three sides and as a canal on the fourth, holding in her full embrace the abode unknown even to celestials.

In this realm the land is made of pure shimmering gold, and the foliage is carefully landscaped into gardens, groves, and bower-houses, which surround a mystical temple made of rare, living gemstones.

This grand temple is called the “great meeting place” (maha-yoga-pitha). It stands at the base of a tall, brilliantly effulgent desire tree that suffuses the forest with its pleasing fragrance and allure.

Eternally present within the yoga-pitha, ever-youthful Srimati Radharani and Syamasundara light up the directions with Their elegance and purity as They sit upon a jewelled lotus-flower throne.

Radharani and Syamasundara are surrounded by Their cowherd girlfriends, who are seated upon the petals of the lotus, each girl absorbed in her own particular service to the youthful divine couple.

O my mind! The love that Radha and Syama bear for each other sweetens and illumines Vrndavana, and that brilliant sweetness can be perceived by meditating upon Their glistening smiles.

That cowherd boy’s enticing smile steals away the mind, but the gentle smile concealed beneath the blue veil of His gopi beloved steals away the heart. May I, from within, see those two smiles forever.

Dear devotees! If you are unable to see the prince and princess of Vraja within you, then chant Hare Krsna and simply gaze upon the same divine couple on Their lotus altar in New Vraja-dhama.

Their faces are said to be just like the moon, and Their smiles like moonshine. Just stand in front of Their Lordships, and the white lotus of your devotion will soon open, one petal at a time.

New Vraja-dhama is like a nursery of kairava lotuses. Everywhere one looks one sees white lotuses caressed by the moonlight of Radha’s and Syamasundara’s smiles and by the sublime sound of Their names.

Those residents of New Vraja-dhama who see Them daily and try to chant Their names without offence nourish their hearts with pure devotion. But the hearts of those who fail to try wilt instead.

**\* \* \* \***

Now let us hear about the fourth excellence of sankirtana, vidya-vadlhu-jivanam. Srila Prabhupada translates it as both “the life and soul of all education” and “the life of all transcendental knowledge.”

The meaning of the word vadhu (“young bride”) further adds to the translation: sankirtana is “the life of the young bride called transcendental knowledge.” We will hear more about this later.

But let us begin our study of this excellence by trying to grasp what is meant here by knowledge. Narada Muni says,

**“Our education should be such that we can become elevated to Krsna consciousness.”**

The purport of this statement (*sa vidya tan-matir yaya*) is that devotional service focused exclusively on increasing our attachment to Krsna is both the momentum for and the goal of real knowledge.

This is supported by Lord Caitanya’s elucidation of the atmarama verse, in which He states that spiritual paths other than devotional service are like “nipples on the neck of a goat.” They yield nothing.

In other words, knowledge resulting from any spiritual process — or for that matter from any endeavour — is tangible and lasting only when linked in some way with devotional service to Krsna.

All this is best expressed by the phrase “bhakti is the life of knowledge.” And since all limbs of bhakti must be accompanied by sankirtana, the Lord says, “Sankirtana is the life of knowledge.”

Why then is transcendental knowledge compared to a young bride? An innocent bride lives only out of loving devotion for her husband, and as she eagerly serves him, she loudly praises his glories.

Srila Prabhupada stated many times that sankirtana could act as the agent for enlightenment in either one of two ways — by itself, or alongside the study of his books. For example, in Bombay he said:

**“The simple thing is that you chant Hare Krsna. But if you think yourself as very learned, thoughtful man, and you want to understand through science and philosophy, all right, come on.**

**“We have got books. Learn it. Two ways... .Otherwise, if you are not so learned to read all these books, chant Hare Krsna. Two things are there. Take advantage, any one of them, and be liberated.’’**

Srila Prabhupada says, “Two things are there. Take advantage, any one of them, and be liberated.” But without chanting Hare Krsna, we will fall away, even if we read Prabhupada’s books very carefully.

And even if somehow we don’t fall away, our book knowledge will be no more than an academic exercise that ultimately leads to dry mental speculation. Like a lifeless body, it will be utterly useless.

What’s more, if we chant but commit offences we will have difficulty staying on the path without fortifying our intelligence by regularly hearing the teachings of scriptures from realised devotees.

Srila Prabhupada’s statement that chanting can liberate us, then, means that offenceless chanting — the life of knowledge — reveals divine truth within our hearts, as it did to Lord Brahma.

Earlier we heard of Lord Brahma’s liberation by sankirtana of the Gopala mantra and Kama-gayatri mantra. Without reference to books, he became intimately familiar with the ocean of truth.

Suta Gosvami speaks of this principle:

**“By rendering devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, one immediately acquires causeless knowledge and detachment from the world.”**

In summary, chanting can reveal all knowledge, but, true to the instructions of the saints, we still must make efforts to mine the gems of transcendental knowledge found in the scriptures.

As we become proficient in nama-sankirtana, Krsna guides our intelligence on bow to come to Him, and so knowledge spontaneously revealed and combined with scriptural knowledge liberates us.

Sukadeva Gosvami tells Maharaja Ambarisa,

**“O King! If you desire to acquire the spiritual knowledge that leads to the supreme goal, then you should respectfully chant Govinda’s holy names.”**

Dear devotees! Allow me to conclude this section by telling you about a particular outfit and matching backdrop in Radha-Syamasundara’s wardrobe. It’s yellow and green, embroidered with flying parrots.

What does this outfit have to do with the wealth of transcendental knowledge, you ask? Just listen to how it came to be and judge for yourself—knowledge comes to those who chant Hare Krsna.

A dream inspired one of Radha-Syamasundara’s servants to create the yellow and green parrot outfit. In the dream a flock of Vraja’s parrots arrived one stormy day to take shelter of the divine couple.

Having found the shelter they sought, the parrots praised the divine couple — the males (sukas) sang of Sri Syamasundara, the females (saris) of Srimati Radharani. Their chatter soon filled the temple.

The sukas praised Syamasundara's disarming smile, colourful turban, and gracefully bending form. The saris praised their Queen Radha’s sweetness, elegant beauty, and artful dancing and singing.

The two groups of parrots competed in glorifying their worshipful Deities and soon became intoxicated, both by the intensity of their sankirtana and by contact with the very objects of their praise.

Drawn by a strong desire to be as close to Them as possible, the parrots flew onto Radha’s and Syama’s garments, where they became embroidered parrots, to the wide-eyed wonder of the divine couple.

The seamstresses of New Vraja-dhama, inspired by this dream, created the outfit, which has enlivened many a Vaisnava with its personal nature and the remembrance it affords of Krsna’s pastimes.

On the days Their Lordships wear this outfit, toy parrots sit on Their shoulders or hands, and the atmosphere on the altar comes alive with the gaiety and spontaneous spirit of a kunja in Vrndavana.

Mundane scholars may dismiss our sankirtana as no more significant than the jabber of parrots, but by chanting the maha-mantra, anyone may attain the pinnacle of knowledge — how to please the Lord.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu met Ramananda Raya on the banks of the Godavari, they discussed many confidential topics, including the essence of all categories of knowledge (*vidya vidya-madhye sara*).

The Lord enquired, “Of all types of education, which is the most important?” Ramananda Raya replied, “No education is important when compared with transcendental devotional service to Krsna.”

Sankirtana directly gives life to transcendental knowledge. But it is also the indirect origin of material knowledge, which, through both false ego and false prestige, causes one to think he is learned.
