By chanting Krsna’s names, we are humbled. In that unassuming state we see our true position in relation to the Lord and then rise to the understanding that we arc Krsna’s servants, forever duty-bound.

This is the purport of nama-sankirtana's fourth excellence. A devotee, decorated with bhakti, the essence of all knowledge, is exalted. A non-devotee, no matter how educated, is condemned.

Dear devotees! At this stage I present the following gem to you. Let it illuminate your minds. You will surely appreciate its value and keep it close to your hearts, cherished and carefully guarded.

Srila Rupa Gosvami quotes the following verse spoken by the great devotee Sri Bhavananda,

**“O Lord Krsna! Just as a miser continually collects, counts, and remembers his money, in the same way let us continually collect, count, and remember Your priceless holy names.”**

**\* \* \* \***

The fifth excellence is anandambudhi-vardhanam: the chanting of the holy name of Krsna “increases the ocean of transcendental bliss,” or “expands the blissful ocean of transcendental life.”

The first three excellences are within the process of anartha-nivrtti, by which our sins and the reactions to previous sins are gradually washed away and our hearts are filled with true happiness.

The fourth excellence refers to chanting enriched with full knowledge of the science of pure devotion. At this stage one’s mind and intelligence are fixed and one’s practices are steady (nistha).

Chanting of this quality soon brings one to goodness and awakens a relish (ruci) for chanting and a selfless attachment (asakti) to Krsna. At this stage one is only slightly tinged by the modes of nature.

Further cultivation of the maha-mantra, however, opens a new galaxy of Krsna consciousness in which the spiritual potencies of existence, knowledge, and bliss transform one’s life, as one has known it.

The aggregate of these three internal energies — the Lord’s superior personal nature — is distinct from His separated material energy. Only one who has perceived this nature directly can truly cherish it.

Bliss (ananda) dominates the other two potencies due to its proximity to Sri Radha, the very embodiment of ananda. It then lends its name to the ocean of ecstasy, which Lord Caitanya calls the ocean of bliss.

This fifth excellence extols nama-sankirtana at the stage of ecstasy (bhava). Amongst its glories arc the effects such chanting has on the waves of spiritual emotion splashing in a devotee’s melted heart.

Although bhava is transcendental, it is still a transitional stage on the way to love (prṛma). In short, the spiritual ecstasies at the stage of bhava and the mixtures of those ecstasies have not yet matured.

Still, at the stage of bhava, spiritual development no longer depends upon material conditions. Its ecstasies act like nuclear chainreactions: once they start they sustain themselves to completion.

At the stage of practice, sankirtana is considered a means to root out material conditioning. But at the liberated state of bhava, sankirtana is simultaneously the process for advancement and its fruit.

This can also be said of earlier stages of bhakti, but at the stage of ecstasy the fruit comes spontaneously, because bhava is the realm of devotional life — vraja-bhakti — that Lord Caitanya came to give.

In the conditioned state different degrees of ignorance — from the oppressive influence of sleep to the intoxicating effect of happiness — obstruct our ability to relish the taste of the pure spiritual name.

In fact our material senses, the instruments for performing-sankirtana, are incapable of perceiving the maha-mantra s qualities, being inherently separate from the spiritual nature of Krsna’s name.

But at ecstasy, our spiritualised senses are under the influence of the spiritual energies (hladini, sandhini, and samvit), and our chanting becomes empowered so that we perceive the wonders of the name.

Such empowered chanting results in a rare flood of ecstasy, the waves of which eradicate any thought of discomfort or inconvenience in ongoing service to Srimati Radharani and Sri Krsna.

Moreover, in reference to the Deity, Jiva Gosvami says,

**“The holy name of the Lord and His Deity form are forms of transcendental bliss. The best evidence of this is the experience of realised souls.”**

As I write, I call out, “O Harinama! Will the day ever come when, with spiritually enlivened senses, my tongue tastes Your sweet names and my eyes see Your beautiful forms of Radha and Syama?”

Srila Prabhupada translates anandambudhi as “transcendental life” to point out that the stage of ecstasy is not a temporary state that we attain and then lose. It is, rather, a permanent state of existence.

It is the future we all hoped for when we heard Srila Prabhupada say, “Chant Hare Krsna and be happy!” Of course, the hope and promise of that future is embodied in the example of His Divine Grace.

Just as moonlight makes water flow from the candrakanta stone, bhava makes waves of ecstasy flow from the melted heart: continuous ecstasy, special ecstasy, sub-ecstasy, and transitory ecstasy.

While Krsna says that an ordinary ocean is always being filled but remains the same, Lord Caitanya says that, agitated by sankirtana s benediction moon, the ocean of bliss goes on increasing forever.

The endlessly rising high tide in the ocean of bliss caused by the pull of the sankirtana moon is one of the dynamic mysteries of loving devotion. It is ever new and fresh, never staid or stagnant.

The presiding Deities of the sankirtana moon are like magicians casting moonbeam spells that charm the tides of bliss to ever-greater heights until those tides crash upon the shore of the heart.

In the end, such tempests of bliss cause an inundation of love in which mature ecstasy makes the throat choke up, the body tremble uncontrollably, and the feet dance with wild abandon.

This wealth of transcendental love can be assessed by the flood of ecstasies, whose symptoms include tears, perspiration, trembling, horripilation, paling of the complexion, confusion, and devastation.

But these bodily transformations arc merely the external symptoms of those very fortunate souls whose hearts drown in the high waves of love for Krsna, waves caused by the full moon of nama-sankirtana.

By the influence of nama-sankirtana, these displays of ecstasy are conspicuous, but the great souls who show them are unaware of their presence, just as madmen are unmindful of their words and deeds.

To such elevated souls, Krsna’s names are like puppetmasters who, according to their will, tug upon the heart-strings in their own independent ways, making their puppets dance, cry, and sing.

These states of ecstasy have a common cause. That cause is the natural awakening of the soul’s eternal relationship with Krsna, in which perfected devotees realise their eternal identity, or svarupa.

Some Vaisnavas assert that realisation of one’s eternal form and the consequent stages of ecstasy are made possible only through the guidance of a fully self-realised spiritual master.

In this first verse of the Siksastaka, however, Caitanya Mahaprabhu makes no such stipulation; rather, He directly praises nama-sankirtana as the direct source of ecstasy and its various symptoms.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda also writes,

**“The holy name takes me to Vraja where He reveals His love dalliance, blesses me with my own divine, eternal body, keeps me near Krsna, and destroys my mortal frame.”**

How do we reconcile the idea that the process of sankirtana in itself is enough to reveal one’s eternal spiritual form with the Vedic injunction that the mantra must be accepted through diksa?

The answer is that the holy name has unlimited independent power that can be accessed through pure chanting. Caitanya Mahaprabhu personally taught this truth to the inhabitants of Kulina-grama.

The Lord said,

**“Chanting the holy name does not depend on initiation, pious activities, or rites observed before initiation. The holy name does not wait for all these activities. It is self-sufficient.”**

But, as Srila Prabhupada explains, our acaryas teach that conditioned souls who chant with offence cannot avail themselves of this inestimable and independent potency of Lord Krsna’s names.

To help free such neophytes from the bodily conception, sages like Narada prescribe Deity worship — which depends upon being duly initiated with appropriate mantras — in addition to chanting.

Obviously, we must all follow this process. But once we reach the stages of taste and attachment, we are qualified to be guided directly by nama-sankirtana how to advance to the perfection of Svarupa.

If a qualified guru is present to help us, surely we should bring our realisations to him for confirmation. But if our guru is not present, and if we are qualified, nama-sankirtana itself acts as our guru.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda sings,

**“That person is a true preceptor, a true father, a true mother, and a true friend only if they teach one to always remember — the holy name of Sri Hari alone is everything.”**

In summary, we may rest assured that if we arc properly initiated, if we worship the Deity and chant the holy names without offence, we will attain perfection by the grace of nama-sankirtana.

Perfected devotees bathe in the soothing moonshine of ecstatic chanting. Actually, that sublime sound’s special tenderness and cooling sheen transforms everyone and everything it touches.

These devotees scoff at liberation: “O Lord! Even though Your impersonal spiritual effulgence is all-pervading, it has not yet torn even a single leaf from the tree of repeated birth and death.

“But the moment Your holy name is accepted by the tongue, it completely shatters the tree of birth and death to its very roots. So which should we serve, the spiritual effulgence or the holy name?"

Yet the priceless treasure of bhava is very rarely attained. Why? Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“This attachment is very confidentially kept by Krsna and is bestowed only upon pure devotees.”**

While listening to the ocean waves crash on the shore outside the Gambhira, what was Caitanya Mahaprabhu thinking as He wrote the words anandambudhi-vardhanam with His own divine hands?

He had appeared to give love of Krsna to everyone. But even the preliminary stage of that love, ecstatic devotion, is very rarely attained. How would Lord Caitanya achieve His mission?

When Krsna came to earth He brought the storehouse of divine love with Him but, true to His nature, He kept it carefully sealed and distributed its contents to a few worthy candidates only.

But now that same transcendental treasurer had appeared as Caitanya Mahaprabhu, and He decided that to achieve His purpose He would have to make bhava much more easily available.

And so in the midst of the Panca-tattva — as He tasted the ecstasies of love and danced, cried, laughed, and sang in divine madness — Lord Caitanya scattered the gems of love for Krsna all over the world.

Casting aside all consideration for who was fit and who was unfit, what place was suitable and what place was unsuitable, Lord Caitanya made everyone, everywhere, objects of His mercy, unconditionally.

While Lord Caitanya walked the earth, the ocean of loving ecstasies swelled in all directions, inundating everyone. To the delight of one and all, its waves left the jewels of love for Krsna everywhere.

The king of elephants, Gajendra, became the object of Krsna's mercy and praised such great fortune:

**“Unalloyed devotees, who have no desire other than to serve the Lord, worship Him in full surrender.**

**“They always hear and chant about His activities, which are most wonderful and auspicious. Thus they always merge in an ocean of transcendental bliss, and never ask the Lord for any benediction.’’**

**\* \* \* \***

The sixth excellence of nama-sankirtana is prati-padam purnamrtasvadanam: it enables us to “taste full nectar at every step,” or “fully taste the nectar for which we are always anxious.”

The word amrta means “that by which one becomes deathless.” To distinguish sankirtana from beverages that are also called amrta but which do not bestow eternal life, the Lord uses the word puma.

Thus nama-sankirtana is purnamrta, or “complete nectar,” because unlike soma-rasa, or even the nectar distributed hy Mohini-murti, nama-sankirtana reinstates the soul in its eternal position in Goloka.

The results of fruitive activities, intense mystic yoga practices, or philosophical efforts to separate spirit from matter are also known as amrta, but without bhakti not a single one will lead to immortality.

Of statements that confirm this principle, a prayer by the demigods to Krsna is foremost:

**“O lotus-eyed Lord! Some non-devotees accept severe austerities and penances to achieve the highest position.**

**“Although they may think themselves liberated, their intelligence is impure and they fall down from their position of imagined superiority because they have no regard for Your lotus feet.”**

Since the stage of ecstasy (bhava) unveils our eternal spiritual body, matures into love (prṛma), and reveals our eternal relationship with and service to Krsna in Goloka, purnamrta actually means prea.

Scriptures and acaryas exalt love for Krsna as the highest goal of life, but they still give singular praise to the special kind of prem that reveals its distinct characteristics through nama-sankirtana.

Indeed, that Krsna’s name is famous for drawing out unique facets of prem is another meaning of the adjective purna (“full”). Love manifests its all-embracing aspects through nama-sankirtana.

How is it that the holy name is so special? The Vaikuntha-dutas tell *Gopa-kumara,*

*sriman nama prabhos tasya sri-murter apy ati-priyam*  
*jagad-dhitam sukhopasyam sa-rasam tat-samam na hi*

**“Dearer to the Lord than even His own beautiful form, His easily worshipped holy name benefits the entire world. Indeed, nothing is as full of nectar \[sa-rasam\] as the holy name of the Lord.”**

The word sa-rasam in this verse is synonymous with purnamrta because nothing is more full of nectar than sankirtana; otherwise, why is Krsna more attracted to His names than to His Deity form?

We may wonder how Krsna can be more attracted to something than He is to His own all-attractive form, but Lord Krsna also declares that He is more attracted to His devotees than He is to Himself.

While speaking to Uddhava, the Lord of Dvaraka said, “My dear Uddhava! Neither Brahma, nor Sankara, nor Sankarsana, nor Laksmi, nor even My own self is as dear to Me as you are.”

Since Krsna says He loves His pure devotees more than He loves Himself, we may wonder why the Vaikuntha-dutas say that this special degree of attraction is unique to His names (*tat-samam na hi*).

There is no contradiction, however, when we consider the prime characteristic of devotees. They always perform nama-sankirtana, so the name imbues them with its own all-attractiveness.

Sanatana Gosvami describes some of the characteristics that make the full nectar of the holy name so special. Sweet-sounding syllables— like ha-re, krs-na, or ra-ma — make sankirtana very gentle.

Because nama-sankirtana is a display of the Supreme Lord’s internal potency, sankirtana also equally inspires the three individual divine potencies of existence, cognisance, and bliss (sac-cid-ananda).

The chanting of Krsna’s names is also unique in that it is an ingredient in every kind of ecstasy in every mellow of devotion — headed by amorous love — whether in meeting or separation.

What’s more, nama-sankirtana quickly evokes attraction to Krsna, drawing not only the Lord’s devotees but also anyone else who hears it — he they saints or sinners, humans or animals —closer to Him.

Other characteristics of this full nectar include its extreme power, its potency to deliver the most fallen, its ability to bestow exceptional happiness, and, as we have all tasted, its uncommon sweetness.

The fact that not even Lord Narayana can bestow love for Krsna gives us a glimpse into the inconceivable attributes invested in nama- sankirtana, the full nectar of Lord Krsna’s holy name.

The Padma Purana portrays the nectarean qualities of the sankirtana of Lord Krsna’s names,nama cintamanih krsnas caitanya-rasa-vigrahah*.*

Surely the followers of Lord Caitanya must know this verse:

**“The holy name of Krsna is transcendentally blissful. It bestows all spiritual benedictions, for it is Krsna Himself, the reservoir of all pleasure.**

**“Lord Krsna’s name is complete, and it is the form of all transcendental mellows. It is not a material name under any condition, and it is no less powerful than Krsna Himself.**

**“Since Krsna’s name is not contaminated hy the material qualities, there is no question of its being involved with mayd. Krsna’s name remains always liberated and spiritual.**

**“It is never conditioned by the laws of material nature. This is because the name of Krsna and Krsna Himself are identical.”**

In short, Krsna’s name, whether chanted silently or aloud, is Krsna.

After hearing these amazing features of the love that issues forth from Lord Krsna’s names, should we be surprised that those names completely wash away our ignorance and put an end to our suffering?

In the following stanzas we will see how nama-sankirtana is the only means to attain ultimate liberation, to revive our original blissful identities, and to understand the secrets of loving devotion.

Jiva Gosvami says that mayd defeats the individual soul and steals his awareness of his original form (atma-svarupa-jnana-lopan). Maya then imprisons the soul within another form — the material body.

Tied to the material world by false attachments, the living entity continues to suffer life after life until he again sees Lord Krsna face- to-face and recalls his own eternal spiritual identity and service.

We attain complete liberation, then, only after we fully realise our spiritual identity and when Krsna appears before us. We are free from suffering only when we regain our original deathless forms.

Thus it is said, muktir hitvanyatha rupam sva-ruðṛna vyavasthitih: “Liberation is the permanent situation of the form of the living entity after he gives up the changeable gross and subtle material bodies.”

Jiva Gosvami comments that this well-known definition of liberation is speaking of both the primary meaning of Svarupa, “the form of the Lord,” and its subsequent meaning, “the form of the living entity.”

We may conclude, then, that only at liberation — when we see both Krsna and our true selves and all vestiges of unhappiness and illusion wash away — do we reach the ultimate goal of life (prea or priti).

Rsabhadeva confirms,

**“Therefore, until one has love \[priti\] for Lord Vasudeva, who is none other than Myself, he is certainly not delivered from having to accept a material body again and again.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Love for Krsna is not acquired from anywhere outside ourselves. It is our constitutional nature. While speaking to Sanatana Gosvami, Lord Caitanya reiterates that nama-sankirtana reawakens this love:

**“Pure love for Krsna is eternally.. .in the hearts of the living entities. It is not something to be gained from another source. When the heart is purified by hearing and chanting, it naturally awakens.”**

This same truth is mentioned both directly and indirectly throughout the Vedas and their corollaries. The aphorism tat tvam asi (“you arc that”), for example, describes the soul’s natural love for the Lord.

Because love is natural for all living beings — sinners and saints alike — and because it makes itself known in our everyday dealings, we must conclude that everyone is looking for someone to love.

Our search for the ideal person to love finds its climax when we fall in love with Krsna, which is why Lord Caitanya taught that love for Krsna is the highest goal of life and the purpose of all knowledge.

A person in love always desires the company of the beloved, and so as Sri Krsna’s devotees we always desire to be with Him in one of two ways: internally within our hearts and externally with our senses.

To see Krsna within ourselves, we must have a heart purified by loving devotion. But to see Krsna externally, we need more than a pure heart, we must also have an intense desire to see Him.

As a result of his meditation, little Narada suddenly saw the Lord in his heart, but his desire was not strong enough to sustain the vision or to sec the Lord face-to-face. He had to wait until his next life.

How does Krsna make Himself visible? Krsna reveals Himself within our hearts, or to our senses, by the same potency that qualifies us to see Him — intense loving devotion. Non-devotees can never see Him.

That said, we may wonder how so many non-devotees, even demons, were able to see Krsna when He was present five thousand years ago. The answer is that they saw Krsna’s reflection, not Krsna directly.

We cannot see Krsna unless we love Him. But Caitanya Mahaprabhu says that if we perform nama-sankirtana with love, we will see Krsna — either internally or externally—at every step (prati-padam).

The phrase prati-padam also means that any stage of life, from that of a student brahmacari to the renounced order of life, sannyasa, is suitable for chanting Krsna’s names and awakening love for Him.

Nama-sankirtana does not require that we renounce household life, as do other disciplines. Narottama Dasa Thakura says, *grhe ba banete thake*: “Whether you live at home or in the forest, just chant.”

The nature of nama-sankirtana performed with loving devotion is to attract Krsna (*sri-krsna-karsini*). In that context, Narada Muni tells what happens to him the moment he begins to sing Krsna’s names.

The sage says, “The Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, whose glories and activities are pleasing to hear, at once appears on the seat of my heart, as if called for, as soon as I begin to chant His holy activities.”

We may wonder what is the essential ingredient in chanting that attracts Krsna so. It is His pleasure potency. The essence of pleasure is love, and the essence of love, emotion, makes Him mad with bliss.

Srimati Radharani embodies the culmination of ecstatic emotion. She is the monarch who reigns over prṛma, and She is the one who nourishes us with ecstatic love and gives Krsna bliss.

Wherever Krsna sees devotees serving Him with unlimited flavours of loving devotion (prṛma), He also sees Srimati Radharani exerting Her potency. Therefore He hastily runs after such fortunate devotees.

In this way Krsna is conquered by His devotees’ love, as His devotees are by His. Maharaja Citraketu describes how master and servant bind themselves to each other with ropes of love:

**“O unconquerable Lord! Although You cannot be conquered by anyone, You are certainly conquered by devotees who have control of the mind and senses. They can keep You under their control —**

**“Because You are causelessly merciful to devotees who desire no material profit from You. Indeed, You give Yourself to them, and because of this You also have full control over Your devotees.”**

Lord Nrsimha also described to Prahlada Maharaja this mutual bond of love, placing special emphasis on how awe and veneration obstruct the spontaneity of love that attracts Him so.

After the Lord had killed Hiranyakasipu, Prahlada offered Him assorted prayers and abundant worship, to which Lord Nrsimha replied,

**“My dear child! Please renounce this awe and veneration.**

**“I do not like those things in My devotees. Show your love for Me spontaneously, as you wish. Although My every desire is always fulfilled, My devotee’s love brings Me newer and newer pleasure.**

**“Because of his unwavering love, a devotee may see Me and converse with me. Although I am always unbound, My devotees bind Me with ropes of love. Although I am unconquerable, devotees conquer Me.**

**“And although I am supremely independent, My devotees control Me. When they renounce the love of their friends and kin to love only Me, I become My devotees’ property, and we become adoring friends.”**

Hearing about Narada’s and Prahlada’s love for the Lord might inspire us to ask, “What makes devotees fall in love with Krsna?” It is the effect of His qualities, beauty, sweetness, and pastimes.

Bhismadeva loved Krsna for faithfully protecting Arjuna under all circumstances during the conflict at Kuruksetra, and for the way He smiled at and moved amongst the gopis during the rasa dance.

Devotees often fall in love with Krsna simply by seeing His charming face and beguiling form, so pleasing to the eyes. The gopis fall for Krsna’s beauty, encouraged by the mystical sound of His flute.

We might expect Krsna’s appeal to entice only humans, but Bilvamangala Thakura says, *krsnad anyah ko va latasv api premado bhavati*:

**“Lord Krsna brings ecstatic joy to the flowering vines.”**

The purity of nama-sankirtana awakens all these sublime exchanges. The holy name acts like a puppetmaster, pulling the strings of divine love to make both the devotees and Krsna move according to its will.

After enumerating all these drops of sankirtana nectar, Lord Caitanya advises us nor just to hear but to taste as well. We should not be like santa-bhaktas who want to see but not to serve Krsna.

But however accustomed we may be to drinking a beverage by our own effort, this purnamrta is not so easily consumed; love for Krsna is just like Krsna Himself, fully independent and self-sufficient.

The nectar of nama-sankirtana can be tasted only by the grace of that very same nectar. As mentioned earlier, Sri Radha is love personified. Only by Her grace can devotees drink and be nourished by prem.

Pure chanting gives rise to love, and chanting with love enables us to taste love’s unfolding ecstasies, the intoxicating effects of which make us even more eager to chant and ascend to higher levels of prem.

All this happens by Sri Radha’s grace. If we chant with offence, however, we live outside (apa) Radha’s influence. Without Her grace we cannot taste even the shadow of love, not to mention pure love.

**\* \* \* \***

We approach Krsna’s names in the maha-mantra through Radha’s name — Hare Krsna or Hare Rama. Based on the order of names, then, it is Radha who allows us to churn the nectar of Krsna’s names.

Just as Krsna attracts anyone who sees or hears of Him — the gopas, gopis, even the animals of Vraja — Krsna’s name attracts all who vibrate or hear it, whether with indifference, attention, or love.

The syllable krs, which connotes the essence of His beauty and sweetness, combines with the syllable na, which emits the pleasure of His presence, to evoke the all-attractiveness of Krsna’s holy name.

Philosophically, this combination of syllables is said to best represent the Absolute Truth, but in terms of taste Krsna’s holy name showers heavenly nectar, the blissful touch of which enlightens us.

When we call out, “Krsna!” the son of Nanda Maharaja who, with His blackish complexion, lotus eyes, and wayward smile, brings unending pleasure to Gokula, we praise the master of supreme bliss.

Spellbound by the name Krsna, we helplessly repeat the name Rama, which draws us closer and closer to eternal Vrndavana by its reassuring taste, the pleasure for which perfected yogis hanker.

When in Vraja, we find that Rama stands for the bliss of amorous pleasure, the very essence of Krsna’s being, and that our own pleasure is derived from assisting Krsna in His sports of love with Radha.

Within the groves of Vrndavana Krsna constantly induces the gopis’ minds and senses to enjoy the charms of His form and beauty, and so they always loudly glorify Him, calling out, “Rama! Rama!”

The taste of the names Krsna and Rama cannot be accurately described. Only one who directly relishes them with a heart full of love can grasp their sweetness, enchantment, and dynamic influence.

Try as they might, such fortunate souls are unable to describe to others the sublime flavours they relish. In the end they can only say, “My dear friend! Chant, ‘Krsna! Krsna! Rama! Rama!”’

The nectar of Krsna’s names as revealed by Radha’s grace is Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s most valuable gift, beyond which we might reasonably imagine nothing else could possibly exist. But there is something else!

That something else is the very means for tasting the nectar of Krsna’s name. For Krsna, and for most Gaudiya Vaisnavas, it is the vessel for sampling the tastiest nectar of all. It is the name of Radha.

Hara in the vocative is Hare. Repeating this name frees us from the three varieties of suffering we encounter in this material world and thus enables us to recite the maha-mantra with fixed attention.

Sri Radha embodies Krsna’s pleasure potency. She steals away His mind, patience, and reputation with the allure of Her twenty-five qualities. We praise that Radha by calling out, “Hare! Hare!”

When the word “Hare” issues from our lips, Lord Krsna knows that in truth we are saying “O Radha!” And the first syllable, ra, inspires Him to eagerly grant us supreme loving devotion.

And the second syllable of Radha’s name, dha, makes Krsna lose all composure. Intoxicated by that nectarean sound, He runs after us, the most fortunate persons, the performers of radha-sankirtana.

This wonder that is the chanting of Radha’s names is encapsulated in the verse

*radhety evam ca samsiddha, ra-karo dana-vacakah*  
*dha nirvanam ca tad-datri tena radha prakirtita*

**“The name of Radha is formed by combining the syllable ra, meaning “a gift,” with dha, meaning “liberation.” Repeating this name, a person achieves the ultimate perfection of complete liberation.”**

These commentaries on the words of the maha-mantra show that chanting “Hare” enables us to taste the sweet nectar not only of Krsna’s names but also of Radha’s. In this way we are doubly blessed.

And that double blessing bestows upon us further insight into the meaning of purnamrta, which is defined as full nectar because the nectar of Sri Radha’s names complements that of Krsna’s.

No doubt we arc all eager to hear a verbal depiction of this full nectar. Unable to give one myself, I cite a verse from one who has so kindly bequeathed it to us, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

The great saint writes,

*radheti nama nava-sundara-sidhu mugdham krsneti nama madhuradbhuta-gadha-dugdham*  
*sarva-ksanam surabhi-raga-himena ramyam krtva tadaiva piba me rasane ksudarte*

**“O my tongue, suffering from thirst! Please mix the delicious fresh enchanting nectar of the name ‘Radha’ with the wonderfully sweet condensed milk of the name ‘Krsna.’**

**“Having done that, please add the fragrant, delightful ice of pure passionate love \[raga-bhakti\] and drink this refreshing full nectar moment after moment.”**

This verse of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami elaborates on nama-sankirtana s sixth excellence, inaccessible and incomprehensible to both materialists and to those whose chanting is marred by offences.

Empiricists may demand tangible proof of the ecstasy contained in Krsna’s name, but the only true evidence is the experience of pure devotees when they chant without offence and with love.

Dasa Gosvami certainly has love for Krsna. His taste for nama-sankirtana is boundless. In order to encourage us to qualify ourselves for tasting nectar, he has kindly recorded his personal encounters.

Unless we are thirsty, we cannot enjoy the taste of a drink. As will be described in upcoming sections, a lack of thirst indicates that we are committing offences to the holy name. Thus we get no taste.

But once our chanting is free of offence, our taste for the name’s sweetness progressively increases, as does our thirst for nama-sankirtana. The tongue, ears, and mind all taste this sweetness.

The more we hear, the more the taste for the name increases; as taste increases, our thirst to chant Hare Krsna grows. Chanting and hearing with thirst increases the taste, and so it goes, ad infinitum.

What is this nectar in the name Hare? It is a fresh, pleasing, and enchanting elixir. Is it like grape juice sweetened with sugar and the touch of the lips of Apsaras? No! It is much tastier than that.

Is it like the nectar of heaven? No! Heavenly nectar keeps demigods young only for the life of Brahma, but this nectar gives love for Krsna and grants immortality by awarding one an eternal spiritual body.

But, O friend! If you really want to taste the nectar of Sri Radha’s name, then I humbly request, “Please drink the name Radha again and again. In time you will be praising its two syllables yourself.”

Dasa Gosvami compares Krsna’s name to the finest, most exquisite, sweetened condensed milk. This is a fitting metaphor, for Krsna is a cowherd boy who daily milks his father’s surabhi cows.

That milk is the liquid form of the cows’ motherly affection for Krsna, sweetened by Krsna’s own touch from milking and Maharaja Nanda’s desire that his son be provided with the best of everything.

Yasoda then saturates the milk with her own motherly affection before giving it to Radha to thicken on the stove. Radha sweetens it with rock candy, Her touch, and the essence of Her youth and beauty.

Finally Madhumangala, generally very talkative, becomes speechless from tasting that condensed milk. Thinking he is drinking the condensed form of love for Krsna, all he can say is “Krsna! Krsna!”

**\* \* \* \***

How much nectar is in Krsna’s names? Although Rupa Gosvami says he doesn’t know, to inspire us he tries to describe the effect it has on his own senses: it makes his tongue dance without stopping.

Krsna’s name is so sweet that Rupa Gosvami desires many tongues to taste it. Similarly, the sweetness of the sound “Krsna” makes his ears want to expand a thousandfold in order to hear it properly.

Not wanting to be left out, Rupa’s eyes visualise the sweetness of the syllables krs-na and hanker to see Krsna’s enchanting threefold-bending form, which is non-different from His name.

Finally, after entering the mind through the ears and eyes, the sweetness of the holy name transforms the heart, where a host of loving ecstasies dance, just as we dance in sankirtana.

Not content with the limited courtyard of the heart, however, these ecstasies roam throughout the body, causing assorted transformations and sweetening Rupa’s limbs with the nectar of spontaneous love.

Dear readers! I have told you about the nectar of Radha’s name and the condensed milk of Krsna’s name. Mixing these beverages together produces a taste as astonishing as the vision of Radha and Syama.

Is there more to say? Dasa Gosvami says that to this astonishing mixture we must add the ice of anuraga, the sixth stage of love’s development, which is the passionate love the gopis bear for Krsna.

This sub-attachment (anuraga) is a very exalted stage of love. At this stage, even after enjoying Krsna’s company, one may feel that his own enjoyment could have been heightened even further.

Such ecstatic emotion allows us to see Krsna in new and novel ways. For example, in order to enjoy Krsna’s company incessantly one may even desire to become an inanimate object, like Krsna’s flute.

This loving ecstasy has its own stages of development, in which symptoms are at first invisible but later appear in or on the body as love escalates to its seventh stage, called ecstasy (bhava).

Chanting the maha-mantra awakens anuraga, which when nourished by more and more chanting brings about a transcendental relish known only to the followers of Rupa and Raghunatha.

And yet we may lament as Lord Caitanya did, *durdaivam idrsam ihajani nanuragah*: “I am so unfortunate that I commit offences while chanting, and therefore I do not achieve attachment for chanting.”

I too lament that due to my offences and my spiritual immaturity, the real wealth of love for Krsna like that of the gopis evades me, as does the intense taste for sankirtana that comes from chanting as they do.

Yet for offenceless devotees whose love has not yet taken birth — the *ajata-priti bhaktas* — their fledgling attachment will certainly mature as they chant and yearn to serve Krsna with anuraga.

Let us take heart! Krsna assures us that by humbly performing devotional service we can move steadily forward, give birth to love within our hearts (jata-priti), and thus fulfil all of our desires.

Krsna says to Uddhava,

**“Everything is attained hy serving Me with devotion. If somehow or other My devotee desires heaven, liberation, or My own spiritual abode, he easily attains such benedictions.”**

Without separate endeavour nama-sankirtana dissolves the false ego and other obstacles that stand between us and perfect love for Krsna, just as the fire of digestion devours everything we eat.

In time the coveted prize of loving devotion appears by its own power, and by its own power causes Krsna to appear. Then, to nourish and develop itself, that same loving devotion causes Krsna to disappear.

Whether Krsna is in front of us or far away, loving devotion acts on a devotee’s transcendental life as food acts on the material body by giving pleasure, nourishment, and relief from material hunger.

To see Krsna face-to-face is the highest perfection of life, and it is most pleasing to the soul. But even more wonderful is that the pleasure one tastes from serving Him in separation is greater still.

In such elevated states one may show outward symptoms of pain, like crying in intense lamentation, but within one relishes incomparable bliss known only to those who have felt it for themselves.

Love in separation is inconceiveable. Its intensely sublime taste generates an addiction that makes those afflicted with it want to feel separation from Lord Krsna over and over again.

This amazing influence of the full nectar of nama-sankirtana reveals another meaning of the phrase “at every step” (prati-padam): the steps are successive events, meeting with and separating from Krsna.

Whether in union or in separation, however, tasting the sweet nectar of love for Krsna is a marginal characteristic of that love; to serve Him is the natural, primary characteristic of loving devotion.

We are not connoisseurs of tastes like the sages whose contact with Krsna consists mainly of looking at Him, sages who would be satisfied if the Lord were to just once cast a merciful glance their way.

Such devotees like Kardama Muni are great souls, but they have no desire to render personal service to Krsna. And because of that shortcoming, Lord Caitanya does not think so highly of them.

Pure devotees make their feelings known to Krsna by serving Him wholeheartedly. They pray for the perfection of being able to serve Him in any condition of life, for no other reason than to please Him.

Lord Siva once praised such devotees to Parvati,

**“For them the heavenly planets, liberation, and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord.”**

Vaisnavas who possess the anuraga mentioned by Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami serve Krsna in two ways: externally by the activities of their senses and internally by the absorption of their minds.

External service includes chanting Hare Krsna, studying Srimad-Bhagavatam, preaching, taking care of those who come forward as a result of that effort, and worshipping the Deity of the Lord.

Internal service means to spontaneously absorb the mind in constant remembrance of Vraja pastimes and to think of ways to assist a Vraja-vasi in his or her service to Srimati Radharani and Sri Krsna.

Devotees aspiring for anuraga and those who have attained it both serve Radha and Krsna, internally and externally. The difference is that the former is like an unripe mango, the latter like a ripe mango.

But how does the unripe mango ripen? And how does the ripe mango become even tastier? Pure nama-sankirtana as taught by Lord Caitanya nourishes, protects, and refines the unripe and the ripe.

Vrndavana is the realm of full nectar (anuraga). It is the abode attained by directing our attachment to serving Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes as we imploringly chant Their mellow-laden names.

Remembering the loving pastimes of the divine couple while chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra is the very life of Gaudiya Vaisnavas and the essence of all regulative principles.

**\* \* \* \***

The seventh and final excellence of nama-sankirtana is sarvatma-snapanam, which means “the whole self is bathed,” or as Srila Prabhupada says, “It gives a cooling effect to everyone.”

These two interpretations reflect the two prongs of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission: chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra to benefit oneself, and chanting it to benefit others.

About Lord Caitanya, Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami says, *apane acari' bhakti karila pracara*: “Assuming the sentiment of a devotee, He preached devotional service while practising it Himself.”

The true glory of nama-sankirtana will be revealed when, following the teachings and example of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the whole world chants and dances in the transcendental ecstasy of love of God.

The preceding sections have dealt with how nama-sankirtana awakens our devotional ecstasy, our spiritual identity, and finally our love for Krsna, the greatest treasure of mankind.

Lord Caitanya’s use of the word sarvatma at the end of His verse glorifying nama-sankirtana amalgamates all that comes before it to indicate rasa, the remarkable taste of fully awakened love for Krsna.

Later we will hear how transcendental mellow (rasa) is the essence of Krsna’s nature, of His eternal companions, and of His eternal abode. We attain that world of rasa exclusively through nama-sankirtana.

The potency to arouse rasa in advanced devotees is inherent in nama-sankirtana because Krsna’s name is itself the conscious form of all transcendental mellows (caitanya-rasa-vigrahah).

Along with awareness of one’s eternal form comes complete rapport with whatever mood of devotion corresponds to one’s Svarupa, which is called permanent emotion, sthayi-bhava, or rati.

In fact this permanent emotion (rati) is what we actually mean when we speak of our “relationship with Krsna.” Rati combined with other ecstasies yields the ever-fresh, sublimely relishable ardour called rasa.

Now let us examine how the four ecstasies — vibhava, anubhava, sattvika-bhava, and vyabhicari-bhava — combine to heighten rati and transform it into rasa, the culmination of devotional service.

The special stimulus that excites sentiments of love, making them more relishable, is called vibhava. For example, the sight of Krsna’s face or form will arouse and intensify the love in one’s heart.

Vibhava precipitates a physical display of aroused love called anubhava. Given the example above, that display may be to call out the Lord’s name, “O Krsna!” or to bow down in obeisance.

These displays of anubhava stimulate further loving exchanges; one may see Krsna’s face and call out, “O Krsna,” and then feel an emotion even more intense called sattvika-bhava.

Sattvika ecstasy differs from anubhava in that it is spontaneous, rather than a response to a particular stimulus for Krsna consciousness. There are eight such symptoms, including crying and horripilation.

The fourth ecstasy is an emotional taste that gives rise to heightened symptoms of love called vyabhicari-bhavas, which differ from vibhava in that various emotions, rather than external forms, arc their cause.

For example, if the sight of Krsna were combined with the sight of a demon attacking Him from behind, fear for Krsna’s safety would dramatically intensify and augment love for the Lord.

When nama-sankirtana combines these four bhavas with permanent emotion (rati), one can taste the mellow of his or her individual relationship with Krsna. That individual taste is called rasa.

We should keep in mind that rati, or one’s sthayi-bhava, dominates the other four bhavas because it is the permanent, foundational ingredient of rasa. It keeps all other emotions under its dominion.

Rupa Gosvami compares devotional service to an ocean in which rati is the water and the other bhavas are the wind, waves, tides, and currents, whose effects appear due to the presence of the water.

The extraordinary feature of rasa is that no matter how many times a devotee tastes it, it always feels as though it’s for the first time. This unprecedented, ever-fresh taste of rasa is called apurva.

When the women of Mathura saw Krsna’s bodily beauty they said,

**“What austerities the gopis must have performed? With their eyes they always drink the nectar of the form of Lord Krsna.**

**“Sri Krsna’s form is the essence of loveliness and is not to be equalled or surpassed. That loveliness is the only abode of beauty, fame, and opulence. It is self-perfect, ever fresh, and extremely rare.”**

To say that Krsna’s sweetness is unprecedented is to say that the sight of Krsna’s nectar-saturated features gives the gopis a taste they are convinced they have never had before. Such is the influence of love.

Great devotees, then, taste not only love and rasa but also the sweetness of Krsna’s form, qualities, and pastimes. And Krsna in turn tastes the sweetness and magnanimity of His devotees’ attributes.

In this way both the Lord and His servants eternally enjoy as they paint Vrndavana with the colours of loving exchange, intoxicating one another with the ever-fresh flavours of divine mellows.

How does ecstasy lead to rasa? For those who have crossed the threshold of transcendence — through either regulated practice or spontaneous devotion — remembering Krsna is effortless.

If we remember Radha’s and Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes as we chant the maha-mantra, the ingredients of mellows gradually blend together within our hearts to produce the full-blown tastes of rasa.

Remembrance of Krsna’s pastimes gives rise to both vibhavas and vyabhicari-bhavas, in turn producing anubhavas and sattvika-bhavas, which combine with permanent emotion (rati) to produce rasa.

The development and blending of the individual bhavas takes place over time by the mercy of nama-sankirtana, passing from the first stage of remembrance to one’s ultimate entrance into Krsna’s lila.

By carefully following the guidance of our preceptors and the dictation of the holy name, chanting will lead us to the ultimate perfection of pure devotion and we will taste endless varieties of bliss.

We will then continuously praise the holy name with wonderful prayers, such as

*narada-vinojjivana sudhormi-niryasa-madhuri-pura*  
*tvam krsna-nama kamam sphura me rasane rasena sada*

**“O life of Narada’s vina! O you who are like waves of essential nectar in the ocean of sweetness. O Krsna-nama! I pray that you please always manifest on my tongue with transcendental rasa.”**

**\* \* \* \***

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu says sarvatma-snapanam He is speaking about the effect of thoroughly mature chanting, in which Krsna’s holy names give rise to the full mellow of devotional service.

The combined shower of divine sound from without and emotion from within, both rich in rasa, permeates one’s being and gets rid of material contamination like a thorough scrubbing gets rid of dirt.

The tongue initiates this shower of nama-sankirtana, the sound of which then passes through the ear, from where it enters into the mind and the intelligence and finally reverberates through the soul.

We may wonder how it can be said that the whole self is bathed when not every sense is actually touched by nama-sankirtana. But every sense is, in fact, touched by the influence of the holy name.

As the Visnudutas instructed Gopa-kumara, they confirmed this phenomenon:

**“When the nectar of the Lord’s names appears in just one sense, all the senses are flooded with their own sweet tastes.”**

In other words, as soon as the transcendental sound “Krsna” escapes the mouth or enters the ear, all the other senses of the body, such as the eyes or nose, are flooded with the sight or scent of Krsna’s body.

And because the holy name arises from the power of speech, its vibration resonates outward from its source, giving pleasure not only to the chanter but also to anyone within range who hears it.

In this way nama-sankirtana benefits more than just the chanter, making it superior to silent meditation. Later we will hear about this benefit, which Srila Prabhupada calls the “cooling effect.”

But first we should thoughtfully consider what Caitanya Mahaprabhu means by “bathing” (snapanam), because in the Vedic culture, as in other cultures, there are different types of baths.

Baths arc most commonly for cleansing the body. In refined cultures it is not unheard of for people to bathe thrice daily. Then there are ritualistic baths, like the avabhrtha-snana, which follow religious rites.

And finally there are purificatory baths for both body and soul in which devotees bathe in sacred water from places of pilgrimage or holy rivers or chant approved mantras, just as we chant Hare Krsna.

The bath spoken of in the Siksastaka, however, stands far above all these others. It is unique in that the purification attained by bathing in nama-sankirtana culminates in awakening love for Krsna.

This bath is so special because Krsna bathes devotees from within. Suta Gosvami says,

**“When people properly glorify the Supreme Personality of Godhead or simply hear about His power —**

**“The Lord personally enters their hearts and cleanses away every trace of misfortune, just as the sun removes the darkness or as a powerful wind drives away the clouds.”**

To bathe in nama-rasa is to transform, by the force of love-inspired mellows, one’s entire being — physical, mental, and spiritual — into something that more closely resembles the original self.

Sruti declares the essential nature of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and of the living entities to be one of rasa, transcendental mellow, rasa vai sah, rasam hy evayam labdhvanandi bhavati.

But until we reach the stage of prem, we arc not qualified to enjoy rasa. And unless we have been transformed by rasa we arc not qualified to have the company of the object of our worship, Sri Krsna.

Just as a subject must fully align himself with the wishes of his king to become a courtier, we must align ourselves through the potency of rasa to serve the emperor of loving mellows, Rasika-sekhara, Krsna.

Indeed, the Vedic aphorism eko brahma dvitiya nasti (“Brahman is one without a second”) implies that we must adopt the rasikd nature of the Supreme Brahman, Krsna, to revive our brahman nature.

This kind of oneness in agreement between the Lord and His servants is acceptable to Vaisnavas, who completely reject the unqualified oneness Mayavadis try to eke out of the self-evident Vedic mantras.

But even this concept of Vaisnava agreement needs further elucidation. In such oneness, Krsna remains the object of love, and the devotees are the shelters of love. Thus there is also a difference.

As the shelters of love, we all have eternal relationships with Krsna in one of five mellows, each of which has a dominant quality, like intimacy in the fraternal mellow or maintenance in the parental.

When the shower of nama-sankirtana bathes advanced devotees, their entire being takes on the specific characteristics of their eternal mellow, which qualifies them to serve Krsna in that particular way.

This means that their senses become completely fit for, their minds spontaneously and exclusively drawn to, and their souls transcendentally one with their eternal service.

The result of such integration is that one is adorned with the qualities of a resident of Vrndavana, and then has no other identity. This is the actual meaning of one's own spiritual body (svarupa).

Such spiritual concepts elude the conditioned mind’s attempt to grasp the meaning of Svarupa through the process of negation (neti neti); in other words, by studying only what the spiritual body is not.

One’s original spiritual identity is not an impermanent one in which the eternal soul temporarily misidentifies itself with a lowly dog’s body in one life and a human being’s body in another.

Once we attain our eternal forms those identities are fixed forever. Krsna Himself says,

**“Established thus, one never departs from the truth, and upon gaining this he thinks there is no greater gain.”**

Just as bell metal is transformed to gold when mixed with mercury, one becomes a fully qualified eternal servant of Krsna when bathed in nama-sankirtana enriched by transcendental rasa.

The great fortune of those who attain their original position in the spiritual realm is difficult to describe; they who once suffered torment at Maya’s hands arc now incessantly overflowing fountains of bliss.

The Visnu Purana says,

**“Attaining the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna is the medicine to cure the suffering soul, and that medicine also fills a person with boundless transcendental happiness.”**

The ãasa-imbucd chanting of Krsna’s names transfers the soul to Vraja. There, the eternal self-manifesting nature of love and pleasure creates an atmosphere full of splendour and sweetness beyond words.

The fountainhead of that blissful reality is Krsna’s never-ending Iila, pastimes overflowing with love-filled mellows that saturate everyone and everything with a sweetness free from anxiety.

Amongst all of Krsna’s pastimes, His dalliances with Radha are supreme because they fully display the qualities of all rasas, therefore connoisseurs of mellows, rasika devotees, make them the goal of life.

**\* \* \* \***

In the realm of transcendence, Goloka, rasa is not just relationship. It is, as the raso vai mantra tells us, Krsna’s very being. And it is the substance from which His associates are made: pure loving devotion.

To give us an idea of what the pinnacle of a body comprised of rasa is like, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami offers his regal prayer, “The Nectar of Pure Love,” which describes Radha’s rasa-laden form:

**“\[The gopis’ love for Krsna\] appears to be a brilliant jewel. Enlightened by such a transcendental jewel, Srimati Radharani’s body is further perfumed and decorated with aromatic kunkuma.**

**“Sri Radha bathes three times daily: in the morning Her body is bathed in the nectar of compassion, in the afternoon, in the nectar of youth, and in the evening, in the nectar of lustre itself.**

**“In this way Her bathing is performed, and Her body becomes as brilliant as the cintamani jewel, thereby confirming that Sri Radha completely eclipses the goddess of fortune, Laksmi-devi.**

**“Her dress is composed of various kinds of silken garments, which may be compared to Her natural shyness. Her beauty is more and more enhanced, being decorated with kunkuma and musk.**

**“The kunkuma is compared to beauty itself, and the blackish musk is compared to amorous love. Thus Sri Radha’s body is decorated with different colours such as red kunkuma and black musk.**

**“Radhika’s ornaments embody the natural symptoms of ecstasy: trembling, tears, jubilation, immobility, perspiration, stammering, blushing, madness, and dullness.**

**“Thus Her entire body is bedecked with these nine different jewels. Over and above this, the beauty of Her body is enhanced by Her transcendental qualities, which hang as a flower garland on Her body.**

**“The ecstasy of love for Sri Krsna is known as dhira and adhira, sober and restless, and such ecstasies constitute the covering of Srimati Radharani’s body. That covering is further adorned by camphor.**

**“Srimati Radharani’s transcendental anger towards Krsna is present in the arrangement of the hair on Her head, and the tilaka of Her great fortune shines forth on Her beautiful forehead.**

**“The earrings of Sri Radha are the holy names of Krsna and the recitation and aural reception of His name and fame. Her lips are always reddish due to the betel nut of ecstatic affection for Krsna.**

**“The black ointment around Radha’s eyes is the tricky behaviour Krsna’s love inspires, while Her gentle smiling and joking with Krsna are the camphor with which She is perfumed.**

**“She sleeps in Her room with the aroma of pride, and when She lies down in Her bed, the transcendental variety of Her loving ecstasies is like a jewelled locket in the midst of the necklace of Her separation.**

**“She has a stringed instrument known as a kacchapi-vina, which is the fame and fortune that actually dries up the faces and breasts of gopis like Candravali, who are Her competitors for Krsna’s attention.**

**“Her breasts are covered by Her sari in the form of affection and anger towards Krsna, and She always keeps Her hands on the shoulder of Her gopi friend, who is compared to Her youthful beauty.**

**“And although Srimati Radharani is highly qualified with so many spiritual assets, She is nonetheless affected by the transcendental Cupid known as Krsna, by whom She is defeated.”**

Dasa Gosvami concludes,

**“O Radha! Taking a straw in his mouth, this unhappy person offers respectful obeisances unto You. Please bring him to life by sprinkling him with the nectar of service to You.**

**“O Gandharvika! Just as Visnu never rejects a surrendered soul, please don’t reject me. One who reads this prayer will attain the direct service that brings with it the mercy of Sri Radha.”**

**In order to highlight the munificence of Lord Caitanya’s mission, Srila Prabhupada translates sarvatma-snapanam, nama-sankirtana s seventh excellence, as “gives a cooling effect to everyone.”**

The purpose of that mission is well conveyed by the phrase sarve sukhino bhavantu: “May everyone be happy.” How can one be happy if one is burning in the forest fire of repeated birth and death?

Caitanya Mahaprabhu says that nama-sankirtana s cooling rays extinguish that blazing fire, not only for the performer of sankirtana but also for anyone who hears the vibration of the holy name.

In this way the sufferings accumulated from past sins and the burning caused by present desires arc mercifully terminated, amnesty granted not only to humans but to all living entities who hear the sankirtana.

Lord Caitanya proved this to be true as He travelled through the forest of Jharikhanda. All the forest creatures, inspired by the Lord’s chanting of Hare Krsna, also danced and chanted in ecstatic love.

Haridasa Thakura says,

**“When loud nama-sankirtana is performed all over the world by those who follow in \[Lord Caitanya’s\] footsteps, all living entities, moving and non-moving, dance in devotional love.”**

The mellow of compassion moves Lord Caitanya to deliver the conditioned souls by His loud sankirtana. Whoever tastes nama-rasa will follow in the footsteps of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

This compassion (karuna-bhakti-rasa), an indirect mellow of love, awakens in the hearts of those devotees sensitive to the suffering of conditioned souls forgetful of their true nature as Krsna’s servants.

One ideal example of such a compassionate soul is Vasudeva Datta, an eternal associate of the Lord who once submitted a plea to Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu that all living entities be delivered.

Vasudeva Datta not only begged for the deliverance of all creatures but also vowed that if any living entities were unfit for liberation he would personally suffer for their sins so that they might be delivered.

By this example it is clear that devotees transformed by rasa are moved by extreme compassion to freely give anyone and everyone a taste of the same nectar of which such fortunate souls freely partake.

Such devotees please the Lord, who then treats them with special affection, as He did Vasudeva Datta; three times Lord Caitanya said,

**“I belong to Vasudeva Datta, and he can sell Me anywhere."**

Moreover, Krsna Himself says about devotees who teach the message of the Bhagavad-gita to others:

**“There is no servant in this world more dear to Me than he, nor will there ever be one more dear.”**

The Lord’s displays of kindness, generosity, and soft-heartedness towards devotees who dedicate their lives to others’ welfare melt our hearts and plunge us deeper into the ecstasies of rasa.

Nevertheless, we may wonder whether the chanting of those not yet liberated is also cooling to one and all. As suggested by the statement of Haridasa Thakura just quoted, the answer is yes.

The namacarya says that sankirtana need only be loud (ucca) to be effective. Whoever hears such loud chanting will be benefited and in time will also remember and chant the holy names.

But one may be concerned that chanting loudly in public will cause practising devotees to lose their spiritual strength. To the contrary, Jiva Gosvami says,

**“You will attain the topmost perfection.”**

Actually, a unique cooling effect descends upon those devotees who preach, as they are bathed in the full rays of the benediction moon. Srila Prabhupada often said, “If you want to attract Krsna, preach.”

The phrase “cooling effect” can also refer to the relief devotees feel from the pangs of separation from Krsna, pangs which feel to them like the intolerable scorching heat from the flames of a blazing fire.

For such advanced devotees the only way to cool their suffering and feel the company of the Lord is through nama-sankirtana, because wherever His names are chanted, Krsna appears (tatra tisthami).

Sri Suta says,

*sankirtyamano bhagavan anantah srutanubhavo vyasanam hi pumsam*  
*pravisya cittam vidhunoty asesam yatha tamo ’rko ’bhram ivati-vatah*

**“When people properly glorify Krsna —**

**“Or simply hear about His power, the Lord personally enters their hearts and cleanses away every trace of misfortune, just as the sun removes darkness or as a powerful wind drives away clouds.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Lord Caitanya concludes His glorification of the seven excellences of nama-sankirtana by declaring, *param vijayate sri-krsna-sankirtanam*: “Let there be all victory for the chanting of the holy name of Krsna.”

Jaya means “victory” and param means “supreme.” One who is supremely victorious is said to have conquered over all enemies. Srila Prabhupada therefore translates param vijayate as “all victory.”

While Krsna walked the earth fifty centuries ago, with assorted weapons He gained victory over the demons, demigods, practising devotees, Cupid, Vraja-vasis, Vraja gopis, and also Srimati Radharani.

To gain victory over demons such as Sisupala and Saiva, Sri Krsna employed weapons like His disc and club. He also engaged weapons like the Gandiva bow through His associates like Arjuna.

To correct demigods like Lord Siva who were falsely proud of their opulence and authority and who foolishly challenged Krsna, the Lord showed the superiority of His supreme weapon, the Narayana-jvara.

Other demigods — who also challenged Krsna, but without waging war on Him — were humbled by the Lord’s mystic powers, powers which thwarted the tricks of Brahma and frustrated Indra’s deluge.

Practising devotees came from all over the creation to join Krsna’s earthly entourage. By the company of His associates and His own attractive features, Hari defeated the ignorance in these souls’ hearts.

At the time of the rasa dance, Cupid mistook Krsna for a lusty boy and shot arrows at the Lord, hoping to incite His passions, but the arrows could not find their mark, because Krsna is never lusty.

Krsna won the hearts of the residents of Vrndavana with childhood pastimes of obedience to His parents and camaraderie with His friends; in other words, with His qualities as the Supreme Person.

The gopis were special objects of Krsna’s affection: influenced by His beauty and the enchanting sound of His flute, they abandoned morality, religious principles, and the ties of marriage to be with Him.

Rupa Gosvami recounts Krsna’s victory over Radha in this way:

**“Thus Lord Sri Krsna spoke of the sexual activities of the previous night. In this way He made Sri Radha close Her eyes out of shyness.**

**“Taking this opportunity, Sri Krsna painted various types of dolphins on Her breasts. Thus He became a very expert artist for all the gopis. During such pastimes, the Lord enjoyed the fulfilment of His youth.”**

And yet Krsna’s final victory, the victory that made Him all victorious, was won not over others but over Himself—curious to taste His own beauty, sweetness, and love, Krsna became Gauranga.

Sukadeva Gosvami’s narration of Krsna’s pastimes ends with the declaration that “Krsna is eternally victorious” (jayati). To celebrate Krsna’s victory, the sage speaks these immortal words:

**“Sri Krsna is He who is known as jana-nivasa, the ultimate resort of all living entities, and who is also known as Devaki-nandana or Yasoda-nandana, the son of Devaki and Yasoda. Although it is said**

**“That Krsna was born of Devaki, He is actually the son of Yasoda. He is the guide of the Yadu dynasty, and with His mighty arms He kills everything inauspicious, as well as every man who is impious.**

**“By His presence He destroys all things inauspicious for all living entities, moving and inert. His blissful smiling face always increases the lusty desires of the gopis. May He be all glorious and happy!”**

That said, we should hear one final truth. Though Krsna is victorious in so many ways, He is conquered by His devotees’ love. Love and its taste (rasa) conquers all, even Krsna, the unconquerable.

We may wonder: Krsna personally protected devotees, destroyed demons, and revived pure devotion on this earth. Now that He has departed, how will He carry out these important missions?

Since Sri Krsna’s departure, this age has deteriorated to the point that the habits of most people fall into the category of the demonic. Should they all be killed for their sins, as was Kamsa?

Demigods no longer come to earth, and practising devotees require more than the occasional company of advanced persons to bring them to perfection. How will these good souls be elevated?

In the form of brahmanas the gopis appeared with Lord Caitanya, hut they also left after His departure, as did Gadadhara Pandita, the form of Sri Radha in gaura-lila. Where are their pastimes of love now?

What remains unchanged is the presence of Cupid, who runs amok in the sensual playground of Kali-yuga. How will the emperor of the rasa dance thwart Cupid’s arrows and shelter His devotees now?

The answer to all these questions is the same: Krsna now achieves the purposes He once realised in person by manifesting Himself fully in divine sound through His equally victorious nama-sankirtana.

The state of affairs in this age has surely degraded — and will continue to do so — but the chanting of Krsna’s all-merciful names will always deliver the highest perfection despite Kali-yuga’s dearth of goodness.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu appeared with His eternal companions to teach us by example how to invoke the holy names and unleash their indomitable potency through dancing and singing in ecstatic love.

Jagai and Madhai, the most degraded persons, were transformed by the power of sankirtana. Even the demigods gave up their pride to dance and chant with the Lord in the guise of ordinary people.

With Caitanya Mahaprabhu, sinners and sadhakas attained perfection, His companions and expansions tasted bliss, and Radha was so subdued that She and Krsna united in one golden form.

Just as Krsna would lose Himself in the wonders of the rasa dance, Lord Caitanya would lose Himself in nama-sankirtana. Obviously, the power of the Lord’s name conquers even the Lord Himself.

The word param (“supreme”) suggests that nama-sankirtana is identical to Krsna’s supreme pastime, the nocturnal rasa dance. The transcendental benefits and ecstasies are the same for both.

The Lord left His sankirtana movement in the care of the acaryas so that ordinary people, practising devotees, and perfected souls alike could all continue to receive their due rewards.

The holy name enters the hearts of both demons and pure devotees to progressively remove all obstacles to awakening love for Krsna and to award all things needed to win over the heart of the Lord.

When pure devotees raise their voices in prema-sankirtana, they conquer Krsna’s heart. Master and servant then dance together as blissful vassals of the all-victorious monarch — nama-sankirtana.

The phrase *param vijayate sri-krsna-sahkirtanam* is also the promised outcome (phala-stuti) of the Siksastaka s first verse, for it blesses those who chant it with all seven excellences — perfect victory.

Sri Suka gave the same blessing,

*martyas tayanusavam edhitaya mukunda srimat-katha-sravana-kirtana-cintayaiti*  
*tad dhama dustara-krtanta-javapavargam gramad vanam ksiti-bhujo ’pi yayur yad-arthah*

**“By regularly hearing, chanting, and meditating on the beautiful topics of Lord Mukunda with ever-increasing sincerity, a mortal being will attain the divine kingdom of the Lord.**

**“In that transcendental kingdom the inviolable power of death holds no sway. For this purpose, many persons, including great kings, abandoned their mundane homes and took to the forest.”**

Dear readers, I conclude this study of the seven excellences of nama-sankirtana with a short summary of the topic. May it add to the glory of the all-victorious chanting of Sri Krsna’s holy names.

Chanting the holy name of Krsna cleanses the mirror of the heart and extinguishes the fire of misery in this world of birth and death. Nama-sankirtana thus inaugurates true auspiciousness for the soul.

Just as an evening lily blooms in the moon’s cooling rays, one’s heart blossoms in the nectar of the holy name, which awakens knowledge of the soul’s lost treasure — life with Krsna in the land of pure love.

By tasting the nectar of the name, the soul dives and surfaces in an ever-expanding ocean of pure joy. The taste of the sweet mellows of Krsna’s holy names thus purifies and satisfies all aspects of the self.

In the words of the great Vyasa,

**“Lord Visnu’s holy name removes all sin, establishes one in a life of piety and makes one disinterested in the attempt to gain an exalted post like that of Lord Brahma.**

**“It grants devotion to one’s spiritual master, brings transcendental knowledge, burns the seed of repeated birth and death, and places saintly devotees in awareness of perfect transcendental bliss.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Let us now conclude this chapter with a synopsis of the universally celebrated process of nama-bhajana, the form of meditation on the name that transports us from the stage of practice to eternal service.

This kind of nama-sankirtana is generally called japa. It is done by absorbing oneself in cultivating the holy name through chanting a prescribed number of rounds of the Hare Krsna mantra on beads.

The only obstacles to perfecting this process arc offences committed to the name. For beginners, offences are common, so the next chapter gives a detailed study of the offences and how they can be avoided.

If still committing offences, or struggling from the reactions to past offences, we must first become free from these dual misfortunes before trying to apply the practices outlined below.

How can one know if he or she is ready to practise meditation on the name? When one can sit still for the duration of sixteen rounds and attentively hear the holy name without the mind wandering.

One who has thus refined his or her chanting, who has cleared away bad habits, and who attentively follows the spiritual master’s guidance on the truths of nama-sankirtana, will make rapid advancement.

If one is sincere but still incapable of taking suitable guidance, or if such guidance is unavailable, all is not lost. Krsna says,

**“I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.”**

Proper worship of the holy name begins with meditating upon the sound vibration of the name itself, tasting its sweetness with the tongue, the ears, and the mind. This process is called nama-smarana.

This type of remembrance of the name is glorified by the Jabali-samhita:

**“Those who desire varieties of bliss should simply chant, remember, sing, and praise the name of Hari incessantly.”**

The symptoms of success in this process are twofold. First, the mind becomes completely inebriated by the taste of the holy name, as a result of which it abandons its capricious tendencies.

And second, the appearance of Krsna’s form, or at least the desire to think of Krsna’s form, arises spontaneously in the mind, at which time the chanter is qualified for the next stage of bhajana.

To meditate upon Sri Krsna’s form is the quintessence of bliss. His shapely limbs, soothing complexion, and enchanting smile reflect in every way the sound of His name’s sacred syllables.

This level of meditation is called rupa-smarana. It may also be executed by fixing the mind on some portrait given in scripture, such as:

**“Then Krsna, a smile on His lotus face, appeared before the gopis.**

**“Wearing a garland and a yellow garment, He directly appeared as one who can bewilder the mind of Cupid, who himself bewilders the minds of ordinary people.”**

We can also practise rupa-smarana by chanting Hare Krsna in front of the Deities, meditating upon Their beautiful forms and assigning syllables to Their limbs, as brahmanas do when they perform nyasa.

But since nama-bhajana aims at training the mind, it is preferable to perform rupa-smarana only within, not directing the eyes to an image or form. Krsna instructs Uddhava in this system of mental absorption:

**“The actual yoga system as taught by My devotees, headed by Sanaka-kumara, is simply this: Having withdrawn the mind from all other objects, one should directly and appropriately absorb it in Me.”**

Maturity at this level of meditation is reached when Krsna’s beautiful form — which is no different from His name — appears naturally and spontaneously in the mind during nama-sankirtana.

One tastes the fruit of rupa-smarana when the purified mind is eager to seek out Krsna’s unlimited and extraordinary qualities, just as a swan dives beneath the water to play amongst lotus stems.

This stage of nama-bhajana is called guna-smarana. At this time the mind recognises Lord Krsna’s qualities from the sound of His names and the movements of His limbs and facial features.

By saying “Hare” one remembers Krsna's infinite kindness, which inspires the Lord to remove all suffering and to grant an opportunity for a new, carefree life. At this thought, such a fortunate soul cries.

Then, when one sees Krsna’s hand holding the flute, that soul becomes fearless in the face of all obstacles and recalls the gopis’ words that glorify this quality: “O best of the Vrsnis! Your lotus-like hand —

“Which holds the hand of the goddess of fortune, grants fearlessness to those who approach Your feet out of fear of material existence. O lover, please place that wish-fulfilling lotus hand on our heads.”

Thoughts of Krsna’s form and qualities naturally lead to thoughts of His transcendental pastimes, which one is eager to remember when the mind is saturated with thoughts of Krsna and His name.

In repeating that verse spoken by the gopis, for example, we may remember how the despondent milkmaids sat on the banks of the Yamuna and tried to attract Krsna with their devotional songs.

We may also recall how the pain the gopis felt from separation became too much for Krsna to bear, and how He reappeared, smartly dressed and ready to join the gopis in the long-awaited rasa dance.

Spontaneous remembrance of Krsna’s pastimes, along with absorption in His name, His form, and His qualities is called lila-smarana. It is the best kind of meditation, the goal of all spiritual practices.

An anonymous Vaisnava records his appreciation for the bhajana of Krsna’s beautiful names:

**“If the opulence or knowledge of many millions of universes were clustered together —**

**“They would hardly equal a small fragment of the glory of Krsna’s holy name. Krsna’s holy name is my life. It is the goal of my life. It is the means I will employ to attain the goal of my life.”**

Practice, pure chanting, and proper guidance are needed at every stage of bhajana to successfully cultivate the five methods of meditative development described by saints and scriptures.

These five successive methods of development are hearing (sravana- dasa)}acceptance (varana-dasa), remembrance (smarana-dasa), application (apana-dasa), and perfection (sampatti-dasa).

Hearing the truths of the holy name constitutes the stage of hearing (sravana-dasa), and the stage of acceptance (varana-dasa) involves embracing those truths. Acceptance culminates in regular chanting.

This stage of acceptance includes both the offensive and clearing stages of nama-bhajana. When all offences are finally removed, situated on the platform of goodness, one can actually meditate.

This stage, called remembrance (smarana-dasa), begins as soon as the chanter earnestly pursues nama-smarana, already described. He or she can then meditate on Krsna’s form, qualities, and finally His pastimes.

The stage of remembrance has five further stages, all worthy of consideration for students of nama-tattva. They are remembrance, concentration, meditation, constant remembrance, and trance.

Typically, one’s first attempts to gain a deeper taste for chanting and hearing are not systematic and do not produce substantial results. This is recollection (smarana) within the stage of smarana-dasa.

Regarding this, the Brhan-naradiya Purana says:

**“Remembrance of the imperishable Lord Narayana, by any means whatsoever, brings happiness even to a sinful person. Of this there is no doubt.”**

Gradually, attempts to control the mind meet with success as techniques for withdrawing the mind from its attachments abound and chanting becomes concentrated. This is dharana.

Krsna defines this stage:

**“The mind of one meditating upon the objects of the senses is certainly entangled in such objects, but if one constantly remembers Me, then the mind is absorbed in Me.”**

Now we come to meditation (dhyana), in which the aforementioned ability to contemplate the name, form, qualities, and pastimes of Krsna is within grasp, and taste comes without obstruction.

It is said that this stage of meditation transports the chanter beyond all dualities, such as heat and cold. Even a sinner thus absorbed by dint of special circumstances can attain the highest benefit.

In the case of one whose practice is mainly regulated, the next two stages — constant remembrance (dhruvanusmrti) and trance (samadhi) — indicate increasingly deep absorption in lila-smaranam.

Lord Kapila describes *dhruvanusmrti*:

**“Just as the water of the Ganges flows naturally down towards the ocean, such devotional ecstasy, uninterrupted by any material condition, flows towards the Lord.”**

Dhruvanusmrti first manifests as mantropasana, which later progresses to svarasiki meditation, in which the heart is purified to the extent that the chanter loses awareness of his or her material body.

Markandeya Rsi displayed this last level of trance. He became so immersed in the Lord that he was unaware of himself or the world around him, including the arrival of Siva and Parvati.

To one whose practice is mainly on the level of spontaneous devotion, constant remembrance brings full absorption in both kinds of meditation, and trance brings identification with those pastimes.

This practice of mentally entering into Krsna’s pastimes — which is rarely recommended, and then only with expert guidance — is distinct from actually gaining admittance into the Lord’s lila.

Let us briefly consider where the stage of samadhi, within the greater stage of smarana-dasa, places us within the general divisions of progressive devotion from attraction (asakti) to love (prema).

The trance (samadhi) achieved in the stage of remembrance places us at the level of attraction (asakti).
