At maturity this trance reaches, but docs not enter, the realm of ecstatic devotion (bhava).The transition from remembrance (smarana-dasa) to application (apana-dasa) marks the division between the conditioned and the transcendental state, a transition that can occur only by divine grace.

Application means that we no longer meditate on something outside ourselves or conceive of ourselves as part of a mental absorption; rather, this degree of remembrance is a direct spiritual experience.

Apana-dasa is the point at which bhava begins and one’s spiritual form (svarupa-siddhi) is revealed. Subsequent stages of ecstatic emotion unfold until culminating in devotional mellow at prema.

At the stage of application, one’s unique, eternal spiritual identity is fully revealed. Through the medium and by the mercy of the holy name, all aspects of spiritual perfection are then thoroughly explored.

But as long as a soul remains entrapped in matter, even though spiritually perfected, the soul must inevitably return from the plane of internal service in emotional ecstasy to this world of suffering.

Thus the soul can only make its final transition to the stage of perfection (sampatti-dasa) upon release from the material body. Such is the process of perfection attained through nama-bhajana.

This is what Srila Prabhupada means by “going back home, back to Godhead.” Such devotees become objects of remembrance that inspire others in their endeavours to achieve the ultimate perfection.

Having considered the stages of absorption, now let us return to our discussion of how devotional mellows develop under the stewardship of nama-bhajana and one advances to the stage of tasting rasa.

**\* \* \* \***

Lila-smaranam is perfected in the conditioned stages of smarana-dasa. As Krsna’s name, form, and qualities integrate seamlessly into His pastimes, the first rays of rasa begin to dawn.

Chanting of this quality may indicate the dawning of nama-rasa, but the full dawn of rasa itself takes place on the transcendental plane. It therefore might be better to call this initial stage nama-rasa-abhasa.

This “semblance of nama-rasa'' appears only after intense purification of the heart. Still, the emotions and realisations it reveals should be taken as shadows of reality, not the transcendental reality itself.

Nonetheless, just as the sun’s rays herald the coming of the sun itself, the glimmer of nama-rasa-abhasa indicates that the sun of spiritual mellows will soon rise by the mercy of the Lord.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda warns that the transition from smarana-dasa to apana-dasa takes place only when one is eligible to receive the transformational mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

The main obstacles to becoming a beneficiary of this mercy are making a show of acquired devotion and seeking to be recognised and worshipped as a great devotee. These are the last snares of maya.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu decries mundane profiteering (labha), mundane adoration (puja)yand mundane importance (pratistha) as weeds that choke the creeper of devotion.

This implies that even though one’s taste for chanting may be intense and the potency of that chanting may be perceptible to others, one may become complacent and fail to take the last step to perfection.

Distracted by the adulation of naive followers and inebriated by an inflated sense of self-importance, these complacent albeit advanced devotees often fail to seek out the company of superiors or even peers.

The material opulence that accompanies prominence and position may further intoxicate such devotees, who are unwilling to pay the final price for perfection — surrendering everything to Krsna.

But, having paid that price — from either the regulated or spontaneous platform — transcendental life awaits. Effortless immersion in Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes accompanies liberation.

The acaryas point out, however, that the ecstatic devotion attained from spontaneous practice is stronger and smoother in the beginning than the ecstatic devotion attained through regulated practice.

The reason for this is that regulated practitioners must gradually adjust themselves as the absolutely spontaneous nature of bhava-bhakti awakens, whereas spontaneous practitioners need not.

At the initial stages of ecstasy, nama-bhajana of Krsna’s pastimes is no longer a function of the mind —meditation or remembrance — hut direct experience, which is the application of spiritual perfection.

In the stage of apana-dasa, ecstasies like vibhava and anubhava mature, bringing about participation in the pastimes of the Lord, because Krsna now grants direct access to the spiritual world.

At this stage, absorption in Radha’s and Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes (astakaliya-lila) concentrates on those services each individual devotee eternally renders to the divine couple.

This emphasis on participation in specific services is a natural part of awakening to the eleven defining characteristics (ekadasa-bhava) of spiritual identity under the guidance of a Vraja-vasi.

The eleven characteristics are name, age, form, attire, group, specific instructions, service, excellence, mood, residence, and relationship to Krsna. They are awakened by help from our Vraja-vasi mentors.

By continuously chanting the holy name, one attains prema, the five bhavas combine to form rasa, and he or she, at this point of full maturity, is always absorbed in direct service to the divine couple.

Through nama-bhajana one can enjoy the ecstatic bliss of loving devotion, and when one's mission in this world is complete, the holy name will give eternal residence in Goloka (sampatti-dasa).

Although it bestows the highest benefit, nama-bhajana is the simplest path to spiritual perfection, a path that depends only upon pure faith and the company of saintly, like-minded devotees.

The goal of bhajana is a love that only pure devotees value. The hearts of all others — from karmis to jnanis — are so filled with competing desires that they cannot appreciate life’s greatest treasure.

Indeed, prana refuses to mingle with non-devotees, even with devotees who associate with non-devotees. In other words, the company one keeps determines his or her spiritual destiny.

In summary, three indispensable factors affect the success of nama-bhajana: saintly company, indifference to mundane distractions, and the presence of enthusiasm, confidence, and determination.

Furthermore, Sanatana Gosvami says that the essential devotional prerequisite for attaining the fruits of bhava, rasa, and prema is utter humility (dainya), without which the pure holy name eludes us.

Sanatana Gosvami goes on to elaborate,

**“Wise men define dainya as the state in which one always thinks oneself exceptionally incapable and low, even when endowed with all excellences.”**

He than concludes,

**“An intelligent person should carefully cultivate speech, behaviour, and thinking that fix him in utter humility, and anything that stands in the way of it he should avoid.”**

True humility is expressed by such traits as tolerance, respectfulness, and feelings of insignificance. Another important aspect of dainya is the tendency to keep one’s own spiritual attainments confidential.

If by the mercy of our spiritual masters and the Lord we realise the transcendental truths regarding devotion in practice or perfection, we should not disclose them, but rather keep them carefully hidden.

Lord Visnu once told Aditi,

**“O lady! Even if someone enquires, you should not disclose this fact to anyone \[that I will become your son\]. That which is very confidential is successful if kept secret.”**

We should be conversant with the confidential methods of worshipping the holy name, but we should not freely discuss those secrets, lest they be heard by the immature or, worse, by imitators.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu warns:

**“Mischievous rascals will degrade the intimate truths of the holy name and create a shroud of ignorance over the entire world.”**

Here the word “rascals” means sahajiyas.

The general rule is that saintly devotees humbly chant Hare Krsna with deep feeling in the mood of separation, while impostors who are actually arrogant fools claim to be constantly seeing Krsna.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission was to give sincere souls with even a minimum of piety and pure faith the opportunity to chant the inestimably valuable and matchlessly pure Hare Krsna maha-mantra.

He left the responsibility for continuing that mission to His followers, of whom the most successful was Srila Prabhupada. His Divine Grace expected us to continue to spread Mahaprabhu’s legacy worldwide.

Some foolish pseudo-Vaisnavas think that preaching will diminish their own chances for vraja-bhakti and, more specifically, service to Sri Radha, but Prabodhananda Sarasvati disproves these views.

*Yatha yatha gaura-padaravinde vindeta bhaktim krta-punya-rasih*  
*tatha tathotsarpati hrdy akasmad radha-padambhoja-sudhamsu-rasih*

**“A very fortunate person may get the mercy of Lord Caitanya.**

**“As much as one can devote his full attention to the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya, to that extent he will be able to taste the nectarean service of the lotus feet of Srimati Radharani in Vrndavana.**

**“The more one engages in the service of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu all over the world, the more one finds oneself in Vrndavana, tasting the nectar of service to Srimati Radharani.”**

Somehow, due to some meager service to Lord Caitanya’s mission, first in Montreal and now in Hungary, the faintest shadow of a taste for service to Sri Radha has awakened in this poor beggar’s heart.

Although this nectar is of the kind distributed to conditioned souls to increase their longing for full nectar (purnamrta), it still dwarfs the temptations of heaven and continually fills my mind with hope.

Living in such a land of hope, at times I ride the wonderful waves of the maha-mantra's promises, floating away on currents of pastimes, waiting and waiting until one day my aspirations become reality.

Let this chapter come to a close with a recollection of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s personal glorification of krsna-nama-sankirtana, as He recorded it for the benefit of all in His Sri Siksastaka.

Lord Caitanya writes,

**“Let there be all victory for the congregational chanting of Lord Krsna’s holy name, which cleanses the mirror of the heart and stops the miseries of the blazing fire of material existence.**

**“That chanting is the waxing moon that spreads moonlight on the white lotus of good fortune for all living entities, and it is the life and soul of the bride of all education — transcendental knowledge.**

**“The chanting of the holy name of Sri Krsna expands the blissful ocean of transcendental life and gives a cooling effect to everyone, enabling them to taste full nectar at every step.”**

Dear readers! Serve the Lords of your heart. Then you will know everything. And if you serve and chant Their names, you will gradually he submerged in the blissful ocean of that service.

*Let us conduct our lives in ways that the mahā-mantra does not take offence with us but instead graces us with its matchless opulences, the crown jewel of which is love for Rādhā-Śyāma.*

## Chapter 37 - Avoiding Offences to the Maha-mantra

Chapter thirty-six extols the glories of nama-sankirtana, particularly the glories of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, the emperor of all mantras and granter of spiritual perfection, selfless love for Krsna.

But despite nama-sankirtana's special potency to facilitate rapid spiritual advancement, obstacles — specifically offences to the holy name (aparadha) —can make such progress very difficult.

Beginners often face difficulties caused by their own mistakes, and we all would like to overcome the effects of offences and the tendency to commit them. This chapter, therefore, deals solely with this topic.

To glorify the name (nama) we need the blessings of the name’s proprietors (namani). I humbly request Radha and Syama to make my words fit for serving Them in Their form as the maha-mantra.

I beg to be freed from the reactions to my offences, which like thieves steal the treasure of my heart — love for the Lords of my life, Radha and Syama — and cast me back into the ocean of sin and suffering.

I pray, “O Nama-sankirtana! O desire tree of mellows! I cannot count how many times I have offended You by word, deed, or simply by neglect. Kindly overlook my sins and correct me from within.

“O Syamasundara! O form of mercy! When Draupadi and Gajendra were in need, You at once came to their aid. Why, then, have You not hurried to my rescue as I suffer torment after torment?

“O Radharani! As I sink deeper into the quicksand of offences, You smile and continue to dance to the sound of Krsna’s flute. Won’t You throw me Your veil as a lifeline and pull me out of this quagmire?

“O Prabhupada! Beaten by the whips of suffering, the horse of my mind runs wild upon the paths of my senses. Please steady this horse with the reins of devotion and tie it to the post of the pure name.

“O holy name of Krsna! O sacred mantra of deliverance! As I delineate the offences to You, please absolve me from committing them and empower me to call upon You with love. Nay, with rasa.”

When Sukadeva Gosvami arrived at the place where Pariksit was fasting unto death, the king begged the sage to

*“...show the way of perfection for all persons, and especially for one who is about to die.”*

Sukadeva explained that he was attracted to hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam, even though he was already liberated, and he urged the king to do the same and thus achieve unflinching faith in the Lord.

The Gosvami then extolled nama-sankirtana as the essential message of Srimad-Bhagavatam,

*etan nirvidyamananam icchatam akuto-bhayam*  
*yoginam nrpa nirnitam barer namanukirtanam*

**“O King! Constant chanting of the holy name of the Supreme Lord Krsna after the ways of the great authorities is the doubtless and fearless way of success for all — “Including those who are free from all material desires, those who are desirous of all material enjoyment, and also those who are selfsatisfied by dint of transcendental knowledge.”**

Nama-sankirtana is known as the best friend of all because it delivers even those who have offended the Lord. Indeed, for one who chants His name with faith, Krsna forgives millions of offences.

But if we are foolish enough to offend the shelter-giving name, not only are we deprived of the blessed results of chanting but we will also inevitably fall down — *hy aparadhat pataty adhah*.

We should therefore carefully monitor our own conduct so that we can avoid offending Krsna’s names. The list of offences, said to contain ten in all, begins with criticising devotees (*sadhu-ninda*).

**\* \* \* \***

To place our hearts in the proper mood of devotion to all Vaisnavas, let us hear this prayer:

**“I offer my respectful obeisances to the devotees of the Lord. Simply by hearing the two syllables krs-na —**

**“Their bodily hairs stand up in ecstasy and they are moved to dance in ecstatic bliss. With their sandals they expertly extricate the fallen souls deeply sunk in the vast mire of repeated birth and death.”**

Markandeya Rsi once told Maharaja Bhagiratha:

**“Fools who blaspheme Vaisnavas fall into the hell called Maharaurava, along with their forefathers, where they are tormented by fearsome rurus.”**

The sage then listed six ways to offend Vaisnavas: to kill, criticise, bear malice towards, become angry with, fail to greet, or not to feel happy upon seeing a Vaisnava, especially after a time of long absence.

To these six offences Sri Suka adds a seventh: to hear criticism of a Vaisnava. And Sati-devi adds an eighth: not to leave the place, or kill the offender, or give up one’s life upon hearing such criticism.

These rules apply to all Vaisnavas, not merely advanced or highly respected ones. No Vaisnava should he neglected. All should be honoured and worshipped, but in proportion to their advancement.

The following two examples from scripture illustrate the importance of treating all Vaisnavas with respect, regardless of the individual devotee’s gender, social status, or level of spiritual advancement.

Once in Vrndavana, Rupa Gosvami was absorbed in devotional trance when a visitor arrived. After offering obeisances to the acarya, the Vaisnava sat down, eager for an audience with the Gosvami.

But Rupa was oblivious to the outside world and did not even notice the arrival of his guest. Instead, the Gosvami laughed at a humorous pastime of Krsna that he was seeing in his ecstatic trance.

Not understanding the actual situation, Rupa’s simple-hearted visitor felt hurt by the Gosvami’s neglect and laughter. Distressed, he went to Rupa’s elder brother, Sanatana Gosvami, to complain.

Meanwhile, Rupa Gosvami’s trance broke and his bliss abruptly vanished. The acarya at once understood that he had done something to lose Krsna’s grace, and so he too went to Sanatana for solace.

When Rupa and his guest met at Dvadasaditya-tila, Sanatana Gosvami brought both sides of the episode to light. The two devotees offered each other obeisances and begged forgiveness for their sins.

In this pastime the Lord used his own associate to highlight the dangers of Vaisnava aparadha. Even if a great devotee inadvertently slights a lesser Vaisnava, he will suffer punishment from Krsna.

Ghanasyama says, *ohe bhai vaisnavete sabadhana babe pranapana kari' aparadha ksamaibe*: “O brothers! Be careful in dealing with devotees. With your heart and soul, beg their forgiveness for any offence.”

The second cautionary tale took place in Radha-kunda. There, a great devotee-scholar, Rupa Kaviraja, once committed an offence to an equally exalted Vaisnavi, Krsnapriya Thakurani.

Rupa Kaviraja had attained a stage of devotional service at which he tasted mellows of love. And Krsnapriya was so elevated that she had been appointed to care for Lord Caitanya’s own Govardhana-sila.

One day, as Rupa Kaviraja was discoursing on Srimad-Bhagavatam publicly, he noticed that Krsnapriya was chanting Hare Krsna as she sat and listened to him. Thinking her inattentive, he said:

“How can you do two things at once? I am disturbed to see that while listening to Srimad-Bhagavatam you also chant.” Krsnapriya replied, “ This is my tongue’s habit. It does not impede my hearing.”

At this Rupa Kaviraja became enraged at the faultless Krsnapriya. That misguided anger lit a fire that would eventually consume the Kaviraja’s body, along with his devotional creeper. Dear devotees!

Please carefully hear the sequence of events that followed this offence to a Vaisnava. After this incident Rupa Kaviraja became contemptuous towards his guru and to the community of devotees.

He then rejected his spiritual lineage and the teachings of Rupa Gosvami. He even lost faith in the divinity of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Needless to say, he also lost the bliss he had previously relished.

Taking shelter of his contaminated intelligence, Rupa Kaviraja fabricated his own bhakti doctrine, one that went against the conclusions of the Gosvamis. In this way his offences multiplied.

Eventually the disease spread from Rupa Kaviraja’s soul to his body. After losing his lustre, beauty, and health, he was afflicted with leprosy in every limb — a testimony to his own misdeeds.

Driven out of Radha-kunda by the devotees, he fled to Bengal and then to Orissa where, after terrible physical suffering, he died, only to become a ghost who haunted offenders of Vaisnavas.

Narahari Cakravarti concludes,

**“By committing a seemingly insignificant offence unto a devotee, even the topmost Vaisnava possessed of the highest standard of love will lose that treasure.”**

Because offending Vaisnavas — especially one’s spiritual master— infuriates the Lord, and because it uproots the creeper of devotional service, it is the supreme offence (paramam aparadham).

Caitanya Mahaprabhu calls it the “mad elephant offence.” He enjoins us to fix the following warning in our minds,

*yadi vaisnava-aparadha uthe hati mata*  
*upade va chinde, tara sukhi’ yaya pata*

**“If, while cultivating the creeper of bhakti a devotee commits an offence at the feet of a Vaisnava, his offence is like a mad elephant that uproots and breaks the creeper, causing the leaves to dry up.”**

To put it most plainly, we should be respectful to everyone. If we speak or act disrespectfully towards others, we may mistakenly offend a Vaisnava in the guise of an ordinary man or woman.

This was the case with Maharaja Rahugana, who spoke harshly to the great devotee Jada Bharata, mistaking him for an ordinary palanquin bearer. Realising his mistake, the king begged pardon from the saint:

**“Although I have committed an offence by insulting you...even though I may be as strong as Lord Siva, I shall be vanquished without delay due to my offence at the lotus feet of a Vaisnava.”**

Scripture repeatedly warns us to carefully protect our hard-earned devotional creepers by fencing them in with gentle conduct and exemplary association, treating all Vaisnavas as our masters.

Now that we have been admitted into the assembly of devotees, Krsna’s names are food for our tongues and the forms of Srimati Radharani and Sri Krsna are soothing balm for our eyes.

Now that the sounds of sankirtana ornament our ears, and our feet dance upon neglected material desires, why would we risk these sublime results for the bitter taste of sadhu-ninda's forbidden fruit?

**\* \* \* \***

The second offence to hari-nama is to make a distinction between the Lord and His names, or to think that demigods like Siva and their names are equal to or independent of Krsna and His names.

We can better understand this offence through the eyes of Krsna’s revelation in the Bhagavad-gita:

**“Know that all opulent, beautiful, and glorious creations spring from but a spark of My splendour.”**

This verse is but one of innumerable scriptural statements confirming that, in all ways and at all times, the demigods are but dependent and subservient expansions of the Supreme Lord, Sri Krsna.

The Kurus once captured Krsna’s son Samba by unchivalrous means as he was eloping with Duryodhana’s daughter Laksmana. To avoid all-out war, Balarama went to Hastinapura to resolve the conflict.

But the Kurus criticised Krsna’s family, in effect criticising Krsna, and thus incited Balarama’s wrath. To punish them, Balarama began to drag their city into the Ganges as He loudly proclaimed:

**“Great demigods like Lord Brahma and Lord Siva, and even the goddess of fortune and I, are simply parts of Krsna’s spiritual identity, and we also carefully carry the dust of His lotus feet on our heads.”**

Just as a part can be neither equal to nor independent from the whole, no demigod, including the great Lord Siva, can be equal to or independent from the supreme whole, Sri Krsna.

This truth is further supported by the fact that Krsna, as the source and shelter of everything, is the origin of all names; thus even the names assigned to the demigods were originally His own.

One of Krsna’s names is Siva, for example, because Krsna is the embodiment of happiness. Just as a king invests his ministers with authority, Krsna assigned His name to the demigod of destruction.

The name of the demigod of destruction, then, is actually “Siva Dasa,” just as the name of the creator is “Brahma Dasa.” This truth is found in books like the Brahmanda, Skanda, and Brahma Puranas.

In conclusion, even though we should not equate demigods with the Lord, we should also not separate the demigods from the Lord’s opulences. The two are one and different as servants and master.

Consequently, it is equally as offensive to think that Siva and Krsna are equals as it is to think that Siva’s potency is distinct from Krsna’s. Due respect should be given to each according to their statures.

Once, on the bank of the Alakananda Ganga in Godrumadvipa, the demigods held a great festival of nama-sankirtana, chanting the names of Lord Krsna and, at times, the names of Lord Caitanya.

At one point the dancing became so surcharged with devotional mellows that the kirtana attracted Lord Visnu, who blessed the demigods not only by His presence but also by joining their revelry.

Lord Siva, who hosted the event, was so elated by this turn of events that he went mad with ecstasy, dancing alongside Lord Visnu in a way that neither the gods nor his wife had ever seen before.

While Lord Visnu and Lord Siva danced together, their common ecstasy in tasting the nectar of Krsna’s names was so powerful that it drew them into one united form called Harihara.

The left side of Harihara was the form of Lord Siva and the right side that of Lord Visnu. In this way the demigods personally witnessed that the two are actually one as master and servant.

One might say that this pastime shows the qualitative oneness of the demigods — especially Siva — and Lord Visnu, but it also shows that the two are eternally distinct, as the created and creator respectively.

Harihara is a united form of two deities. The preservation of their individual features — half Hari and half Hara — also proclaims the distinct characteristics we must always bear in mind to avoid offence.

To this day in Navadvipa there is a deity of Harihara at a place where Lord Caitanya would regularly rest. The locals call it Harihara-ksetra. Learned Vaisnavas also recognise it as Maha-Varanasi.

Equating the demigods with Krsna not only belittles the Supreme Lord, it also exaggerates the status of the demigods, thus compounding the offence to the Lord with offence to His devotees.

A graphic example of how the demigods arc offended at being equated with the Lord is found in the pastime of Lord Rama’s establishing the famous deity of Lord Siva called Ramesvara.

At the time, common people — as they do today — interpreted the name Ramesvara to mean “the Lord of Rama.” But the demigods at once objected. They said it means, “Siva, like Rama, is also the Lord.”

But both these erroneous interpretations distressed the master of destruction, Lord Siva, who personally spoke these words from his deity form (siva-linga), “Neither explanation is correct.

“The name Ramesvara means ‘He whose Lord is Rama.’” In this way, not only was the controversy over Ramesvara settled hut also the leader of the demigods gave a clear warning to one and all.

Just as we know the spiritual master to be “as good as Hari” (saksad-haritvena) without equating him with Krsna, we must also know the demigods to he as good as Hari, hut the Lord’s servants just the same.

**\* \* \* \***

The third offence to the holy name is to disrespect or disobey the spiritual master (guror avajna). This offence is a severe form of the first offence — to vilify Vaisnavas great or small, in any way.

Amongst Vaisnavas, the instructing and initiating spiritual masters are special because they are confidential servants of Krsna who have dedicated their lives to bringing conditioned souls closer to the Lord.

They have endeared themselves to Krsna by connecting their disciples to Him, especially through the holy name and other mantras, and by giving relevant instructions on how to serve the Lord.

Therefore, although we give all Vaisnavas due respect, we must give our spiritual masters special honour. We follow their orders under all circumstances, or risk bearing the results of guror avajna.

In the following deliberation on offences to the spiritual master, although Sri Guru is referred to in the singular, it should be noted that these principles apply equally to initiating and instructing gurus.

Because the spiritual master is a representative of both Krsna and the holy name, disrespecting him is the same as disrespecting Krsna or Krsna’s names. In fact, it is the same as offending all of them.

As disciples, our responsibility is to select our spiritual master with great care. It is also our duty to learn and follow the proper etiquette required to serve and worship him without committing offences.

Let us now enumerate the offenses to the spiritual master. The first is to consider the guru to be an ordinary man and thus deny that he is a manifestation of Krsna’s own potency, an empowered emissary.

In this regard Narada Muni says,

**“The spiritual master should be considered to be directly the Supreme Lord because he gives transcendental knowledge for enlightenment. Consequently —**

**“For one who maintains the material conception that the guru is an ordinary human being, everything is frustrated. His enlightenment, Vedic studies, and knowledge arc like the bathing of an elephant.”**

It is also an offence to dwell upon any defect in the spiritual master from a time before pure devotion awoke in him, or to see caste, bodily defects, nationality, or race as disqualifying him for his position.

Srila Prabhupada was fond of quoting the Padma Purana verse that begins arcye visnau, which portrays those who harbour such doubts about a Vaisnava spiritual master as “residents of hell.”

During Narottama Dasa Thakura’s lifetime, caste-conscious brahmanas criticised him because he offered initiation to those born in brahmana families although he was born of ksatriyas.

Some of these brahmanas saw the error of their ways and rectified themselves, taking shelter of Narottama. Others clung fast to their bigotry, even as the acarya was passing away, and thus they perished.

Since the guru is the medium through whom transcendental knowledge descends, it is offensive to be inattentive to him or disobedient to his orders, just as it is to be ungrateful for a gift.

Devotees sometimes argue that the order of the spiritual master is “too difficult to follow.” But scriptures say, “The order of the spiritual master must be obeyed without personal consideration.”

The book Raghu-vamsa recounts how Laksmana — for whom Rama was guru — committed Himself to His brother’s orders upon hearing how Parasurama once killed his own mother at his father’s behest.

Disloyalty to Sri Guru also includes neglecting the vows we make to the Lord, the spiritual master, and the Vaisnavas at initiation. For this we suffer for our sinful deeds as well as for breaking a covenant.

By the influence of Kali-yuga the last leg of religion, truthfulness, is fading rapidly, and even devotees accept trifling excuses as legitimate reasons to break their vows of initiation or marriage.

Lord Ramacandra taught us to reflect carefully before taking an oath; once our word is given, we should never go back on it. To fulfil His father’s promise, Lord Rama abdicated the throne of Ayodhya.

And even though the citizens were so distraught that Bharata went to His brother in the forest and urged Rama to sacrifice His vow for the greater welfare of the citizens and the state, Rama refused.

As a bastion of virtue the Lord said,

*raghukula riti sada cali ayi*  
*prana jayi para vacana na jayi*

**“The tradition of the Raghu dynasty is to forfeit one’s life before forfeiting one’s promise.”**

As Srila Prabhupada’s sincere followers, we should be so determined to keep our vows. We may wonder how to be so determined in the face of the myriad allurements of this age. Prabhupada answers:

**“It is not very difficult! But one has to practise the determination, ‘Now I have taken vow before the Deity...before the spiritual master that I’ll not have illicit sex. That is promised. How can I break it?’**

**“This is tapasya...'I have promised it. If I am gentleman, how can I break my promise?’ This is called jnana. With knowledge one has to respect. Otherwise, to become attracted, that is not unnatural.”**

The next infraction in the category of offences to Sri Guru is called maryada-vyatikrama, by which a disciple loses lifespan, opulence, fame, piety, and the blessings of the Vaisnavas.

This offence takes different forms, such as either accepting disciples while one’s spiritual master is still living or instructing others in the presence of one’s guru, without being specifically told to do so.

Although we may take instructions from Vaisnavas other than our own spiritual master, it is offensive to do so without prior permission or to neglect confirming with our guru what we have learned.

A final and most deplorable type of impertinence to Sri Guru is the attempt to instruct or correct one’s otherwise faultless pure devotee spiritual master, as Ramacandra Puri did to his own guru.

When Madhavendra Puri was at the last stage of his life he would chant Krsna’s names and at times cry out to Him in lamentation: “O my Lord Krsna! I did not get shelter at Mathura. O my Lord Krsna!”

Unable to understand his spiritual master’s exalted position, Ramacandra Puri dared advise him, “Why are you lamenting? You should now remember only Brahman. Why are you crying?”

Hearing this, Madhavendra Puri angrily rebuked his disciple, saying, “Get out, you sinful rascal! Go anywhere you like, but don’t show me your face. If I die looking at you, I shall not achieve my destination.”

Crying out to Krsna, the great saint prayed,

**“O my Lord! I could not reach You, nor could I reach Your abode, Mathura. I am dying in my unhappiness, and now this rascal has come to give me more pain.”**

Thus Ramacandra Puri’s guru rebuked him. For his offence, material desire and speculative attachment awoke within him. He became a critic of Vaisnavas and, in the end, criticised Lord Caitanya directly.

It is also an offence to fail to worship the spiritual master, worship that includes offering obeisances upon seeing him, glorifying him in a suitable manner, and offering respect to his personal belongings.

From one to another, spiritual masters may vary in spiritual potency, yet their disciples are duty bound to respect them as they would respect Lord Krsna. This is the meaning of *saksad-haritvena*.

Indra, the king of heaven, once failed to properly greet his spiritual master, Brhaspati. As a result, the demons, who had become powerful by serving their guru, Sukracarya, ousted the demigods from heaven.

The lesson is that if we offend our spiritual master, we lose not only our spiritual assets but also our material opulence. Defeated by the material energy, we are victimised by illusion once again.

As shown by Ramacandra Puri, anyone who offends his spiritual master in any way loses the protection of the holy name, again falls under the influence of the material energy, and engages in sinful life.

One of Srila Prabhupada’s Sanskrit editors serves as an example of an offender of this sort. After regularly hearing from a Radha-kunda babaji, this disciple also accepted some form of initiation from him.

Srila Prabhupada was very sorry to hear of his disciple’s disloyalty. Some time later he received a letter from the same disciple asking for blessings to attain love for Krsna. Srila Prabhupada was very angry.

Though he very rarely did, Srila Prabhupada took offence. Disclosing the fate of that disciple — and others who offend Sri Guru — he said, “I bless him to not get love for Krsna for a hundred thousand births.”

What should we do if we have either intentionally or inadvertently offended Sri Guru? Are we, too, condemned for many births, or is there hope for our redemption? To paraphrase the Skanda Purana:

**“Just as the earth is the only support for those who lose their footing and fall, the spiritual master remains the only shelter for those who offend him and lose their way in Krsna consciousness.”**

In conclusion, if one has offended his guru in some way, he should admit the offence, repent, and beg forgiveness. Then, by divine grace he will be restored to a healthy state of spiritual life.

But if one fails to make amends for one’s of fences — as we daily recite them together—even meticulous service to Krsna will be futile, *yasya prasadad bhagavat-prasado yasyaprasadan na gatih kuto'pi*.

**\* \* \* \***

The fourth offence is to “blaspheme the Vedic literature” (sruti-sastra-nindanam). Srila Prabhupada’s translation expands this definition to include “literature in pursuance of the Vedic version.”

The Vedic scriptures, such as the four Vedas and eighteen Puranas, are called apauruseya, meaning they have no human origin. They emanate directly from the breathing of the Supreme Lord.

Since the Vedic literature is not subject to human defects, its teachings are indisputable truth. Still, to be properly understood such truth must be heard from self-realised souls in disciplic succession.

Although the Vedic library contains a vast array of laws, rituals, histories, sacrifices, and spiritual practices and their goals, when their essential message is distilled, ten fundamental principles emerge.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu taught His followers these ten truths (dasa- mula-tattva) : (1) The Vedas are the source of perfect knowledge and the ultimate evidence of that which is to be known.

(2) Sri Krsna is the Supreme Absolute Truth, (3) He possesses unlimited and multifarious potencies, and (4) He is the ocean of mellows. (5) The living entities are His separated parts and parcels.

Because of their marginal nature, the living entities (6) in their conditioned state are under the influence of matter, and (7) in their liberated state, free from matter, they are sheltered by divine potency.

The living entities (8) are simultaneously different from and one with Krsna. (9) They may elevate themselves to the liberated state by sadhana-bhakti and (10) attain the goal of life — pure love for Krsna.

Inherent in these ten truths is the fact that offenceless chanting of the maha-mantra easily and quickly gives conditioned living entities the perfection their liberated counterparts possess — krsna-prema.

Krsna-dvaipayana Vyasa compiled the original Vedas, and Vaisnavas who followed him composed “literature in pursuance of the Vedic version,” or books embodying these same ten essential Vedic truths.

The Padma Purana uses the same word, ninda (“blasphemy”), for both the first and fourth offences to the holy name. As it does for sadhu-ninda, it also describes several ways to offend the sacred scriptures.

In the fields of Indology, Sanskrit, and Asian studies, most scholars reject the self-declared, absolute authority of the Vedas. They mislead their students by dismissing the histories in the Vedas as “mythology.”

Such scholars who reject the Vedas — as do the atheist Carvaka Muni and Buddhists — are also offenders of the Vedas and, consequently, Krsna’s holy name, the Vedas' most valuable treasure.

In the early 1970’s, as I was searching through India’s gurus and sacred texts for the answers to life, I attended a lecture in Boulder, Colorado, given by the alleged child prodigy Guru Maharaj Ji.

In his talk he made this statement: “What Krsna spoke five thousand years ago is no longer relevant in this modern age. We need a new way of enlightenment, and that is what I have come to give.”

I didn’t know much about the Bhagavad-gita at the time, but I had read enough to feel that what I was hearing was not right. It wasn’t! Guru Maharaj Ji was offending the most sacred of all scriptures.

Other pseudo-spiritualists seem to accept the eternality of the Vedas, but actually reject their teachings and conclusion, krsnas tu bhagavan svayam. Their eclectic approach is also contemptuous.

These sages erroneously promote subsidiary teachings as the final Vedic conclusion, and in this way they cover Krsna’s supremacy. Jaimini, for example, promoted fruitive rituals as life’s goal.

The atheist Kapila denied God’s existence and advocated atheistic metaphysics as the way to self-realisation. Gautama taught that logic was the path to liberation, which to him was devoid of consciousness.

But if deviant philosophers are to be graded according to their degree of insolence, then Mayavadis headed by Sankaracarya, Astavakra, Dattatreya, and Gaudapada would certainly top the list.

Their distortions of the Vedas are the worst. They reinterpret the statements of the Vedas so as to disembody and depersonalise Krsna, the eternally youthful cowherd and Supreme Personality of Godhead.

The books of our acaryas are also Vedas. To criticise them — as the scholar Vallabha did passages of Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu and Sridhara Svami’s commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam — is also an offence.

Further examples of sastra-nindanam are found in the ignorant critiques of Srila Prabhupada’s purports as short-sighted or overly conservative interpretations of classical Vedic texts.

Even today, just a few decades after Srila Prabhupada’s departure, the offence of qualifying the words of our scriptures and, even worse, of Srila Prabhupada’s purports, has reared its head in iskcon.

For example, some devotees take exception to apparently sexist passages in Srimad-Bhagavatam and in Srila Prabhupada’s purports, proposing to edit the passages out for the sake of political correctness.

Srila Prabhupada cites a graphic example of how Krsna once reacted to an attempt to alter sastra: the history of Arjunacarya that comes to us through Yamunacarya’s line of succession.

Yamunacarya’s follower Arjunacarya, while writing a commentary on the Bhagavad-gita, came across a verse that made him doubt whether one of Krsna’s statements was literally true. The verse read:

**“But those who always worship Me with exclusive devotion, meditating on My transcendental form — to them I carry \[vahamy aham\] what they lack, and I preserve what they have.”**

The acarya doubted that “I carry” (vahamy aham) actually meant that Krsna personally provided His devotees’ needs. He thought, “It must mean ‘I provide for My devotees through someone else.’”

Convinced that he was correct, Arjunacarya crossed out the word vahamy and replaced it with another, changing the meaning to “I have it done.” The sage then walked to the river for his midday bath.

While Arjunacarya was absent, two beautiful boys came to his home carrying a large quantity of food on their backs. When the acarya’s wife asked where the food came from, one of the boys replied:

“Your husband instructed us to bring it.” But the brahmani doubted the boys’ words because it was unlike her husband to demand from young boys such strenuous duties as carrying heavy weights.

“Not only that,” said the younger of the two, “he also beat Me with a stick.” Turning around, He showed her the lash marks on His back. “What has my husband done?” thought Arjunacarya’s wife.

She then comforted the boys, sat Them down, and quickly prepared a meal for Them. Soon after the boys had left, Arjunacarya returned home to an unusually cold reception from his wife.

When she explained the reason for her anger, the acarya pleaded ignorance of the entire incident. But as soon as his wife described the boys, Arjunacarya at once understood what had happened.

Arjunacarya said,

**“To expose my misinterpretation, Krsna personally brought enough food to fill my storehouse. And the welts on His back were evidence of the pain I caused Him by changing His words.”**

Srila Prabhupada said,

**“Because I wanted that God docs not deliver, so He has delivered these goods, and because I cut these alphabets that He does not give personally, so He has shown that beating mark.”**

Srila Prabhupada told this pastime to show us that to disbelieve scriptural statements and to wrongly qualify them is a serious offence against the Lord, from whom the teachings of scripture come.

Finally, scriptures outside the Vedic canon, like the Koran or Bible, should also be given due respect because they promote a concept of God and a life of piety by which people can please Him.

Such scriptures may not directly present the Vedic conclusion, but their teachings make the sinful people in this Age of Kali more qualified to accept the Vedic way of life as taught by Krsna.

The acceptance of Krsna consciousness by Srila Prabhupada’s followers, for example, was often a natural and spontaneous continuation of their Judaeo-Christian upbringing.

In essence, if we follow Krsna’s advice and always speak words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and that do not agitate others, then we will automatically avoid offending the Vedic literature.

If we regularly recite texts like the Bhagavad-gita, we will naturally come to love them, and if we mistakenly offend these sacred works, we should confess and make amends by glorifying them publicly.

Arguably, the best remedy for blaspheming the Vedas is to personally distribute transcendental literature, a practice Srila Prabhupada established as the inviolable basis of his mission.

The Vedic literature describes the stepwise cultivation of nama-sankirtana that leads us to eternal life with Krsna. One should therefore never fault the Vedas and thereby displease the holy name.

**\* \* \* \***

Now let us examine topics related to the offence of blaspheming scriptures, topics that at first might not appear directly related but under scrutiny will be seen to be in the same category of offence.

Srila Prabhupada established transcendental literature as the basis of the Krsna consciousness movement. We should, therefore, be wary of misconduct that undermines our very foundation.

Books like the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam authenticate our spiritual tradition and its practices. The worldwide distribution of such books is the lifeblood of Srila Prabhupada’s mission.

We must always be alert not to mistreat our scriptures in ways that would weaken our spiritual lives, cast aspersions on the credibility of our movement, and corrupt our preaching efforts.

Such malpractices begin with mistreating our scriptures’ printed text. We should treat these books with the same care and attention with which we serve and worship the Deity of Lord Krsna.

Srila Prabhupada speaks of how Sikhs revere and worship their sacred text Guru Granth Sahib, and he encourages us to deal just as respectfully towards the Bhagavad-gita and our other scriptures.

Krsna’s song of absolute wisdom is identical with Him. Indeed, Lord Visnu once explained to Laksmi how the eighteen chapters of the Gita constitute the Lord’s limbs, from His head to His feet.

The Bhagavad-gita should therefore always he kept in a clean, sacred place, handled with clean hands, and read with the utmost reverence. In other words, it should be given the same respect as a Deity.

Or as Suta Gosvami says,

**“Therefore, because it is the inaugurator of all religious wisdom and the spotless essence of all scriptures, the Gita should he offered all respects at all times and in all places.”**

The Padma Purana also describes that before one reads the Srimad-Bhagavatam one should offer full arati, obeisances, and prayers. The same applies to all Vedic scriptures and books that elucidate them.

Similarly, Srila Prabhupada says,

**“India, when we speak on the Bhagavad-gita, or on the Srimad-Bhagavatam, we worship regularly with flower, with other paraphernalia required for worshipping.”**

Since Srila Prabhupada did not personally follow this ceremonial worship, we are not obliged to do so. Yet we should retain the spirit of such worship by offering due feelings of respect before giving class.

If we neglect to offer due respect and worship to sacred scriptures, then we also offend the holy names glorified therein, because the scriptures ultimately inspire us to perform nama-sankirtana.

It is also disrespectful to neglect the regular study of sacred texts, especially those books Vyasadeva compiled that were translated and commented upon by Srila Prabhupada for the benefit of his followers.

Even though we may enthusiastically sell Srila Prabhupada’s books, if we do not know and apply the wisdom they impart, then we show disrespect to those transcendental texts and their authors as well.

Suta Gosvami entreats us to serve Srimad-Bhagavatam by regular study (nityam bhagavata-sevaya).And with even stronger language he condemns those who fail to read the Bhagavad-gita:

**“There is no one more fallen than the person who fails to study and learn the Bhagavad-gita. Condemned are all his undertakings, reputation, worship, charity, and good qualities.”**

Srila Prabhupada once voiced displeasure by noting that although he took so much trouble to stay up late every night to translate and comment on the scriptures, we did not take the time to read them.

And even when devotees were enthusiastic to distribute Srila Prabhupada’s books, when he noticed that many distributors did not read them, His Divine Grace publicly commented, “What is the use!”

Srila Prabhupada repeatedly instructs us:

**“So I am requesting all of my students to read my books very seriously every day without fail. In this way, if your mind becomes absorbed —**

**“At least one or two hours daily in the transcendental subject matter of Srimad-Bhagavatam, Bhagavad-gita, and other books, then very easily you will make your advancement in Krsna consciousness.”**

Another offence — one that is quite prevalent in this “information age” in which nearly anything can be easily and instantly accessed — is to peruse scriptures that we have little or no qualification to grasp.

Scriptures and their commentators often delimit the qualifications of the audience for whom a book is written. Srimad-Bhagavatam, for example, says that it is intended for the pure in heart.

Krsna says that the confidential knowledge of the Bhagavad-gita should only be explained to those who are austere, devoted, practically engaged in active service, and free of envy towards Him.

Educators know this fundamental principle of learning when classifying students. Pupils are not taught subjects that they have no capacity to understand. The same holds true for revealed scriptures.

Just as a young child cannot be taught nuclear physics, a neophyte devotee should not delve into the elevated philosophy of the Vedanta- sutra or hear Krsna’s intimate pastimes in Gita-govinda.

Such premature attempts to study elevated scriptures above one's adhikara will lead to confusion, arrogance, and deviation from the path of pure devotion chalked out by our acaryas. Krsna thus says:

**“It is firmly declared that the steady adherence of transcendentalists to their respective spiritual positions constitutes real piety and that sin occurs when a transcendentalist neglects his prescribed duty.”**

The next affront to the works of our acaryas is the notion that iskcon has distributed sufficient numbers of books, or that book distribution is an outdated preaching strategy, or that it is ineffective.

Srila Prabhupada established books as the basis of his Krsna consciousness movement. Never, not even in his final days, did he even hint that distribution of scripture would ever be outdated.

Just the opposite! Srila Prabhupada said that we could know him by reading his books and that he would continue to live in his books. His enthusiasm for mass distribution of his books is common knowledge.

What’s more, His Divine Grace repeatedly stressed that we measure the success of our preaching by the success of book distribution. To that effect he wrote the following to a leading member of the GBC:

**“So distribution of literature is our real preaching. Now if you cannot handle the matter nicely, that is your fault. But the success of your preaching will be substantiated by how many books are sold.”**

No doubt we need to develop outreach programs to cultivate those who have received books. But such programs should be in addition to not a replacement for book distribution, which is iskcon’s basis.

**\* \* \* \***

Another offence to sastra is to forbid devotees from reading books other than those by Srila Prabhupada, including the books of the previous acaryas, or those written by Srila Prabhupada’s followers.

Certainly Srila Prabhupada’s books arc sufficient for devotees to attain perfection, and devotees with little time to read will do best to concentrate on the four main books of His Divine Grace.

But that does not preclude those devotees who have the time, interest, and qualification to read other books from doing so. Such extreme conservative protectionism is wrong-headed.

About our previous acaryas’ books, Srila Prabhupada clarified his position long ago. The following excerpt comes from a conversation focused on the argument over whether they should be read or not.

Disciple: “I thought you said that we should not read the previous acaryas’ books.”Prabhupada: “No, you should read.”Disciple: “We should?”Prabhupada: “It is misunderstanding \[that we should not\].”

And regarding future publications, Srila Prabhupada made it clear that he expected all his followers, especially the sannyasis, to go on publishing books. In fact, he called publishing our “family business.”

To forbid devotees from reading the books of previous acaryas and of current devotee authors is to obstruct the ongoing glorification of Krsna (sankirtana), which is the life-breath of every true Vaisnava.

Indeed, hearing Krsna’s teachings and pastimes protects us from material allurements. Why should we give it up? As Sri Sankaracarya once wrote,

**“May Lord Madhava’s pastimes —**

**“Which bring sense-pleasure stronger than that experienced by hedonists, liberation more real than that felt by yogis, and bliss more intense than that tasted by expert drinkers of nectar, protect you.”**

We should encourage one another to hear scriptures we are qualified to hear, but we should not read books that have not been authorised by our spiritual masters; otherwise, we risk another type of offence.

The number of unauthorised Vedic texts, or books posing to be Vedic, is extensive. Many original texts are either poorly translated, are not supported by a parampara, or have been interpolated.

To discriminate between authorised and anomalous texts requires realised spiritual guidance, for there are as many excuses for such deviant literature as there are types of pseudo-Vaisnava cults.

One example of a spurious edition of an otherwise authentic text is given in a letter written by Srila Prabhupada in early 1968 in which His Divine Grace instructs his followers not to read the bogus book.

Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“I have seen one copy of Narada-pancaratra sent here from San Francisco, and it is not good. Please stop circulation of this book, which is not authorised.”**

Even though Srila Prabhupada instructed his followers not to read Gaudiya Matha publications printed after his spiritual master’s disappearance, he validated books written before that time:

**“I am glad to learn that Donald has purchased Professor Sanyal’s book, Krsna Caitanya. The late N. K. Sanyal was my godbrother, and his book Krsna Caitanya is approved and authoritative.”**

There are many examples of books whose philosophical conclusions fall outside of or are in conflict with those of authentic disciplic successions, especially our own Gaudiya Vaisnava sampradaya.

For example, Srila Prabhupada explained that Sri Rama-carita-manasa was “not very authorised” because its author, Tulasi Dasa, was not a pure Vaisnava, and his parampara was tainted with Mayavada.

And in the introduction to his commentary on Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura speaks about contemporary but fraudulent biographies of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

In this regard, Sri Caitanya-caritamrta gives the general principle to bear in mind,

*bahu-sastre bahu-vakye citte bhrama haya sadhya-sadhana srestha na haya niscaya*

**“If one becomes a bookworm —**

**“Reading many books and scriptures and hearing many commentaries and the instructions of many men, this will produce doubt within his heart. One cannot in this way ascertain the real goal of life.”**

In addition to the above transgressions, yet another offence is to manipulate the scriptures in ways that suit one’s whims or preconceived ideologies. A few examples follow.

Some pseudo-devotees extract one part of scripture and leave another part aside. For example, to support their desire to freely mix with women, they highlight Krsna’s rasa dance but ignore His divinity.

Others — eclectics like Emperor Akbar — gather doctrines and practices from different texts and combine them to create what they think is a synthesis of all scriptures but what is in reality a sham.

Mayavadis are not only insolent in their ideologies but also in the method by which they arrive at them, which is to concoct indirect interpretations of direct statements regarding the personality of God.

Sometimes we dwell on topics — such as the origin of the jiva — that even scriptures do not dwell upon. At such times we exhibit the defect Srila Prabhupada referred to as over-intelligence.

It is also an offence to fault an acarya — scripture’s spokesperson — for making comments that appear contradictory, for instance that apani-pado means “God has spiritual hands and feet.”

In cases such as these, scriptures sometimes speak in esoteric terms. When acaryas describe a text’s underlying intent, their commentaries may thus appear to conflict with the scriptures’ direct meanings.

The last offence I will deal with in this section is to think that one has surpassed the previous acaryas, just as Vallabhacarya thought he had surpassed Sridhara Svami’s commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu received Vallabhacarya's request to hear his commentary, the Lord smilingly replied, “One who does not accept the svami \[husband\] as an authority I consider a prostitute.”

In conclusion, anyone who rejects the authority of the scriptures — whether those scriptures are in written form or delivered verbally from the mouths of self-realised souls — offends the holy name.

This is not only because chanting the holy name is the goal to which the Vedic literature directs us but also because the Hare Krsna maha-mantra is itself the condensed form of all holy scriptures.

To warn us of the folly of sruti-sastra-nindanam and of the even greater folly of refusing to atone for such a sin, Suta Gosvami gives offenders a glimpse of the punishment that awaits them:

**“The fool who, inflated with egotism, insults the purport of the Gita, must remain in boiling oil in the hell known as Kumbhipaka up to the time of annihilation at the end of that millennium.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Dear reader! Before I conclude this topic please hear a passage from Teachings of Lord Caitanya, a passage that struck me the first time I read it as a new devotee, due to its beauty, richness, and purity.

As I read this excerpt for the first time and felt the emotions it stirred in me, I thought, “This is not earthly literature, and Srila Prabhupada is no ordinary author. They are both emissaries of Krsna.”

That conviction was instrumental in convincing me to give myself to Srila Prabhupada’s mission. Now I hope that my pen will similarly inspire someone to accept Srila Prabhupada’s divine authority.

Lord Caitanya concludes His teachings to Sanatana Gosvami on “The Opulences of Krsna” in this excerpt:

**“The manifestation of His internal potency is not even exhibited in the kingdom of God —**

**“Or on the planets of Vaikuntha, but He does exhibit that internal potency within the universe when, through His inconceivable mercy, He descends from His personal abode.”**

Lord Sri Krsna is so wonderful and attractive that He Himself becomes attracted by His own beauty, and this is proof that He is full of all inconceivable potencies.

**“As far as Krsna’s ornaments are concerned, when they decorate His body it appears that they do not beautify Him, but the ornaments themselves become beautiful simply by being on His body.**

**“When He stands in a thrice-curved way, He attracts all living entities, including the demigods. Indeed, He even attracts the Narayana form which presides in each and every Vaikuntha planet.”**

The excerpt continues in “The Beauty of Krsna,” which is the following chapter:

“Krsna is known as Madana-mohana because He conquers the mind of Cupid. He is also known as Madana-mohana —

“Due to His accepting the devotional service of the damsels of Vraja and rendering favours unto them. After conquering Cupid’s pride, the Lord engages in the rasa dance as the new Cupid.

“He is also known as Madana-mohana because of His ability to conquer the minds of women with His five arrows called form, taste, smell, sound, and touch.

“The pearls of the necklace which hangs about the neck of Lord Krsna are as white as ducks, and the peacock feather which decorates Krsna’s head is coloured like a rainbow.

“His yellow garment is like lightning in the sky, and Krsna Himself is like the newly arrived clouds. The gopis are like bells on His feet, and when the cloud pours rain on the grains in the field —

“It appears that Krsna is nourishing the hearts of the gopis by calling down His pastime rain of mercy. Indeed, ducks fly in the sky during the rainy season, and rainbows can also be seen at that time.

“Krsna freely moves amongst His friends as a cowherd boy in Vrndavana, and when He plays His flute, all living creatures, mobile and immobile, become overwhelmed with ecstasy.

“They quiver, and tears flow from their eyes. Of His various opulences, conjugal love is the summit. He is the master of all riches, all strength, all fame, all beauty, all knowledge, and all renunciation.

“And out of these, His perfect beauty is His conjugal attraction. The form of Krsna, the conjugal beauty, is eternally existent in Krsna alone, whereas His other opulences are present in His Narayana form.

“When Lord Caitanya described the superexcellence of Krsna’s conjugal attraction, He felt transcendental ecstasy, and, catching the hands of Sanatana Gosvami, He began to proclaim how fortunate —

“The damsels of Vraja were, reciting a verse from Srimad-Bhagavatam,

*gopyas tapah kim acaran yad amusya rupam lavanya-saram asamordhvam ananya-siddham*  
*drgbhih pibanty anusavabhinavam — durapam ekanta-dhama yasasah sriya aisvarasya*

**‘What great penance and austerities the damsels of Vrndavana must have undergone, for they are able to drink the nectar of Krsna, who is all beauty -**

**All strength, all riches, all fame, and whose bodily lustre is the centre of all beauty.’**

The body of Krsna, the ocean of the eternal beauty of youth, can be seen to move in waves of beauty \[taranga—lavanya-sara\].

“There is a whirlwind at the sound of His flute. And those waves and that whirlwind make the hearts of the gopis flutter like dry leaves on trees, and when those leaves fall down at Krsna’s lotus feet —

“They can never rise up again. There is no beauty to compare with Krsna’s, for no one possesses beauty greater than or equal to His. Since He is the origin of all incarnations, including the form of Narayana —

“The goddess of fortune, who is a constant companion of Narayana, gives up Narayana’s association and engages herself in penance in order to gain the association of Sri Krsna.

“Such is the greatness of the superexcellent beauty of Sri Krsna, the everlasting mine of all beauty. It is from that beauty that all beautiful things emanate.

“The attitude of the gopis is like a mirror upon which the reflection of Krsna’s beauty develops at every moment. Both Krsna and the gopis increase their transcendental beauty at every moment —

“And there is always transcendental competition between them. No one can appreciate the beauty of Krsna by properly discharging his occupational duty, or by austerities, mystic yoga, or by prayers.

“Only those who are on the transcendental platform of love of God, who out of love engage in devotional service, can appreciate the transcendental beauty of Krsna.

“Such beauty is the essence of all opulences and is only appreciated in Goloka Vrndavana and nowhere else. In the form of Narayana the beauties of mercy, fame, etc., are all established by Krsna —

“But Krsna’s gentleness and magnanimity do not exist in Narayana. They are found only in Krsna. Lord Caitanya, greatly relishing all the verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam which He was explaining to Sanatana —

“Quoted another verse,

*yasyananam makara-kundala-caru-karna-bhrajat-kapola-subhagam savilasa-hasam*  
*nityotsavam na tatrpur drsibhih pibantyo naryo naras ca muditah kupita nimes ca*

“The gopis used to relish the beauty of Krsna as a ceremony of perpetual enjoyment. They enjoyed the beautiful face of Krsna, His beautiful ears with earrings, His broad forehead, and His smile.

“‘And when enjoying this sight of Krsna’s beauty, they used to criticise the creator Brahma for causing their vision of Krsna to he momentarily impeded by the blinking of their eyelids.’

“The Vedic hymn known as Kama-gayatri describes the face of Krsna as the king of all moons. In metaphorical language, there are many different moons, but they are all one in Krsna.

“There is the moon of His mouth, the moon of His cheeks, the moon-spots of sandalwood pulp on His body, the moons of the fingertips of His hands, and the moons of the tips of His toes.

“In this way there are twenty-four and a half moons and Krsna is the central figure of all of them. The dancing movement of Krsna’s earrings, eyes, and eyebrows is very attractive to the damsels of Vraja.

“Activities in devotional service increase the sense of devotional service. What else is there for two eyes to see beyond the face of the Supreme Lord, Sri Krsna?

“Since one cannot adequately sec Krsna with only two eyes, one feels incapable and thus becomes bereaved. Such bereavement is slightly reduced when one criticises the creative power of the creator.

“The unsatiated seer of Krsna’s face nonetheless laments: ‘I do not have thousands of eyes, hut only two, and these arc disturbed by the movements of my eyelids.

“‘Therefore it is to he understood that the creator of this body is not very intelligent. He is not conversant in the art of ecstasy but is simply a prosaic creator.

“‘He does not know how to arrange things properly so one can see only Sri Krsna.’ The gopis’ minds arc always engaged in relishing the sweetness of Krsna’s body.

“He is the ocean of beauty, and His beautiful face and smile and the lustre of His body are all-attractive to the minds of the gopis. In the Krsna-karnamrta, His face, smile —

“And bodily lustre have been described as sweet, sweeter, and sweetest. When there are three kinds of contamination in the bodily constitution, convulsions take place.

“Similarly, a perfect devotee of Krsna experiences convulsion when he is overwhelmed by seeing the beauty of Krsna’s body, face, and smile. Before Krsna’s beauty, the devotee sometimes stays —

“Immersed in this ocean of transcendental convulsions without receiving treatment, just as a patient suffering ordinary convulsions may be prevented by a physician from receiving a drink of water.

“The devotee increasingly feels the absence of Krsna, for without Him one cannot drink the nectar of His beauty. When the transcendental sound of Krsna’s flute is heard —

“The devotee’s anxiety to continue to hear that flute enables him to penetrate the covering of the material world and enter into the spiritual sky where the transcendental sound of the flute —

“Enters into the ears of the followers of the gopis. The sound of Krsna’s flute always resides within the ears of the gopis and increases their ecstasy.

“When it is heard, no other sound can enter into their ears, and amongst their family they are not able to reply to questions properly, for all these beautiful sounds arc vibrating in their ears.

“Thus Lord Caitanya explained the transcendental constitution of Krsna, His expansions, His bodily lustre, and everything connected with Him.”

In short, Lord Caitanya explained to Sanatana Gosvami the process by which one can approach Krsna. The verdict of all Vedic literature is that the only process, said Caitanya Mahaprabhu, is devotional service to Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

The fifth offence is to consider the glories of the holy name — propounded by self-realised acaryas and recorded in authoritative scriptures — to be imaginary or exaggerated praise (artha-vadah).

It is true, a portion of the Vedas offers exaggerated praise of fruitive sacrifice and philosophical speculation in order to awaken spiritual activity in those persons addicted to gratifying their senses.

No such exaggeration exists, however, in the glorification of nama-sankirtana. The Jaimini-samhita says,

*sruti-smrti-puranesu nama-mahatmya-vacisu*  
*ye ’rtha-vada iti bruyur na tesam niraya-ksayah*

**“Persons who claim that the glories of the holy name described in the sruti-smrti and Puranas are exaggerations live always in hell.”**

But because karmis and jnanis are used to some inflated claims in sastra —

They assume that glorification of the holy name is also exaggeration intended to create a taste for nama-sankirtana. Speculation such as this is nothing short of blasphemy against the holy name.

A certain materialistic speculator once decried the glories of the holy name and suffered the effects of that offence. His folly is recounted in the Caitanya-caritamrta's glorification of Haridasa Thakura.

One day in the Bengali village of Candapura, a group of gentlemen were discussing the glories of Krsna’s holy names. Some said chanting frees one of sinful reactions, others insisted that it gives liberation.

But the great authority of hari-nama, Haridasa Thakura, proposed that these boons were only incidental to the pre-eminent result of offenceless chanting — to awaken ecstatic love for Krsna.

To show that liberation was a mere by-product of chanting the holy name, Haridasa quoted this verse:

**“As the rising sun immediately dissipates all the world’s darkness, which is deep like an ocean—**

**“So the holy name of the Lord, if chanted once without offence, dissipates all the reactions of a living being’s sinful life. All glories to that holy name of the Lord, which is auspicious for the entire world.”**

Haridasa explained that liberation is a trivial result of the slightest glimpse of offenceless chanting (namabhasa), and this disturbed a local scholar named Gopala Cakravarti who became extremely angry.

He considered the verse Haridasa had quoted to be exaggeration and Haridasa’s explanation to be mere sentiment. Gopala Cakravarti said, “Dear Sirs! Just hear the conclusion of this emotional devotee.

“After many millions of births, when one is complete in knowledge, one still may not attain liberation, yet this man says that one may attain it simply by awakening a glimpse of the pure holy name.”

Haridasa then cited another verse to show that chanting awards liberation: “O master of the universe! Since I have directly seen You, my transcendental bliss has taken the shape of a great ocean.

“O my Lord! Being situated in that ocean, I now realise all other so-called happiness, even the bliss of liberation (brahmananda) to be like the water contained in the hoofprint of a calf.”

Again Gopala Cakravarti dismissed this reference as exaggeration and challenged Haridasa, “If namabhasa does not give liberation, then make no mistake — I shall cut off your nose!”

Haridasa Thakura accepted the challenge in a humble mood, but the others present, outraged by Gopala Cakravarti’s offence to the holy name and to the name’s great devotee, expelled the offender.

It is said that within three days Gopala Cakravarti contracted leprosy and his beautiful bodily features quickly melted away. From this we can learn the danger of belittling the holy name or its servants.

Like Gopala Cakravarti, ritualistic caste-conscious brahmanas do not believe scripture when it states that low-born devotees who chant the holy names are purer than vipras such as themselves. For example:

“To say nothing of the spiritual advancement of persons who see the Supreme Person face-to-face, even a person born in a family of dog" eaters immediately becomes eligible to perform Vedic sacrifices —

“If he once utters the holy name of the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna or chants about Him, hears about His pastimes, offers Him obeisances, or even remembers Him.”

This statement is like a pinprick to smarta-brahmanas, who offend the holy name by insisting that the verse means the chanting of dogeaters begins the process of purification, nothing more.

Sridhara Svami refutes this misinterpretation, however, by pointing out that the word sadyah (“immediately”) in this verse means that the holy name at once fully purifies the offenceless chanter’s heart.

To stress this point the acarya says, anena pujyatvam laksyate: “By the quality of their chanting, devotees become worshipable.” In other words, the power of the name elevates devotees to twice-born status.

Any person is a great offender who thinks — out of envy, malice, or ignorance — that the glories of the holy name are exaggerated and thus tries to qualify scriptural statements that extol those glories.

The Kurma Purana says, “Enmity to one’s guru is a million times worse than enmity to the Lord, but to contradict scriptural wisdom \[that praises Krsna’s names\] is atheism a million times worse still.”

In conclusion, I recall a time I spoke with one of Guru Maharaj Ji’s “saints” at a program in Montreal. In the course of our conversation I asked him about chanting Hare Krsna.

His answer went something like this: “How can anyone attain perfection just by repeating some words?” But by then I had already begun to chant Hare Krsna and to taste the benefits of hari-nama.

Instinctively I knew that to minimise the power of nama-sankirtana was wrong, and that any guru who would do so must also be wrong. So I scratched Guru Maharaj Ji off my list of potential saviours.

**\* \* \* \***

The sixth offence against the maha-mantra is to imagine or speculatively interpret the meaning of the holy name or the potency of the chanting to give the goal it promises (hari-namni kalpanam).

Caitanya Mahaprabhu says that nama-sankirtana purifies the heart of all bad habits, giving us not only relief from material suffering but also a taste of sublime happiness through contact with the Lord.

But empiricists want to explain everything in terms of material cause and effect, so scientists search for bio-chemical or psychological reasons for the relief and joy devotees feel from chanting.

Such explanations are improper, as arc attempts to interpret the maha-mantra in any way or for any purpose other than that presented by revealed scriptures and our predecessor acaryas.

Some tantrics, for example, say that by using a krsna-yantra, purchased for only one hundred and fifty dollars, chanters of the maha-mantra can acquire the same charm that attracts everyone to Krsna.

Unfortunately, even gross materialists have heard of Krsna’s dealings with the gopis. And because they have no faith in the Lord’s divinity, their only interest is to imitate Him for their own sensual enjoyment.

Since the word krsna means “all attractive,” the tantrics say that a krsna-yantra can help the chanter extract charisma from the name and thus dramatically increase his ability to attract the opposite sex.

Other equally contemptuous people say that krsna means “dark,” and because darkness connotes mystery, they can unveil the as yet unknown mysteries of the universe by chanting the holy names.

In this way they claim to be masters of the esoteric enchantments of darkness and in yet another way attempt to enrich themselves and exercise power over others in pursuit of unrelenting selfishness.

To concoct these sorts of so-called meanings of the maha-mantra is insolent, not only because they malign the holy name but also because they mislead gullible people away from the truth.

As Sri Isopanisad says,

**“Those who engage in the culture of nescient activities shall enter into the darkest region of ignorance. Worse still are those engaged in the culture of so-called knowledge.”**

When our acaryas speak of entering into the transcendental realm of Vraja, full of desire trees and surabhi cows, by the power of Krsna’s holy names, they are not promoting a form of self-hypnosis.

When they speak of serving, by the maha-mantra's grace, in their eternal forms as maidservants in Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes, they are not expressing some form of latent transsexuality.

Genuine Vaisnavas who admit to tasting loving ecstasies in meditative trance partake of a reality incomprehensible to empiricists, who evaluate all of it as the false rapture of escapists.

Just as it is offensive to relegate to mere psychological phenomena the transcendental symptoms of chanting Krsna’s names, it is offensive to dismiss as sahajiyaism the encounters of sincere practitioners.

Too often neophytes, without knowing the truth of the matter, are quick to denigrate the spiritual encounters of other Vaisnavas as sahajiyaism or hallucinations brought about by sentimentalism.

While only liberated devotees can lay claim to factual transcendental encounters, practitioners may have strong impressions — albeit materially tainted — of Krsna’s names, forms, qualities, and pastimes.

The taste we get from devotional service in practice is not illusion. It may not be full in spiritual maturity, but the tangible delight it gives keeps us far from Maya’s enticements. As confirmed by Isvara Puri:

**“Let the twice-born enter the fearless kingdom of yoga, Vedic study, and solitary meditation in the forest. Let them become liberated in that way. As for us, we will spend hundreds of thousands of births —**

**“Chanting the holy name of Lord Krsna, whose splendid dark complexion and yellow garments are like a host of blue lotus flowers blooming in a grove of yellow-flower-bearing kadamba trees.”**

Of course, it is improper to consider perceptions in the conditioned state equal to transcendental encounters of liberated souls; still, we should also not discard — or be told to discard — them as illusion.

As a devotee chants Jaya Radha-Madhava, for example, he may think of Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes as depicted by the wonderful phrases Thakura Bhaktivinoda chose to include in his beautiful song.

While singing the words yamuna-tira-vana-cari he may envisage Radha and Krsna walking together upon a path along the side of the Yamuna, surrounded on all sides by Their gopi friends.

He may think of how some gopis sing Their glories, others fan Them, and yet others throw flower petals at Their feet, filling the air with colour and aroma and covering the ground with a fragrant carpet.

Dear Vaisnavas! Let us encourage one another to taste the benefits of the holy name according to our individual qualifications, knowing well that only such taste will draw us into the realm of transcendence.

In summary, we should always keep in mind that the maha-mantra is completely transcendental, and any attempt to understand it by the speculative power of the conditioned mind is futile.

If material objects like trees, cows, and our own bodies display inconceivable potency, how much power must there be in a purely spiritual object like Krsna’s personal name. It is inconceivable.

Shouldn’t we have faith, then, in the glories of the holy name? Only with such rational faith can we follow the Lord’s teachings, spiritualise our intelligence, and realise the truth of nama-sankirtana.

**\* \* \* \***

The seventh offence, a symptom of Kali-yuga’s hypocrisy, is to “commit sin on the strength of the chanting of the holy name,” namno balad yasya hi papa-buddhir na vidyate tasya yamair hi suddhih.

The word nama, as indicated by this verse, represents all the limbs of pure devotion, the most important of which is nama-sankirtana, the devotional practice that accompanies all the other limbs.
