Conditioned souls, ignorant of their eternal spiritual identities, have a penchant for enjoying through material senses the forbidden fruits of this temporary world, committing sin or acting against God’s laws.

Sinful acts not only cause reactions but also sow seeds of desire that impel the sinner to sin again. This cycle of sin, desire, more sin, more desire, more sin, and so on, is the cycle of birth and death (samsara).

Samsara is like a forest fire in which the conditioned living entities are consumed like helpless animals. Their only relief is Krsna’s cloudburst of mercy descending from the spiritual master.

The spiritual master awards his disciples the gift of the holy name, which is the means to purify the desire to sin and to control the tendency to commit sin. On its strength we become sober (dhira).

As we become steady in our chanting (nistha), our inclination to sin decreases to a trace, and as our taste for chanting matures, we abandon temptation, no longer giving it a second thought.

The key to gaining freedom from sinful life is the sincere desire for such freedom. But if one is not sincere, if one chants Hare Krsna with ulterior motives, the desire to sin cannot be controlled.

Some take up devotional service to make their livings as learned scholars or renowned kirtaniyas or, even worse, to prey on innocent followers or helpless children in the guise of guru or teacher.

Duplicity reigns over the hearts of such pseudo-devotees. They either give up both chanting and devotional service, or they succumb to the urges of their senses and subdue their guilt through rationalisation.

The rationale for such sinful activity is the hope that the power of the holy name will gradually free and forgive them for sins — often some form of forbidden sex — in which they engage remorselessly.

It is true that continuous chanting can free us from offences to the holy name of the Lord, even the grievous offences under discussion, but it will take many births to achieve hrsna-prema in that way.

Why is this offence so deplorable? Because to misuse the power of the holy name meant for attaining Krsna’s lotus feet—just to enjoy sense objects we should have long ago abandoned — is to abuse the Lord.

Thus the offence of committing sin is further compounded by the offence of abusing the holy name. The aggregate of these offences both generates sinful reactions and plants the seed of future desires.

The sinful reactions and desires resulting from such offences are more impervious to the influence of the holy name than those coming from past impious activities — they persist even at transcendence.

And no amount of atonement, no matter how extensive or severe, can purify the offender from such reactions. This is the meaning of the second line of this offence, na vidyate tasya yamair hi suddhih.

The only way one can be relieved of sinning on the strength of the holy name is nama-sankirtana itself,

*namaparadha-yuktanam namany eva haranty agham*  
*avisranti-prayutani tany evartha-karani ca*

**“Even if in the beginning one chants the Hare Krsna** ***maha*****-mantra with offences, one will become free from such offences by chanting again and again.”**

This is the verdict of the Padma Purana.

But unless offenders give up their devious, exploitative mentalities and chant hari-nama with sincere and repentant attitudes, their chanting will be like the bathing of an elephant (kunjara-saucavat).

An elephant enters a body of water and carefully cleanses itself, but as soon as it returns to land it throws dirt all over its head and body, the effect of which is that he appears not to have bathed.

Offenders to the holy name must chant with the desire to be freed of offences or, even better, they should chant without offence and in that way regain the mercy of Lord Krsna’s holy names.

There is a gulf of difference between the mentality of those who sin accidentally, even if repeatedly, and those whose sins are premeditated; the former is corrigible, the latter incorrigible.

Krsna repeatedly speaks about devotees who sin accidentally. To Uddhava He says,

**“My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.”**

And to Arjuna He says,

**“Even if one commits the most abominable action, if he is engaged in devotional service he is to be considered saintly because he is properly situated in his determination.”**

In both of these verses Krsna is describing a sincere devotee who is determined to attain His lotus feet but who, due to some weakness, temporarily succumbs to the demands of the mind and senses.

By continued engagement in devotional service (bhajate mam ananya-bhak), such a devotee is quickly rectified of fault, and Krsna concludes, “he attains lasting peace” — he goes back to Godhead.

But unless intentional sinners change their mentality and acquire a desire to give up their sinful ways, they cannot be rectified and will continue to suffer from the results of their sins, birth after birth.

**\* \* \* \***

Pariksit Maharaja and Sukadeva Gosvami discuss this truth at the beginning of the Sixth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam. The king is concerned about how sinful living entities can be saved from hell.

At first Sukadeva Gosvami suggests atonement:

**“Before one’s next death comes, as long as one’s body is strong enough, one should quickly adopt the process of atonement according to sastra.”**

But Pariksit Maharaja reasons that there must be something better than acts of atonement, which do nothing to eradicate one’s desire to sin; instead, “one is forced to commit sins again and again.”

Sukadeva Gosvami admits,

**“Unless one is freed from the mode of ignorance, trying to counteract one action through another is useless because this will not uproot one’s desires.”**

Though the cultivation of knowledge, which helps to control the mind and senses, is better than the path of fruitive work, it also cannot root out from within the heart the tendency to commit sin.

Finally, Sukadeva Gosvami reveals the confidential perfection, the path of pure devotion, which is above the paths of fruitive work and knowledge, and which frees one of the desire for and reactions to sin.

He says,

*kecit kevalaya bhaktya vasudeva-parayanah*  
*agham dhun-vanti kartsnyena niharam iva bhaskarah*

**“Only a rare person who has adopted complete, unalloyed devotional service to Krsna —**

**“Can uproot the weeds of sinful actions with no possibility that they will revive. He can do this simply by discharging devotional service, just as the sun can immediately dissipate fog by its rays.”**

In this verse the words kevalaya bhaktya vasudeva-parayanah spell out how a sinner can become absolutely free of the desire for and effects of sin: he must embrace the path of pure devotional service.

Only by sincerely submitting to the process of devotional service, a process headed by chanting Krsna’s names without offence, can one he completely freed from sin’s vicious and entangling network.

To further illustrate the power of Krsna’s names upon innocent sinners, Sukadeva Gosvami tells the story of Ajamila, a qualified brahmana who accidentally fell under the influence of a prostitute.

Nonetheless, at the time of death Ajamila helplessly called out the name of his youngest son, Narayana. As a result, he was cleansed of his past sins and awakened to his original pure consciousness.

Ajamila regretted his sins and the years of his life he had wasted. He then left his family, absorbed himself in pure devotional service, attained perfection, and went back to Godhead.

Ajamila’s regretful prayer for his past misdeeds and his revelation of what he planned to do in order to redeem himself serve as a model from which we can compose our own prayers. He prayed:

**“Simply because I chanted the Lord’s holy name in the association of devotees, my heart is now becoming purified. Therefore I shall not fall victim again to the false lures of material sense gratification.**

**“Now that I have become fixed in the Absolute Truth, henceforward I shall not identify myself with the body. I shall give up false conceptions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ and fix my mind on Krsna’s lotus feet.”**

Having now heard about the offence of committing sin on the strength of chanting, let us hear examples of such offences, beginning with the sins we may fall victim to during our everyday activities.

Many devotional practices, such as Deity worship, cooking, or going on Parikrama, may conclude with prayers of forgiveness intended to absolve us from mistakes made during those services.

But if we intentionally make mistakes and think, “It is all right, I will say the prayer afterwards and be excused,” that premeditated abuse of bhakti, requesting that our error be legalised, is the seventh offence.

One example would be a pujari who neglects to place tulasi leaves on offerings prepared for the Lord and then notices the mistake. Out of laziness he may think, “The Lord is very kind. It doesn’t matter.”

The mistake of forgetting a tulasi leaf is minor, hut the mentality that excuses it is the same as that by which others commit more serious sins, such as having sex with another’s spouse — “Krsna will forgive.”

The unwanted habit of duplicity created in reaction to the small mistake becomes as pervasive, destructive, and ongoing as it is for a more grievous sin, haunting us until we attain pure love for Krsna.

A blase attitude towards devotional service becomes a breeding ground for what may appear to be minor transgressions hut that arc, in reality, serious sins on the strength of chanting the holy name.

The danger is that this hypocritical mentality is habit-forming. Repeatedly rationalising small mistakes may escalate, bit by bit, to justifying the most horrendous deeds by the same perverted logic.

It should not be surprising, then, that in Bhauma Vrndavana so-called renunciants and babajis indulge in illicit sex or smoke ganja, all the while reassuring themselves that the dhama is all-merciful.

This offence is also common in religious traditions outside Vaisnavism in which the confession of sins or a system of payment for redemption is used as an excuse for ongoing indulgence in sinful acts.

At this point one might ask about Arjuna’s situation. If on the battlefield he knew that Krsna would absolve him of the sin of killing, did he offend the holy name by shedding his enemies’ blood?

The answer is no! Arjuna’s motive for fighting was to please Krsna. He was not fighting for personal gain. Neither was he interested in freeing himself from sin by invoking Krsna’s mercy.

In conclusion, we can protect ourselves from the seventh offence against the holy name by always strictly adhering to the regulative principles of devotional service, without compromise.

There is no doubt Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami was transcendentally situated. And yet his adherence to the regulative principles was said to be “like lines on a stone.” We should follow his example.

Given the opportunity, the cheating propensity intrinsic to all conditioned souls will dominate our hearts and, in the name of devotional service, attempt to fulfil the latent desires in our minds.

But by the strength of the holy name and the company of pure devotees we can avoid what Dasa Gosvami calls “bathing in the trickling urine of the great asses of deviousness and hypocrisy.”

And if lust and his cronies have lured us into the pit of wicked deeds, then with an honest heart we must cry out to Krsna and His devotees, who will doubtlessly help restore us to our natural healthy condition.

**\* \* \* \***

The eighth offence is to consider nama-sankirtana to be one of the auspicious ritualistic activities prescribed in the karma-kanda portion of the Vedas — *dharma-vrata-tyaga-hutadi- sarva-subha-kriya-samyam*.

In this age of irreligion it is rare to find persons who can appreciate selfless acts of pure devotion like public nama-sankirtana or book distribution, much less a life dedicated to chanting Hare Krsna.

The mass of people more readily value mundane welfare work, and so they tend to judge a spiritual organisation’s value more on its acts of charity than on its efforts to disseminate transcendental knowledge.

The Vedic literature prescribes acts of piety such as yoga, sense control, charity, ablutions, penances, sacrifices, pilgrimages, holy baths, altruistic work, and adherence to varnasrama-dharma.

With the promise of a better life attained by following scriptural injunctions, sastra recommends acts of piety — materialistic religious practices meant to elevate the performer to the mode of goodness.

Following Vedic principles, even with material motivation, accustoms one to some degree of regulation, austerity, self-control, selflessness, renunciation, and regular contact with scripture and saints.

Visnu is the presiding Deity in most sattvika pious acts, but those acts are still deemed to be material because they are self-serving, devoid of the pure devotion that has Krsna’s happiness as its only motive.

Pious acts are not spiritual; rather, they are a means to gradually qualify practitioners for spiritual life. But in this Age of Kali, sastra does not recommend this indirect, stepwise progression to bhakti.

Instead, Lord Caitanya introduced nama-sankirtana as the means by which people in any condition of life can, by practising sadhana-bhakti, elevate themselves to pure devotion and then to love of God.

Foolish people sometimes think that chanting Hare Krsna is a form of material piety akin to planting trees or digging wells, and they take to nama-sankirtana with this misconception, ignorant of sastric truth.

Just as a person with jaundice sees everything with a yellow tint, one infected with a mundane conception of religion — piety and impiety— sees even the ultimate religious sacrifice as a mere pious act.

Such persons, afflicted by the jaundice of ignorance, can neither taste the sweetness of chanting Krsna’s name, nor appreciate its cintamani effect, though it is glorified throughout scripture.

For example, “Of all that is sweet, the holy name of Krsna is the sweetest, and of all that is auspicious, the holy name stands supreme. It is the transcendental fruit of the desire tree of the Vedas.

“O best of the Bhrgus! If someone utters the holy name without offence even once, either with faith or inattentively, it immediately delivers that person from the bondage of illusion.”

Krsna’s names arc not ordinary. They are so powerful that one who purely chants them realises the purport and reaps the benefit of all the mantras in the Vedic literature. The Visnu-dharma says —

*Rg-vedo 'tha yajur-vedah sama-vedo ’py atharvanah*  
*adhitas tena yenoktam harir ity aksara-dvayam*

**“One who chants the two syllables ha-ri has already studied the four Vedas — Sama, Rg, Yajur and Atharva.”**

The difference between pious acts and chanting Hare Krsna is like the difference between night and day. To overlook this distinction is to tragically mistake the material for the spiritual and vice versa.

This mistake not only offends the holy name and the Lord Himself but also undermines the basis for all spiritual understanding: to be able to distinguish spirit from matter, reality from illusion.

To accept nama-sankirtana as pious activity and at the same time the means for perfection, as stated in scriptures, is to accept the illusion that material effort can bring one to transcendence.

Such a conclusion ignores the independent nature (svarat) of the Absolute Truth and defies logic, experience, and scriptural conclusions. In other words, it is utter nonsense.

Krsna Himself tells Uddhava that pious activities are not sufficient to attain Him:

**“My dear Uddhava! Even though one engages with great endeavour in the mystic yoga system, philosophical speculation —**

**“Charity, vows, penances, ritualistic sacrifices, teaching of Vedic mantras to others, personal study of the Vedas, or the renounced order of life, still one cannot achieve Me.”**

In summary, one who equates any amount of pious activity with the chanting of Krsna’s name likens a piece of coal to gold. He is considered an atheist and a candidate for Yamaraja’s punishment.

This offence, if not rooted out at the beginning of devotional life, will gradually poison offenders’ minds with its misconceptions and transform them into Mayavadis. A greater curse cannot be found.

It is possible to attain every goal of every pious act by chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, but using the holy name for such trifling gains is like using a priceless diamond as a hammer.

Pious activities are generally abandoned after their purpose has been served, but nama-sankirtana is never given up by the spiritually enlightened, who perform it as practitioners and as perfected souls.

This offence is born of ignorance; therefore, it can be eradicated by transcendental knowledge that discriminates between the elevated blessings of the holy name and the paltry benefits of pious acts.

If we are careless in chanting Hare Krsna, and if we keep bad company, we may lose our spiritual intelligence, relate to nama-sankirtana as if it were mere piety, and thus perpetuate our offences.

Prior to Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s appearance, devotees would meet at Advaita Acarya’s house, where they would hold kirtana, only to be ridiculed by the materialistic smarta-brahmanas of Navadvipa.

These smartas thought that nama-sankirtana was a pious ritual meant for a fixed time and place. Moreover, they faulted the devotees for chanting during Caturmasya, the four months when Visnu sleeps.

One brahmana said, “If the Lord’s sleep is disturbed, no doubt He will be angered and curse this land with famine.’’ Another brahmana worried about how such a famine might affect the price of rice.

These brahmanas would also chant the Lord’s names, but kirtana was for them part of a ritual they performed to earn their livelihood. They were ignorant of the fact that pure sankirtana always pleases Krsna.

As a result of this offensive attitude towards the holy name, the brahmanas became offensive to the Vaisnavas, and later to Caitanya Mahaprabhu, demonstrating the rule that offence begets offence.

A final point: the well-known expression “Service to man is service to God” (*manava-seva madhava-seva*) is symbolic of the eighth offence, for it equates pious acts like feeding people with pure devotion.

Feeding people is service to God only if the food is krsna-prasada, which naturally leads man towards God. Simply filling a stomach without feeding the soul is, from the absolute perspective, futile.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda offers the following sublime remedy for one who has committed the eighth offence. First, the offender should find a Vaisnava householder who is originally from a low caste.

He should then smear the dust of that Vaisnava’s feet all over his body, eat the remnants of his food, and drink the water that has washed his feet. This will destroy false caste distinctions.

Then the proper attitude towards the Lord’s name will reawaken in the offender’s heart. Bhaktivinoda cites the example of Kalidasa as one who was thus saved from this eighth offence to the holy name.

**\* \* \* \***

The ninth offence to the holy name is to relate the glories of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra in ways that are beyond the faith and intelligence of listeners to comprehend and thus accept.

If we explain confidential things to a faithless person and he simply finds fault with Lord Krsna, it is also our offence (asraddadhane vimukhe 'py asrnvati yas copadesah siva-namaparadhah).

Srila Prabhupada directs this verse to preachers in general as a warning, but Bhaktivinoda Thakura and Jiva Gosvami specifically direct it to initiating (diksa) spiritual masters. We’ll discuss that later.

Both views, however, follow Krsna’s order:

**“Steadiness in one’s own position is declared to be actual piety, whereas deviation from one’s position is considered impiety. In this way the two are ascertained.”**

The point is that we should invest others with knowledge of the holy name in proportion to their ability to accept what they have heard. Of course, such ability is dependent on the degree of their faith.

Srila Prabhupada instructs us to engage newcomers simply in hearing and chanting the maha-mantra, thus giving the holy name a chance to purify their hearts and plant the seeds of faith.

As faith grows in them, their ability to understand the truths of the holy name will increase proportionately. We should then give them incremental knowledge according to their burgeoning faith.

When we impart wisdom beyond the hearer’s ability to accept it, doubts can awaken and consequently stifle enthusiasm. This is just the opposite of what a preacher is meant to instil in others.

If Sri Nama Prabhu sees his representatives producing the opposite of the result for which they were empowered, he becomes offended, as would a king to see ministers fomenting discord amongst the citizens.

By losing the mercy of the holy name, preachers not only forfeit their power of attorney, but also lose their own taste for the holy name; the opportunity to garner special mercy instead results in disfavour.

One example of this offence is to expect too much of beginners, such as insisting that they must first follow the four regulative principles or chant at least sixteen rounds daily before they can advance.

Other examples of the ninth offence arc instructing newcomers in advanced techniques of meditation on the name or encouraging them artificially to remember esoteric pastimes while they chant.

Indeed, to explain the maha-mantra to neophytes in any other way than “O Lord! O energy of the Lord! Please engage me in Your service!” is also offensive, especially if it involves Krsna and the gopis.

As already mentioned, Srila Prabhupada generally directs his comments regarding this offence to preachers introducing new devotees to the practice of chanting Hare Krsna.

They must be careful to preach according to the lowest common denominator of understanding in their audience, reserving higher truths only for those who have developed the required faith.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu was amongst the people in general, He simply chanted Hare Krsna. But with His own devotees and more educated persons, He spoke of Krsna’s teachings and general pastimes.

And only when He was with confidants like Ramananda Raya and Svarupa Damodara would He delve into the most intimate pastimes of Radha and Krsna, revealing His own divine encounters.

In this way the Lord disclosed to various groups of devotees various degrees of Krsna consciousness and, by example, taught His followers to preach according to audience, time, and circumstance.

This topic — preaching the glories of the holy name to the faithless — also includes needlessly wrangling over philosophical issues beyond the purview of the parties involved, issues like the origin of the jiva.

We often see devotees mechanically rehashing the same quotes, logic, and arguments of that well-trod debate without ever reaching a conclusion or increasing anyone’s faith in Krsna.

By discussing subjects inconceivable to conditioned souls, we speak above our own qualifications, and in so doing disregard Srila Prabhupada’s direct order as well as scriptural injunctions.

Bhismadeva advises,

**“One should not try to understand by logic that which is inconceivable. Things that lie beyond material nature are said to be inconceivable to persons subjected to the modes.”**

Therefore, it is as offensive to speak above our own realisations as it is to speak above the realisation of others. Both acts transgress Krsna’s edict cited earlier, sve sve ’dhikare ya nistha.

To speak according to one’s qualification or that of one’s audience is virtuous, but to present a position one is unqualified to speak about or one’s audience is unqualified to hear is irresponsible and offensive.

As mentioned earlier, some acaryas consider that this offence — instructing the faithless about the glories of the holy name — is meant as a warning to spiritual masters not to initiate unfit disciples.

Again, the rule of thumb is sve sve’ dhikare ya nistha, which enjoins that preachers distribute and listeners receive knowledge of the Lord according to their respective levels of advancement.

Both scriptures and acaryas confirm that it is the duty of the spiritual master to test his disciples’ qualification, waiting until a suitable time before initiating them with the holy name or other mantras.

If, however, the spiritual master ignores this warning and initiates disciples prematurely, the offence will cause his spiritual power to diminish, and he may even leave the path of devotion altogether.

Giving the touchstone of the holy name to those who cannot appreciate its value is akin to throwing pearls before swine. The holy name is offended when its wealth is squandered in this way.

And since it is the spiritual master who gives disciples access to the holy name, in addition to the offence of abusing his distinguished post, he also shares in all the offences of his errant disciples.

Since we all chant the maha-mantra before we are initiated, let us now clarify what it means to receive the Hare Krsna mantra from the spiritual master at the time of initiation.

Lord Caitanya has freely given the maha-mantra to everyone. Generally, we first chant without making any formal vow and without formally recognising the parampara, or even Krsna.

But this level of chanting qualifies us for initiation by bringing us to a point of maturity at which the spiritual master acts on behalf of Krsna to accept our formal vows in our worship of the holy name.

Those vows include avoiding the ten offences, following the four regulative principles, and chanting a minimum of sixteen rounds daily. In exchange, Krsna relieves us of the burden of our sins.

As a recognised member of Krsna’s family, our continued chanting qualifies us for chanting with love, which in turn will qualify us for attaining Krsna. Lord Caitanya taught these mysteries of diksa.

To Sanatana Gosvami, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu said,

*diksa-kale bhakta kare atma-samarpana*  
*sei-kale krsna tare kare atma-sama, cid-ananda-maya*  
*aprakrta-dehe tanra carana bhajaya*

**“At the time of spiritual initiation, diksa, when a devotee fully surrenders unto the devotional service of the Lord, Sri Krsna accepts that devotee to he as good as Himself.**

**“When the devotee’s body is thus transformed into spiritual existence, the devotee, in that transcendental body, renders service to the lotus feet of the Lord.’’**

In summary, chanting first instils faith in us, inspires us to associate with Vaisnavas, and begins the eradication of bad habits. In this way we qualify ourselves for initiation into the disciplic succession.

Empowered by initiation, our chanting qualifies us to free ourselves of bad habits completely. But even more important, we become qualified to awaken our spiritual identity and enter into Krsna’s loving service.

If we chant without being initiated, the process of freeing ourselves from bad habits and gaining entrance into a fully spiritual existence is so difficult and overlong as to be almost impossible in this age.

**\* \* \* \***

But we may still question the need to be initiated at all, considering that it is the chanting of Krsna’s names that can fully reawaken our connection with the Lord. After all, Caitanya Mahaprabhu says:

**“One does not have to undergo initiation or execute the activities required before initiation. One simply has to vibrate the holy name with his lips. Thus even a man in the lowest class can be delivered.”**

The conclusion of Srimad-Bhagavatam and great souls is that the holy name, the bestower of liberation and of love for God, is so powerful that anyone who chants it can feel an immediate effect.

The maha-mantra is Krsna Himself; therefore, chanting the mantra does not depend upon initiation, pious activities, or preparatory rites. Being fully independent, it acts according to its own sweet will.

Yes, these glories of the holy name are factual, but they do not apply to everyone automatically. Sadly, the vast majority of us distance ourselves from the holy name’s glories by our offences.

We are, by and large, riddled with bad habits from former lives, which makes for chanting that is slow to clear away impurities, not to mention reveal the holy name’s full splendour.

For this reason great sages like Narada Muni have made initiation and Deity worship prerequisites by which we can get quick relief from bad habits, bodily identification, and the enjoying spirit.

Once, Lord Narayana instructed Narada on the benefits of Deity worship. At that time the Lord stressed the power of the pancaratrika system to free conditioned souls from persistent impurities.

The Lord said, “O sage! My devotee who worships My Deity form according to the rules and regulations never meets, even in dream, any troubles or obstacles but becomes completely fearless.”

By the process of initiation we establish a relationship with Krsna through our connection with the spiritual master, which is then further fortified by worship of the Lord in His Deity form.

In addition to freeing us from sinful reactions, initiation is said to awaken our transcendental knowledge with mantras describing the Lord’s form, helping to solidify our relationship with Krsna.

To get the most benefit from nama-sankirtana, scriptures enjoin that we surrender to a spiritual master, accept initiation from him, receive diksa-mantras, and worship the Deity of the Lord.

Technically, liberated souls may be free from the necessity to accept initiation, but conditioned souls are not. By Deity worship our Krsna consciousness grows, as does the quality of our chanting.

The more purified we are of bodily attachment, the more we realise our identities as Lord Krsna’s servants, and at the stage of liberation we realise our eternal spiritual identities (svarupa).

At that stage of transcendence, our chanting of the maha-mantra is at last freed from any taint of material contamination and displays the wonderful qualities that scriptures and saints incessantly praise.

In spite of hearing all these arguments, we may insist, “But scriptures say that chanting is not dependent upon initiation. Why can’t we simply go on chanting without initiation and still attain perfection?”

The answer is that while scriptures have described the absolute power of the holy name, great sages have explained how that power can be accessed through a process that includes initiation and Deity worship.

These two statements are not mutually exclusive, but complementary aspects of Sri Krsna’s inviolable will, which He Himself voiced: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master.

“Enquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realised souls can impart knowledge unto you \[through the process of initiation\], because they have seen the truth.”

The process, given by Narada and others, of receiving initiation and worshipping the Deity is the method whereby conditioned souls of this world can get the full benefit of chanting Krsna’s holy names.

Those who follow these instructions reap favourable results, those who do not, struggle and fail. In this regard, Bhumi-devi says to King Prthu,

**“A foolish person who, through mental speculation —**

**“Manufactures his own ways and means and does not recognise the authority of the sages who lay down unimpeachable directions is simply unsuccessful again and again in his attempts.”**

Although these answers should satisfy sincere enquiries, a final and conclusive piece of evidence in support of the necessity for initiation is found in the example of our self-realised acaryas and of the Lord.

Vaisnava history records that Krsna and Balarama, before They went to gurukula, accepted initiation from Garga Muni, and Caitanya Mahaprabhu received initiation from Isvara Puri in Gaya.

The followers of Lord Caitanya, many of whom are His eternal corn-panions, who are doubtlessly above the regulations governing conditioned souls, all took initiation and worshipped Deities.

This consistent precedent leads us to conclude that our liberated predecessors were convinced of the benefits that initiation would bestow upon them and upon their followers, including us.

Now let us return to the topic of the guru’s offence: initiating unqualified disciples. We have already shown that initiation is not a trifling affair hut a momentous occasion in the life of a disciple.

Service to the spiritual master literally opens the gates of Goloka to the disciple (mahat-sevam dvaram ahur vimukteh). But if he allows unworthy candidates to enter, he is punished for his negligence.

Why would a mature Vaisnava knowingly accept unqualified disciples? Such conduct is not found in liberated gurus who are above the four material defects, including cheating and illusion.

But conditioned souls who are not spiritually powerful, or who are overburdened by the sins of their disciples, may very well succumb to the allurements of their post — greed, adoration, and distinction.

Anyone, initiating gurus included, who hears and chants without trying to give up offences becomes attached to sense gratification. To such gurus, disciples are natural, submissive, and favoured objects.

The temptation to collect disciples and benefit from monetary gifts and adoring worshippers blinds such gurus from seeing their proper duty: to elevate followers through supervised spiritual education.

Upon careful analysis, it is clear that such deviant spiritual masters include in their offences more than merely transgressing the law of the disciplic succession regarding who is qualified for initiation.

Such offences not only feed the cheating propensity of unfit disciples by failing to guide them to the actual goal of spiritual life, hut also sow seeds of doubt in qualified disciples who see through the charade.

Finally, by setting a bad example these gurus bring disrepute upon the institutions of which they arc a part, upon the disciplic succession as a whole, upon their own spiritual masters, and ultimately upon Krsna.

In Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s words:

**“To initiate a faithless person is an abominable offence, and the spiritual master who gives initiation to a faithless person for material benefit goes to hell.”**

**\* \* \* \***

What happens if a spiritual master unknowingly accepts an unqualified disciple? No doubt Krsna will bring the error to his notice, at which time the spiritual master must take appropriate steps.

He must chastise the disciple for misleading him and then arrange a program of rectification that can bring the disciple to the proper standard. And if the disciple is incorrigible, he should be rejected.

Then the spiritual master should disclose everything to senior Vaisnavas and ask them to relieve him of his offence on behalf of the disciplic succession. Caution in this regard is the better part of valour.

In this age people in general arc habituated to many sinful activities, even in their means of livelihood. Before initiating aspirants, a spiritual master must ensure that they have stopped their sinful ways.

Before the initiation, aspirants should have followed the regulative principles strictly for at least six months and should have developed enough strength from chanting to live a pure life.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda insists that a disciple study and understand the ten essential principles of the Vedas (dasa-mula-tattva) before beginning the purificatory process that includes initiation.

These principles are to be learned from the lips of a spiritual master as he reveals them from the pages of the Bhagavad-gita, Srimad- Bhagavatam, and Sri Caitanya-caritamrta.

After prospective disciples have assimilated the basic philosophy, they may then undertake the five purificatory rites described in scriptures as tapah, pundra, nama, mantra, and yajna.

Hearing and accepting the basic Vedic truths strengthens one’s faith, and for the faithful, austerity (tapah) is the spontaneous outpouring of repentance that flows from a purified, penitent heart.

We express this tapah in words such as: “O my Lord! O dearly beloved of Radha! Having suffered in this world for so long I have finally discovered You, the personification and source of all happiness.

“I have turned my back upon Your illusory potency, although by habit my heart is still drawn to it. I beseech You! Please give me the shelter of Your more advanced devotees, the only path to You.”

When a spiritual master hears these words uttered with true feeling and sees the disciple humbly fallen at his feet, he may then further test that devotee’s determination for initiation with pundra.

In Vaisnava tradition, pundra meant to brand the symbols of Visnu upon the body. One’s repentance would be confirmed by a willingness to accept the painful inconvenience of being permanently marked.

But Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the spiritual master of everyone, kindly removed this severe and stringent requirement, asking us instead to mark our bodies after bathing with gopi-candana-tilaka.

The Lord also asked His followers to show their sincerity in identifying themselves as Vaisnavas by engaging in public nama-sankirtana, the ultimate expression of pundra and tapah.

After these two stages of purification, the spiritual master confirms the depth and stability of the disciples’ repentance by testing how well they have understood and assimilated the fundamental truths.

In iskcon this requirement is met by the aspirant having to pass a compulsory pre-initiation examination before being recommended for the next stages of purification: nama, mantra, and yajna.

First initiation means to receive the order and the privilege to chant nama without offence. Once sufficiently steady, second initiation means to receive mantra-diksa and perform Deity worship (yajna).

Spiritual masters must protect the integrity of these stages of purification by ensuring that they are met according to the well-known and already mentioned principle — *sve sve ’dhikare yd nistha*.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu set the example when He delivered Jagai and Madhai. Lord Nityananda pleaded on their behalf, and so Mahaprabhu implanted transcendental knowledge in their hearts.

Enlightened with the ways of truth, the two begged forgiveness from the Lord and His companions and feelingly promised to give up their sinful ways. Only then did Lord Caitanya accept them as His own.

From this pastime it is clear that as merciful as Lord Caitanya is, He makes repentance a condition for official recognition as His follower. Locana Dasa sings of this prerequisite of the Lord —

*Bhajo bhajo bhai, Caitanya nitai sudrdha biswasa kori*  
*visaya chadiya, se rase majiya, mukhe bolo hari hari*

**“My dear brother! Just worship Lord Caitanya and Nityananda with firm faith.**

**“If one wants to he Krsna conscious by this process, one has to give up one’s engagement in sense gratification and chant without any motive, ‘Hare Krsna! Hari Hari!’ That is all!”**

This offence has another facet that deserves mention. That facet is activated when gurus give initiation to qualified disciples but after having done so neglect to properly care for their dependents.

The initiation ceremony marks the beginning of a long process in which the spiritual master plays the role of teacher and agrees to steadily enlighten his student with transcendental knowledge.

A guru who neglects the responsibility of delivering his disciples, either personally or through the agency of others he has empowered, is like a teacher who leaves his students to their own devices.

Even qualified disciples may lose their fledgling faith in such a case and abandon the vows that qualified them to serve the Deity, chant Gayatri, and so on, for which the guru is again liable.

Maharaja Rsabhadeva, while instructing his sons, stressed the competence of an authorised spiritual master by stating that the guru is able to take his disciples back home, back to Godhead.

The Lord says,

**“One who cannot deliver his dependents from the path of repeated birth and death should never become a spiritual master, a father, a husband, a mother, or a worshipable demigod.”**

This concludes my account of the ninth offence to the holy name. I pray to Nrsimhadeva, “O Lord! Protector of devotees! Please shelter me from the all-devouring demon of offences to Krsna’s name.

“My life, my spiritual assets, and my aspirations are solely the result of the holy name’s mercy. Please give me the intelligence and the purity of heart never to succumb to the allurements of my position.”

**\* \* \* \***

While the ninth offence pertains to those who give instructions about or initiate others into chanting the name, the tenth pertains to those who receive those instructions or who have been initiated.

*Srute ’pi nama-mahatmye yah priti-rahito narah*  
*aham-mamadi-paramo namni so ’py aparadha-krt*

**“If one has heard the glories of the Lord’s name but still continues his materialistic way of life —**

**“Thinking ‘I am this body and everything belonging to this body is mine’ (aham mameti) and does not show respect and love for the chanting of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, that is an offence.”**

Learned Vaisnavas sometimes refer to this transgression as the worst of the ten because it is the root of all other offences to the holy name, even those of blaspheming Vaisnavas and the spiritual master.

And so until one rises above material attachment in its various forms — such as envy, ignorance, greed, and pride — this tenth offence continues to be the source of all kinds of offences to the holy name.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu says that initiation means we fully surrender to Krsna. Freed of material designation and blessed by the Lord, we can then serve Him with our spiritual bodies, aprakrta-dehe.

Generally it is seen, however, that in spite of receiving the name Dasa or Dasi, “servant of Krsna,” we don’t act as though liberated from initiation onward but continue thinking of “I” and “mine.”

At initiation, the vast majority of us do not become aware of our spiritual identities in the way that, for example, Caitanya Mahaprabhu did when He was initiated by Isvara Puri.

When Lord Caitanya received initiation He became mad with the ecstasy of love, indicating that — in His role as an acarya —He had full realisation of His eternal relationship with Krsna.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu played the role of an ideal initiate, but because today so few of us meet that standard, there is a good chance devotees will become offenders after having taken initiation.

The holy name takes offence when non-liberated devotees maintain or cultivate material attachments after having accepted initiation into a path dedicated to conscious detachment, vairagya-vidya.

In other words, if we externally commit ourselves to progressive surrender as the means to please the maha-mantra, but internally we actually do not want to surrender, then we are offenders.

This offence and the risk of perpetuating it cease only when we abandon all pretence and with purified hearts fully surrender ourselves as humble servants of the holy name.

Surrender has six divisions: (1) accepting whatever is favourable to devotional service, (2) rejecting whatever is unfavourable, (3) being convinced that Krsna will give all protection—

(4) Accepting the Lord as one’s guardian or master, (5) desiring only what Krsna desires, and (6) utter humility. By following this process in our pursuit of surrender, Krsna helps us forget our attachments.

By sincerely practising this process of surrender, we become increasingly submissive to Krsna’s will until surrender finally becomes spontaneous. Then we are situated in the state of atma-nivedanam.

The surrender of pseudo-devotees, however, is but an external show in the name of devotion. They secretly enjoy this world with their senses, so naturally Maya makes them forget devotional service.

Taking shelter of the misconceptions “I” and “mine,” such persons act only for their own selfish interests and arrogantly think of themselves as masters of their fate and lords of their possessions.

One example of such an offender is Sukracarya. As the spiritual master of the demons, he was present when Vamanadeva begged Bali Maharaja for all the land He could cover with three steps.

Bali Maharaja readily agreed to forfeit everything he had to please the Lord, hut because Sukracarya feared to lose his comfortable way of life, he advised the king not to surrender to the Lord.

Even at the cost of disobeying his guru, Bali Maharaja thought it wiser to surrender to the Lord than be a hypocrite like Sukracarya; thus he gave Vamana everything, including his very self

Bali said, “I do not fear hell, poverty, an ocean of distress, fall- down from my position, or even death as much as I fear cheating a brahmana.” Equally so, we should be fearful to cheat the name.

Another example of such an aparadhi is Dhrtarastra. Although Bhisma, Vidura, and Krsna repeatedly advised him to tread the path of righteousness, due to weak-heartedness he could not surrender.

No matter how much good advice he received to abdicate the throne to Yudhisthira, Dhrtarastra would not give up his attachment to being king, either directly or through evil-minded Duryodhana.

Once, after hearing about Krsna’s greatness from his father Vyasa, Dhrtarastra said, “I know that Krsna is the Supreme controller! I know that He has ordained that Yudhisthira rule the kingdom.

“And I know my sons can never conquer the Pandavas in battle. Yet I cannot refuse Duryodhana’s desire to be king, for I am helpless in the throes of my attachment to him. I cannot resist.”

And Srila Prabhupada tells a story that epitomises the foolishness of clutching onto our attachments while calling out the holy names: An old woman was carrying a bundle of wood through theforest.

Because it was very heavy, the bundle fell from her head to the ground. Unable to pick it up, she became disturbed and thought, “Who will help put this bundle back on my head?”

Desperate, the woman cried out, “God help me! Help me!” In response, God soon appeared and asked, “What do you want?” The old woman replied, “Please, sir, put this bundle back on my head.”

This fable illustrates the foolishness of the tenth offence: Krsna appears in the form of the maha-mantra to liberate us, yet we would rather have Him put the bundle of material pains back on our heads.

Traditionally, the only way to rid oneself of such a sinful mentality was to abandon the objects of one’s attachment, accept a vow of poverty, and wander from land to land chanting the Lord’s names.

Freed from the intoxicating effects of home and family, the company of pure devotees quickly absolves one of false ego, instils in one a taste for the holy name, and eradicates the false notions of “I” and “mine.”

Once we have finally abandoned false bodily designations, we can sincerely surrender to the Lord and, under the merciful shelter of the holy name, finally unearth the ultimate treasure, love for Krsna.

People can no longer adopt the mendicant’s way of life, but they can derive the essence of such practice, which is to distance themselves from attachment by strength derived from being with pure devotees.

At last able to gauge the comparative merits of sense enjoyment and pure devotion, we are — even though past offenders — able to pray like Dhruva Maharaja, who was saved by his contact with Narada:

**“O my Lord! Because I was seeking an opulent material position, I was performing severe types of penance and austerity. Now I have gotten You, who are very difficult for demigods, saints, and kings to attain.**

**“I was searching after a worthless, broken piece of glass, but instead I have found a most valuable jewel — Your Holiness. Therefore I am so satisfied that I do not wish to ask any benediction from You.”**

The question I hear most often regarding this offence is whether or not those who have material attachments but sincerely want to abandon them are in the category of offenders.

The answer is no. The holy name has descended with Lord Caitanya to deliver the fallen people of this age. How could it take offence at the very condition from which it wants to purify us?

But we commit a punishable offence when, despite our chanting, we resist or have no intention of being purified of our attachments, which is the natural effect of chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra.

And our punishment is the loss of enthusiasm and spiritual shelter, as a result of which the material desires once kept at hay by the holy name again take control over our lives and victimise us.

Krsna speaks of this condition:

**“The spirit soul bewildered by the influence of false ego thinks himself the doer of activities that are in actuality carried out by the three modes of material nature.”**

The punishment meted out to offenders is amplified by sinful reactions from breaking initiation vows and practising duplicity, which reinforce existing attachments and create new ones as well.

The end result is a pseudo-devotee who makes a living by accepting materialistic disciples or by chanting Hare Krsna but who remains deeply entrenched in a life devoid of pure devotion.

And as long as the selfish desire to enjoy remains unpurified, it follows us birth after birth, just as the smell of camphor lingers in a pot even long after the camphor has been removed.

One who offends the holy name in this way is like a sick man who rejects the treatment prescribed by his physician, all the while claiming to be on the road to recovery. Ultimately he dies.

Srila Prabhupada adds that to not show respect or love for chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra is a further cause of this offence. This profound truth can be understood in the following way:

The holy name is our guru, guide, well-wisher, and means for progress, regardless our stage of spiritual advancement; a sincere practitioner therefore shows both respect and love for the process of chanting.

Nama-sankirtana is the altar at which we all worship. Any sincere practitioner, at whatever stage of advancement he may be, cannot fail to show respect and affection for the object of his worship.

But those for whom chanting is not a worshipable deity hut merely a dry ritual, a means of livelihood, or a way to win recognition from the foolish have neither respect nor love for the holy name.

Such pseudo'devotees may claim to be servants of the holy name, but in truth they are servants of their minds and senses. They vibrate something that sounds like the mantra, but they are far from it.

One who clings to ignorance in this way is like a man who pretends to be asleep, refusing to “wake up” despite all efforts to rouse him — a hopeless situation in a discipline dedicated to spiritual awakening.

The Vedas call out to awaken us from slumber,

*uttistha jagrata prapya varan nibodhata*

**“O living entity, you are sleeping in this material world. Please get up and take advantage of the human form of life.”**

And Lord Caitanya personally pleads,

**“I have brought medicine to awaken every living being from perpetual sleep. Please receive the holy name of the Lord, the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, and awaken.”**

In conclusion, those who reject the mercy of the holy name remain offenders until pure Vaisnavas finally succeed in shaking them out of their stupor and setting them on the path of honest sadhana.

Only straightforward conduct leads to prema-bhakti. It is said that nothing is more sinful than untruthfulness. Indeed, Mother Earth says, “I can bear any heavy thing except a liar.”

**\* \* \* \***

In addition to the ten offences to the holy name analysed in this chapter and recorded in scripture, our acaryas have added an eleventh: to be inattentive while chanting the maha-mantra.

One of the four defects of the conditioned soul is to be subject to illusion (pramada), which means to accept the temporal as permanent. This distraction from reality gives rise to inattention.

Inattention is the root of all other offences because if we are not attentive to avoid pitfalls in chanting — and in devotional service in general — our conditioned nature will inevitably betray us.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructed Sanatana Gosvami in Jagannatha Puri and Gopala Bhatta Gosvami in South India about the importance of chanting Krsna’s holy names with loving attention.

Even if we carefully avoid all ten offences, if we are inattentive while chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, surely the ecstasy that should come from pure chanting will elude us.

Inattention sows the seeds of additional unwanted habits that in turn grow into more weeds of inattention. This proliferation of pramada transforms the garden of the heart into an unsightly patch of weeds.

Pramada gives rise to unwanted habits: apathy — lack of fixed resolve in sadhana; laziness — sleeping in japa or while hearing about Krsna; and distraction — indulging sensual thoughts during japa or kirtana.

How inattention is offensive can be understood in this way. When we chant the maha-mantra we are calling out to Krsna, just as we would call for a loved one to come near by crying out his or her name.

Krsna hears His name and comes to our side as any beloved would, but if we ignore Him — if our attention is distracted by some trifling thing — then Krsna, like a spurned lover, is offended and upset.

We may argue, “I don’t see Krsna when I chant His name. If I did I would not ignore Him.” But Krsna is His name. When one says the syllables krs-na, the Lord is present on the tongue of the chanter.

Indeed, Rupa Gosvami says that the holy name of Krsna dances in the mouth of the chanter. Again, one may argue, “What is the evidence that Krsna in the form of His name dances within one’s mouth?”

Listen carefully, and from your mouth Krsna will enter your ears, and from there, the courtyard of your heart, where you will see Him alongside Radharani, dancing to the sound of Their names.

At the sight of Radha’s and Krsna’s wonderful dancing, your mind will cease wandering. And without the mind’s prompting, your senses will become idle. All this you can directly perceive by being attentive.

As long as we are inattentive, this spontaneous attraction to the name, called anuraga, stays far away. But once anuraga awakens, we are, at long last, indifferent to everything but the name.

Chota Haridasa paid dearly for the offence of pramada: While engaged in getting rice for Caitanya Mahaprabhu, he allowed his mind to wander momentarily to a young maidservant.

For this apparently minor transgression, Lord Caitanya banished Chota Haridasa from His company. And in sorrow, hoping to atone for his offence, Chota Haridasa gave up his body by drowning.

Such severe atonement is no longer acceptable, but we can still rectify the sin of inattentiveness by sincerely chanting the maha-mantra in the close company of devotees who have achieved anuraga.

By trying to follow in the footsteps of such pure devotees without duplicity, we will start to feel spiritually anxious to taste the nectar of the holy name, and our inattentiveness will gradually wane.

When circumstances permit, like on Ekadasi or other holy days, it is advisable that one make an extra effort to chant sixty-four or even one hundred and ninety-two rounds in some secluded place.

By such sacrifices we overcome inattentiveness and all other offences, and by continued enthusiastic chanting all impurities are swept from the heart and we attain the stage of pure chanting.

Allow me to summarise what I have said regarding the offences to the holy name — repetition is good. We who seek pure Krsna consciousness must tremble at the thought of offending Krsna’s holy name.

Scriptures say that the holy name’s and Krsna’s power are equally inestimable. Reciting the maha-mantra is devotional service, and because bhakti begets bhakti, chanting brings more devotional service.

Whether chanted properly or improperly, pronounced correctly or incorrectly, spoken or remembered millions of times or but once, the holy name without doubt delivers us from material bondage.

But misusing the name of Krsna for sensual pleasure, for accumulating wealth, and for collecting followers, or committing any of the offenses described earlier, delays the results of chanting.

Offences are like heavy weights placed upon a bullock cart: they slow down its forward progress. The Padma Purana says, na phala-janakam sighram: “The desired result will not come soon.”

Although Krsna says that in executing devotional acts like chanting the maha-mantra “there is no loss or diminution,” the time it takes for devotion to mature depends on how free we are from offence.

O dear devotees! Please try to understand the seriousness of offences to the holy name. Because these offences are the basis of atheism, the scriptures call one who commits them just that — an atheist (pasandi).

Also, the word aparadha means “to be distanced from worship,” which in a deeper sense means to be distanced from Radha, who departs with the benefits of bhakti when we offend Krsna’s name.

We must therefore diligently avoid offences in chanting the holy name of the Lord. But if somehow or other we do commit offences, we must continue to chant with increased effort to chant purely.

The holy name of Lord Krsna is all-powerful, transcendental. It is Krsna. Thus only the name can wash away sins accumulated from offending it. For this reason we should never stop chanting.

In the following verse, Krsna explains that only two spiritually powerful yoga systems (jnana and bhakti) can rectify sinful activity resulting from an accidental downfall.

But if we commit premeditated sins or other offences, the word yoga in this verse refers only to the chanting of the Lord’s holy names. Krsna says,

**“If, because of momentary inattention —**

**“A yogi accidentally commits an abominable activity, then by the very practice of yoga he should burn to ashes the sinful reaction, without at any time employing any other procedure.”**

If we commit an offence to a Vaisnava, however, then we should also beg forgiveness directly from the Vaisnava or Vaisnavi whom we have offended, as did Durvasa from Maharaja Ambarisa.

In this regard, the book Nama-kaumudi says,

**“An offence to a great devotee is removed either by suffering the result (while chanting Hare Krsna\] or by the mercy of that devotee.”**

Dear devotees! If you are greedy for the pure devotion relished by great souls, then pray constantly at the lotus feet of the holy name, avoid offences to that merciful saviour, and chant, chant, chant!

**\* \* \* \***

Still, to be free of offences, we must do more than try to avoid them. The Lord ordered Brahma to learn the science of devotion by both direct and indirect means, in all circumstances, in all space and time.

Thus we should cultivate the saintly qualities of pure Vaisnavas as related in scriptures, for even attempting to do so will keep offences at bay. Kapiladeva recounts these qualities and their effects:

**“The symptoms of a sadhu are that he is tolerant, merciful, and friendly to all living entities. He has no enemies, he is peaceful, he abides by the scriptures, and all his characteristics are sublime.**

**“He engages in staunch devotional service to the Lord without deviation. For the sake of the Lord he renounces connections, such as family relationships and friendly acquaintances within this world.**

**“Engaged constantly in chanting and hearing about Me, the Supreme Lord, the sadhus do not suffer from material miseries because they arc always filled with thoughts of My pastimes and activities.”**

From these teachings of Lord Kapila we should learn to serve and honour devotees, great or small, according to Vaisnava etiquette, and to worship Sri Krsna as the one Supreme Lord without a second.

We must honour our spiritual masters, especially the initiating spiritual master, and, while respecting all scriptures, strictly follow those pre-eminent texts that reveal the glories of the holy name.

Practitioners who are convinced of the glories of the holy name and are faithful to the teachings of their gurus will neither doubt the power of the holy name nor try to explain it in unauthorised ways.

By strictly following devotional disciplines, such as attending mangala-arati, we gain the spiritual strength to resist and root out sinful habits and to abandon all other religious and ritualistic acts.

Always careful to speak to the level of advancement of those to whom we are speaking, fully surrendered to the maha-mantra, we become exemplars who inspire others to chant Hare Krsna without offence.

In addition to these divine attributes, we cultivate the quality of attentiveness. Once Srila Prabhupada was leaving the Indian Embassy in New York and he asked the devotee accompanying him:

“Did you notice the painting in the Ambassador’s reception room?”  
The devotee looked around blankly and said, “No, Srila Prabhupada.”  
His Divine Grace replied, “That is a fault. You should be attentive.”

Armed with these virtues, we quickly cleanse our hearts of all remaining impurities. Then we can chant the pure name of the Lord and taste the many wonderful symptoms of ecstasy.

But if such divine bodily symptoms have yet to appear, then we should know that our chanting is still riddled with offences. Saunaka Rsi explicitly states,

**“Certainly that heart is steel-framed which —**

**“In spite of one’s chanting the holy name of Lord Sri Hari with concentration — does not change when ecstasy takes place, tears fill the eyes, and the hairs stand on end.”**

About this verse, Srila Prabhupada says,

**“If the reaction does not take place, even after continuous hearing and chanting of the holy name of the Lord, it may be considered to be due to offences only.”**

Leaving behind all offences and adopting the conduct of a true Vaisnava, we enter the clearing stage of chanting, the stage at which all manner of bad habits are systematically wiped away.

As unwanted habits disappear, the taste for and pleasure derived from chanting the maha-mantra increase step by step, as does our hankering for the perfectional stages of devotional service.

As feelings of separation develop, so docs the eligibility to receive Krsna’s mercy. And by crying and crying for it, we will one day successfully secure the Lord’s causeless grace.

With a mere touch of His personal potency, Krsna relieves His devotees from the influence of maya and awakens in them spontaneous ecstatic devotion, the first stage of loving devotion.

Beginning at the stage of ecstasy, our chanting opens the bud of love, petal by petal, diffusing the sublime fragrance of transcendence and mixing it together with various raptures to create the elixir of rasa.

When the mature mellow of devotion awakens in us, the chanting of the holy names opens a transcendental realm that is known only to the eternal residents of Vrndavana and no one else.

Dear Vaisnava readers! Please hear the confessions of an offender to the touchstone that is Sri Krsna’s holy name. By the intercession of your blessings may I be freed from my transgressions.

When I first chanted Hare Krsna I was filled with extraordinary feelings that made me wonder, “If this is just the beginning, what realms of rapture do the coming years have in store for me?”

Seated in the temple room in Montreal, I would watch the devotees enter what I thought was deep trance, only to realise later that these were not symptoms of ecstasy but of ignorance, known as sleep.

In time my own bliss peaked and then descended into what at times took the form of a struggle with drowsiness and at other times with mental images of past sensual experiences, much to my dismay.

Why, I wondered, was my taste for the holy name waning? The answer was clear: By overfamiliarity with devotees, I was offending them, and by overfamiliarity with the name, I was offending it.

Many years have come and gone since those days, and with them, many attempts to eradicate bad habits, to beg forgiveness from the name, and to cultivate the qualities of a true Vaisnava sadhu.

Sometimes the sun of Krsna’s names would shine through the clouds of my had habits and warm me to the very core of my being with its benevolent rays and soothing vibration. Once again I would rejoice.

On one such occasion, during a *hari-nama* in London, I felt as if Lord Caitanya were personally singing and dancing in the *sankirtana* party. I was not the only one who felt that way on that night.

Now and then, to attract the holy name’s mercy, I secluded myself to follow Haridasa Thakura’s regulation. And I held extended *sankirtana* sessions — now called “Holy Name Day” — in New Vraja-dhama.

Sometimes I would fast, sometimes cry, and sometimes do *parikrama* of Navadvipa. But the service most endearing to the holy name, I believe, was Srila Prabhupada’s own simple formula — preaching.

Just as the thick darkness of night gives way to the rising sun, which colours the horizon bright shades of red, the gradual dissipation of offensive habits gives way to the colourful pastimes of *namabhasa.*

While pronouncing the shadow of the holy name, I felt, amongst other things, absolved of sin, protected from Kali’s grip, freed from evil influences, and blessed with depth in my study of scripture.

But most importantly, I felt my taste for the *maha-mantra* return, a taste more pronounced in the company of like-minded Vaisnavas. Once again I felt the delights of bygone days.

It was just as Rupa Gosvami describes:

**“By carefully chanting these sweet names every day, a natural relish awakens within his tongue, and his disease \[of ignorance\] is gradually destroyed at the root.”**

The dawn that follows a storm is clear, cloudless, filled with birdsong, and blessed with tranquillity. In that pristine state, Mother Nature blithely displays her colourful sweetness and majesty.

Now, at times, while chanting *japa* or *sankirtana,* as soon as I pronounce Krsna’s name I feel Krsna’s presence and raise my arms to the sky to offer Him my one and only possession — my heart.

At other times, as I chant before Radha-Syamasundara, I become inexplicably absorbed in Their forms, qualities, and wonderful pastimes. Speechless, I am left to wonder, “What do I do now?”

Sometimes tears come to my eyes, my limbs quiver, my voice chokes up, and my heart fills with a happiness that makes the accumulated treasures of the three worlds seem as insignificant as bits of straw.

And yet I know that because I continue to suffer the residual effects of my past offences this joy is immature in comparison to the bliss felt by pure souls, a shadow of what I would feel if I weren’t an offender.

I worship some incredible, indescribable sound that goes by the name of the *maha-mantra.* Of its own volition, at times that sound dances in my heart with such abandon that it forces me to dance along.

Then again, like a cloud looming on the distant horizon, some bad habit appears to engulf me, obstructing the sun of the pure name for the duration of the sentence meted out by my past offence.

At these times I know, once again, I have somehow offended the holy name, and before I am allowed to relish its full taste once more, I must wait — chanting all the while — until I am pardoned for my sin.

Such are the foibles and offensive mentalities of imperfect souls. Dear devotees! Please bless me to draw back the curtain that separates me from constant, direct communion with my worshipable Lordships.

By repeating Their names with love, we can live always with the divine couple. Their constant companionship is the singular desire of my heart, a desire that only your blessings will transform into reality.

Having disclosed my heart’s burden and its secret desire, I pray to the forms of Radha and Syama that reveal Themselves through the medium of divine sound: “O playful youths of Vraja!

“One moment it appears that I can almost touch You, the next that You are gone. Again I savour Your names, and once again Their sweetness fades, like the taste of candy once it has been eaten.

“I know You free Your servants of impurities and increase their attachment to You by swinging them back and forth between the intense emotional poles of separation and meeting.

“I am Your plaything. Do with me as You like! But please free me from the misdeeds by which I cause You pain and burden my soul, misconduct that saints say is like heating You with a stick.

“What to speak of actually committing such a crime, who can even tolerate the thought of it? O Radha! O Syama! Do with me as You like! But please, please let me be Your pure servant, free of offence.

“O prince and princess of Vraja! I have heard from the lips of great souls that Your endless pastimes flow in waves of nectar. When, by the mercy of Your names, will those waves wash over me?

“The taste we derive from drinking a nectar-blend of Your names, forms, qualities, and pastimes is so agreeable to the heart that it immunises us from every enticement *maya* might use to capture us.

“And when that beverage is further sweetened by Your personal presence on the altar in the temple and iced with the enthusiasm of other devotees, it defies this lowly poet’s ability to describe it.

“O Radha! O Syama! I have disclosed my desire to one day be worthy of Your kindness, of this wonderful abode I call home, of the treasure that is Your personal service, and of Your devotees’ companionship.

“I have neither means nor wealth to requite Your gifts, save to ‘return’ the most valuable gift of them all by chanting Your names to You. I hope against hope this will please You and fulfil my aspirations.

“I know that desiring Your eternal service is a sign of my impertinence. But am I to blame? These ambitions have come as a result of seeing You, hearing about You, and living in Your abode.

“O merciful Hari-nama! Despite my doubts, offences, and years of negligence, You have never abandoned me but are always willing to let me redeem myself. O treasure of Vraja, obeisance to You.”

*Śrīla Prabhupāda wrote, “Hare Kṛṣṇa—O my Lord, O energy of the Lord, please engage me in Your service!” (Teachings of Lord Caitanya)*

## Chapter 38 - The Maha-mantra. Part I

The following four chapters praise the *maha-mantra* in a : succession of four equal parts: (1) Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna,' (2) Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare, (3) Hare Rama, Hare Rama, (4) Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

In the preceding chapter, we heard about the obstacles to chanting the Hare Krsna *maha-mantra* purely. In this and the following three chapters, let us hear the wonders of that pure name *(suddha-nama).*

Before elaborating on the meanings of the names in the m*aha-mantra*, let me share with you a well-known pastime of Radha and Krsna, traditionally performed as a drama in Bhauma Vrndavana.

This pastime gives us a glimpse of how profound the names Radha and Krsna are by showing how the divine couple Themselves worship, understand, and taste even just one syllable of those names.

Srimati Radharani, Krsna, and Lord Caitanya are all incomparable connoisseurs of *nama-sankirtana*. They enjoy a proficiency that neither practising nor perfected devotees can ever hope to attain.

Hearing about how Caitanya Mahaprabhu tasted unique ecstatic symptoms and also strictly followed the principles of regulated devotion inspires us to strive for perfection through *sadhana-bhakti.*

And hearing about the sweetness and potency of the unparalleled *nama-sankirtana* performed by Radha and Krsna will inspire us to chant and relish the *maha-mantra* according to our capacity.

May the following four stanzas, which praise the divine couple’s names and reciprocal love, invoke Their mercy and empower me to properly glorify Their names. And may you be pleased by my attempt.

Sri Radha, the daughter of Varsana’s king, is also known as Syamasundari, the supreme potency of Vraja’s blackish prince, Syamasundara, also known as Sri Krsna, the potent Supreme Being.

The goddess of learning, Sarasvati-devi, is nothing but an expansion of Sri Radha; still, Srimati Radharani cannot say how much nectar is to be found in the nectar-ocean of Sri Krsna’s names.

When the cooling breeze of Radha’s names enters Krsna’s ears, He trembles, the hairs on His body stand erect, and the heart of He upon whom self-satisfied yogis meditate is completely lost to Her.

Rapt in wonder at such transcendental exchanges, Vaisnava poets praise the names of Radha and Krsna, thereby pleasing saintly persons and increasing their desire to hear the divine couple’s glories.

Once in Vrndavana, by the independent course of pure ecstatic love, Srimati Radharani developed and displayed attachment for Syamasundara before He displayed attachment for Her.

After all, the inclination for love awakens in young women before young men. Thus the foremost doe-eyed *gopi* of Vrndavana felt the pangs of passion even before the divine couple met.

Radha and Krsna had not yet come face-to-face, but the instant Radha first heard His name, She lost Her equilibrium. Confused, She confided in Lalita, speaking in a voice heady with the aroma of love.

“O friend! Who uttered that name ‘Krsna’? Somehow it slipped in through My cars and from there crept into My heart. Now the timid doc of My life-airs trembles at the fragrance of newborn excitement.”

Like a lotus dancing in a gusty breeze, Radha’s restless eyes darted in all directions. Taking Radha’s hand, Lalita said, “If this name causes You so much distress, we will never utter it again.”

But Krsna’s name had already risen like the full moon and melted Srimati Radharani’s moonstone heart. Oblivious to Her friend’s vow, Radha continued, “Lalita! Why is the name ‘Krsna’ so sweet?

“Now that My lips have tasted this name, I can do nothing but repeat it again and again. It must be some kind of mystic mantra! I know I would be better off if I could forget it. But I cannot.

“To forget this name seems impossible! By its mysterious effect I feel like I’ve been deranged. I am afraid!” Tightening Her grip on Lalita’s hand, Radha whispered, “O Lalita! What will become of Me?”

Lalita whispered in reply, a mischievous smile on her face, “Radhika! Why should You fear? You have never even met this person. What harm could possibly come to You simply by hearing His name!”

Radha sighed as if the word ‘Krsna’ were a volley of Cupid’s arrows. Her voice faltered as She said, “If the mere sound of this name agitates Me so, what would happen if its owner were to touch Me?”

Radha chattered on, “Were He to come before My eyes, surely I could not continue to tread the path of righteousness.” But Lalita admonished Her, “Forget Him! Why dwell on thoughts of a stranger?”

Again Radha faltered, then opened up the innermost recesses of Her heart. She confessed, “I have tried! With all My heart and soul. I have tried My best to forget Him. But He will not be forgotten.”

Looking into Her friend’s eyes, Radharani stammered, “What will I do now? What will I do?” With a feigned air of resignation, Lalita shrugged her shoulders and replied dramatically:

“Behold a saintly young girl on the brink of defaming Her family!” At this Radha lowered Her face and covered Her mouth with Her hands. But Lalita could sense a drop of joy concealed in Radha’s heart.

Some time later, Krsna, along with Balarama and Their cowherd friends, entered Vrndavana forest. It was springtime, and when Cupid beheld Krsna’s soft, bluish-black limbs, he thought:

“Ah! Some thoughtful person has created a spring festival for me in the form of this delightful cowherd.” To provoke Krsna’s senses, Cupid showered Him with flower arrows from above.

From below, Cupid enticed Krsna with the fragrance of the earth, and from all sides he assailed Him with the hum of honeybees, the call of cuckoos, and the aromatic caress of spring breezes.

Just then Krsna glanced back over His shoulder and caught a glimpse of Radha standing amidst Her friends. He pretended not to see Her, but the sight of Her struck His heart like a thunderbolt.

Absorbed in thoughts of Radha’s beauty, all day He stumbled through the forest, dazed, tending cows, and playing His flute merely out of habit. Hairs on end, shivering in ecstasy, Krsna thought:

“What did I see? That gopi was like a flash of lightning on a jewelled temple dome. Her sari was shimmering like a cloud. Is She human or celestial? Is She a goddess? A human could never be so beautiful.

“Perhaps She is the celebrated princess of Varsana. My mothers often speak of Her. They say that Her glories arc without limit, and that She is as delightful as moonlight mixed with camphor.”

Absorbed in thoughts of Srimati Radharani, Krsna concluded, “It must have been Her! Vrsabhanu-nandini is none other than Sri Radha! The mere mention of this girl’s name fills Me with bliss.”

His heart entrapped by Radha’s qualities, Krsna lost all interest in playing with His friends. He put the cows in Balarama’s care and wandered through the forest with Sridama, Subala, and Madhu.

In time the boys came upon a secluded grove by Yamuna’s shore where trees and creepers played in a restless breeze, jasmine flowers spread their sweet aroma, and bumblebees sang in chorus.

Krsna whispered, “Sridama! Have you ever seen the jewel named Radha, the most beautiful girl in the universe?” Sridama silently lowered his face, his dark complexion now softly glowing red.

Subala blurted out, “Krsna! Why would You ask Sridama if he has seen Radha? Of course he has: Radha is his sister!” Embarrassed, Krsna meekly glanced at Sridama from the corners of His eyes.

Krsna let out a deep sigh and made a proposal, “Dear friends! Let’s go sit beneath the *kadamba* trees on the bank of the Yamuna. There I can pour My melted heart out through the holes of My flute.”

Madhumangala placed a hand on Krsna’s shoulder to comfort Him and said, “Friend! I will bring Radha to You.” “Madhu,” asked Krsna, “I know you to be honest, but are you telling Me the truth?”

With his hands upon his belly Madhu said, “I swear by Gayatri, the mother of the *Vedas,* that I’m telling the truth.” Krsna’s happy face glowed with faith. He placed Madhu’s hands upon His heavy heart.

“Where is She? Please bring Radha here at once!” “I will place Her in Your hand,” Madhu replied, “but first You must give me *daksina.* To accept gifts from a *brahmana* without compensation is irreligious.”

Krsna begged a jasmine garland from a desire tree and respectfully garlanded His friend. Admiring the majestic garland on his chest, Madhumangala plucked a leaf from his belt and offered it to Krsna.

With a voice full of respect, he said, “Now You may take Her.” Krsna gazed in disbelief at the palm-sized leaf Madhu held out to Him and thought, “How can he treat Me like this? This is no time for jest.”

Krsna could not have looked more forlorn. His tear-filled eyes met Madhu’s, but Madhumangala simply smiled wider and held the leaf enticingly closer to his friend. “Here, Krsna! Take Her!”

Krsna reached forward cautiously and took the golden leaf from Madhu’s hand. In large, hold letters He saw the word “Radha.” Stunned, His hand trembling, Krsna fixed His gaze on Radha’s name.

He felt as if His parched eyes had crossed a desert of formlessness and plunged into a nectar-ocean of transcendental form. The syllables *ra-dha* appeared like the sun and moon united to soothe His heart.
