Radha’s name was a divine proclamation of love, the ultimate relief for His distress, an irrepressible source of happiness. Krsna prayed, “O Radha! Your auspicious name is sweeter than glistening nectar.

“It makes the residents of the universe ecstatic and causes the hairs on their bodies to stand on end. Today I have seen the matchless form of perfection, the victory banner of Your holy name.”

Full of gratitude, Krsna smiled at Madhu, “Friend! You have truly done a great service. In My hour of need you revealed Radha’s form to Me. For this I am forever indebted. I cannot thank you enough.”

Pleased with himself, thumbs in his belt, Madhu rolled back and forth on his heels. Overjoyed by Krsna’s gratitude, he glanced at Sridama as if to say, “Such are the benefits of brahminical prowess.”

The other boys smiled. The bees, the parrots, even the creepers and trees blissfully sang the name of Sri Radha, and their *kirtana* resounded throughout the forests, valleys, and hilltops of Vraja.

When the syllables of Radha’s name enter Krsna’s ears or eyes, they satisfy Him completely, filling Him with bliss. How much benefit can we, who are but sparks of Sri Krsna, derive from Her name?

Let us contemplate the divine couple’s admiration for each other’s names as we recite Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s prayer:

**“O my tongue, tortured by thirst! If you desire complete satisfaction —**

**“Mix the delicious nectar of the name ‘Radha’ with the wonderfully sweet condensed milk of the name ‘Krsna,’ add the fragrant ice of pure love, and drink this elixir at every moment!”**

**\* \* \* \***

When Radha and Krsna meet it is due to the prerogative of divine fate. To increase Their longing for each other, and in turn increase Their mutual love, destiny obstructed Their first meeting.

They had seen and heard of each other, so Radha and Krsna were fully absorbed in thoughts of each other. But as much as They desired to meet one another, Providence would not allow it.

Despite Her best efforts and the false pretexts supplied by Her friends, Radha could not escape from Her in-laws. Smouldering like fire, She sat in Her chambers or toiled with Her household duties.

In contrast, Krsna was free to wander Vrndavana, to tend cows and play games. His heart, however, was firmly chained to Sri Radha. He could see nothing, hear nothing, and think of nothing but Her.

Without Her companionship He felt as restricted as She did. His only meditation was, “Let Me meet Radhika, if even momentarily.” Late one morning, Radha sat at Her window, gazing towards Nandagrama.

She was dressed in a black sari and decorated with pearl ornaments and a garland of flowers. Her complexion was like golden tinged with *kunkuma,* Her lips red like betel, and Her eyes lined with black *kajjala* ointment.

The *tilaka* of good fortune graced Her forehead, jewelled earrings framed Her cheeks, sweetness shone from Her limbs, and yet sorrow filled Her heart and tears rolled down Her cheeks as She sat silently.

Radha’s girlfriends attended Her. They knew well of Her unhappiness hut were unable to console Her. Radha wanted to see Krsna, and neither gifts nor promises could replace the encounter She longed for.

Lalita-devi rose quietly and walked towards Radha. She placed an affectionate hand on Radha’s delicate shoulder and said, “Sundari! Why do You needlessly pine for Nanda’s son? Time fulfils all desires.

“Your meeting with the prince will arise when destiny wills it.” Sri Radha continued to gaze out the window. She could see Nandisvara Hill in the far distance, enveloped in a warm summer haze.

Upon the crest of that hill sat the marble palace of King Nanda, and in that palace lived the heart of Her heart. Radha sighed but said nothing. Meanwhile, Lalita looked to the far end of the room.

A silent group of gopis huddled against the marble wall, absorbed in empathy for their friend. Lalita silently called Visakha, whose rustling skirt and tinkling ankle bells lightened the sombre mood.

Lalita and Visakha are wise. What is unknown to them is not to be known by anyone else. Their only concern is Radha’s pleasure; indeed, they constantly think, “How can we make Radha happy?”

Distraught, Radha undid Her serpentine braid, removing the jewel- lotus and silk ribbon from its end. As She gazed at the blackness of Her own hair, innumerable desires rose to the surface of Her heart.

Radha’s hands froze, and She stared in stunned silence at Her hair. Lalita and Visakha exchanged glances. “If we do not pacify the princess,” they thought, “Her melancholy will spread like a plague.

“First we will die, then Vrndavana will perish, and finally the universe will be consumed by Her sorrow.” Lalita stroked Radha’s hair, “Friend! When You heard Krsna’s flute, I blocked Your ears.

“When You gazed at Krsna’s handsome form, I covered Your eyes. Yet despite my efforts, You were determined to be captivated.” Radha sighed, and Her heavy breath withered the flowers in Her garland.

“O beautiful girl!” Lalita continued. “Day by day You are more and more enchanted by that bluish-black boy. But what will be the result? In the end You will have passed Your entire life simply weeping.”

Now Visakha spoke up, “Friend! For no reason You pine for Madhava. Look at what has become of You! Faded complexion, sunken eyes, emaciated — Your body wastes away, Your life at risk.

“You planted a tree of love in the private garden of Your heart and expected the Krsna-cloud to water it. Alas! The only rains are the tears from Your lotus eyes. What good can such salty water do?”

Radha raised Her pitiful face. Voice quivering, She said, “What can I do? I do not understand what has happened. This is all very new to a chaste girl like Me. When I see Krsna, I lose My composure.

“When I do not see Krsna, I am tossed upon high waves of anguish. See Him or not, My condition is the same. How can I look away? I burn in flames, but My heart is still enchanted.”

Looking from Lalita to Visakha, Radha continued, “O friends! You are very wise. What can I say to you? I am possessed by a host of longings. If I cannot meet Krsna, I fear I shall soon lose My life.”

Radha returned to staring out the window. As if possessed She whispered, “Please help Me.” This was all too much for Lalita. Visakha, equally upset, squeezed Lalita’s hand, and with a glance said:

“Lalita! This is no time to lose hope. Make Radha write a letter to Her beloved. That will steady Her.” Lalita felt encouraged. What better way to engage Radha’s unhinged mind than composing a love letter?

A message to Krsna would appeal to Him, and a heartfelt entreaty would surely bring the two together. Lalita smiled. Stroking Radha’s head, she gently lifted Radha’s chin and looked into Her eyes.

Radha took heart at the hope in Lalita’s face. And comforted by Lalita’s touch, She braved a slight smile. Lalita ventured, “Overcome by unhappiness in separation from You, Krsna lies awake all night.

“Absorbed in thoughts of You, He embraces His yellow *dhoti,* speaks nonsense, and repeatedly falls to the ground. His friends say that He is in such a state He cannot even taste the sweetness of sugar.”

Visakha added, “They say He just gazes at the moon. Separated from You, He feels distraught. His body is gaunt and lustreless. To hide in darkness He calls the clouds, and when they depart He sighs.”

“He lives by the sound of Your names. While singing Your praises, the hairs on His body stand on end and tears stream from His eyes. Radha! Fortune has blessed You. You are the object of Krsna’s love.

“All these symptoms reveal His deep love for You. I have never heard of such an able, considerate, and kind-hearted lover as Krsna.” Seeing Radha encouraged, Lalita suggested, “Now write a letter.

“Tell Krsna how You feel and insist that only a meeting — if even for the twinkling of an eye — will save You from death. Friend! He who drowns in an ocean of sorrow will rush to Your side and give You joy.”

Taking her cue, a demure young *gopi* quickly brought ink, a writing stylus, and a lotus petal on a golden tray. As she approached her mistress, the girl smiled bashfully at Srimati Radharani.

The princess thought of Krsna lying on His bed, eyes closed, lips still, hands folded over His heart. She saw tears flow in waves from eyes that were once unable to resist the amorous glances of other *gopis.*

In Her mind’s eye Radha saw sad, drawn-out sighs escape like a tempest from a mouth that once always smiled. Her friends were right: Krsna was suffering from the poisonous effects of love in separation.

Too shy to reveal Her heart, Radha said, “O Lalita! You write the letter! You are the wisest of My friends, and you know the secrets of My heart. Can Krsna refuse your request? I think not.

“Describe My condition. I beg you! Tell Him, ‘If Radha does not see You, She will not continue to live.’” Lalita took Radha’s hand and said, “If You do not compose the letter with Your own hand —

“If You do not woo Him with Your own heart’s singular affection, Krsna will not be pacified. He wants no substitute for Radha. If You want Him, the letter must be from You and no one else.”

Radha’s blue eyes looked to Her friends for confirmation. They all nodded in agreement. Visakha-devi placed the tray on Radha’s lap and said, “Radhika! You must write. We will help You.”

Radha was like a flash of lightning as it strikes the ocean shore, a golden lake full of newly blossomed lotus flowers, a jasmine vine of sublime love. She was everything pure, good, young, and lovely.

When She gazed at the writing tray before Her, it was as if Krsna was sitting on Her lap eagerly waiting for Her attention. Radharani held the stylus aloft as if to seal the fate of a million universes.

**\* \* \* \***

Radha gazed at the lotus petal and saw dark Krsna gazing at Her with bumblebee eyes. As She closed Her eyes, She saw His youthful form within Her heart. Where was He not, this black apparition of love?

The ink was vermilion, the colour of Radha’s ecstasy. She dipped the stylus into it and then touched stylus to leaf. Carefully She wrote “Krs”— and that was all. A torrent of emotions overpowered Her.

Countless volumes of Vedic wisdom are unable to describe what Radha perceived in but an instant. She erupted with divine passion, like a volcano from which flowed the molten lava of pure love.

The waves of Her ecstasies crashed on all sides. The walls melted and the floor gave way as Her friends looked on. In an instant, the *gopis* were forcibly dragged into the vortex of Radha’s absorption in love.

It was as if they were one with Radha — seeing, feeling, smelling, hearing, and tasting as She did. And Radha saw Krsna dressed in yellow silk, playing the flute, and smiling more sweetly than Cupid.

In the syllable *krs,* Radha saw Krsna’s form, His many qualities, His daily pastimes, His sublime abode. Through *krs* She entered Krsna’s heart, saw His love, knew His anguish, desired and felt His desires.

In the syllable *krs,* Radha saw the one who attracts the *gopis, gopas,* cows, calves, birds, beasts, plants, and rivers of Vrndavana. In *krs* She perceived Herself as His transcendental counter-whole.

In the syllable *krs,* which is eternally joined with the syllable *na,* Her own self in sound, Radha realised that Krsna is the complete form of the Absolute Truth sought by great transcendentalists.

In the syllable *krs,* Radha perceived the whole of existence, notably the one thing universally beneficial: service to Krsna. She saw the syllabic *krs* as the source and repose of all things that be.

In the syllable *krs,* Radha saw Her own joy and suffering, hope and despair, Her purpose and Her very life. In *krs* She saw a bridge spanning the chasm of adversity and leading to a meeting with Krsna.

To describe the other things Radha and Her *gopi* friends found in just half of Krsna’s name would require one of those *gopis* to dictate to the great Vyasadeva, who could then put them into words for us to read.

Like miners who finally strike a vein of gold and cannot stop until their bounty has been extracted, Radha and the other *gopis* distilled ecstatic truths from one half of Krsna’s name — and hours passed.

Finally, as the afternoon sun peeked through the window, Yogamaya gently broke Radha’s and the *gopis*’ trance and gradually brought them back to awareness of their external surroundings.

Radha was still sitting with the letter before Her, stylus in hand, and the *gopis* were still surrounding Her, looking on. As if awakened from deep sleep, the *gopis* stared at one another, at Radha, and at the sun.

One *prahara* had passed.Visakha spoke to Lalita through a glance, “Friend, at this rate the letter will take millenniums to write!” Her hand still on Radha’s hair, Lalita said, “O Radha, beloved of Krsna!

“You have composed a very nice letter. I think You have included everything that needs to be said, and more. In repeated lifetimes, Krsna may someday come to the end of this letter.”

Puzzled, Radha stared at the petal in Her hand. Her ecstasy would not allow Her to comprehend what Lalita meant. All She could see was “Krs— ”. Again, with a quizzical look, She glanced at Her friends.

Visakha added, “Let us send this excellent letter to Krsna through a reliable messenger.” With a flick of her eyebrows Visakha-devi called Rati-manjari, who shyly stepped forward.

Visakha carefully took the lotus petal from Radha’s hand, rolled it up, put it into a golden container, and handed it to Rati, who touched the container to her forehead before hiding it in her outer cloth.

Srimati Radharani reached out and took Rati’s hand. Neither of them spoke, but Radha caught Rati’s innocent gaze and for what seemed to be a very long time looked deep into her dark eyes.

The senders of hand-delivered letters usually give fitting instructions to their messengers. In the silent language of glances, Radha told Rati what to do and when finished, let go of her delicate hand.

Shadowed by a few close friends, Rati left for Vraja’s pastures — and for Krsna. She had no idea where Krsna was, but from within her heart Radha would guide her so that not a moment would be lost.

**\* \* \* \***

After leaving Nandagrama, Krsna and the *gopas* herded their cows towards Govardhana Hill. Govinda busied Himself by playing games with His friends to keep His mind from running to Sri Radha.

Despite His best efforts, Krsna was unable to ignore His heartache. The cows followed Vraja’s fresh grasses and grazed their way to Manasa-ganga, where they and the boys drank its cool water.

The *gopas* happily splashed in Ganga’s waves until tired and then they returned to shore, where Krsna sat in their midst and laughed as He fed them savouries, mangoes, condensed milk, and yogurt.

Once everyone was full, Krsna announced, “O friends! Please rest awhile with the cows. Subala, Madhu, and I want to roam the forest and enjoy the beauty of the season. We’ll be back shortly.”

Krsna wandered pensively through the valleys of Govardhana with His two friends following behind. Wherever He turned, Krsna saw Radha — in the water, in the trees, even in Vraja’s forest creatures.

With every step Krsna’s heart ached more and more. His smile faded into a frown, His face lost its lustre. To ease their dear friend’s pain, the birds sang, deer played, and peacocks danced.

But Krsna remained morose. Can a few palmfuls of water satisfy a thirst for an ocean of nectar? Soon the trio came to an ancient *bakula* tree, where Krsna sat upon its tangled roots and stared into space.

Subala and Madhu, painfully aware of Krsna’s plight, sat to cither side of Him exchanging worried looks. As Krsna sighed, the hot breath of sorrow swept through the valleys like a searing wind.

Subala, his voice heavy with affection, said, “Friend! What is wrong? Why have You left Your blissful cows and *gopas* to sulk in this lonely place? Obviously You are distressed. Please tell us what is wrong.”

Madhumangala said, “Your peacock feather and flower garland fell to the ground some time ago, hut You didn’t even notice. Only dire straits could cause such bewilderment. Gopala! What is it?”

“Nothing is wrong,” Krsna replied. But Subala insisted, “Friend! You can’t hide from us! We can see Your heart.” Madhu added, “I think Your troubles come from having seen something beyond compare.”

“How could Madhu understand My mind?” thought Krsna. Though silent, the floodgates of Krsna’s heart had burst, and as Subala slowly rubbed his dear friend’s chest, hot tears fell upon his hand.

Startled, Subala called out, “O Govinda!” He then went on, “What are these tears? Why are You crying? O friend! You are my life. Seeing You in such a state breaks my heart into a hundred pieces.

“Hari! Gopala! For Your happiness I will walk to the ends of the earth and back and give up my life a thousand times. Tell me what it is You want, and I will get it. Reveal Your pain to me, and I will cure it.”

“How can I deceive such loyal friends?” thought Krsna. Now openly sobbing, He blurted out, “Friends, My heart is yours! What can I hide? To you, I am an open book. Listen, I will tell you My secret.”

Madhu held Krsna close to his rotund belly and said, “Tell us. There is nothing we will not do for You.” Krsna began, “It is like this: every morning as I enter the forest, a girl comes into My vision.

“Endowed with magical charms, She enters My heart and enchants My mind like a tantric abducts the spirit of his victim. Though I play My flute and tend the cows, I cannot think of anything but Her.”

To Subala, Krsna said, “I have tried to forget Her but, alas, I cannot. O Subala, My friend! I am forced to admit that I can no longer live without this bewitching girl. Therefore, I am undone.”

Subala said, “O Krsna! Who is this girl?” Madhu added, “What does She look like?” Krsna closed His eyes and envisioned Radha, framed by a palace doorway, like a gold deity in a jewelled temple.

“I do not know who She is. Although She can only be compared to Herself, I can say that She shines like lightning, Her sari is like a cloud, Her ornaments are like swans, and Her beauty is unlimited.”

Wide-eyed, as if possessed, Krsna concluded, “I can’t tell if She is human or an enchantress from heaven. Sometimes I see Her walking in the sky, sometimes upon water, sometimes within My heart.”

Having said this, Krsna fell silent. A moment later Subala slapped his thigh gently and laughed with surprise. Glancing at Madhu he said, “Syama! Worry no longer. I know who Your beloved is.

“Who else could stand upon the turret of a palace like lightning in a cloud but Radha, the daughter of King Vrsabhanu? The unparalleled beauty You speak of is to be found in Her alone, and no one else.”

But when Krsna heard the name Radha He became even more disturbed. His body shook and His hairs stood on end. Madhu, with His chubby arms, embraced His friend and tried to console Him.

“Friend! Fear not!” Madhu said. “With my command of Vedic spells and skill in mixing potions I shall bring this girl to You without delay. I will gather herbs from the forest and chant the mantras at once.”

And Subala said, “On the strength of my arms, which never fail in subduing demons, I vow to You that we will arrange a meeting with Your beloved. She will become a flower garland around Your neck.”

Madhu added, “Friend! Now all we need to do is find Radha and think of some way to approach Her. If only one of Her friends were picking flowers nearby, we could find Radha and plan our next step.”

The words and desires of Krsna’s dear friends moved the compass of divine fate. Just as the boys were speaking, Rati and her girlfriends arrived, as timid as wide-eyed does stepping out into a forest meadow.

At the sight of Krsna the girls were apprehensive. But, spurred on by their fealty to Radha’s love, they strode bravely into His presence, albeit with eyes turned shyly towards the ground.

Making much of this divine coincidence, Madhu bragged, “Just witness the mystic power of a pure *brahmana.* Simply by my desire these girls, led by Radha’s dearest Rati, have appeared.”

From the basket on her arm, Rati handed Madhumangala a garland, prepared by Radha and still fragrant from Her touch. Krsna craned His neck to see the garland and then marveled at its artistry.

And when a laughing Madhumangala hung it around Krsna’s neck, Krsna felt not only the garland but also the touch of Radha’s hand. Eager to see Radha, He asked: “Friend! Is your mistress well?”

Rati spoke directly to Krsna, “By the grace of the Supreme, She is well.” Krsna asked, “Where is She now?” Looking back at the path, Rati answered, “At home with Her friends.”

Krsna could not hide His disappointment, “Won’t She come to the forest to worship Her deity?” Rati replied, “Lord! It will not be possible. She is a young bride and Her elders will not let Her out.”

Krsna was despondent. He asked, speaking almost in a whisper, “Then what is She doing?” Feeling Krsna’s pain, Rati replied, “Mad in separation from You, She was churning water in the yogurt pot.”

A moment’s silence passed and then Krsna prodded, “Then...?” Rati replied, “Thinking Her to be possessed, Her in-laws locked Her in the house. Desperate to see You, She cries pitifully like a caged bird.”

Krsna was filled with conflicting emotions. He was overjoyed to hear that Radha loved Him in return, but unhappy to hear that She was confined to Her home. Would fate ever smile upon Them?

Krsna’s disappointment distressed Rati. But spurred on by her friends’ glances, she said, “O joy of Vraja! Don’t be sad! Your beloved desires to meet You, and for that reason She has written You a letter.”

“A letter!” Krsna exclaimed. “She wrote Me a letter?” Rati reached into her apron for the golden container and, while Krsna watched excitedly, she removed the lotus petal as if it were a priceless treasure.

Rati held out the love letter and said, “Krsna! Please take this lotus petal.” Krsna looked at the petal in Rati’s hand but before taking it He removed a *gunja* necklace from His neck and garlanded her.

Still looking at the lotus petal in Rati’s hand, Krsna said to Himself, “Heart! Be peaceful! Be happy! This flower petal is the fully ripened fruit that has grown from the seed of your desire.”

Tossed by turbulent emotions, Krsna was afraid to read Radha’s letter, and so He requested Madhu, “Dear friend! Please read this letter. I have no doubt it must be a reservoir of nectar for the ears.”

Madhu eagerly accepted the letter, but upon opening it he saw “Krs” and nothing else. Madhu may be greedy for sweets and given always to humour, but he is also a peerless connoisseur of *rasa.*

“Only Krsna is qualified to read this letter,” he thought. When Krsna impatiently insisted that he begin reading, Madhumangala rolled his eyes and replied, “Friend. This is an exceedingly long letter.”

“Friend! Read it!” Krsna demanded. But Madhu shook his head good- naturedly and handed the letter to Krsna, saying, “Better You read it. This sort of letter is best read only by the one for whom it is meant.”

**\* \* \* \***

As Krsna took the letter His body shook as if He were directly seeing Radha. He said, “As the full moon in the month of Jyaistha causes violent waves in the Ganga, so does Radha act upon My heart.”

Madhumangala asked curiously, “By the touch of this letter does this girl now stand before You?” Krsna answered, “Friend! Due to your blessings and to My own good fortune, Radha has come to Me. Look!

“With the flowering vines of Her eyebrows, the restless glances of Her eyes, Radha teaches graceful deer the art of casting sidelong glances.” Krsna laughed and continued to speak as if Radha were present.

“Whenever I look at this girl with *bimba-f*ruit lips, angry Kamadeva aims his flower arrows at Me.” Eager to encourage his friend, Subala wondered aloud, “Perhaps You two have met before?”

“No, no!” protested Krsna. “How could We have met? Whenever Radha’s soothing moon-like face treads lightly upon the pathway of My eyes, My mother forces Me to return home for supper.”

Madhumangala teased, “Friend! There are so many beautiful *gopis* in Vrndavana. Why do You love only Radha with such feeling?” Smiling slightly and speaking in a far-off voice, Krsna answered, “Madhu!

“In Radha there resides such sweetness that upon seeing Her beautiful lotus eyes I feel like rejecting the moon. If you simply think about Radha, you too will know something of Her glory.”

Still eager to hear the letter, which after all was the subject at hand, Subala curiously craned his neck to look over Krsna’s shoulder, and softly enquired, “Krsna! What does the letter say?”

Krsna blinked to clear His lotus eyes and obediently looked at the letter. He saw before Him the syllable *krs* and nothing more, but it was effulgent like a hundred suns and cooling like a hundred moons.

Each character was an expansive ocean of knowledge that encompassed Cupid’s teachings in condensed form, a revelation of Radha’s love, and the essence of sweetness, beauty, and bliss.

Krsna marveled at the beauty of the characters — their ink’s dark glossy lustre, their mysterious calligraphy, their effect on His heart. From the syllable *krs* He saw His hundred names expand.

Nay, He saw His thousand names — rather, His million names — as sung by saints. Krsna fell headlong into the bottomless well of infinite significance that is the syllable *krs,* and He saw Himself as Radha did.

Still curious, Subala again enquired, “Friend! What does the letter say?” Krsna tried to speak, but His throat was choked with emotion. After some time He cleared His voice, wiped His eyes, and read aloud:

“‘O supremely beautiful Syamasundara! This letter is not made of words. Your humble maidservant petitions You from the innermost core of Her heart. Please spare a few moments to hear Her plea.

“‘In this letter love has personally appeared upon a lotus petal to declare its own desires and to make those desires known to You. Listen carefully, for the life of a certain *gopi* hangs in the balance.

“‘O Krsna! The artistic loveliness of Your form is permanently etched in My mind. Because Your beauty causes Me constant distress I run here and there for relief, but wherever I go You block My path.

“‘This is My dilemma. Tell Me what to do! Your youthful beauty surpasses all things in this world. If the gently splashing waves of Your smile make Kamadeva faint from bliss, what will become of Me?

“‘Each time You smile — and smile, and smile — Your limbs sway to and fro, sharp arrows shoot from Your eyes, jasmine garlands sway on Your chest, and *tilaka* glistens on Your forehead. Oh, what a wonder!

“‘I do not know what happened when I first saw You. It felt as if an arrow had pierced My life’s breath. My normally peaceful composure fled to a faraway place, and restlessness took hold of Me.

“‘Now, for no apparent reason, I constantly weep. Fearful of what My elders might say, I’ve told no one of My plight and I simply hide in My room. No one knows what has happened to Me — not even I.’’’

Krsna looked up at His friends, His cheeks wet with tears. Madhumangala wiped Krsna’s tears away with his shawl and softly said, “Friend! Her love is indeed great. You are uniquely fortunate.”

Gazing at the letter with eyes full of emotion, Krsna continued, “‘I hide My face behind My veil, but tears soak My garments. I repeatedly laugh without rhyme or reason. Ever so often I sigh deeply.

‘“My body burns with fever. Not a slight fever, but the fever that comes just before death. Torn by agony, I roll on the ground. Except for Your image My mind is vacant, thus I can say nothing to others.

“‘My dear girlfriends are tossed into an ocean of sorrow to see the state I am in. They have discussed the matter amongst themselves, hut they do not know how to help Me. O Hari! If I die, so will they.

“‘The thought of their demise is intolerable for Me. Please do not be the cause of death for young girls! By Your wish I shall live, and if I do, so will My friends. I place this petition at Your lotus feet.’”

Krsna cried, as did Madhu, Subala, Rati, and her friends. Their tears flowed to the ground and pooled together, forming a pond in which the glistening aquatics of ecstatic separation swam playfully.

“Hari!” Rati sobbed. “If You do not meet Radha, I cannot say what will happen. Separated from You, Her heart is overwhelmed by pain, and that pain is clearly dragging Her towards death’s doorstep.

“Her beautiful eyes, once petals in Her lotus face, are now two Gangotris from which flow rivers of tears. Her breath is like searing fire. Restless, She has lost all patience, and She is always unkempt.

“Because She repeatedly falls to the ground, She is constantly covered with dust. And although intelligent *gopis* try their best to speak with Her, She cannot, or will not, utter a single word in reply.

“At this very moment She is unconscious. I cannot say whether or not Her life’s breath will stay within Her body. O Lord! I have been witness to these things, and I implore You: please meet Her.”

Rati’s friends supported her testimony by nodding but had nothing else to add. Krsna looked at Madhu and then Subala. For several moments everyone tolerated a prolonged and awkward silence.

At this chance to serve his dear friend — as well as Radha — Subala said, “Such a heartfelt letter soaked in emotion deserves a proper reply. Krsna! You must write to Radha and fulfil Her heart’s desire.”

Rati needed no prompting. At once she reached into her basket and produced a lotus leaf, stylus, and ink. With uncharacteristic boldness she leapt before Krsna and thrust the stationery into His hand.

Having placed the leaf upon His lap, Krsna readied the stylus to begin His letter. Slowly, He wrote “Ra” and stopped. That was all He wrote. Radha could only write “Krs.” And all He could write was “Ra.”

But why? What was it about this one syllable, ra, full of wonder, which at once captured His mind, forced itself from His lips, unsettled His senses, and set His distress free to run rampant?

What was this wonderful syllabic ra, which shows love Tilled devotees the futility of all material goals, whose letters represent the goddess of fortune Rama, and the foremost *gopi,* Sri Radha Herself?

What was this wonder ra, which when combined with *dha,* reverberated in His heart like a drum roll, and which caused Him to fly haphazardly in the sweet wind of *radha-nama* like a drunken bee?

What was *ra*? It was the magic mirror in which Krsna saw the future — the bank of the Yamuna on a full-moon night, a lamp-lit *kunja,* and Himself waiting for Srimati Radharani.

In these two letters Krsna could hear ankle bells and the music of the *rasa* dance, see mind-enchanting dance steps, and feel the joy of a meeting that would begin with the words “You have come!”

The syllable *ra* was a crystal ball in which Krsna could see dance- fatigued *gopis,* water sports in the Yamuna, a dinner beneath the stars, and the calm before sunrise only lovers can know.

Those letters, shaped like a string of pearls, were a hidden path to Sri Radha, a bridge that spanned the chasm between separation and meeting, a mantra that would award Krsna full freedom.

Finally, *ra* was a wise sage who detected Krsna’s heart’s longing, who knew of His love for Sri Radha, who championed His eagerness for meeting with Her, and who advised Krsna how to realise His goal.

Since Krsna is the origin of everything, and the syllable *ra* meant everything to Him, what could *ra* not have been? Still, more important than all else, *ra* declared Krsna’s submission to Radha.

**\* \* \* \***

Still gazing at what He had written, convinced that this syllable alone would secure a meeting with His beloved, Krsna handed the letter to Madhu. Subala and Madhu read it and exchanged knowing glances.

As the birds in their perches jostled with one another for a vantage point from which to read the letter, Madhu rolled it up, touched it to his forehead, and gave it to Rati, who received it with great respect.

Placing the lotus leaf into the gold container, Rati bowed before Krsna and His friends and then, like the morning mist, vanished along with the other girls, leaving only dainty footprints behind.

Just then Krsna heard the distant sound of bugles and lowing cows, a sign that the rest of His companions were anxious for His return, and so He left to meet them, now confident that happiness would be His.

Krsna had received Radha’s letter and read everything She had wanted to say. In return, He had also revealed His heart in a letter of His own. In two syllables Radha and Krsna had said everything.

As morose as Krsna had felt that morning entering the forest, He now felt happy leaving it. He had full faith in the power of Radha’s name. And He had no doubt that She would fulfil His request.

That evening He would accommodate His parents as usual. But after His mother had put Him to sleep, Krsna would climb out His bedroom window and head for the shore of the Yamuna River, alone.

Just as the written syllables of the divine couple’s names had conveyed Their mutual affection, those same syllables, when spoken, would also direct Radha and Krsna to the unknown meeting place.

Meanwhile, Rati had returned to Yavata, where she proudly placed Krsna’s letter in her mistress’s hands and watched Radha— tentative yet eager — gaze at the lotus petal glowing with splendour.

“O Radha!” said Rati. “Krsna was swept away with emotion when He received Your jasmine garland. Tears of love streamed from His eyes, and He incessantly chanted a mantra composed of Your glories.

“My dear beautiful friend! Syamasundara’s love for You runs deep, like an underwater stream. The girls of our village may flatter Him, but even in His dreams Krsna loves no one but You.

“Smitten with love, that jewel amongst men rolls on the ground chanting *ra* and then *dha.* And as streams of tears flood His eyes, He is unable to utter anything but the sound of Your name.

“O Vrsabhanu-nandini! I fall at Your feet and beg: Remove Your own suffering by removing His. Meet Krsna on the moonlit bank of the Yamuna and bring peace to the hearts of Your friends.

“Now You must read that gentle cowherd’s letter. Even the petal upon which He has written it is pleasing to the eyes and the heart. Just imagine, then, the many wonderful things waiting within.”

Looking again at the letter She held in Her hands, Radha trembled, perspired, and cried tears of joy as She slowly unrolled it and then read with a trembling voice, ‘“O beautiful princess of Varsana.

‘“From the day I first saw You, My life changed. I was a carefree *gopa* playing in the fields of Vraja, hut now I am held captive by the tiny hope that You may bless Me with a casual, sidelong glance.

‘“My friends try to console Me, not knowing the reason I am so morose. But I find solace in the image of Your smile, Your complexion, Your hair, and Your matchlessly beautiful form.

‘“O Radha! Your transcendental beauty is a reflection of Your heart. That which is within You is revealed by Your peerless form. I am but a part of what We are together; without You, I have no life.

‘“What wings are to a bird, what the sun is to the world, what the soul is to the body, You are to Me. If You think I should live, if You think I deserve to see You in person, meet Me by the bank of the Yamuna.

‘“Beneath the *kadamba* trees, where cuckoos sing and bees hum, please allow Me to serve You, for You are the queen of My heart, My Radharani, My worshipable Deity, and I am Your servant, eternally.

Radha fell silent and placed the letter gently on Her lap. With Her face still turned down, an uncontrollable smile appeared on Her lips — the kind of smile Her friends had not seen for many days.

Suddenly raising Her head and looking around, Radha excitedly said, “He has accepted Me! O My friends! I must meet Krsna by the Yamuna tonight. Please help Me to look My very best.”

And so it was that the gloom over Yavata lifted. After selecting clothes and ornaments that would be most pleasing to Krsna, Radha was bathed, anointed, dressed, and ornamented by Her happy friends.

And when the *gopis* had finished, they all stood back to see their handiwork. “Do you think He will like Me?” Srimati Radharani humbly asked. Visakha wiped tears of wonder from her face.

“Devi!” she exclaimed. “In a bathing dress and otherwise unadorned, Your beauty could make demigods fall from the sky like rain. But words cannot do justice to the way You appear just now.

“Yes, He will like You! I only hope the fainting spell He has upon seeing You does not delay Your pastimes forever.” Unable to restrain herself, Visakha embraced Radha as the other *gopis* crowded around.

At nightfall, followed by Her happy friends who each carried the accoutrements for her particular service, Radha crossed beyond the threshold of Her home — and of Vraja’s religious traditions.

Radha did not hesitate to plunge into the forest. With Her great love and eagerness to please Krsna, She ground into dust any obstacle between Them, dust that then mingled with the dust of Vraja.

When everyone in Nandagrama had gone to sleep, Krsna left home and, with the heat of His excitement, turned the sand beneath His feet into diamond dust, which also mixed with the dust of Vraja.

Krsna had neither map, nor guide, nor lamp with which to find His way. But by chanting “Radha! Radha!” His journey was quick, without incident, and — at His destination — greatly rewarding.

Upon arriving at the riverside Krsna finally beheld Radha. At the sight of Him, Her girlfriends crept into the shadows of the forest to watch in silence as Krsna gazed at Radha, and She gazed back at Him.

After so much waiting, so much anticipation, the divine couple finally stood face-to-face. It was Their first meeting; or was it? They were both certain that They had met many, many times before.

By having spoken each other’s names many times in separation, They had seen and felt each other’s presence many times before. Those meetings were no less real than the meeting They now relished.

Both Radha and Krsna thought, “The person here before Me is the embodiment of the name I have been cherishing in My heart.” The first words They spoke, then, where each other’s names.

And as They did, the *gopis* hiding nearby, the forest creatures and foliage alike all repeated those same two names — Radha and Krsna — as they fully relished the divine couple’s first meeting.

**\* \* \* \***

By the grace of just one syllable of Krsna’s name, Sri Radha had won His heart, and by the grace of one syllable of Radha’s name, Sri Krsna had won Hers. Such is the inconceivable power of *hari-nama.*

By the grace of those two sacred syllables, every obstacle to Their meeting was removed. And by the grace of the syllables not yet uttered, even Their untold desires would be completely fulfilled.

By the power of those syllables, the intimate companions of Radha and Krsna entered Their pastimes, became aware of Their love for each other, and, most important, tasted the mellows of that love.

If such wonders can come to pass by uttering just two syllables, what can happen if one recites Radha’s and Krsna’s full names thousands of times daily? Those devotees who are eager to know will find out.

By chanting the nectarean names of Radha and Krsna, worldly men are absolved of their sins, practising devotees attain perfection, and pure devotees swim in an ocean of unparalleled mellows.

The esoteric truths of Radha s and Krsna’s names are Goloka’s emporium of divine gems that become glistening ornaments on the cars of pure-hearted devotees who chant those names with love.

Dear reader! Please relish and treasure within your heart of hearts the following verse, which is a veritable wellspring of the truths spoken of in this pastime. It is the essence of the *Vedas.*

Narottama Dasa Thakura sings,

*krsna-nama-gane badi radhika-carana pai radha-nama-gdne krsnacandra*  
*sanksepe kahila katha ghucahamaneravyatha duhkha-maya anya-katha-dvandva*

**“O brother! If you chant the name of Krsna, Radhika, being pleased with you, will bless you in many ways, and if you chant the name of Radha, Krsna will be pleased to fulfill your innermost desires.**

**“This instruction is the essence of all advice, beyond which there is nothing, and by which all troubles fly away. If you hear words to the contrary, ignore them, for they will only bring you sorrow.”**

This concludes the pastime of how Radha and Krsna displayed Their incomparable love for each other through a mutual attraction to the wonders and sweetness inherent in each other’s names.

Hearing this pastime will increase our affection for the Supreme Lord’s names and considerably enhance our taste for chanting the *maha-mantra.* What greater gain could there be?

Now let us hear the glories of the Deities of Radha-Syamasundara alongside those of the Hare Krsna *maha-mantra.* They are not different from each other as the named and the names, respectively.

Many great *acaryas* have praised the divine couple through their glorification of the *maha-mantra*. I feel inspired to follow in their footsteps. May they permit me to do so in my own words and style.

Of course, my effort will likely resemble a child trying to catch the moon. May the saints forgive my audacity. I am not qualified to make such an attempt, but I am impelled by my faith in the holy name.

In comparison to Radha and Krsna, great devotees see the sun to be a firefly, *cintamani* gems mere pebbles, desire trees thorn bushes, and the universe a clump of straw. I seek the blessings of such Vaisnavas.

O Radha and Syama! At the beginning, middle, and end of my nights and days, my meditations and wanderings, my fasts and feasts, my sacrifices and diversions, You — and You alone — are my goal.

As Sri Sarvabhauma once said,

**“We are not poets, not logicians, not eloquent speakers, nor philosophers who have crossed to the farthest shore of** ***Vedanta.*** **We are the servants of a rascal cowherd youth.”**

O sublime mantra of deliverance! O supreme wealth of Goloka! I desire to say something about the vibrations embedded in the letters and syllables that make up Your names. Please allow me to do so.

In this and the following chapters, I praise but a few drops from the nectar-ocean of the holy name’s glories, the tiniest of samples gleaned from the rare privilege of serving the divine couple.

I hope one day to directly taste the joy of serving Their pastimes; still, the ambrosia of simply aspiring for such a privilege is so excruciatingly sweet that my mind and senses regularly drown in happiness.

The kindness and generosity of pure devotional service mixed with *nama-sankirtana* is so relishable that at every stage of practice — from the first to the last —one tastes a joy uniquely his own.

This is because Krsna reciprocates our attempts to offer ourselves as His servants. He gives us a chance to taste loving service by revealing its potency in proportion to the purity of our hearts.

This loving reciprocation is enacted through the transcendental medium of the all-merciful guide, friend, and guardian of practising and perfected devotees alike — the Hare Krsna *maha-mantra.*

To invoke blessings and to help us drink from the *surabhi* cow of Krsna’s holy names, let us chant

*Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare*  
*Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare*

**\* \* \* \***

O, noble readers of refined judgement! The chanting of Krsna’s jholy names is the priceless key to the kingdom of Vraja, where joyful cowherds engage in never-ending, ever-fresh pastimes of love.

The eight pairs of names that comprise the *maha-mantra* are just one of many groups of “eights” found in the realm of pure devotion. Let us meditate upon these divine groupings according to our moods.

These “eights” include the stages of pure devotion leading to love, the stages of love from *prema* to *mahabhava,* the parts of Krsna’s day and their related pastimes, and the divine couple’s limbs.

In *Bhajana-rahasya* Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that the eight pairs of names correspond to the eight verses of Lord Caitanya’s *Siksastaka*, composed to elucidate the *maha-mantras* many meanings.

*Sri-caitanya-mukhodgirna hare-krsneti-varnakah*  
*majjayanto jagat premni vijayantam tad-ahvayah*

**“Glory to the** ***maha-mantra*****, whose names flow from Sri Caitanya’s mouth to drown the world in love.”**

This and the following three chapters follow the structure of *Bhajana*-*rahasya,* citing scriptural verses quoted by the Thakura that elaborate on his statements. My own realisations are also included.

Allow me to share with you, to the best of my ability, what I have assimilated from the teachings of Lord Caitanya and His followers regarding the eight pairs of names that comprise the *maha-mantra.*

The *maha-mantra* is said to he both the means and the end of pure devotion. But this “end" is not the kind that stops; rather, this end stays with us forever as we chant Krsna’s names eternally in Goloka.

The *maha-mantra* is an *avatara* of Radha and Krsna. It has descended from Vraja to enact a lengthy and dynamic performance upon the stage of our tongues for the sole purpose of delivering us.

But when the curtain has closed on the final act of our deliverance, the *maha-mantra* does not retire. Rather it acquires another stage for its eternal purpose —it dances forever upon our spiritual tongues.

The first Hare Krsna is a desperate call for help uttered by those souls lost in the material wilderness who have by some untold fortune come to subdue their ignorance and invest their faith in the Lord.

The second Hare Krsna conveys the relief that we feel under the shelter of devotional service in practice and the joy we relish by making Goloka Vrndavana our ultimate destination.

The names Krsna Krsna suggest our firm faith in Krsna’s divinity and our ongoing commitment to pure devotional service or, more specifically, to the attainment of the pure name *(suddha-nama*).

The names Hare Hare reveal the purified hearts of devotees who, by serving Krsna, have come to realise that Radha is not only Krsna’s confidential energy but also the centrepiece of His pastimes.

These eight names in the *maha-mantra* also symbolise regulated devotion, the stage of Krsna consciousness meant for the world at large to see, and for neophyte and intermediate devotees to practise.

The first Hare Rama is the sacred threshold we cross to enter the *sanctum sanctorum* of purified thoughts of Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes, wherein our minds are drawn to the bliss of *vraja-bhakti.*

The second Hare Rama expresses the ecstatic yearning that comes from having been embraced by the Lord’s internal potency as we finally realise the divine consciousness for which we have long toiled.

The names Rama Rama are a call for service like that of the Vraja- vasis, for whom Krsna is everything, and especially the *gopis,* for whom Krsna is the transcendental Cupid who incites their passion.

The final Hare Hare is the recognition that Krsna is owned and controlled by Srimati Radharani, and our plea for the shelter of *gopis* like Lalita, who is the be-all and end-all for maidservants like Rupa.

The last eight names of the *maha-mantra* encapsulate Goloka’s treasure — spontaneous loving service — which is hidden in the hearts of great souls and is rarely spoken about, even amongst them.

O my deliverer, friend, guru, and constant companion! O sacred *maha-mantra* joyfully chanted by the topmost amongst saintly devotees! O immovable anchor in this ever-changing world!

O *maha-mantra*, no different from my worshipable Radha-Syama, I am an unqualified aspirant rolling in the *cintamani* dust of Your lotus feet. Please forgive my impudence as I attempt to glorify You.

Since only You know Yourself, please guide my hand, that I may record only that which You desire — no more, no less. Sivarama Dasa, the servant of Your lotus feet and Your mission, bows before You.

**\* \* \* \***

Uttering the first two words of the Hare Krsna mantra removes the curtain of ignorance covering conditioned souls and reveals the ultimate reality to he the forms of love and beauty, Radha and Krsna.

Hare, the vocative form of Hara (or Hari), pervades the other names of the mantra, Krsna and Rama, and refines the chanter’s mood to one of humble entreaty that grows in intensity as chanting develops.

Krsna’s words *pranipatena pariprasnena sevaya* establish submission, enquiry, and service, as prerequisites to acquiring transcendental knowledge and gaining access to the mysteries of mantras.

Lord Caitanya explicitly applies these principles to *nama-sankirtana:* “One should chant the holy name of the Lord in a humble state of mind, thinking oneself lower than the straw in the street.

**“One should be more tolerant than a tree, devoid of all sense of false prestige, and should be ready to offer all respects to others. In such a state of mind one can chant the holy name of the Lord constantly.”**

As beginners we generally call to Krsna by saying “O Hari!” Hari means “one who takes away.” In this way we pray to be freed from all obstacles to pure devotional practice, especially to *nama-sankirtana.*

We also call out to Krsna as the all attractive Lord, whose superexcellent beauty can draw our minds and senses away from the illusory forms of *maya* to the original forms of transcendence.

In summary, the first pair of names in the *maha-mantra* (Hare Krsna) depicts our quest for shelter from the pitfalls of ignorance and our relief at finding the new life promised by faithful *nama-sankirtana.*

This promise of a meaningful life, culminating in spiritual perfection and a return to Krsna’s eternal abode, is outlined in the first verse of *Siksastaka: ceto-darpana-marjanam bhava-maha-davagni-nirvapanam.*

Lord Caitanya prays:

**“Let there be all victory for the congregational chanting of Lord Krsna’s holy name, which cleanses the mirror of the heart and stops the miseries of the blazing fire of material existence.**

**“That chanting is the waxing moon that spreads moonlight on the white lotus of good fortune for all living entities, and it is the life and soul of the bride of all education — transcendental knowledge.**

**“The chanting of the holy name of Sri Krsna expands the blissful ocean of transcendental life and it gives a cooling effect to everyone, enabling them to taste full nectar at every step.”**

Chapter thirty-six analyses this verse in depth. But one point especially deserves repeating: Please assiduously avoid the main obstacle on the path from pious deeds to selfless love.

That obstacle is bad company *(asat-sanga)*. It is said, “Better to embrace a snake, a tiger, or an alligator than to keep company with persons who worship demigods or are driven by material desire.”

The words and conduct of atheists or gross materialists — or the plethora of pseudo-Vaisnavas common in Kali-yuga— cause vicious weeds to choke the creeper of devotion within the heart.

Such weeds invite conduct destructive to pure devotion: diplomatic behaviour, violence, profiteering, and desire for adoration or importance. If we allow these weeds to victimise us, we fall down.

Bad company may be easily identified when it comes in the form of atheists or hedonists, but when it comes subtly disguised it can act as a Trojan Horse and make us unsuspecting victims.

Two of *asat-sanga's* disguises are persons or things extraneous to devotional service, and pseudo-Vaisnavas, whom Thakura Bhaktivinoda has identified as thirteen different types of *sahajiyas.*

Bharata Maharaja is an example of a devotee who was tainted by the company of something unrelated to *bhakti,* in his case a deer. One would hardly expect an innocent animal to cause such misfortune.

But despite the fact that Bharata Maharaja had attained the platform of *bhava,* his attachment obliged him to accept two additional lives — one as a deer, the other as Jada Bharata — before attaining perfection.

For *sannyasis,* attachment to luxury or accepting too many disciples in the name of preaching are similar to King Bharata’s deer. For *grhasthas,* excessive attachment to family, home, or business is similar.

Bad company’s second Trojan Horse comes in the form of pseudo-Vaisnavas, whose precepts and conduct deviate from the principles of pure devotional service. Such people presently abound.

By definition, neophyte devotees lack the knowledge to discriminate between genuine and counterfeit Vaisnavas, and so beginners are easily fooled by external shows of devotion lacking in real substance.

A pretender who is friendly, sings nice *bhajanas,* and freely discusses esoteric topics can easily mislead neophyte devotees, who tend to fall prey to philosophical deviation or illicit conduct.

Of such deviants, Bhaktivinoda Thakura warns, *eo to*’ *eka kalir cela:* “Just look, here comes Kali’s servant. He is dressed as a Vaisnava, hut in truth he deviates from the conduct and beliefs of real Vaisnavas.”

Lord Caitanya has given us a guideline by which to identify the behaviour of genuine Vaisnavas: they reject the company of nondevotees and anyone who represents untruth *(asat-sanga-tyaga).*

To avoid the pitfall of had company we should seek out — and never abandon — the company of pure Vaisnavas, especially advanced Vaisnavas, as defined by revealed scriptures.

Moreover, we should — without hesitation and with full confidence— take exclusive shelter of *nama-sankirtana,* abandoning or at least desiring to abandon all material attachment.

By chanting Hare Krsna and making Krsna’s pleasure our life’s goal we can advance on the path chalked out by Lord Caitanya in His *Siksastaka* and arrive at the perfectional stage of Krsna consciousness.

That path begins when we first chant with faith. As our hearts are purified our chanting matures and we can increasingly concentrate on our *bhajana*, as portrayed in *Siksastaka's* third and fourth verses.

The fifth verse describes the stage at which we develop attachment to the Lord’s spiritual form, and the sixth, the attainment of our own spiritual form (*siddha-deha*) in the realised stage of ecstatic devotion.

Verses seven and eight depict the mood of loving devotion under Radha’s shelter, further nourished by feelings of separation as we encounter them in perfection, both in this world and in Goloka.

*Sastra* warns that we should not imagine our spiritual forms without qualification and proper guidance because meditation of that sort bewilders the intelligence and increases the likelihood of downfall.

Just as a fruit naturally ripens with rain and sun in its proper season, the devotional creeper naturally blossoms when it is watered by *nama-sankirtana* and enriched by remembrance of Radha and Krsna.

And even if we cannot practise remembrance, we should never stop chanting, because the power of the name, when chanted with faith in Lord Krsna, gradually frees us from bodily demands.

Eventually, the result is perfection, as Suta Gosvami describes,

*sankirtyamano bhagavan anantah srutanubhavo vyasanam hi pumsam*  
*pravisya cittarh vidhunoty asesam yatha tamo 'rko ’bhram ivati-vatah*

**“When people properly glorify the Lord or simply hear about His power, He, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, personally enters their hearts and cleanses away every trace of misfortune —**

**“Just as the sun removes the darkness or as a powerful wind drives away the clouds.**

Suta spoke these words at the very end of *Srimad-Bhagavatam* to remind us of the bliss *nama-sankirtana* bestows.

I have not the dimmest shadow of the devotion needed to qualify me for the purification Sri Suta mentions or to taste the bliss of love other great souls describe. I do, however, have a clear goal — and hope.

My hope rests in the merciful nature of Radha-Syamasundara. Although They are worshipable by all the three worlds, I have seen Them display profound kindness to the unworthy, even to offenders.

Daily I bow before Them, offer my *pranamas,* and appeal to Them: “I am not worthy of receiving Your grace, but just as an example to encourage others, please be merciful to me.”

If Radha-Syamasundara were to say, “But that may make Our mercy seem cheap,” I would be ready with my reply: “Not at all. Great people often show mercy to the less fortunate or impious.

“I am a wicked person, but because I sometimes chant Your names, the shadow of which can drive away unlimited sins, can’t You fulfil my request on the pretext that I have chanted Hare Krsna?”

Of course, They have heard my appeal many times before, but if just once the divine couple were to ask, “Say again, what is your request?” I would place my *uttariya* between my teeth and say:

“On the strength of chanting Your names this fool asks You to sprinkle upon him but a drop of Your mercy and give him the pure love You bestow upon those whose hearts overflow with ecstasy.”

**\* \* \* \***

The first two names (Hare Krsna) introduce the *maha-mantra.* They correspond to Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes at dawn which also begin the divine couple’s daily pastimes.

Both Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura begin their epic compositions depicting Radha’s and Krsna’s daily pastimes with narrations of Krsna’s *nisanta-lila*.

Srila Prabhupada has invited all of us to begin the day by participating in this pastime, as enacted by the Deities in our temples. It starts just before dawn at four with the soft tinkling of bells.

I recall, even as an uninitiated devotee, chanting rounds in the temple room and hearing the *pujari* ring the bell, enter the Deity room, and in a sweet voice say, “My dear Lordships, please get up.”

Radha-Syamasundara exchange the most confidential moods with Their servants from the time They first awake, through Their morning refreshment, and then Their first worship at *mangala-arati.*

The entire devotee community should be present at *mangala-arati* to greet Their Lordships and relish the intimate mood with which Radha and Syamasundara embrace Their servants.

During the tranquil singing of *Gurvastaka,* each devotee can have the special feeling that “Radha and Syama are looking at me,” just as the cowherd boys had when each thought Krsna was looking only at him.

As the verses beginning *sri-radhika-madhavay or apara* and *nikunja*-*yuno rati-keli-siddhyai* resound in the temple room, we can meditate upon the *nisanta-lila* remembered and served by our gurus.

**“I offer my respects to my spiritual master, who is eager to hear and chant at every moment about the unlimited conjugal pastimes of Radhika and Madhava, and Their qualities, names, and forms.**

**“I offer my respects to my spiritual master, who is very dear because he is expert in assisting the** ***gopis*** **as they make various tasteful arrangements for Radha-Krsna’s loving affairs in Vraja’s groves.”**

At night’s end in Vraja, the faint rays of dawn first awaken the cuckoos, causing them to softly coo, and then the peacocks perched in the *kadamba* trees, making them search the sky for clouds.

As if preparing for a concert, other creatures like parrots, pigeons, bees, and crickets quickly awaken one after another to add their own songs to the increasingly rich chorus thickening the air.

The stars, pleased to hear this ensemble’s recital, gradually follow their lord the moon and conceal themselves out of shame as the sun and its subjects display their effulgent opulence.

In a riverside grove laden with blossoming flowers and furnished with every accoutrement for amorous diversions rests a youthful couple — Radha and Krsna — the forms of paramount loving enjoyment.

As the supreme lover and the supreme beloved, these two are the original dual features of the Absolute Truth, who also manifest Themselves as Sri Vrndavana-dhama, the supreme setting for love.

Outside the grove, making preparations to greet the divine couple, are countless *gopis,* each with her own unique features. Expansions of Radha’s body, these *gopis* complement Her service to Krsna.

The service the *gopis* perform for the divine couple is the essence of unlimited, eternally expanding pastimes, an essence that nurtures the Vraja-vasis with its nectarean taste and heady aroma.

The eternal residents of Vrndavana — be they vines or cowherd men — each taste a unique mellow of devotion whose influence makes them constantly dance and sing in a festival called *prema-sankirtana.*

Female parrots inside the grove, their chatter sweet like the name Hare, stir Radha from Her sleep. And male parrots, their chatter sweet like the name Krsna, rouse Him from slumber.

Gradually the divine couple open Their eyes and drink in the image of each other’s faces. Divine love, however, quickly blurs Their vision with tears, filling Them both with intense unhappiness.

Fortunately, the sense of touch as They embrace reassures each of the other’s presence. Nonetheless, knowing that They must return to Their respective homes, Radha and Krsna sit up in bed.

As They yawn Their teeth sparkle and gleam, filling the riverside with heart-warming peace. Then, They offer *mangala-arati* to each other with the light beaming from Their twinkling eyes.

But alas! Feelings of imminent separation chase the drowsiness away from Radha’s blue and Syama’s dark eyes, and those sad feelings grow steadily as the light on the eastern horizon increases.

Hastily, Radha and Krsna get dressed in the semi-darkness, accidentally exchanging articles of one another’s clothes. Finally,'They leave the grove to be greeted by enthusiastic *gopis.*

As Radha and Krsna linger for a moment Their maidservants enter the grove to collect clothing or ornaments left behind and claim any betel, garlands, or food remnants to share amongst themselves.

The divine couple then walk along the forest path, arms resting on each other’s shoulders, minds disturbed by the fear of being discovered by Their elders but more so by the dread of having to part ways.

At the junction that leads to Nandagrama in one direction and Yavata in the other, They must finally part. Only Vidyudvari, where Krsna and Balarama boarded Akrura’s chariot, is more disliked by the *gopis.*

After one last embrace, Krsna heads home alone, and Radha hurries towards Yavata followed by Her friends. Every so often, each looks back to see the other until a cruel turn in the road blocks Their view.

The growing fear that They might see a familiar face on the way home helps check the growing suffering They must endure as the distance between Them increases. All glories to that fear!

Those Vaisnavas who feel distress by hearing of Radha’s and Krsna’s separation from each other, can mitigate the pain in their hearts by uniting the divine couple through chanting Their names.

**\* \* \* \***

If we embrace the *maha-mantra* as we pronounce its first pair of names, we will feel the ignorance of countless lives being washed away, like debris dragged from a beach by a strong riptide.

If we perform *nama-sankirtana* with faith, we will feel sheltered from the madness of the world and freed from the effects of illusion as we place our feet on the first step of the stairway to Vaikuntha.

Our spiritual sojourn by *nama-sankirtana* begins with meditating upon the lotus feet of the divine couple, whose rosy pink soles bear many divine marks like the fish, lotus, umbrella, and cow’s hoof print.

Their feet are so soft and beautiful that poets always compare them to lotuses. And like the lotus, which stands above the water, those feet always dance far above the material realm, and even Vaikuntha.

Just as humming bees always surround lotus flowers, eager to taste honey, devotees loudly singing *sankirtana* always surround Radha-Syamasundara’s lotus feet, eager for Their mercy.

As the petals of a lotus unfold to reveal the flower’s breathtaking beauty, so too do Radha-Syama’s charming toes uncurl to show Their toenails’ breathtaking blend of translucent red and white.

Lotuses are surely beautiful, aromatic, majestic, and ever fresh, but we know that these flowers have such qualities only due to having been in constant touch with Radha’s and Krsna’s lotus feet.

As we meditate on those ornaments of the three worlds, we call out, “Hare!” — which means both “O Hari!” and “O Hara!”— and come to know the amazing influence of Radha-Syama’s tender lotus feet.

What is that influence? These cunning youths steal away the mind and fashion anklets from it. Then They cheerfully tie those anklets on Their lotus feet and make them jingle with Their dancing steps.

At first we may object to having been taken hostage by wayward royalty, but soon we drop our protest, as we notice Maya’s shackles loosening from our necks, her myriad allurements becoming slack.

“Is it true?” we then ask ourselves. “Are Radha and Syama, by the wonder of Their sweetness and inconceivable kindness, delivering us from painful bondage to this world of relentless suffering?”

Knowing that the slightest kick of Krsna’s lotus feet can decide the fate of a million universes, we cry out, “Yes! Take my mind! Take my soul! Free me from my self-imposed fate. Save me!”

Their eyes melting with compassion, Radha’s and Krsna’s lotus faces then appear within the mind. How wonderful! Saints and yogis pray to Them, *gopas* and *gopis* wait on Them, yet They have time for us.

How could we not be attracted to Them? As we consider how attractive Krsna is to everyone, are we not forced to conclude that His all-attractive features can be summed up in one word — sweet?

With that sweetness He captures all wayward souls. And yet there is one more thing that truly completes the full meaning of the name Hare — the enticing effect Radha has on Krsna.

By Her feminine traits, artistic talents, and above all by Her peerless love for Krsna, She turns Him into a helpless drunkard, intoxicated by the wine of Her loving affection. So it is that She is called Hara.

In calling out Hare do we mean Krsna or Radha? Srila Prabhupada gives the answer:

**“In the beginning of the Hare Krsna** ***maha-mantra*** **we first address the internal energy of Krsna, Hare. Thus we say —**

**“‘O Radharani! O Hare! O energy of the Lord!’ When we address someone in this way, he usually says, ‘What do you want?’ The answer is, ‘Please engage me in Your service.’ This should be our prayer.”**

If we call out, “O Hare! O Radha!” and get no answer, we may again cry out, “O Hare! O Radha!” this time adding, “Sri Gurudeva has instructed that I ask You for some service.”

If Radha were to enquire, “Why not serve Krsna instead of Me?” we might then reply: “You have stolen Krsna’s mind. That means He is best served by serving You. So please engage me in some service.”

Once again we may recall Their lotus feet, sparkling with rings, glistening with splendour, the shelter of Their *gopi* friends and maidservants, and then think, “O beautiful queen of Vrndavana!

“Let me take shelter of Your lotus feet. They are fountains of cool and pleasing nectar. Doesn’t Krsna Himself place them upon His heart to extinguish the blazing flames of desire that torment Him?”

Once Sri Radha waited for Krsna in a grove. He had promised to be on time but was late. Feeling neglected, Radha was overwhelmed with hopelessness and sorrow. Such are the ways of youthful love.

And then Krsna finally appeared. At first Radha was glad to see Him, but Her hot-tempered nature got the better of Her. To spurn Him She covered Her face with Her veil and turned Her back on Him.

Deeply despairing at this rejection, Krsna decided to surrender to Radha’s feet as His only shelter. As She sat upon Her throne, ignoring Him, He took advantage of Her huff and clasped Her feet.

Lord Sri Krsna, whose own foot-dust is sought by great devotees, craftily pressed reluctant Radha’s feet to His chest and at once felt the same happiness He would feel by embracing Her.

What’s more, by submitting to those embodiments of bliss, just as devotees do, Krsna was able to fulfil His heart’s desire: Radharani’s pique vanished, and She again welcomed Him to Her side.

With the name Hare I worship the red lac markings on Krsna’s chest, marks filled with a splendour that makes the mark of Srivatsa and the Kaustubha gem seem as pale as mist before the rays of the rising sun.

May the magnificent red remnants of Radha’s feet on Krsna’s chest that resemble a red lotus floating upon the rising and falling waves in the Yamuna’s blackish waters protect and bless us all.

**\* \* \* \***

Chanting the first Krsna in the *maha-mantra* at once attracts all Vaisnavas to the sound, and their hearts cry out in unison, "O Krsna! Let us be attracted to You, to Your form, and to Your pastimes.”

He who steals the life of Putana, the garments of young *gopis,* and the sins of surrendered souls, will He not someday steal our hearts and make us as rich in love as He did the fruit vendor with jewels?

Tinkling anklets crown the upper portion of both His bluish feet, which slope gracefully to meet a pinkish line that encircles His soles like a garland of roses and gives way to saffron-red beneath.

Accompanying nineteen auspicious marks on those reddish feet, which leave impressions Mother Earth counts amongst her many treasures, are colours neither the *Vedas* nor *Puranas* can identify.

The occasional smudge of pink *kunkuma* comes from the *gopis’* breasts when they carefully place Krsna’s lotus feet there. This *kunkuma* indicates the passionate love within their hearts.

Like twinkling stars amidst the blackness of the night sky, *cintamani*- dust particles from Vraja’s soil also cling to Krsna’s feet and beg to be empowered by their touch, ointment, and the symbols on their soles.

If only we could collect a few particles of that dust, then the Brahmas of all the universes would eagerly offer to exchange their kingdoms for just a single speck of that treasure. But we should not accept.

Until we obtain the Vraja dust from these divine monarchs (*vraja*-*rajah-raja),* let us chant the name Krsna to nourish the hope that one day Krsna’s special footprints might be visible to our eyes.

As we call out to Krsna, let us remember that His appeal extends even to the foremost *gopi*, Radharani, whose mind is hopelessly ensnared by His divine attributes, like a doe hypnotised by a hunter’s flute.

Once, as Radha chanted the *maha-mantra* in separation from Sri Krsna and remembered Her past encounters with Him, She contemplated the name Krsna and the effect it had upon Her.

Radha thought, “This name, Krsna, is a combination of two special syllables: *krs,* which refers to all existence, both temporal and eternal, and *na,* which indicates an identity steeped in boundless bliss.

“Combined together in one name, these syllables denote the eternal form of bliss and knowledge, the form that tempts all beings in all directions with a joy far superior to any other.”

Just as Srimad Radharani was thinking like this, She heard the sound of Krsna’s flute. But not just that, She heard something else as well. She heard “Radha! Radha!” a secret call discernable to Her alone.

Alas, it was midday. Confined to Her husband’s home, how could She escape and follow that beckoning song? But the second time She heard that call it was suffused with the essence of Krsna’s loveliness.

That potion, a blend of Krsna’s flute-song and His beauty, made Radha jump to Her feet, run out the door, and disappear into the forest. Thus I call out “Krsna” to that Lord of enchanting virtues.

Dear readers! Allow me to conclude this praise of the *maha-mantras* first two names by describing an outfit of Radha-Syamasundara that I take to be related to these two wonderful names, Hare and Krsna.

Radha and Syama have a “net dress,” a latticework of white pearls over a separate silk underdress of pastel blue, green, lilac, and pink. To see it is to become enmeshed in the charm of the two who wear it.

A pearl dress should be complemented by pearl earrings, necklaces, and bracelets. Indeed, it is. But I lament that, for the most part, Radha-Syamasundara’s pearls are not precious natural ones.

What a waste of the Lord’s energy! Endless wealth is squandered decorating flesh, bones, and blood with gold and gems, while the Lord’s beautiful Deity form is bedecked in costume jewelry, at best.

Oh, if I were a king I would procure the finest natural pearls for this outfit. I would also stock a treasure house with priceless jewels that I could use to decorate Radha-Syamasundara’s exquisite forms.

Royalty and commoners alike revere pearls as objects of rare and precious beauty due to their roundness, smoothness, and iridescence. Yet pearls appear from the insides of lowly mollusks.

In the same way, Radha-Syamasundara are like priceless pearls—one black, one gold-—who have made Their appearance within this ordinary country to beautify the eyes and hearts of the Hungarians.

When Radha-Syamasundara don this gown, They resemble “fishers of men.” Casting Their net-dress into t he ocean of suffering, They drag all who see Them to the secure shore of Their lotus feet.

Having delivered not only Their devotees but also Their guests, these fishermen, with no one else to catch, cast Their nets upon each other, and both willingly submit to being caught in loving pastimes.

As the name Hare tosses its net of love over Krsna to contain Him, the name Krsna also opens the net of its inconceivable beauty, with which it catches and draws in the floundering fish of Radha’s heart.

Because the task of hauling in a full catch is hard work, Radha’s and Syamasundara’s hair is sometimes tied up in a net of pearls to keep it in place, an arrangement upon which I meditate.

The first time Radha-Syamasundara wore this outfit, They also wore specially prepared lotus-crowns made from pink cloth stretched over wire frame. Now those crowns exist only in pictures.

The backdrop was also special. *Gopis* stood on lotuses, serving the divine couple. And lastly, both Gaura Nataraja and Govardhana Lala had blue lotus thrones to match Their own net dresses.

O wise readers! If you too want deliverance from this ocean of birth and death, then come see Radha and Syama in Their incredible net-dress, first offered to Them on the appearance day of Sri Radha.

When we say, “...no one can escape the unique loving network of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu,” we can include this net outfit as part of Lord Caitanya’s movement meant to deliver the conditioned souls.

By chanting the *siddha-mantra* of inconceivable names that contains the pair Hare Krsna, and by serving Vraja’s divine couple day and night in New Vraja-dhama, when will I attain the goal of life?

**\* \* \* \***

I have attempted to glorify Radha-Syamasundara by explain- hag the *maha-mantras* first pair of names. Now I will continue that attempt by elucidating some truths of the second pair of names, Hare Krsna.

Dear friends! Have Radha’s and Syama’s names and forms entered your ears and eyes to enchant your mind and fill you with an irrepressible desire to chant the *maha-mantra?*

One of my god brothers visiting New Vraja-dhama coined a phrase to describe the effect of Radha-Syamasundara’s *darsana* combined with Their devotees’ *kirtana.* He called it the “Radhe-Syama experience.”

Indeed, I often hear that phrase used to describe the effect New Vraja-dhama’s ambience has on visitors, an ambience that originates from Radha-Syamasundara as They are stirred by devotees in *kirtana.*

Or do Radha-Syamasundara stir Their devotees’ *kirtana*? It is both. The “Radhe-Syama experience” is created as the Lord and His devotees compete to better serve and please one another.

The inaugurators of that *nama-sankirtana* are the devotees, but it is Their Lordships who so kindly respond. Lord Krsna says, “As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly.”

Krsna has so kindly arranged that we may chant His holy names. As in other places in ISKCON, in New Vraja-dhama we endeavour to do so, yet we find our taste for chanting sometimes wanes.

In His *Siksastaka,* Caitanya Mahaprabhu speaks of the state of consciousness in which we encounter difficulty as a result of chanting the Hare Krsna *maha-mantra* without attachment.

The Lord says,

*namnam akari bahudha nija-sarva-saktis tatrarpita niy-amitah smarane na kalah*  
*etadrsi tava krpa bluigavan mamapi durdaivam idrsam ihajani nanuragah*

**“O my Lord! In Your holy name there is all good fortune for the living entity, and therefore You have many names, such as Krsna and Govinda, by which You expand Yourself.**

**“You have invested all Your potencies in those names, and there are no hard and fast rules for remembering them. O Lord! Although You bestow such mercy upon the fallen, conditioned souls by liberally —**

**“Teaching Your holy names, I am so unfortunate that I commit offences while chanting the holy name, and therefore I do not achieve attachment for chanting.”**

How can such misfortune come upon us just as we have crossed the threshold of auspicious life? It is due to the effects of had habits from past lives, and offences we have incurred while chanting.

We are directly freed from these unwanted things by following the process, in which chanting is the most important part, and indirectly by desisting from the four prohibitions all initiates vow to accept.

For example, when we say we cannot chant our rounds, the reason generally is that because we have not controlled the six urges we have succumbed to their influence and thus lost our taste for chanting.

And even if the six urges are controlled, unless we root out more subtle habits — like deceit, fault-finding, and the desire for fame — we will be unable to develop attachment to *nama-sankirtana.*

In addition, as already detailed in the preceding chapter, we must strictly guard against committing the ten offences to Krsna’s holy name, especially the offence of criticising devotees.

Along with these prohibitions, there are six principles favourable to the proper cultivation of *nama-bhajana*, beginning with enthusiastically pushing forward and endeavouring with confidence.

We must also be patient, strictly follow the regulative principles, abandon the company of non-devotees by keeping company with devotees, and follow in the footsteps of the previous *acaryas*.

Krsna Himself summarises the underlying mood of these activities, a mood that overcomes indifference and arouses taste for chanting:

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories —**

**“Being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee remains happy and worships Me with —**

**‘‘Great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.”**

In short, with determination we must embrace the rules and prohibitions pertaining to Krsna consciousness. Then we will develop attachment to chanting and the conviction to advance further.

Only with determination can we access the secrets of chanting, just as only with determination do Radha and Krsna meet again after They are forced to separate from each other at night’s end.

The pain felt by the divine couple as They walk side by side along the forest path, surrounded by Their equally unhappy but outwardly cheerful and supportive friends, is impossible to describe.
