Remembering Krsna’s qualities without being able to taste them is like baking a beautifully decorated cake without sugar — devoid of sweetness. Yet I continue to chant with faith in Sri Rupa’s words:

**“The holy name, character, pastimes, and activities of Krsna are all transcendentally sweet like sugar candy. Although the tongue of one afflicted by the jaundice of ignorance cannot taste anything sweet —**

**“It is wonderful that simply by carefully chanting these sweet names every day, a natural relish awakens within his tongue, and his disease is gradually destroyed at the root.”**

Gradually my mind searches for Radha’s and Krsna’s forenoon pastimes, and with its jaundiced tongue tries to taste the various sweet stages of those pastimes. The taste is barely detectable.

But continued remembrance of the transcendentally sweet holy names intensifies my taste for Lord Krsna’s forms, qualities, and pastimes, a taste that by its nature makes me eager for more.

I am particularly fond of recalling Srimati Radharani’s pastimes of cooking, especially when She is in Yasoda-devi’s kitchen. I also like to hear the names of the many dishes She lovingly prepares for Krsna.

A few acaryas, especially Kaviraja Gosvami, elaborately tell of the fare relished by Lord Caitanya and Krsna. Bhaktivinoda Thakura, for example, wrote a song for arati that lists the names of these dishes.

In the morning, the cooking starts with Radha receiving Yasoda’s and Rohini’s blessings to enter the kitchen. Meanwhile, Dhanistha secretly exchanges Krsna’s yellow cloth for Radha’s blue veil.

Maidservants wash and dry the lotus feet of Sri Radha. She then follows Rohini into the kitchen, followed by Her friends and finally Her maidservants, all in single file like ducklings follow their mother.

Rohini-devi gives each gopi a place to cook, a menu, and the necessary ingredients. But knowing Radha’s fine culinary skills, Rohini encourages Radha to cook whatever Her heart dictates.

Surrounded by a few eager maidservants who know just what ingredients and utensils are needed for each preparation, Radha sits on a wooden stool and inaugurates Her devotional culinary sacrifice.

We can just imagine the opulence of Mother Yasoda’s kitchen and Sri Radha’s cuisine when sandal and aloe are used for firewood and when the dishes they cook are not found even on Brahmaloka.

Radha is gravity personified while cooking. She puts Her full concentration into each and every dish She prepares, like a mantra-brahmana meticulously pronouncing each and every syllable.

Let us hear the enchanting names of but a few of the preparations She cooks, beginning with the sweets that are cooled before eating and ending with the rice and vegetables that are served hot.

Manohara-laddu with camphor and nutmeg; kadamba, a round hard sweet shaped like a kadamba flower; padma-cini, a sweet made from the lotus flower; amrta-keli, a favourite milk-sweet of Krsna’s —

Gaja and khaja, sweets made of flour, the latter for which Krsna will literally run; pera, milk cooked down with sugar; candra-cura, the taste of which can only be compared to powdered moonlight —

Misri, rock candy; sarabhaja, a sweet made from cream; sarapuri, a puri made by frying cream; bundi-ladu, sweet balls made of chickpea-flour;and rasa-kara, the last of the sweets, made from coconut.

Radha prepares various beverages, like a fruit juice called rasala, and a cream drink called mathani, as well as yogurt, milk, coconut milk, flavoured whey, and freshly made ghee, the staple of Vedic cuisine.

She makes various kinds of fresh pickles and selects a variety of aged pickles as well, placing each kind in a separate container. Radha also slices fresh fruits especially selected by Mother Yasoda.

In the last phase of Her cooking, Radha prepares exquisitely fragrant rice and then cuts, cooks, and spices countless vegetables, who sesucculent aroma could easily break the meditations of great sages.

All these preparations are placed on golden plates, covered with thin cloths, and carried to tables, where Mother Yasoda inspects them before serving, just as a general reviews his troops.

Krsna’s mother is well aware that anything Sri Radha touches becomes nectarean and does not require to be checked; still, out of her natural maternal instinct, Mother Yasoda feels obliged to do so.

But the real test of Radha’s cooking comes when Krsna’s friends, especially Madhumangala, sample one beautiful dish after another, expressing their approval by producing all manner of funny sounds.

Radha’s cooking not only tastes like nectar but is also pleasing to the eyes, putting the eater in a quandary: How can one eat something so gorgeous? Then again, how could one resist something so inviting?

But the final touch comes when Srimati Radharani demurely serves the meal Herself, one dish after the other. After all, doesn’t food taste most delicious when served by the one who cooked it?

Consequently, because Radha cooks and then serves the meal, each dish is so filled with Her love that it overwhelms Krsna’s mind and senses, and so He often loses His appetite and sits picking at His plate.

Worried that Krsna’s appetite is weak, Mother Yasoda becomes upset: “Son! I have asked Radha, the best cook in all of Vraja, to come a great distance just to cook for You, but You’re playing with Your food.

“Listen! Lalita and Visakha have told me that if You don’t cat properly, then Radha will not come back again. And why should She?” At this, Krsna looks back and forth from Radha to His mother.

Then, to please the two women who love Him most, Krsna consumes everything on His plate by invoking the same potency with which He accepts unlimited food offerings in an infinity of Deity forms.

Such are the pastimes of Radha’s morning cooking. Though they are the pinnacle of happiness for the Vraja-vasis, as those pastimes draw to a close they portend a great sorrow — Krsna’s departure.

With a hundred hearts may we worship Yasoda’s motherly concern,which only reluctantly allows her son to leave each morning for the pastures of Govardhana with His friends and His cows.

After Yasoda ties amulets and protective stones to Their wrists and arms, Krsna and Balarama offer her prostrated obeisances, discreetly laughing at Their mother’s efforts to protect Them from harm.

As Yasoda accompanies her sons down Nandagrama Hill she pleads, “O child! We have so much wealth. We are not a poor family. What need is there for You to go to the forest? Let others go. You can stay!

“I know none more dear than You! If misfortune were to befall You I would perish. I shiver in fright to think of Your body scorched by the sun’s harsh rays and Your soft soles pricked by sharp stones.”

At these words, Krsna holds Yasoda’s hands and says, “Mother! You need not fear. In the presence of Balarama, what harm can come to Me? Besides, there are no demons left in the forest. They are all dead.

“The trees shelter us everywhere like big umbrellas, and the stones obligingly become like cotton balls under our feet. Please Mother!How could I neglect our tradition and My duty to care for the cows?”

While Krsna talks like this, one gopi tells Yasoda, “O Queen! If you don’t send Radha back to Her home, Jatila might become suspicious and forbid Her from returning tomorrow to cook for Krsna.”

Persuaded by this warning and her son’s reassuring words, Yasoda embraces her boys one last time and then gives Them permission to depart, watching as They leave with Their enormous herd.

After sending Krsna off, Yasoda returns to her palace with a sad heart and consoles herself by seating Radha on her lap. Let us recall that Yasoda’s love for Radha is just as intense as her love for her son.

In a faltering voice, Yasoda says, “O Radha! Consider me to be just like Your mother, Kirtida, and this house just like Your own home. Alas! Because of gossip, I cannot even keep You here for a full day.

“Unfortunately, the small-minded villagers are too harsh.” Tears moisten Mother Yasoda’s breasts as she binds an assortment of sweets in the border of Radha’s sari and prepares to send Her home.

As Mother Yasoda weeps, the palace walls melt in sympathy, and the young gopis weep along with her. Radha uses Her own sari to wipe the tears from Yasoda’s face and then falls into her loving embrace.

Yasoda repeatedly kisses Radha’s beautiful face and then embraces each of Radha’s girlfriends. Unable to control her feelings, she follows the gopis for some distance until Rohini finally restrains her.

I worship the lotus feet of Mother Yasoda, who loves Radha as much as she does Krsna, and who is very affectionate to Radha’s friends. May we all feel her loving embrace one day. O Krsna! O Krsna!

**\* \* \* \***

Sometimes while meditating on Krsna’s pastimes I don’t remember things in order; overwhelmed by thinking of Yasoda’s adoration for Radha, I now return to their exchange at the conclusion of breakfast.

During nama-bhajana we may find that the mind does not follow the natural sequence of Lord Krsna’s pastimes but sometimes jumps to a particular pastime to which we are especially attracted.

This restlessness of the mind is not undesirable, for it hints at spontaneous attachment and sometimes appears in our acaryas’ narrations at the times when their love inspires them in that way.

After breakfast Krsna and His friends take a nap. Perspiring from the heat and shivering from fatigue, Srimati Radharani comes out of the kitchen and sits nearby, beaming smiles at Her friends.

Maidservants wash Her feet and hands with cool, fragrant water while Lalita-devi lovingly wipes Her face and arms with a cold, damp cloth,chiding Radharani for having over-exerted Herself.

Just then Mother Yasoda appears and escorts the girls into another room to rest. Yasoda seats Radha on her lap and pleads lovingly, “My girl! Now that You have fed everyone, You must also eat.”

At Yasoda’s insistence, Srimati Radharani and Her friends, laughing and joking, accept the assorted preparations brought by Rohini, dishes that Kundalata had previously mixed with Krsna’s remnants.

When the girls finish, Radha cleanses Her mouth and accepts betel nuts to chew. Satisfied, She lies back against the pillows of a large couch, looking like the queen of majestic swans at rest.

But before long Yasoda’s voice can be heard calling, “O daughter!” Immediately one of the housemaids comes in and ushers the girls into the queen’s apartment, where she has arranged to dress Radha.

Yasoda motions for Radha to take Her place on a seat in the centre of the room and, with great affection, begins to dress and ornament Her by first retying Radha’s soft curly hair into a graceful braid.

Vraja’s queen applies fresh vermilion in the part of Radha’s hair, tilaka on Her forehead, and collyrium over Her eyelids, then steps back to get a better look, marvelling at her own artistry.

Yasoda then replaces Radha’s nose ring with her own most precious golden pearl, which sways with Radha’s breath and will later,unbeknownst to Mother Yasoda, capture the restless eyes of her son.

With a piece of cotton Yasoda removes the faded drop of musk on Radha’s chin and carefully applies a fresh one, exclaiming, “There! It looks like a black bumblebee sitting on the golden lotus of Your face.”

Radha shyly lowers Her head as Mother Yasoda gently removes the simple white clothes Radha had worn for cooking and quickly replaces them with fresh ones. First she deftly slips on a new blouse.

Then she wraps Sri Radha in a beautiful blue sari. Its colour matches Krsna’s complexion and invokes thoughts in Radha that make Her hide Her blushing face, lest the queen read the contents of Her mind.

Yasoda-devi, as if she senses the heat of passion welling up in Srimati Radharani, lovingly dabs and smears the young girl’s limbs with cooling sandalwood paste and then personally fans Her.

Meanwhile, one of Mother Yasoda’s maidservants delivers a tray of ornaments that glitters like a thousand suns. The queen selects a string of diamonds and hangs it around Sri Radha’s graceful neck.

Yasoda-devi then places ivory bangles on Radharani’s wrists, jewel-studded armlets on Her lower, middle, and upper arms, and a ring with an orb-like jewel on the ring finger of Sri Radha’s right hand.

From the tray of jewels, Krsna’s mother selects a string of alternating coral and black pearl beads she had fashioned earlier, letting out a sigh of bliss as she uses it to frame Radharani’s golden forehead.

Moving behind Varsana’s princess, Yasoda takes Radha’s braid in her hands and decorates it with various hairpins: one gold, one diamond,one pearl, and others made of jewels like ruby and emerald.

Coming around to face Radha, Yasoda tilts Her chin with her thumb and forefinger and decorates Radha’s hair with tiny flowers, finishing by tucking a single yellow campaka flower behind each of Her ears.

Yasoda looks for the next item on the tray of jewellery, but before the queen can even try to put the anklets on Radha’s feet, the Princess of Varsana, smiling enchantingly, reaches for the ornaments Herself.

But before either Radha or Yasoda can touch them, one of Radha’s maidservants takes the ankle bells from the tray, deftly places them on Radha’s delicate lotus feet, and steps back out of sight.

While this intimate exchange takes place between Radha and Yasoda, the gopis are spectators, like an audience enthralled by expert players in a dramatic theatrical performance directed by love itself

The gopis are witnesses to Yasoda’s dressing and decorating Radha, and they see the clothes, ornaments, and flowers offered to Her as different manifestations of the queen’s love for their princess.

Actually, the queen of Nandagrama resembles a great reservoir of nectarean love in which Radha fully immerses Her body, like a graceful dolphin, to swim within its cool, sweet, boundless waters.

Yasoda’s voice quivers from that love, “O my precious little girl! Your form and qualities soothe my heart; I dream of them always. What sins have I committed that I cannot have You as my daughter?

“You and my son are like the two halves of my life, or the pupils of my two eyes. The king of Vraja also shares this sentiment, just as we share the sadness that You are not the wife of our dear Krsna.”

Yasoda’s words bring an irrepressible smile to Sri Radha’s face, which She quickly conceals with Her veil. As Krsnas mother embraces Her, Radharani exchanges knowing glances with Her smiling girlfriends.

Radharani is Krsna’s eternal consort, but for the sake of Their pastimes as paramours They never wed. And so, even though Mother Yasoda’s desire is eternally fulfilled, she never realises that it is.

As Yasoda and Radha embrace, they both think of Krsna. The pair of names, Krsna Krsna, can thus be said to denote the embrace of the two women dearest to the Lord. May their blessings be upon us.

O Krsna! I call out Your name once, twice, with no idea how much time goes by. Yet I go on dutifully worshipping Your pastimes, in spite of being distanced from them by my conditioned state.

**\* \* \* \***

Perhaps the dress we call the “Vrndavana outfit” goes best with the two names Krsna Krsna, for upon seeing its unique style and colours everyone immediately exclaims in bliss, “Krsna! Krsna!”

This outfit is expertly sewn from fine satin silk — Srimati Radharani in blue and Syamasundara in green — with a variety of Vrndavana’s animals and foliage hand painted on its background.

To complete the scene, an exquisite backdrop places the divine couple within a forest grove in Vraja overlooking the Yamuna River,as a full moon peeps through the night clouds.

To anyone who sees this dress, its name is instantly self-evident. It paints a picture of Vrndavana forest that is complete with the very life of Vraja, Radha, and Syama. Thus it is complete in every way!

Let me begin the glorification of this outfit by portraying Radha’s pale-blue skirt, which is dominated by two swans facing each other in waters filled with pink lotuses floating over rippling waves.

At the level of Radha’s knees is a green shore with rabbits, deer, and squirrels amongst flowering bushes and trees. From there to the waist is a light blue sky with birds in flight, singing of their good fortune.

Words can hardly do justice to this fine blend of form and colour. It creates such a harmonious theme, is so pleasing to the eye, and is yet so practical — essentially a skirt with a scalloped bottom.

Radha’s belt is also fabric: painted flowers with a central hanging pink lotus upon a leafy background. Her blouse is a dark turquoise-blue but with a lesser array of flowers and animals than on Her skirt.

Her chiffon veil is scalloped like the hem of Her skirt but with a border of flowers and leaves similar to Her belt and an assortment of flowers and butterflies on the halves that hang to either side of Her.

Radha’s outfit is complete with a specially made crown, a choker, bracelets, anklets, decorations for Her long black braid, and a silk garland fixed at Her ears and the part in Her hair, framing Her face.

A collection of matching necklaces and gemstones also go with this dress. Simply thinking of ornamenting Radha with them increases my eagerness to serve Her and deepens my taste for nama-sankirtana.

I hope that some day I am able to arrange my services in such a way that I can also regularly make flower garlands for Srimati Radharani, especially garlands that match this Vrndavana dress.

What better service can there be than picking flowers with one’s own hands, spreading out a silk cloth on the ground before you, and creating matching flower garlands for Radha and Syama?

Radha’s garland requires more attention to detail than does Syama’s because it is so petite. As my hands grow clumsier with age, I worry I won’t be able to make garlands when I finally have the time.

I find solace, however, in Krsna’s assurance that whatever service we meditate upon at the end of this life, we will be able to perform in the next, in a body perfectly suited to the service we desire.

As Lord Krsna Himself says, *yam yam vapi smaran bhavam*: “Whatever state of being one remembers when he quits his present body, in his next life he will attain to that state without fail.”

Even though so many services are available for spreading Krsna consciousness in this world, it is nonetheless a place of suffering from which we must ultimately seek release as soon as possible.

At a certain point, even Sri Krsna Himself—the ornament of this insipid world whose value to conditioned souls is verily incalculable — did not desire to keep His transcendental body here any longer.

Sukadeva Gosvami, referring to Lord Krsna’s disappearance, says,

**“Thus He revealed the destination of those fixed in the self and demonstrated that this mortal world is of no intrinsic value.”**

Commenting on this statement, acaryas Jiva and Visvanatha explain that Krsna does not want those devotees engaged in His mission to save the fallen souls to stay in this world any longer than necessary.

The Lord’s desire is that we perfect ourselves as quickly as possible and go back home, back to Godhead. To emphasise this point, and to not give undue esteem to this world, He left when He did.

I am far distant from such perfection, but my desire to engage fully in service to the divine couple is steadily increasing. It is offset onlyby the services that Radha-Syamasundara mercifully provide for me.

And if such services as garland-making are no longer available, what else hut those duties given to me by Srila Prabhupada, such as preaching, could enthuse me to stay in this world any longer?

Such thoughts may seem distant from the Krsna Krsna meditations of nama-sankirtana, hut when those thoughts become inevitable reality, what else but calling out, “Krsna! Krsna!” will there be?

Thus Krsna Krsna is my passionate plea to the holy names: Please drag me to perfection now so that no obstacle can prevent me from thinking of Radha and Syama when the time comes for me to leave.

As King Kulasekhara said,

*krsna tvadiya-pada-pankaja-panjarantamadyaiva me visatu manasa-raja-hamsah*  
*prana-prayana-samaye kapha-vata-pittaih kanthavarodhana-vidhau smaranam kutas te*

**“O Krsna! At this moment let the royal swan of my mind enter the tangled stems of the lotus of Your feet. Otherwise, how will it be possible for me to remember You at the time of death —**

**“When my throat will he choked up with mucus, bile, and air?”**

Srila Prabhupada was very fond of this verse. He quoted it often and even sang it during his daily activities or when alone in his room.

Repeating, “Krsna, Krsna” reminds me of Syamasundara in His green Vrndavana dress. Indeed, my mind is enchanted by the Vrndavana scenes hand-painted onto every part of His outfit.

On the front fold of Syama’s dhoti is a peacock facing Radha. Its crown begins at Syama’s belt and its feathers fan out through the space between Syama’s legs and off towards His right side.

On Syama’s left leg is a fox peering out from behind a bush, and on His right, monkeys play in a flower garden. My mind wants to stay there but it naturally moves to the outfit’s other fascinating features.

Over Syamasundara’s dhoti is a small ruffled skirt tied to His waist with a belt of leaves. The skirt extends to mid-thigh and is home to coloured parrots that sit upon branches blossoming with flowers.

His shirt is the only part of the outfit that is not green. It shares the same turquoise-blue of Radha’s blouse and has similar flowers, birds,and borders, accented by similar necklaces and strands of beads.

Syama’s upper cloth is generous in area as well as design, with many birds and flowers, but unlike Sri Radha’s blue chiffon veil, it is green and made of the same satin cloth as the other parts of His outfit.

Syamasundara has armlets, anklets, and a matching choker that all resemble Radha’s. But if you were to ask which of the two looks more attractive, I would reply, “Please ask someone else.”

In conclusion, the hems of both dresses are jari or sequins, their colours matching the dominant shade nearest them. The dress isVrndavana not only in appearance but also in detail and elegance.

May vraja-bhakti, the mere touch of the shadow of which can make an emperor abandon his kingdom, or the perfect yogi his meditation,enrich our hearts when we chant, “Krsna! Krsna!”

This third pair of names in the maha-mantra also indicates a rigorous cleansing of the heart, by which we pave the way for the Lord’s transcendental pastimes to unfold in that newly purified place.

One day in Puri, Lord Caitanya asked His devotees to join Him in cleaning the Gundica temple in preparation for Lord Jagannatha’s arrival at the conclusion of the first leg of the Ratha-yatra.

The Gundica temple and its gardens are non-different from Vrndavana, and the Ratha-yatra procession to Gundica is Jagannatha’s return to Vrndavana after a long stay in Dvaraka.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu engaged the devotees in sweeping the temple, collecting even the smallest grains of dust, and washing the walls and floors thoroughly with water. They did all of this twice.

During this cleansing process the only sound the devotees would utter was the name Krsna. Thus the sound “Krsna” became the common language for anyone who needed to say something.

When someone wanted a broom, he would say, “Krsna! Krsna!” When someone wanted a water pot, he would say, “Krsna! Krsna!” Those to whom they spoke would also say, “Krsna! Krsna!” with a smile.

In this way, by cleaning the Gundica temple, Caitanya Mahaprabhu taught us how to cleanse our hearts in preparation for Krsna’s return there by the simple process of chanting “Krsna! Krsna!”

By Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s grace, those who arc serious about steadily cleansing their hearts will soon see the day when Krsna and His pastimes appear there as they chant Krsna’s holy names.

May the carefree prince of New Vraja-dhama smile each time I call out His name — “Krsna!” And may His dearest, Sri Radha, cast a loving glance my way at the sound of Her beloved’s name — “Krsna!”

May the shower of Radha-Syamasundara’s divine mercy fall upon those who keep company with pure devotees and chant Krsna’s name with firm faith as they remember His forenoon pastimes.

And may those who are fortunate enough to regularly behold the charming forms of Radha-Syamasundara in Their “Vrndavana outfit” extend that good fortune to the other people of this country.

**\* \* \* \***

Having discussed the first three of the eight pairs of names comprising the maha-mantra, let me now explain the fourth — Hare Hare — which indicates the awakening of taste for nama-sankirtana.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says,

**“The fourth pair \[of names\] indicates the awakening of unmotivated devotional service.”**

This commen treveals why loving devotion may still be beyond our grasp.

It may be because our devotion has not been, in the strictest sense of the word, unmotivated. One may contest my statement, citing the definition of faith:

**“Sraddha is confident, firm faith that -**

**By offering transcendental loving service to Krsna one automatically performs all subsidiary activities. Such faith is favourable to the discharge of devotional service.”**

We may further argue that since such faith is “favourable to the discharge of pure devotional service,” why shouldn’t our devotion be unmotivated at the initial stages of faith, practice, and steadiness?

The reason our devotion may still be motivated is that two imperfections inherent in practising devotees (sadhakas), in whom real taste (ruci) has not yet awakened, may still be present.

First, even if one is without the conscious desire for impersonal liberation, the desire to be freed from anarthas — which cause suffering— is also a subtle desire for liberation by devotional service.

Second, although we may not want thoughts of sense gratification, such thoughts do enter our minds, even up to and including the stage of steadiness; such thoughts also contaminate our devotion.

But when real taste awakens, its effect is so powerful that neither the desire for freedom from bad habits nor thoughts of material enjoyment can enter the mind to dilute the purity of our motivation.

Prior to acquiring full taste our purpose in serving Lord Krsna strives to he unmotivated (*anyabhilasita-sunyam*); but at the stage of taste (ruci) it is actually unmotivated (*anydbhilasa-sunyam*).

Similarly, though devotion is said to be pure when it strives to be unmotivated, it is absolutely pure only when it is completely untainted by the modes of nature at the stage of ecstasy (bhava).

For this reason, when scriptures mention bhakti, they often mean to say “loving devotion,” as they do in the verse *sraddha ratir bhaktiranukramisyati*, “then real devotion and devotional service begin.”

In other words, the name Hare is repeated to indicate that purity of motivation comes about beyond the preliminary stage of taste, when one finally attains the more developed stages of ecstasy.

One imperfection present up to and including the preliminary stage of ruci is that one’s appreciation for the various limbs of bhakti depends in part upon how expertly those activities are performed.

For example, a devotee in this category will thoroughly appreciate kirtana when sung sweetly and melodiously to expert musical accompaniment. But in the absence of these things his taste wanes.

This kind of taste, then, cannot be considered truly unmotivated. Only a taste for devotional practices that is independent from the material quality of those practices can truly be called pure.

In summary, the first Hare of this pair indicates a degree of taste that depends upon material excellence, while the second Hare indicates a taste for devotion, unfettered by material conditions.

Calling out the first Hare may also be known as a request for unconditional service in general, while calling out the second Hare, the request of a qualified devotee for a specific service to the Lord.

We pray to He who removes the obstacles in devotional service,

*nadhanam na janam na sundarim kavitam va jagad-isa kamaye*  
*mamajanmani janmanisvare bhavatad bhaktir ahaituki tvayi*

**“O Lord of the universe! I do not desire material wealth, materialistic followers, a beautiful wife, or fruitive activities. All I want, life afterlife, is unmotivated devotional service to You.”**

This prayer of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu epitomises the mindset of devotees who have achieved taste (ruci) for nama-bhajana. They desire nothing but unalloyed devotion to Sri Krsna.

The Lord lists the obstacles to pure devotion: attachment to wealth, followers, family, or sense enjoyment. By studying the dangers of wealth, we can recognize the dangers posed by other attachments.

Material affluence poses two significant stumbling blocks: those who possess it are always gripped by anxiety over potential loss and gain, and it increases a false sense of ownership of “I” and “mine.”

Obviously such obstacles distract the wealthy from taking shelter of the Lord. Their greed to taste honey in the form of wealth prevents them from tasting even the slightest drop of the holy name’s nectar.

The most degraded way of earning wealth, however — one that robs even aspiring transcendentalists of the taste of devotion — is preaching Krsna consciousness to amass wealth from disciples.

Such so-called gurus can never attain a real taste for chanting. Even if they have achieved some taste, they will certainly lose it when the holy name punishes them for their corrupt mentality.

How can one cultivate real taste? “With one-pointed attention, one should constantly hear about, glorify, remember, and worship the Lord, who is the protector of the devotees.”

With such one-pointed attention we can struggle valiantly to root out our anarthas and remain equipoised while either losing or gaining any of the attachments already mentioned by Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

Krsna Himself directs us to be equipoised in loss or gain and to accept only those things that are necessary for executing devotional service,no more and no less, and in that way mitigate all material pains.

We have heard about the consciousness that manifests at the stage of taste (ruci) and the obstacles that slow our progress to the next stage. Now let us hear about the symptoms of one who tastes the name.

At that stage, chanting Hare Krsna gives real pleasure, nourishes one’s enthusiasm to continue chanting, and relieves the new foundhunger for tangible reciprocation from the holy name.

Our objectives at this point are to awaken attachment for Krsna’s pastimes, to learn the techniques of meditating on them, and to keep company with devotees whose superior taste can elevate our own.

And since taste is ultimately individual — meaning that it leads to one’s own individual mood — Lord Caitanya’s followers naturally long for the company of such devotees, just as Lord Brahma did.

Brahma recognised the superiority of the Lord and of the Vraja-vasis’ love for the Lord when he prayed,

**“My dear Lord! I therefore pray to be so fortunate that in this life as Lord Brahma or in another life —**

**“Wherever I take my birth, I may be counted as one of Your devotees. I pray that wherever I may be, even amongst the animal species, I can engage in devotional service to Your lotus feet.”**

At the stage of ruci, the taste of nama-bhajana — whether coming from one’s own chanting or from others’ — is so palatable that it make seven the concept of liberation wholly unattractive.

Therefore, the objective is not to free oneself from suffering or to attain the bliss of Brahman, but to reach the next stage of devotion,which is attachment to Krsna and His eternal companions.

And finally, the effect of performing nama-bhajana with taste is that all the good qualities of the demigods, such as religiosity, knowledge,and renunciation automatically develop in the chanter.

This is understandable, for devotional service gradually severs the knots of karma. False ego and bodily identification then literally dissolve as we are fixed in a spiritual self-conception.

But when we have taste we want a spiritual identity more substantial than “spirit soul,” and more specific even than “Krsna’s servant.” We want to know the particulars of our eternal identity and service.

Those specific details are revealed only at the stage of bhava. Still, driven by taste, the presence of that curiosity in the heart, reinforced by cultivated remembrance, nurtures a shadow of one’s sthayi-bhava.

In other words, our reading, chanting, and association attract us to taste the company of a Vraja-vasi associate of Krsna. We then prefer to hear about, remember, and emulate that particular devotee’s mood.

**\* \* \* \***

Without reservation I raise my arms and call out, “O Hari! O Hara! One way or another, please make this proud and ignorant fool, who fancies himself Your pure devotee, actually worthy of serving You.”

By pronouncing these two names, Hare Hare, we repeat Srila Prabhupada’s succinct elucidation of the maha-mantra:

**“O Lord! O Energy of the Lord! Please engage me in Your service.”**

When we hear that advancement in nama-sankirtana naturally leads us to take shelter of the mood of the gopis, specifically Srimati Radharani, we might wonder, “Why not some other devotee?”

We may think, “There are many great transcendentalists. Can I not take shelter of any one of them?” In principle, this argument is perfect, and devotees have been doing this throughout countless ages.

Just as we may chant the names of whichever form of the Supreme Lord we are attracted to, we may also aspire to serve whichever devotee of the Lord that we worship as our superior.

Devotees of Lord Nrsimhadeva, for example, will choose to chant His sacred names and mantras. And they will serve Him by serving Lord Nrsimhadeva’s greatest devotee, Prahlada Maharaja.

In fact, the Lord said to Prahlada,

**“Those who follow your example will naturally become My pure devotees. You are the best example of My devotee, and others should follow in your footsteps.”**

But in Kali-yuga Lord Caitanya came to give everyone an opportunity to relish the mellow of amorous love, which can only he appreciated when one has taken shelter of the gopis in their loving mood.

What’s more, according to transcendental science, bhakti's amorous mood is love of God in the fullest and most elevated form. It is complete because it contains all the other moods of loving devotion.

Lord Caitanya instructed Rupa Gosvami in the different mellows of pure devotional service and told him the details of all these truths, citing evidence from revealed scriptures like Srimad-Bhagavatam.

No other incarnation of the Lord — and not just any devotee of the Lord — bestows this confidential type of spontaneous love. Since itis the highest mellow, only the most elevated persons can bestowit.

Lord Caitanya’s followers therefore generally become followers of the gopis and of their unique service, which is the best of all forms of worship, *ramya kacid-upasana vraja-vadhu-vargena yd kalpita*.

According to Lord Siva, Prahlada Maharaja is the best amongst Krsna’s devotees, for Lord Nrsimha put His hand on the boy’s head, a favour never shown to Siva, Brahma, or even Laksmi.

But Narada told Yudhisthira that the Pandavas were more fortunate than Prahlada because the Lord lived in their home and became their intimate relative, a privilege never enjoyed by Sri Prahlada.

Still, some members of the Yadu dynasty are more exalted than the Pandavas, for Lord Krsna lives with them continuously and He is even more closely related to them by family ties.

Amongst the Yadus, Krsna’s cousin Uddhava is considered the best,for even as a child he would personally worship a Deity of the Lord. Thus he was always known as a great devotee of Sri Krsna.

And Uddhava wanted to place the dust of the gopis feet upon his head, even if it meant taking birth as grass in Vrndavana. It must be concluded, then, that the gopis are superior to Krsna’s cousin.

Uddhava went to Vraja on Krsna’s order and met the gopis. Amazed by the depth of their love, he said,

**“Among all persons on earth, these cowherd women alone have actually perfected their embodied lives —**

**“For they have achieved the perfection of unalloyed love for Lord Govinda. Their pure love is hankered after by those who fear material existence, by great sages, and by ourselves as well.**

**“For one who has tasted the narrations of the infinite Lord \[the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna\] what is the use of taking birth as a high-class brahmana, or even as Lord Brahma himself?”**

Krsna Himself substantiates— in statements made to both Uddhava and Arjuna — the fact that the gopis’ devotion is superior to that of all other servants of the Lord, regardless of their place or relationship.

And to differentiate Radha from the other gopis, the Padma Puranasays, *sarva-gopisu saivaika visnor atyanta-vallabha*: “Amongst all the gopis, Srimati Radharani is the best and most dear to Lord Krsna.”

Since all devotees and incarnations of Godhead can only taste their own mellow of devotion, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu offered them all,as well as us conditioned souls, a very special opportunity.

That rarely bestowed opportunity is to relish the amorous love the gopis have for Krsna through the method of nama-sankirtana and, having taken shelter of Sri Radha, to serve Krsna as Her maidservant.

In this regard Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati says,

**“Those who engage in the service of Nityananda Prabhu and Advaita Prabhu generally have relationships of parental love, fraternity, servitude, and neutrality. When such devotees develop great attachment for Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, they too become situated within the intimate circle of devotees in conjugal love \[as described in the song gauranga balite\]”**

And Prabodhananda Sarasvati says,

**“When, because I have finally understood the secret of this golden form \[Lord Caitanya\], will the splendour of Radha’s jewel toenails shine in my heart?”**

Srimati Radharani is like a golden chalice overflowing with affection for Krsna. Whether She is with Him or away from Him She alwayspraises Krsna’s pastimes — sometimes to Herself, sometimes out loud.

Because Radha’s peerless kirtana draws Krsna to Her side, with even greater strength and speed than the kirtanas of any of the Lord’s other devotees, those learned in the secrets of rasa call Her “Hara.”

Radha’s constant absorption in thoughts of Krsna makes Her see Him everywhere. Similarly, Krsna’s constant absorption in thoughts of Radha causes Him to see Her in all directions, wherever He may go.

As He tends cows with His friends, Krsna sees Her by His side. While He is at home eating supper, He sees Her serving food to Him. And whenever He sleeps, He sees Her in His dreams.

An advanced devotee sees Sri Krsna everywhere and in everything,and Krsna sees Srimati Radharani, His ista-deva, in the same way; that makes His mind like a whirlwind of thoughts about Her.

Unless we call our ista-deva with intense feeling, that worshipful Deity stays far away. And so while chanting Hare Krsna we must try to abandon all false ego and chant with complete abandon.

For example, as Krsna fought with Aristasura, Srimati Radharani, beside Herself with anxiety, called out “Krsna!” with such intensity that She stole His mind. For this She is also called Hara.

Another time, just by thinking about Him with love, Radharani stole Krsna away from the cowherd boys and enticed Him to Her kunja, confirming once again why everyone calls Her Hara.

Hare Hare reminds me of Krsna’s chest and arms, whose image, touch, and aroma arouse mellows of amorous love not only in Srimati Radharani but also in all young girls in the three worlds.

Krsna’s broad chest boasts its own natural ornaments, including the Srivatsa mark to the right, the goddess of fortune in the form of a stripe to the left, and a light covering of soft dark hair.

The Kaustubha gem hangs from His neck, resting upon His heart in the middle of a garland of forest flowers of five different colours that proclaims Him to be the Lord of Vaikuntha in the form of a gopa.

Radha meditates on being held by Krsna, close to His chest, a throne upon which Her mind rests. Of course Krsna is very happy to play host to these constant meditations of Srimati Radharani.

When I massage Syama’s chest with oils then wash and dry it, His two arms seem like wish-fulfilling trees that have grown from the garden of His chest in answer to Radharani’s desire for His affection.

Krsna’s arms bring great joy to Radha when She is with Him, but when She is away from Him the horse of Her mind suffers, tied fast to those stake-like arms by ropes of longing and remembrance.

Could it have been Radha’s plan that at the end of Krsna’s arms two hands would sprout, hands that behave at times as Her adversary, holding Her against Her will and doing what they please?

The soft, pinkish palms of those hands may show emblems of divinity like the conch, goad, and umbrella, but the ways they behave often contradict what one would expect from the protector of religion.

Aside from their dubious conduct, Krsna’s hands have a kind of electrifying effect upon Sri Radha, making Her bodily hairs stand on end and Her steady heart palpitate in excitement at their touch.

Tvasta wrongly chanted a mantra and brought danger upon himself. Did Srimati Radharani’s worship of Krsna’s arms similarly backfire and produce enemies in the form of Krsna’s fingernails?

I use the word “enemies” because sometimes those nails leave marks on Sri Radha’s chest when Krsna scratches Her during a dalliance,or on Her neck when He contends with Her in a water fight.

Whatever Radha’s intentions or discrepancies in worship, She has no doubt created two unique flowers, the backs of which appear like blue lotuses, the palms like red lotuses, and their fingers like petals.

Aside from the wonder these petal-like fingers cause as they entwine one another, they are crowned with the full moons of Krsna’s nails and armed with Cupid’s arrows, their sharp fingertips.

Just as Krsna’s chest and arms are objects of Srimati Radharani’s thoughts, Her chest and arms are objects of His. But always bear in mind that all Her features are embodiments of Her pure love for Him.

By that I mean that Radha’s body is not like the curvaceous form of an Apsara or heavenly damsel. She is the personification of selfless love, and Her features appear as they do only to please Krsna.

The female forms of this world, from Svarga to Patala, are perverted reflections of Sri Radha’s form, expressions not of pure love but of the lust that binds humans and demigods alike to birth and death.

Sri Radha’s chest is Her heart’s home, and Her heart is the source of love for Krsna — from which Her body is made — and the source of the joys and ecstasies Krsna tastes in His form as Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

By proximity to Her heart, Radha’s beautiful breasts are like water pots that contain the bounties of Her love. Thus they are a sourceof great happiness for Krsna, who is their humble devotee.

All the gopis enhance the beauty of their breasts by smearing them with kunkuma. We do the same when dressing Radha, for it attracts and pleases Syama by showing Her passionate love for Him.

As true as these descriptions of Srimati Radharani are, they are rarely visible, for She keeps Herself so carefully covered that even Her husband cannot see any exposed part of Her form below Her neck.

Radharani’s arms extend from beneath Her shoulders like two snakes who, with their slightest movements, hypnotise the mice of Krsna’s eyes. What then of their effect when She dances for Him!

To be sure, Srimati Radharani’s arms and hands attain the pinnacle of beauty when locked in Krsna’s own arms and hands during the rasa dance or the many dances Cupid choreographs.

As She casually pushes Her hair back with Her hand or makes Her bangles jingle to attract Krsna’s attention, Sri Radha’s arms possess the power of magic wands, putting Krsna under their spell.

In that bewitched condition Krsna loses Himself in the high waves of ecstasy, just as He does when She places Her two pink palms on His arms or chest and leaves their auspicious emblems to show He is Hers.

These are some meditations on the physical features of the divine couple invoked by the first Hare Hare. They release such an addictive taste for this pair of names that one cannot stop repeating them.

**\* \* \* \***

The sound and taste of the maha-mantra submerges my mind in remembrance of beautiful Radha-Syamasundara in Their elegant, blue-hued dress with blue sequins and blue stones.

This stunning outfit was originally intended to be a night dress, but as soon as I saw the Deities wearing it, I requested the head pujari to schedule it as a day outfit because of its beauty and opulence.

Some devotees say this outfit accentuates Radha’s blue eyes, others say it blends with Syama’s dusky complexion, and still others say that its outstanding beauty comes from its sheer simplicity.

The shades of Syama’s kurta and dhoti go from dark blue at the bottom to light blue at the top, and Sri Radha’s skirt and blouse change shade in the same way but from Her left to Her right.

Syama’s shawl and Radha’s veil are made of very fine silk and display both shades of blue in whirling patterns of medium size. The same two shades pervade the patterns marking the sequinned and jewelled hems.

There are two more outstanding features of this outfit. The first is an elegant necklace of large black pearls I acquired for Radharani so that She could always be reminded of Her Syamasundara.

The second is Syama’s topknot, fashioned with strings of flowers,peacock feathers, and blue pearls. It looks like the work of gopas or gopis, so the pujari who designed it is certainly most fortunate.

The outfit’s overall effect is to see Radha and Syama like a dark and white cloud hanging in a dark-blue evening sky that is gradually transforming into the brilliant darkness of a star-studded night.

Hare! Hare! The blue hues pervading the outfit evoke thoughts of the transcendental connection between the colour of the blue sequinned outfit and the mystery of Syamasundara’s bodily complexion.

It almost appears that Syama has invested the aspects of His bodily complexion into the blue dress, infusing His hue into its colour and imparting His divine sheen into the sparkle of its stones and sequins.

Many things are suffused with the colour of Krsna’s body. Srila Prabhupada explains that Krsna’s bodily effulgence, the brahmajyoti, is responsible for tinting the sky with its bluish rays.

Srila Rupa Gosvami remarks that the touch of Krsna’s cheeks change the color of His flute from its natural bamboo-yellow to the deep blue-black of a sapphire. These statements support my claim.

Syama is not the only one with this power—Sri Radha has it as well. Once Krsna placed a white lotus bud in the curly locks of Radharani’s hair and the flower at once turned blue (indivara).

A sceptic might argue that because His colour is black and the dress is dark blue our notion of Syama lending His colour to the dress is an exaggeration at best, hut a closer look shows that it is not.

Vaisnava poets, including Srila Prabhupada, repeatedly use the words “blue” and “black” interchangeably in their descriptions of Krsna’s complexion without conclusively choosing one or the other.

The main reason they are reluctant to do so is that, because of its indescribable sweetness, the color of Krsna’s complexion cannot be adequately expressed in words, a characteristic called madhuryam.

Srila Prabhupada says,

**“There \[is\] nothing comparable to the bodily features of Krsna....The most beautiful object in the material world may be compared to the blue lotus flower or the full moon in the sky.**

**“But even the lotus flower and the moon are defeated by the beauty of the bodily features of Lord Krsna, and this was certified by the demigods, the most beautiful living creatures in the universe.”**

Jayadeva Gosvami describes Krsna’s body as bluish-black:

**“With His \[Krsna’s\] soft bluish-black limbs, which resemble blue lotus flowers, He has created a spring festival for Cupid.”**

And Srila Prabhupada uses the two colours interchangeably, for example,

**“… \[Krsna’s\] complexion is like a dark blue cloud,” and “… \[Krsna’s\] bodily colour resembles a fresh black cloud.”**

Another possible reason for this literary paradox is the effect Krsna’s dark colour — the colour of the amorous mellow-has on the minds of those who try to describe it in words. They are intoxicated by it.

Indeed, intoxication leads one to liberality in conduct and speech. Why not in writing as well? Saints inebriated by Krsna’s complexion describe it as blue (nila), black (syama), and bluish-black (syamala).

Syama’s complexion is not only intoxicating but also contagious. This contagion spreads to the fully transcendental souls of Goloka, and even to the conditioned souls of this world. It affects everyone.

As already mentioned, the brahmajyoti sometimes transmits Krsna’s blackish complexion to other things — such as the sky — which then become objects to which Sri Krsna’s bodily hue is rightly compared.

What are these fortunate objects to which Krsna’s complexion is compared? The most common are blue lotuses, sapphires, rain clouds,the tamala tree, collyrium, a swarm of bees, and the Yamuna.

Sri Advaita says,

**“Fragrant as a host of suddenly blooming blue lotuses, glorious as a host of dark clouds, dark as a forest of flowering tamala trees, and brilliant as a heap of sapphires.**

**“What is this flood of splendour that robs My eyes? A dark glory in each limb flooded with sweet nectar that expertly plays the flute, a divine splendour that is brother to the dark clouds, stands before Me.”**

Our acaryas verify that Krsna’s complexion is just like the colour of these objects. Sanatana Gosvami, for example, gives one such description of Krsna playing in the river with His friends.

To hide from the gopas and pretend he had drowned, Krsna once submerged His body in the dark waters of the Yamuna and concealed His face behind a cluster of blue lotuses, making it unrecognisable.

Searching, but not finding Him, His grief-stricken friends wept terribly until Krsna emerged from the lotuses, laughing in front of the boys, who were wide-eyed in amazement at His disappearing act.

Kaviraja Gosvami records how Radharani, love-blind and unable to recognise Her beloved, mistakes Krsna for a varied list of things. She wonders aloud, “Is this a cloud, a tamala tree, or a sapphire sprout?

“Is it a mountain peak of collyrium, a swarm of black bees, or a new stream of the river Yamuna? Or is it a cluster of blue lotus flowers created by the glances of the doe-eyed gopis of Vrndavana?”

These black objects are not only useful as points of comparison but also as causes of ecstatic love (uddipana), for the mere sight of them awakens remembrance of Krsna in those whose hearts are pure.

For instance, a young gopa once informed Krsna that lotus-eyed Srimati Radharani had seen a bluish cloud in the sky, remembered Krsna at once, and thus became eager for His company.

Radha is keen to always surround Herself with and to wear things that remind Her of Her lover. In the words of Lalita-devi, this practice is known as “Her blue emblem of constant love” for Krsna.

Sri Radha generally wears blue clothes. In this way She feels as if in Krsna’s constant embrace. She also wears sapphire jewellery, blue lotus garlands, kajjala on Her eyes, and a dot of musk on Her chin.

In addition to these personal items, Radha likes the dark sky of the waning moon, newly blossomed blue lotuses, black deer, dark tamala trees, monsoon clouds, and the blackish waves of the Yamuna River.

Perhaps Syama gave this blue-hued outfit its colour to reciprocate the constancy of Radha’s love for Him, because even in the material world blue is recognised as a symbol of truth, confidence, and fidelity.

Blue also symbolises peace and attachment to tradition, while black conveys elegance, sophistication, sexuality, and a touch of mystery— characteristics having their origins in Krsna Himself.

Krsna’s complexion has other qualities that sing of its extraordinary spiritual nature. Amongst these is its aroma. In short, Krsna’s bodily hue has not just the colour but also the fragrance of a blue lotus.

Sri Suka’s description of the rasa dance confirms:

**“Upon a gopi's shoulder Krsna placed His arm, whose natural blue-lotus fragrance was mixed with that of the sandal wood pulp anointing it.**

Actually, Krsna’s complexion is the colour of His essential nature, the amorous mellow (syama-rasa). The Upanisads indicate this with the words raso vai sah: Krsna is the reservoir of pleasure.

When Krsna’s transcendental desires are agitated, His complexion sometimes exhibits an aura that obscures His form, and because of this, living entities may mistake Him for something else.

Yogamaya Paurnamasi once said to Krsna,

**“Seeing Your glistening peacock-feather crown, the peacocks think You are a blue rain cloud, and they begin to dance with jubilant abandon.”**

There is another quality of Lord Krsna’s mysterious complexion that I will mention. It effects whomever looks upon it, especially those who are in a mood to reciprocate the amorous love it proclaims.

The young cowherd girls of Vraja are always looking at Krsna with amorous desire, and so their eyes are generally tinted blue. This is especially so of Srimati Radharani, of whose eyes it is said:

**“The beauty of Srimati Radharani’s eyes forcibly devours the beauty of newly grown blue lotus flowers, and the beauty of Her face surpasses that of an entire forest of fully blossomed lotuses.”**

In speaking about Krsna’s bodily complexion, it should be mentioned that rare references to the colour of His eyes indicate that they too are blue-black, which is further confirmation of His amorous nature.

Bilvamangala Thakura writes,

**“When will Sri Krsna cast upon me His sidelong glances, which are as dark blue as the blue lotuses growing in the Yamuna and tremulous with waves of mercy? Please tell me.”**

Because Radha’s blue sari steals Syama’s mind by sending Him amorous signals, I call her Hara, and because Syama steals Radha’s mind by dressing in blue to reciprocate Her love, I call Him Hari.

Dressed in this way, with similarly coloured necklaces, rings, earrings,ornaments, and garlands, and by the influence of the maha-mantra, They remind me of Their midday pastimes. Hare! Hare!

Radha-Syamasundara appear as Deities upon the altar of New Vraja-dhama, but in Their unmanifest forms They continuously engage in eightfold daily pastimes, just as They do in Goloka Vrndavana.

Prabodhananda Sarasvati says that Radha and Krsna sometimes feelunsatisfied with the expressions of love They can show each other asa single couple. They then expand Themselves into many couples.

**“When Radha-Krsna, thirsting after the sweetness of transcendental pastimes, are not satisfied by being a single couple, They become limitless couples and enjoy passionate pastimes in the rasa dance.”**

In this way Radha and Krsna manifest not only as Deities, but in aprakata pastimes as well. Sometimes They also appear in multiple forms to play dice, drink wine, swing, joke, and so on, all at once.

**\* \* \* \***

The midday pastimes begin when Srimati Radharani and Her cowherd girlfriends leave Yavata to worship the sun god. At that time Krsna leaves His gopa friends and the cows to wander in the forest.

Radha and Krsna may give different reasons for Their respective departures, but Their purpose is one: They will meet at Radha-kunda to fulfil Their mounting desire to be with one another.

These pastimes begin with a conversation at Yavata. Radha does Her best to shelter Her mother-in-law’s mind from the winds of village gossip that whisper of an illicit relationship between Her and Krsna.

Villagers are conservative. If a young bride goes daily to the house of another man to cook, that fuels the fire of gossip, and if she is seen in the forest with that man, it will surely fan those flames.

Yasoda hears the gossip in her own village and curses Providence for obliging her to send Radha home immediately after breakfast. She cries, “I cannot even keep Radha with me for a single day.”

Jatila, her daughter Kutila, and son Abhimanyu also hear the gossip, but because Radha always returns with gifts from Yasoda, Jatila is unwilling to refuse the revenue that fills her family’s coffers.

The one who suffers most from all this small-mindedness is Radha, for whom Yavata is like fire, Her in-laws like condemnation personified, and Her husband like the embodiment of Lord Siva’s anger.

Sometimes Srimati Radharani laments, “Had I known that I would suffer so, I would never have entered into this love affair with the son of Maharaja Nanda. What have I done? Oh, what have I done?”

Of course, such words don’t reflect Her eternal commitment to please Krsna at all costs. They are words meant to enrich the mood of pastimes and bring smiles of amusement to Her friends.

Upon Her return from Nandagrama, Radharani shows Jatila the costly ornaments and silken garments given by Yasoda, knowing well that Jatila has already heard an earful of gossip that morning.

Clever Radharani lowers Her head as if dejected and for some time sits silently beside Her equally morose gopi friends, Her lotus face red from crying, Her eyes still brimming with tears.

Jatila swallows the bait and asks with concern, “Daughter! Why is Your face downcast? Why are Your eyes red with tears? Tell me honestly, has someone said or done something to upset You?”

Radha replies, “Everyone must suffer the results of his or her karma. Apparently My fate is to tolerate the slander of villagers for whom Ihave become like sand in the eyes. At least that is how they treat Me.

“They say I am so foolish that I cannot hind the hair on My own head. They criticise Me for going to another’s home to cook. How can a chaste wife and the daughter-in-law of nobility tolerate all of this?”

Worried that Radha will no longer visit Nandagrama and that the gifts from Mother Yasoda will cease to come, Jatila the miser pleads, “Princess! Don’t say such things. What if Yasoda were to hear!

“She decorates You with ornaments and asks You to cook for her son out of affection for me. She could hire so many cooks. Just understand. There is no difference between her house and mine.

“For You to cook in her kitchen is the same as cooking in this house. Have no doubts. Besides, Paurnamasi says that Durvasa Muni has blessed Your cooking to possess the taste and potency of nectar.

“Since our two families are so intimately related, and since the creator has blessed Your cooking, why should You hesitate to cook in Yasoda s house? Rest assured that whoever criticises You will perish.”

Eager to change the topic, Jatila concludes, “You must now prepare to worship the sun god. Girls! Rest a little, then collect the paraphernalia for worship and find a local brahmana to assist you.”

The gopis follow Jatila’s orders and retire to Radha’s apartment,where they lounge like resting swans while Radha entertains them with jokes about the recent conversation with Her mother-in-law.

As soon as the maidservants have prepared everything, including an offering of sweets and savouries for the sun god, the gopis dress and ornament Radha so that She can enchant the enchanter of Cupid.

At midday the footpaths in Vraja are quite hot, and the eyes of the villagers alert. But Radha casts aside Her family’s reputation and Her famed chastity and ignores the enmity of the low-minded villagers.

With Cupid as Her charioteer, Radha rides the chariot of love out of the scaring sun into the forest, and onwards to Her lake, all the while reciting mantras to attain Her desire. All obstacles be damned!

Sometimes Krsna arrives early at Radha-kunda and has to wait for Her, but at other times, like this one, it is She who has to wait in the creeper-shaded cottage within Her private garden until He arrives.

When He does arrive, beautifully dressed and ornamented, Radha is visibly receptive to Krsna. She greets Him with great respect, placing a garland on His neck and sandalwood paste on His limbs.

And though the sandalwood paste cools and refreshes Krsna’s body,inside Him desire burns. By Her proximity to Him, Radha feels the heat of ecstatic love growing in both Their hearts and She perspires.

Seeing His beloved decorated by pearl-drops of attachment for Him, Krsna suggests that They do something to relieve the heat of midday, and so the divine couple begin Their pastimes by swinging together.

After pleasing Themselves and Their girlfriends with games on the swing, Radha and Krsna greet the hottest part of the day with diversions in the cool, aromatic waters of Radha-kunda.

Radha’s and Krsna’s water sports may resemble the play of infatuated adolescents, but actually they are expressions of selfless love, disclosed only to devotees with the deepest faith in and a grasp of the sublime.

After Their water sports They come to shore, and Their friends dress Them in fresh clothing and flower decorations. Looking like two moving gardens, Radha and Krsna then sit down for a game of dice.

Under the boughs of a grove of desire trees Radha and Krsna take Their places to play dice. The stakes? Loving exchanges. Radha rolls black dice, Krsna rolls gold ones, and Their friends look on with glee.

Of the two, Krsna is more controlled by the competitive spirit. And because He is so eager to win the first round — and collect the wager — when He wins, His friends shout, “Hare! O Hari!”

But Radha is more skilled at throwing dice. Krsna wins some throws, but Radharani wins the game. As She collects the total wagered stakes, in the excitement of victory Her friends yell, “Hare! O Hara!”

Krsna accepts His inevitable defeat and feigns being a good sport. He places the dice in Radha’s hands and says, “Today the goddess of fortune has smiled upon You. I submit Myself at Your lotus feet.”

After such physical exertion, naturally They are hungry. Srimati Radharani feeds Krsna fruit collected from a nearby forest, savouries brought from home, and sweets She prepared earlier in the day.

After Krsna has eaten His fill, Radha and Her friends honour His remnants, and then the divine couple retire to a beautiful jeweled temple to enjoy amorous pastimes on the pretext of taking rest.

Meanwhile, the sakhis also rest in their respective groves while the maidservants joyfully finish the remnants of the meal before busying themselves to prepare for Radha’s visit to Surya-kunda.

**\* \* \* \***

Amidst this lull, a parrot suddenly arrives with news that Abhimanyu and Jatila, incited by village gossip, are on their way to find out why it always takes Radha and Her friends so long to worship the sun god.

This news is like a bucket of iced water tossed on Krsna and the gopis,who leap to their feet and hastily make a plan. Radha and Her friends are off to Surya-kunda, Krsna heads to Kunjara to change clothes.

Carrying the items with which to worship the sun, Radha and the gopis are the first to arrive at the beautiful altar standing at the centre of a flower-filled grove within a forest of wish-fulfilling trees.

Srimati Radharani and Her maidservants sit down near the deity, place the gifts and items of worship on a silken cloth before the altar, and begin to sing traditional songs that glorify the sun.

A little while later, Madhumangala appears along with Krsna, who is disguised as a brahmana. Dressed in white cloth, His tousled black hair tied in a topknot, He resembles a lifelong brahmacari.

A scarf hangs from Krsna’s neck, a large red spot of tilaka graces His forehead, and rings decorate His fingers. With kusa grass in one hand and a sacred book in the other, He moves with an air of detachment.

It’s not long before Madhumangala notices the sweets waiting to he offered to the deity and says, “We should not keep the lord of the sky waiting for his worship or offering. Let us do the needful, post-haste.”

Radha nods in agreement to Madhu’s proposal and offers a seat to the two brahmanas. Then She places the tray of sweets in Krsna’s hands for offering, along with gifts of garments and ornaments.

At that moment, Abhimanyu, who is sometimes called Ayana, arrives with Jatila. On the way to Surya-kunda, they had been speaking harshly about Radha, unable to contain their slanderous words.

But since they are now in the presence of a demigod and two brahmanas, mother and son control themselves and sit down in the corner of the courtyard, constantly scowling at the proceedings.

Srimati Radharani acknowledges their arrival hy bowing Her head, but Krsna is already reciting mantras, so She remains silent. She just sits there, shaking with fear, not knowing what to expect.

Radha is clearly at wits’ end, Her veil fallen to the ground. The other cowherd girls, recognising the impending danger, whisper amongst themselves, “Ayana will recognise Krsna. What will we do?”

But Krsna is serene as He chants mantras in praise of the sun. Suddenly He throws His voice to make it sound as if it’s coming from the deity, who speaks angrily at Sri Radha. The deity says:

**“O chaste Radha! No matter how many sacrifices You perform for me, in return for their sins I will send death to your husband and ruin to Jatila, to her relatives, to her cows, and to the people of her village.**

**“You, Radha, are as pure as my rays. Thus I cannot tolerate those who falsely accuse You of misconduct. I will free the earth of such filth.”**

Because Radha misses this cue to speak, Krsna, as the brahmana, says:

**“O Lord! O jewel of day! I am here only for your service, but I must also represent this girl who is speechless due to your terrible curse. If you kill Her husband, how will She continue to live?”**

Astute Kundalata then speaks up, “O Lord of the skies! I know how dear Radha has become to you by Her daily worship, and how you cannot stand to see your pure devotees defamed or disgraced — ”

Prompted by these cues, Radha finally interrupts, “With folded hands I pray to you, My worshipable deity, whom I have served all My life. What will be My fate if My friends and relatives all die?

“My husband is My life. If he dies how can I live? My mother-in-law always treats Me with affection. If she is destroyed, how will your Radha survive such a calamity? Oh, please be kind to them!”

Radha and Krsna then both rise to Their feet. Standing side by side, palms joined, They offer prayer after prayer to the sun god as Jatila and Abhimanyu stand by, wide-eyed and mouths agape.

At last the deity of the sun says, “O chaste one! Your devotion always pleases me. Rest assured that no calamity shall befall You. Your husband, family, and friends are safe. Be at peace.”

At these words of reassurance from the deity of Surya, Radha and Krsna take Their seats to complete the offering by chanting mantras and to worship the sun god with incense, lamps, flowers, and garlands.

To milk the positive turn of events for its full worth, Radha prays aloud, “O Lord! If you are still My protector and well-wisher after all I have asked, please throw Me a flower. Then I will be reassured.”

As soon as Radha finishes speaking, the deity smiles and shakes his body, causing all the offered flowers to fall in a shower to the floor. The gopis all jump to their feet and joyfully cry out, “Jaya! Jaya!”

While Madhu ties all the offered sweets in his cloth, Krsna very gravely goes to each gopi, places His hands on her head, and blesses her with the words, “May you be happy with your husband.”

Abhimanyu, taking advantage of the happy confusion, sneaks away with his mother, heading for the forest road that leads back to their home. Relieved to be alive, he even drops his shawl on the ground.

On the way home mother and son praise Radha profusely, hitting their heads with their hands, although along the same road not long ago they had accused Her of heinous deeds and called Her ill names.

At home Abhimanyu tells his mother, “Never again listen to the advice of your foolish neighbours, who will be the death of me. And never again fault your daughter-in-law, lest the Lord ruin you.”

Mother and son talk for a long time about the incredible things they saw and heard at Surya-kunda, and they agree not to speak about them to anyone, but to simply praise Radha when She returns home.

But Radha would be a little late in coming home that day, for after her husband had gone, She and Krsna returned to Radha-kunda and continued the pastimes that had been so rudely interrupted.

To free Themselves from the stress of the episode at Surya-kunda, They again immersed Themselves in the refreshing, nectarean waters of Radha-kunda and splashed Their worries away in games of love.

Such are the blissful pastimes Radha and Krsna perform during the twelve dandas of midday. Even though these pastimes occur daily, they always look and feel as if they arc happening for the first time.

When devotees of faith hear, remember, or repeat these pastimes,their hearts are filled with joy, and they cannot help but praise the hero and heroine of Vrndavana by repeatedly saying, “Hare! Hare!”

Indeed, Krsna, who is also known as Hari for taking away Radha’s sadness with His affectionate ways, is unlimitedly pleased when He hears devotees call out to His beloved Radha, “Hara! Hara!”

O swan of my mind! Swim always in the waters of nama-sankirtana, play amongst the lotuses of Radha’s and Krsna’s midday pastimes, and reject thoughts of religiosity, wealth, sensual pleasure, and liberation.

**\* \* \* \***

My heart, tongue, and hands, each in their own way, praise New Vraja-dhama, where Radha-Syamasundara enact Their pastimes and the residents have every opportunity to meditate upon Them.

Chanting Hare Hare reminds me of how a devotee once boldly enquired, “Isn’t it self-serving of Krsna to inspire His devotees to chant His own names, pastimes, and other glories?”

This pair of names, Hare Hare, answers this challenge, insisting by repetition that it is Radha who inspires us to praise Krsna in so many ways. But, in esoteric terms, Hare Hare says even more.

Since the words Hare Hare invoke the pleasure potency’s essence, mahabhava, we recognise that it is love itself that inspires us to glorify Radha and Krsna, thus neither can be accused of being self-serving.

Though I compile various meanings for the names that comprise the maha-mantra, my readers may think remembering such things to bean unnecessary burden that only makes nama-bhajana more difficult.

But my intention in presenting these meanings is not to force anyone to think of formulas to be memorised or mindlessly repeated. My purpose is to present avenues for contemplation on the maha-mantra.

My hope is that these discussions will stimulate my readers’ comprehension, which will then crystallise in genuine realisations and devotional moods compatible with their individual natures.

Such mature knowledge and sentiment will guide chanters on the path of nama-bhajana to their own unique relationships with Krsna and to the special relish associated with those relationships.

For example, in order to teach someone how to cook a single dish, an expert chef may explain what each individual ingredient contributes to the whole and why they are added in a particular sequence.

Such a chef will also indicate the proper temperature, the variance sin cooking times, and how to mix or stir the ingredients, all in order to produce the desired taste, texture, and aroma.

Once the student has mastered the complexities of what he has seen, heard, and tasted, all the variables come together in a very natural way and the result is very tasty.

Similarly, when knowledge of the maha-mantra — in terms of relationship, practice, and goal — is combined with sincere chanting blessed by divine grace, the resultant nama-bhajana is also quite tasty.

I thus conclude this explanation of the maha-mantra’s fourth pair of names, hoping to please the all-merciful holy name and receive blessings for unconditional devotion and truly refined chanting.

To Radha-Syama I pray, “O playful couple! In my quest for knowledge I once gave up a beautiful wife, the prospects of a lucrative career, and the allure of sensual pleasure. Please give me Your shelter!

“I now have many submissive followers, material facilities for service,and respect from both Vaisnava and civil society, but I am not looking for these things. I desire only to be Your menial servant.”

Daily I utter these prayers, first to Syama and then to His beloved Radha,

*premadam ca me kamadam ca me vedanam ca me vaibhavamca me*  
*jivanam ca me jivitam ca me daivatam ca me deva na 'param*

**“\[O Syama!\] You and You alone are my worshipful Deity, the giver of love and the fulfiller of desire. You alone are the object of my knowledge, my power, and wealth, my vital force, and my very life.”**

*Tavaivasmi tavaivasmi na jivami tvaya vina*  
*iti vijnaya devi tvam nayamam caranantikam*

**“\[O Radha!\] I am Yours! I am Yours! I cannot live without You! Please understand this and bring me to Your feet.”**

Having completed my description of the first four pairs of names — the first half of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra — I offer my humble obeisances to these cintamani forms of the Lord in sacred sound.

I offer my obeisances at the lotus feet of my readers and at the lotusfeet of my worshipable Lordships, Radha-Syamasundara. May theyall be kind enough to bless me with the fulfilment of my desires.

*O son of Maharaja Nanda, I am Your eternal servant, but because of My own fruitive acts I have fallen into this horrible ocean of nescience. How, please be causelessly merciful to Me. Consider Me a particle of dust at Your lotus feet. (Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu)*

## Chapter 40 - The Maha-mantra. Part III

The maha-mantra is like a great ocean in which all of one’s troubles dissolve. Its waves, the sounds of the ultimate names of the Lord — Hare, Krsna, and Rama — mercifully purify everything.

Exquisite jewels are found in the depths of that ocean: devotional service in practice, in ecstasy, and in love of God. And of those jewels, the most precious is service to the divine couple’s lotus feet.

Knowing that such treasures abound within the ocean of Krsna’s holy names, bhakti-yogis relentlessly plumb its depths and adorn themselves with the priceless jewels they inevitably find.

In this way Vaisnavas and Vaisnavis grow increasingly opulent with the trove of pure devotion, which unlike earthly riches is the source of all good qualities, all good fortune, and all perfection.

As the preceding two chapters extol and elucidate the first four pairs of the maha-mantra s names, this and the following chapter attempt to magnify the glories of the remaining four pairs of divine names.

These chapters follow the structure of Sri Bhajana-rahasya, as did the preceding two, citing scriptural verses Bhaktivinoda Thakura uses to corroborate his statements. They also include my own realisations.

In Sri Bhajana-rahasya the Thakura describes the development of love for Krsna in the wake of the amorous mellow, specifically themellow of Radha’s maidservants, and these chapters follow his lead.

The development of love following the Vraja-vasis’ other moods, such as those of Krsna’s friends, are just as worthy of a portrayal, along with the corresponding truths of their mellows and pastimes.

Nonetheless, Srila Prabhupada points out that a part of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s specific mission was to personally exhibit and freelybestow the amorous love displayed by the gopis of Vrndavana.

And while we may seek perfection in any of the five mellows, His Divine Grace also points out,

**“Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His followers mainly worship Lord Krsna in madhurya-rasa."**

For this reason the process of nama-bhajana chalked out here leads to the development of devotional service in amorous love, a path no doubt helpful for devotees in every other mellow as well.

From my own lowly position, I sometimes express my own feelings towards the service of Sri Radha, specifically in the context of service to New Vraja-dhama’s presiding Deities, Radha-Syamasundara.

These feelings are no more sublime than a budding attraction that awoke in me as I studied Srila Prabhupada’s books, served Lord Caitanya’s mission, and worshipped Radha-Syamasundara.

I pray that, by the mercy of His Divine Grace and Krsna’s holy names, this budding attraction may one day develop into the mature attraction described by our acaryas. And I am confident that it will.

Srila Prabhupada himself outlines the path to awakening and developing mature attraction to the service of the divine couple in these words,

**“This development of conjugal love can be possible —**

**“Only with those who are already engaged in following the regulative principles of devotional service, specifically in the worship of Radha and Krsna in the temple.**

**“Such devotees gradually develop a spontaneous love for the Deity, and by hearing of the Lord’s exchange of loving affairs with the gopis, they gradually become attracted to these pastimes.**

**“After this spontaneous attraction becomes highly developed, the devotee is placed in either of the above mentioned categories \[direct contact with Krsna as a sakhi or indirect as a manjari\]."**

Let us now hear of the fifth pair of names, Hare Rama, which suggests a strong attachment to Krsna. Such attachment is the final stage of chanting in practice and the precursor to pure chanting in ecstasy.

This stage of devotion (asakti) appears when the taste for nama-bhajana is enriched by attachment to Krsna, a bond that develops naturally through regular hearing of Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes.

By meditating upon how Krsna’s daily activities unfold, we cultivate attachment to Him. A part of our prayers to the holy name, then, includes a request for the privilege to remember Sri Krsna’s pastimes.

Our endeavour to please Krsna by thinking of Him, along with the blessings of the holy name, nourishes our taste for Krsna’s pastimes. In time that taste transforms into attachment to Krsna (asakti).

This attachment is a sublime emotion that closely resembles true spiritual love. Nama-bhajana touched by this degree of affection polishes the mirror of the heart almost to the point of purity.

But to go beyond this stage we require divine intervention from the Lord or from one of His empowered agents, for our endeavour to prayor meditate cannot by itself effect the change we desire.

How and why the Lord intercedes to awaken ecstatic love is a topic related to the sixth pair of names. For now let us hear more about the symptoms and practices of nama-bhajana imbued with asakti.

When taste and attachment mature, an exhilarating, at times even intoxicating joy arises in the heart. That electrifying joy is nourished by the spontaneous flow of thoughts about Krsna.

Now, with no conscious effort on our part, the joy of attachment to Krsna plunges us headlong into thoughts of Krsna’s pastimes, just as a strong river current swiftly carries a helpless person downstream.

At this stage the heart’s only remaining ambition is to be accepted as a qualified servant, which enables one to cross from the near shore of hankering for direct service to the far shore of entering Krsna’s lila.
