Even the demigods respect one who has attained this stage of devotion, but humility reminds such a devotee that it was his or her rebellious, sinful nature that first caused separation from the Lord.

**\* \* \* \***

At this point in our development we often recall our past sins. These shameful memories fill us with regret for having disobeyed the Lord’s will and for having taken the Lord’s endless patience for granted.

Asakti also fuels our ardent desire for service. As the Lord Himself says,

*ayi nanda-tanuja kinkaram patitam mani visame bhavambudhau*  
*krpaya tava pada-pankaja-sthita-dhuli-sadrsam vicintaya*

**“O My Lord, O Krsna, son of Maharaja Nanda, I am Your eternal servant, but because of My own fruitive acts I have fallen into this horrible ocean of nescience. Now, please be causelessly —**

**“Merciful to Me. Consider Me a particle of dust at Your lotus feet.”**

In this famous verse Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu points out two qualities of an advanced devotee: repentance and aspiration.

Even as one feels strong attachment to the Lord, such a soul is still conditioned and painfully aware of all disqualifications, knowing that only Lord Krsna’s causeless mercy can bestow transcendence.

Still, Mahaprabhu’s followers do not pray for liberation from material suffering, instead preferring the privilege of being accepted as Krsna’s own to engage in service to the Lord while living in this world.

While chanting Hare Rama I often think, “What else can I do but wait, suffer the burden of my sins, and beg, cry, and pray for the mercy Radha and Syama will shower upon me? Surely They will!’’

The reader may wonder, “How can you be so sure that you will receive Krsna’s mercy? How can you say it ‘will’ happen?” My answer: Srila Prabhupada has promised that we will go back to Godhead.

What’s more, Krsna promises, “You will come to Me.” And scriptures declare that constant endeavour, unflinching devotion, and detachment surely bring the practitioner spiritual success.

An example of a determined devotee who waited patiently to be reinstated in eternal service to Krsna is Vrtrasura, who, as the great devotee Citraketu, was cursed by Parvati to become a demon.

Citraketu was a great Vaisnava, powerful enough to nullify any curse,but he accepted his fate as the Lord’s will, along with the suffering that came from having to fight and kill some of the demigods.

Yet Vrtrasura never abandoned the conviction that supreme good fortune would one day be his. Even as he was on the verge of death at Indra’s hands, he still prayed to the Lord with complete certainty:

**“O my Lord, O Supreme Personality of Godhead! Will I again be able to be a servant of Your eternal servants who find shelter only at Your lotus feet? O Lord of my life, may I again become their servant —**

**“So that my mind may always think of Your transcendental attributes,my words always glorify those attributes, and my body always engage in the loving service of Your Lordship?”**

We should also note that as our aspiration for service intensifies, it becomes more specific. For the followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the desire may emerge to be one of Srimati Radharani’s maidservants.

As are all stages of devotional service, asakti is accompanied by a corresponding aspiration, which for those aspiring to he gopis is a semblance of the inimitable mood of Sri Radha’s maidservants.We cannot imitate the mood — not to mention the service—of the gopis, hut we can certainly revere them. After they had answered the call of His flute, even the gopis had to convince Krsna to accept them.Similarly, we may follow in the gopis’ footsteps by praying to Krsna,

**“O Lord! Through Your personal teachings and the words of Your agents, You have asked us to become Your servants.**

**“We have followed Your instructions. If You think it proper and us fit, guide us in the wake of Your maidservants.”**

This selfless service attitude is the basis of the mood at the stage of attachment.

In the progression of attachment, next is that one’s aspiration to he a soul surrendered to Sri Radha naturally awakens, just as one earlier identified oneself as a servant of Krsna in a more general sense.

From the beginning of one’s devotional life one thinks, “I am Krsna’s eternal servant,” and as one advances, the process of devotional service gradually discloses a preferred mode of service.

One’s aspiration thus develops naturally by degrees, gradually becoming more specific, from being a servant of Krsna, to a servant of a Vraja-vasi and, in the case of a maidservant, a servant of Radha.

Inherent in aspiring service to Radha is knowledge that such service entails the mood of the paramour love of Vrndavana and not the wedded love of the queens of the Lord in Dvaraka.

As Kaviraja Gosvami says,

**“All glories to the mellow of amorous love, which is the most excellent of all rasas and is propagated in Vraja by Sri Krsna in the form of the divine parakiya-bhava \[paramour love\]."**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami expresses his sentiment for such service thus:

**“Without worshipping the pollen of Sri Radha’s lotus feet, without taking shelter of Vrndavana, which bears Her footprints —**

**“And without respectfully greeting the great souls whose hearts are filled with deep love for Srimati Radharani, how will one be able to plunge into the nectar ocean of love for Lord Krsna?”**

The cumulative effect of the development of attachment is called abhimana, a self-identification in which the conception of one’s original identity awakens but is completely devoid of false ego.

Some people may find this identification born of attachment artificial or even unattractive, but devotees in whom it has actually awakened through nama-bhajana will not be deterred by opinions.

Uddhava, an eternal associate of Krsna, also expressed his willingness to be born as the ground cover in Vraja solely to attain the gopis’ mercy and to be able to relish their selfless attitude of service.

Although Lord Caitanya directed His prayers to Krsna, acaryas offered similar prayers for service to Radha, and we currently pray to the divine couple for the same purpose — service to Sri Radha.

The following words of Prabodhananda Sarasvati Thakura summarise the mood and attachment of *asakti-nama'-bhajana*, a mood one meditates upon as represented by the pair of names, Hare Rama.

**“By always remembering Lord Sri Krsna, who wears a peacock feather in His crown, by performing sankirtana, by engaging in the service of His lotus feet, and by chanting the best of mantras —**

**“By remembering the most cherished service of the lotus feet of Sri Radha within my heart, when will I relish the most amazing festival of attachment to the daughter of King Vrsabhanu?”**

Dear devotees, beware! We should avoid the company of immature persons who speak of attraction to Radha in a way that minimises Krsna. Such ideas are defective in terms of both tattva and rasa.

We may think of Radha’s lotus feet as our goal in life, and She maybe our worshipful Deity, but we can never reject or minimise attachment to Radha’s beloved and at the same time expect to please Her.

Radha may control Krsna in Their pastimes, but He is always the supreme controller, even when Radha treats Him as Her plaything. Ultimately, such an attitude exists only because it is pleasing to Him.

Therefore we can determine if real asakti has awakened in us, or in anyone else, by noting the presence of the characteristics described and summarised in the following verse by Uddhava Mahasaya.

**“Simply by decorating ourselves with the garlands, fragrant oils, clothes, and ornaments that You have already enjoyed, and simply by eating the remnants of Your meals, we, Your servants —**

**“Will indeed conquer Your illusory energy.”**

In short, attached devotees have firm faith that Krsna’s mercy will free them from maya and reinstate them in their coveted eternal service to Him.

While chanting Hare Rama let us contemplate the meaning of the word kinkara (“servant”) used by Lord Caitanya in His Siksastaka and pray that direct service to Radha and Krsna attracts us.

**\* \* \* \***

In the sequence wherein the divine couple’s bodily features correspond to the pairs of names in the maha-mantra, the fifth, Hare Rama, reminds me of Their shoulders and neck.

Syama’s threefold-bending pose, holding a flute to His lips, makes His broad, lion-like shoulders slope downward from His right to His left. When He dances, the angle of that slope appears even greater.

His shoulders are perfectly symmetrical and proportioned. Garlands and necklaces decorate them, as does His soft, shiny hair gently falling in waves and curls over His shoulders and back.

Some say Krsna’s shoulders resemble the backs of bulls, indicative of the power of the Supreme Person. Others say that His shoulders are raised due to constantly embracing Srimati Radharani.

And yet others believe that the broadness of Krsna’s shoulders is caused by their constantly expanding themselves in eagerness to seethe dark sweetness of His neck decorated by the Kaustubha gem.

Krsna’s neck is short and marked with three conch-like lines, which are symbols of auspiciousness. His neck is also lustrous, resembling a sapphire mirror, and it tilts gracefully to His left.

This tilting of the neck is also seen in Sri Radha as a symptom of ecstatic love that accompanies the blossoming of the eyes, eyebrows, and other features in happiness, symptoms called hava.

Strands of pearls and a choker decorate Krsna’s neck, as does a tiger’s nail set in gold that Mother Yasoda hung there when Krsna was still a child, in the conviction that it would ward off evil influences.

Lord Caitanya says that Krsna’s pearl necklaces resemble a flock of flying swans, and Srila Prabhupada explains that they denote Krsna’s devotees, whom He always protects by holding them to His bosom.

Krsna’s neck is the throne for His throat and His words. It is likened to a lake wherein the Kaustubha swan swims and from where flow graceful rivers of amusing jokes, artistic poems, and melodious songs.

What can be said about these waves of sound rippling across the lake of Krsna’s neck that could eliminate the need to hear them ourselves? They defeat the sounds of cuckoos, bees, the flute, and the vina.

I am not so fortunate as to have heard the sound of Krsna’s voice,and so I am unable to describe it or to compare it to something. Nonetheless, the next best thing for me is the sound of Hare Rama.

In this way, Krsna’s devotees are so pleased by the sight of His shoulders and neck that they involuntarily call out, “Hare Rama!” and offer obeisances to this feature of the Lord’s youthful good looks.

Syamasundara’s original, eternal form (svarupa) is that of an adolescent in the last stage of youth (sesa-kaisora or nava-yauvana). This transcendental svarupa is the source of all other forms and ages.

In His form as an eternal youth, Krsna’s dress, actions, features, and excellences surpass those of His childhood, boyhood, or any one of the other phases of youth. As nava-yauvana, He is simply wonderful.

Srila Prabhupada called his favourite painting “Wonderful Krsna.” In this picture Radha is kneeling and offering flowers at Krsna’s lotus feet as He stands in His classic threefold-bending pose.

Three things have always struck me about that painting: the breadth of Krsna’s shoulders, Radha’s humble demeanour at His feet, and the gopis’ faces in the bushes. These are pastimes of that eternal youth.

Each time I massage Syamasundara with oils to prepare Him for His hath, I marvel at the strength, elegance, and artistic poise with which His chest blooms into wide shoulders and a pillar-like neck.

These are the same shoulders upon which tired gopis rest their arms, Sri Radha leans Her head, Sridama sometimes rides, and upon which Krsna once slung Kuvalayapida’s severed tusk after killing the beast.

It is said that the great sages of Maharloka reside upon the Lord’s neck, but these saints must be ignorant of their own good fortune; otherwise, they would worship Him directly instead of through fire.

From Syama’s neck hangs the famous Kaustubha gem. A friend of the Syamantaka jewel, it rests on His chest as a symbol of His divinity. I lament that here in New Vraja-dhama we offer Him a mere replica.

Another divine symbol that decorates the Lord’s neck and shoulders is the knee-length Vaijayanti garland. Made of fragrant sylvan flowers and tulasi-manjaris, it attracts a constant swarm of bees.

A flower garland always embraces Krsna’s tilaka-marked neck, and so envious Radha cursed the Vaijayanti to always meet with destruction by being crushed on Krsna’s chest by Her embrace.

Brahma once told Narada that whoever regularly wears flower garlands that have hung from Krsna’s neck becomes freed of all disease, sinful reaction, and, ultimately, all material contamination.

And to answer a prayer, or to give special mercy, the Lord sometimes makes His garland slip from His neck, just as Madana-mohana did when He gave blessings to Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami.

Who does not long for a rare sign of recognition such as that? I must admit that, as merciful as They have been to me, Radha-Syamasundara have yet to show me that particular token of affection.

But on one occasion I went into the Deity room with a small stool to sit and watch Their Lordships being dressed. Just as I was sitting down, the pujari asked me, “Will you dress Srimati Radharani?”

I joined my palms and shook my head to decline, only to have the sturdy stool collapse beneath me. And so I at once gave up my plan to he an observer and happily accepted Radha’s “demand” to dress Her.

Being praised or chastised by the Supreme Lord or His consort are both signs of Their recognition, equally welcomed by those eager to he accepted as menial servants of their worshipful Deities.

When we come to the stage of loving surrender, Krsna takes us into His circle of confidential companions and directly reciprocates with us, either by His loving neglect, His indifference, or His embrace.

As Radha and Krsna were once wandering through the forest, She felt a little proud and asked Him to carry Her. He told Her, “Climb on My shoulder,” and then disappeared, leaving Her to lament.

Contrast this with how Krsna sometimes allows His friends to climb on His shoulders after He loses a mock fight, or to pin His shoulders down while wrestling and to call out, “I have won! Krsna has lost!”

Krsna’s purpose in reciprocating with His associates or His devotees is to increase loving relationships with them through the dynamics of praise and chastisement, as He does through meeting and separation.

The sight of Krsna’s shoulders reassures us that for those who meditate on His transcendental form and who worship Him exclusively, He carries what they lack and preserves what they have.

For me, “carries what they lack” means Krsna will accept His devotees’ offerings, however imperfect; “preserves what they have” means He will reciprocate by increasing His devotees’ love for Him.

The ultimate reciprocation comes when Krsna offers His shoulder to His companion to ride or to lean upon. In this way, the sloping of Syamasundara’s shoulders portends promising things to come.

In the soft sands of Vrndavana, Krsna stands in a youthful pose with Balarama amongst His cowherd boyfriends. And Balarama, who is taller than Krsna, rests His elbow on Krsna’s raised right shoulder.

And when He stands amongst the gopis in the soft sands by Yamuna’s shore, His pose is quite the same, hut because Radha is smaller than Him, She rests Her right arm on Krsna's left, lower, shoulder.

To onlookers, exchanges such as these are bliss. A gopi said, “Dear Subala! I know that Krsna is your friend and that you always enjoy joking with Him. The other day I saw you both standing together.

“You were keeping your hand upon Krsna’s shoulder, and both of you were joyfully smiling. When I saw the two of you standing like that in the distance, my eyes at once overflooded with tears.”

As I chant, “Hare Rama” I am reminded of Krsna’s shoulders, upon which He carried the stolen clothes of bathing gopis, and from which He also handed their clothes back to them, one by one.

I meditate upon He whose shoulders are always elegantly draped with a silken garment with which lovely Radharani sometimes wipes the perspiration or the tears of joy from Her face during the rasa dance.

Where is that artistic, clever Krsna, who moves His neck like a dancing peacock as He entertains His friends or as He dances with Sri Radha, who also moves Her neck like a dancing peahen? Where is He?

**\* \* \* \***

The bending of Sri Radha’s neck is one of seven signs of love She sends to Syama, signs that also include six different glances: smiling, roving, crooked, sidelong, half-closed, and turned-away.

Once, on the shore of the Yamuna, doe-eyed Radharani tilted Her neck in this way and glanced at Krsna with dancing eyes, severely wounding His heart with the sharp tip of one of Cupid’s arrows.

Radha bends Her neck, feet, and waist and moves Her eyebrows as She looks at Krsna, all in a manner more overpowering than Cupid’s how. A pose such as this is a sign of love’s ornament called lalita.

Sri Radha’s slightly arched neck rises from the placid stream of Her shoulders as if it were the graceful stem of Her lotus face hut, unlike the green stem of the lotus, Radha’s neck is golden.

Poets and scriptures extol the elegance of Her neck’s three lines, its unique jewelled choker, its strands of pearls, and its priceless Syamantaka gem. But these ornaments are not its greatest glory.

The most wonderful ornament of Radha’s neck is invisible, for it resides like a cintamani gem within her throat: it is the constant vibration of Krsna’s names, which also appears on Her tongue.

Could it be the effect of Krsna’s names that has transformed the stem of Her lotus face to the golden colour of love, and also given the ornaments covering Her neck such extraordinary lustre?

Radha favours necklaces that remind Her of Krsna, cither because of their blackish colour or because they were gifts from Him, like the necklace of gunja berries Krsna gave Her during the rasa dance.

Once, as Radha walked with Citra, Radha’s necklace caught on a creeper and broke. She called out in alarm, “Friend! This necklace was Krsna’s favourite. Come help Me pick up the scattered pearls.”

Amongst the different chokers and necklaces we use to decorate Srimati Radharani in New Vraja-dhama, I favour the velvet and lace hands due to their soft and feminine appearance.

When I dress Radha, I take special care in selecting the ornaments for Her neck. Because they stand out more than the jewellery on Her dress, wrists, and fingers, they should be especially neat and attractive.

When decorating Radha’s neck with pearls, I generally use three strands to represent the three lines on Her throat, lines which arc home to the goddesses of beauty, poetry, and song.

If Krsna’s voice is indescribable, then what can be said of Sri Radha’s? When Krsna hears that irresistible, hypnotic sound, it captures the deer of His heart and forcibly drags it, and Him, into the forest.

Once in the forest, Krsna drinks from the flowering vine of Sri Radha’s voice — honey-sweet with the fragrance of pure love — and, intoxicated, He loudly hums just like a black bee.

Because She attracts Him like this, Krsna helplessly calls after Radha, “O Hara!” And because His submissive, affectionate voice completely soothes Radha’s heart, She replies with Her own call, “O Rama!”

Radha’s shoulders are low, soft, and slightly sloping, which makes them a perfect resting place for Sri Krsna’s arms while they are absorbed in the spontaneous romantic gestures of the rasa dance.

Her shoulders display strands of pearls, jeweled necklaces, and fine garlands, but none of these ornaments can compare to the arm of Sri Krsna, anointed with scents and sandalwood paste.

Sometimes, as Radha and Krsna stroll with Their girlfriends through the gardens of the six seasons, Krsna places His left arm across Radha’s shoulders, His hand swinging freely from Her left shoulder.

But when Krsna’s hand becomes too carefree, roving where it’s unwelcome, Radha slaps it decisively and, with a look meant to reprimand, places it securely back on the edge of Her shoulder.

Some poets say that Radharani’s shoulders are low because of so frequently bearing the weight of Krsna’s strong arms when They stroll through Vrndavana or dance together in the rasa dance.

Other poets say that Radharani’s shoulders appear low because She holds Her head high out of pride, being more qualified and more favoured by Krsna than all other gopis. Both opinions must be true.

Uddhava praises the gopis’ unique fortune at being embraced by Krsna’s arms in ways unknown even to the goddess of fortune. But Krsna’s praise of Radha as the most fortunate goes even further.

Even as Krsna’s arm rests on the shoulders of each gopi, He dances with Radha at the centre of the rasa dance and both His and Her arm rest on the other’s shoulder, declaring Radha’s supremacy.

The gopis sometimes pretend to be lost so that Krsna will place His arm on their shoulders and lead them home. But Krsna goes out of His own way to find excuses to touch Sri Radha and escort Her home.

But Radha, contrary as She is, sometimes bends Her neck as if afraid of His touch. She garlands Him with blue-lotus glances, but then walks away as if rejecting Him and chastises Him with crooked words.

Let there be no doubt why Krsna favours Srimati Radharani. Her unique love in separation from Him shines bright like the full moon before the twinkling stars of the other gopis’ affection.

Rati-manjari once praised Sri Radha’s madness in separation:

**“May Radha, who once anointed Her body with black musk in imitation of Krsna’s complexion and dressed in yellow silk garments —**

**“\[Who\] wore a garland of flowers, placed a charming peacock feather in Her braided hair, and played a bamboo flute, tilting it to touch Her shoulder just to imitate the appearance of Krsna, protect us all.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Radha and Krsna can never get enough of each other’s company, but in Vrndavana the movements of eternal time ordain that midday give way to afternoon, thus opening a new chapter in Their daily pastimes.

The duration and intensity of Their midday pastimes, and the facility they give Radha and Krsna to be close to one another, can only be equalled by Their intimate nocturnal pastimes (nakta-lila).

In the periods between these two parts of the day, the divine couple contact each other either by messages or meditation, and the time and distance between Them intensify Their upcoming meeting.

The thankless task of reminding Radharani and Krsna that They must part ways falls to the weakening rays of the sun and to an apologetic gopi who must say the words, “The day is ending.”

These words are worse than a proclamation of death. They cause Radha and Krsna heartache that wipes away Their smiles, makes Their speech falter, and unleashes a flood of tears from Their eyes.

And so it is that in the afternoon the divine couple become so forlorn at Their impending separation that the gopis fear the earth might crack open under Their feet out of sympathy for Their plight.

To divert the divine couple’s attention, one gopi says, “O Radha! O Syama! Don’t dally now. If You are late, Your parents might become suspicious and prevent You from ever meeting again. Please hurry!”

These words of warning strike fear into the hearts of the divine couple. They quickly, albeit reluctantly, leave the shelter of Radha-kunda and, after walking together for some time, finally part ways.

Srimati Radharani unwillingly returns to Yavata, and Krsna to His friends, who are anxiously waiting for Him along with their cows, all of them eager to make their own journey home to Nandagrama.

The midday pastimes last five hours, but the gopas think they have been separated from Krsna for no longer than ten minutes. How could they manage, after all, to be without Him for longer?

Earlier, Krsna told the cowherd boys He was going for a walk in the forest, so they had spent the afternoon resting happily in the shade. When Krsna returns as promised, their play simply resumes.

Had Krsna been absent any longer, however, the boys would not have lounged about but gone off in search of Him, fearing that He had been waylaid by a demon or gotten lost in the depths of the forest.

Just as the Lord’s pastime potency extends the night of a rasa dance with the gopis to last as long as a night of Brahma, it contracts Krsna’s midday absence from the gopas to no more than a few minutes.

Thus the cowherd boys think that they have been with Krsna for almost the entire period of midday, during which they play endless games while tending the cows throughout the twelve forests of Vraja.

The time Krsna spends travelling from Radha back to the gopas is difficult for Him. He feels alone with the pain of separation and, with nothing to distract His mind, He muddies the ground with His tears.

But as soon as He arrives, the gopas happily greet Him with loving embraces and demand that He play with them. His mind drawn into the joy of fraternal love, He thus forgets His sorrow.

Krsna doesn’t hesitate to take charge of the boys and the cows, allowing Balarama and a few friends to go off in search of strays in the forests and near the watering holes in the pastures.

Krsna accepts the challenge of a ball game which, in no time at all, leads to a shoving match with Sridama and then a friendly scuffle. In the end, of course, the two cowherd boys make up and embrace.

As the boys wander here and there from forest to forest, Krsna visits various groups of gopas and engages in friendly exchanges with each group according to their loving mood and service.

At the foot of Govardhana Hill the boys engage in an exuberant game of tag, until the sound of Balarama’s buffalo horn announces that it is time to collect the herd and return home.

The call of the buffalo horn reminds each hoy of his own cows, so they all abandon their play and run here and there calling their cows and searching for strays in the caves and nearby groves.

Krsna sees that His friends are getting too worked up as they try to gather their herds and locate strays, so He calls out, “O friends! Don’t be upset. Listen as I call the cows with My flute.”

Climbing onto a rocky crag overlooking one of Govardhana’s many meadows, Krsna plays His flute in a way that sounds just like the names of the various cows, urging them all to come to Him at once.

And come they do, galloping from all sides, tails and heads raised, ears spread wide, the sound of their hooves keeping perfect time to Krsna’s lively flute music and the boys’ calls of “Hai! Hai!”

Very quickly the clearing fills up with mooing cows trying to get close enough to lick Krsna, smell Krsna, or brush Krsna with the soft switch of their tails, all the while showering Him with loving glances.

Sridama calls to Subala, “O friend! Look! Who amongst us can bring our cows together just by playing his flute? Only Krsna is capable of such a feat, just as only He can kill ferocious demons.”

Since all the cows have been assembled together so efficiently, the boys take advantage of the time Krsna has saved by collecting fruits, which they happily eat along with their leftovers from lunch.

A few servant boys go to collect flowers while the others drink fresh water, wash their hands and mouths, collect their belongings, and blow on their bugles and flutes, raising a heavenly din.

Sudama and a few other friends approach Krsna with baskets of flowers and, in plain view of the lowing cows and trumpeting boys, they artistically decorate Krsna from head to toe like a forest sprite.

The audience of cows and cowherds all praise the boys’ talent in floral artistry, and Krsna responds to their loving words by affectionately glancing at all of them as He plays enchanting melodies on His flute.

Subala runs to Krsna’s side and embraces Him tightly to show Him the affection all the other boys are feeling; actually, all the cows and cowherd boys feel as though they are embracing Krsna themselves.

Finally, Subala twirls his stick in the air and, over a mooing chorus of cows, calls out, “Let’s go!” The boys cheer, blow their horns, and call the names of leading cows, “Kali! Dhavali! Rangi! Hamsi!”

The herd suddenly moves like a rolling wave breaking onto shore. The white cows are its whitecaps, the other cows of many colours its body, their mooing its roaring, and the excited gopas its aquatics.

The cows, eager to return home, need little prodding, but the boys play their roles as cowherds anyway, beating drums, blowing on instruments, clapping their hands, and shouting, “Hai! Hai!”

These sounds mix with the natural reverberations of the forest to provide a symphonic background for Krsna’s solo flute, and create auspicious vibrations that draw the demigods from heaven to Vraja.

The demigods, however, can only trace these celestial sounds to a vast golden cloud of dust. Despite the strength of their mystic powers and sublime vision, they can see nothing more than that.

Without the essential prerequisite devotion, how can ordinary conditioned souls, however powerful they might be, penetrate through the billows of cintamani dust to see Krsna and His pastimes?

When the sounds of the demigods’ prayers catch Krsna’s attention, only then, by His empowerment, can they behold His pastime of herding the cows home in the afternoon (go-carana).

That same empowerment — and even more — comes to our own eyes by the strength of nama-sankirtana, in which Hare addresses dustcovered Krsna, and Rama addresses Balarama by His side.

**\* \* \* \***

Earlier on, at the fork in the road where Krsna took the path leading to His friends, Radha left a depression in the ground by nervously digging there with Her toes as She watched Him depart.

Krsna’s heart urged Him to turn back, to wave, and to look at Radharani, but knowing that such gestures would merely prolong Her agony, He walked briskly to the bend in the road and out of sight.

Now Radha’s eyes are so filled with tears, Her head spinning so fast, that She forgets where to turn. And as She dithers at the crossing, the heat of Her burning heart makes the plants in the clearing wilt.

Her radiant body becomes so pale and Her limbs so thin that Her bracelets and anklets slip to the ground, and Her shoulders collapse to the point that Her outer garments fall in a heap at Her feet.

In an attempt to express Her deep longing for Krsna and the pain His absence is causing Her, Radha tries to speak, hut Her words are completely nonsensical, like that of a mad or intoxicated woman.

Eager to relieve their friend’s anxiety, the gopis say, “Behaving this way out in the open, You will disclose Your own secret and open a storehouse of gossip for Your enemies to share. Friend! Be grave.”

At this Radha takes a deep breath and tries to compose Herself as Her friends quickly replace Her fallen ornaments and clothes, all the while trying to encourage Her, “Why should You be so afflicted?

“Krsna is not a mundane personality. He resides in Your heart, just as He does everywhere else. Instead of relying on Your imperfect eyes, look within Yourself and be with Him any time, day or night.”

These words bring hope to Srimati Radharani’s heart, a hope that shows in Her face, shines through Her eyes, and dances upon Her lips. She thinks, “Yes! I will see Him again! I will!”

Thus begins the trek back to Yavata, a short distance by road but an endless march on a bed of thorns for Radha. And what awaits Her at home? Nothing more than a walking, talking thorn bush—Jatila.

But Jatila has been chastened by what she thought were the angry words of the sun god, and so she receives Radha with respect and offers blessings to Her friends, who have delivered Her unsullied.

All afternoon the old woman has been constantly thinking, “The gossip of small-minded people made me doubtful of my own daughter-in-law. With that corrupted intelligence, I cruelly mistreated Her.

“But then I heard the angry words of the sun god, Radha’s lord, with my own ears and saw him rain mercy upon Her with my own eyes. I repent. May a thunderbolt strike me down for my sins!”

The gopis offer obeisances to Jatila, noting the drastic change in her attitude, and they chat about the happy turn of events all the way back to their own homes. Once again clever Krsna has saved the day.

Jatila speaks of her affection for Radha, whom she now sees as the jewel of her family: “O daughter! You have been away from home in the heat of the day. Now bathe in cool water and refresh Yourself.”

Srimati Radharani bows to Her mother-in-law and follows her order. Relieved at the unusually favourable greeting She has received from Her family, She thinks, “Perhaps fate is finally smiling on Me.”

Before bathing, Radha enters the kitchen and quickly prepares laddus and fancy rice, placing them on golden trays along with pan, sandalwood paste, and a flower garland — all for Krsna.

Knowing that Krsna will be returning soon from the pastures, Radha takes the help of a maidservant to bathe, dress, and ornament Herself in a way that will please Him and capture His heart.

Then She enters Her sitting room, sits before a picture of Krsna painted by Visakha, and softly chants His names as She waits for the sounds of bugles, flutes, and cows to herald His arrival.

But no sounds come. Had Krsna’s herd already passed? Perhaps they had not come through Yavata. After all, it is not on the way to Nandagrama. If they had, surely Her friends would have told Her.

Radha peers out the window for a sign of a dust cloud, but sees none. As She paces back and forth, She repeatedly looks out the window, and with each futile pass She displays more signs of madness.

She repeatedly sits down and again rises to Her feet, sighs out loud, paces back and forth, then again sits down. A tiny sound startles Her, which again brings Her to Her feet and then again to the window.

Disappointed at not seeing what She was hoping for, Srimati Radharani turns away from the window, shivers as if from severe fever, and chokes as if forcibly held under water, gasping for air.

She bitterly kicks at nothing with Her left foot, as if kicking aside the reputation of Her dynasty and the personal chastity that keeps Her from running to the forest to live there as Krsna’s kept maidservant.

As tears blind Her eyes and despair impairs Her hearing, Radha’s consciousness withdraws from the external plane, so She is unable to hear Krsna’s flute or see the dust cloud approaching at long last.

Only when a maidservant pulls Her to the window and calls into Her ear do Radha’s senses awake, like a morning lotus opens to the sun, eager to relish the best of all mantras, “Krsna is coming!”

And indeed He is! But before entering Yavata, Krsna stops at a banana orchard along with Madhu and Subala, picks as much fruit as they can carry, then joyfully passes it out to the other boys.

The gopas eat the bananas and then hurry to catch up to the cows, who are now over-eager to return to their calves. They trot with raised ears and tails, their hooves kicking the dust even higher.

Intoxicated with love for Krsna, Balarama alternates between blowing His horn and calling the cows, His deep affection visible in His unsteady gait, rolling eyes, and unintelligible speech.

With a rope for tying cows on His shoulders, Balarama occasionally calls out, “Krsna! Krsna!” To prevent Him from wandering off in that intoxicated condition, His friends keep Him at the centre of the herd.

Finally, to announce their arrival to the residents of Yavata, and even the residents of far distant Nandagrama, all the boys, Krsna included, play their horns and flutes in unison on the same note.

This tumultuous sound is like sweetest nectar to the ears of young gopis like Radha, as well as to elder gopis like Yasoda, all of whom at once trade their lamentation for jubilation and ecstasy.

As the great dust cloud approaches the town of Yavata, the procession stops to allow some local boys to separate their cows from the herd and to say goodbye before heading off to their own villages.

While this is going on, Sri Radha hurries to the top of the moontower, where from the balustrade She can see the cowherd boys parting ways and, in their midst, She can see Krsna, looking Her way.

Then suddenly, shyness, like a strong north wind, pushes Radharani back a few steps. She wraps Her veil around Her shoulders and face, leaving only Her eyes exposed, so that She can still see Krsna.

Nonetheless, as the divine couple’s eyes meet, what They are able to exchange by way of glances is enough for Them to feel and say everything that needs to be felt and said — and more.

Pierced by Cupid’s arrows, unable to even blink, Radha and Krsna are rooted to the ground, where They stand like statues, tottering back and forth until They collapse into the waiting arms of Their friends.

Radha gradually comes back to consciousness, but Krsna is still in a swoon because of seeing Her, and so Subala, as he gestures to Radharani to reassure Her, tells the other boys to carry Krsna.

The boys carry Krsna to a grove where they are able to bring Him back to consciousness by chanting mantras, putting a damp cloth on His forehead, and reminding Him that He will soon see Radharani.

Once Krsna has come to and the boys have resumed their march, Radha cannot see Him, but She can hear His flute, so She feels reassured that He is all right and on His way towards Nanda’s capital.

Radha visualises Krsna and Balarama arriving at Their home, offering obeisances to Their parents, and then happily receiving the blessings, kisses, and embraces of Their elders and the villagers.

Suddenly Srimati Radharani remembers the trays of food She prepared earlier for Krsna. Running down the stairs as fast as She had come up, She calls behind Her, “Rati! Quick! Come, follow Me.”

In the privacy of Her bedroom, Radha whispers instructions into Rati’s ear. She then sends Her friends off with the trays of sweets, rice, pan, and a garland, calling out, “Hurry back!”

Rati and her helpers quickly cross the divine lotus of Vrndavana to Nandagrama, where they hand the offerings to Dhanistha, who also receives Srimati Radharani’s private message to Krsna.

Because Radha is the embodiment of the topmost loving service to Sri Krsna, we call out to Her, “Hare!” And because Krsna is the source of the bliss Sri Radha derives from serving Him, She calls Him “Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna’s pastime potency imparts a sense of newness to every event in Krsna’s day, even as these events repeat day after day, forever. Therefore, Krsna’s enjoyment is always fresh and never, ever, hackneyed.

Krsna and the gopas herd the cows through Yavata every day, but it always seems like the first time. In the same way, every time Radha’s and Krsna’s eyes meet it feels to Them like the very first time.

The primary cause of this “eternal newness” (*nitya-nava-navdyamdna*) is eternal time, in which everything and everyone is eternally present, and not a moment has a sense of passing away.

This truth is described by both Sri Brahma-samhita and by Srila Prabhupada, who once explained,

**“In the spiritual existence there is no past, no future, only present. Only present.**

**“Everything \|is\| fresh, present,** ***nitya-\[nava\]-navayamana*****, only feelings, new... new. That is spiritual existence, anandambudhi-vardhanam, only present — no future, no past.”**

This eternal freshness can be tasted even in this world through devotional activities like chanting Hare Krsna, hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam, and for me, especially serving the Deity of the Lord.

Whenever I dress Radha-Syamasundara in the serenity of brahma-muhurta, I recall the service the gopis perform in Goloka Vrndavana at the end of each night, and I taste a drop of their ever-fresh joy.

Radha-Syamasundara have a soft-pink and white lace outfit with a white lace umbrella to protect Radha from the intense afternoon sun. This outfit brings out the sweet innocence of Their mutual affection.

The colours of this outfit reflect Radha’s softness, its simplicity the Vraja-vasis’ love for Syama, and its delicate lace Syama’s beauty. Strands of white and pink pearls remind me of Their gopi friends.

O friend! If your eyes ache to see true grace and elegance, if your heart yearns to taste sweetness and joy, if you have not yet found these, visit New Vraja-dhama when Radha-Syama wear this outfit.

The divine couple stand on the bank of the Yamuna amidst trees with delicate pink blossoms and a small bevy of swans attracted by the melodious tinkling sounds of Radha’s and Syama’s ankle bells.

Syama’s turban is also pink and white. His hands hold a flute made of white gold, His ankles are decorated with small pink flower garlands, and pearl and rose-quartz rings sparkle on His fingers and toes.

Radha’s braid, plaited with tiny white jasmine flowers, curls around Her hips. Sometimes, while absorbed in nama-bhajana, I think of how fortunate I would be to take birth as one of those flowers.

Along with garlands and ornaments, Radha-Syamasundara have other captivating items in common: soft-pink velvet chokers with white lace on both edges, exquisite enough to take one’s breath away.

This pink outfit is one of three that Radha-Syama wear on Ekadasi. The other two are made from heavier material — one pink, one red. Both have silver trim and ornaments appropriate for this holy day.

Astrologically, Mars rules Ekadasi. Mars and its colour, red, tend to promote conflict, whereas cooler, moon-like silver and white soften that fiery effect, just as mixing white with red produces pink.

The phases of the moon influence bodies of water here on earth, as well as fluids in the body. Thus on Ekadasi the demands of the senses increase, and we arc advised to fast in order to avoid quarrel and lust.

And yet Srila Prabhupada said that “fasting means feasting.” In part this means that whereas practising devotees are advised to fast on Ekadasi, perfected devotees and the residents of Goloka feast.

Mother Yasoda and Mother Rohini think that Ekadasi will influence Krsna to eat more than usual, giving them an opportunity to increase Their service to Him by cooking Him a wonderful feast.

During the time of the Gosvamis, one of Gopala Bhatta’s disciples advocated that devotees not be required to fast on Ekadasi. For this transgression, Gopala Bhatta Gosvami rejected his disciple.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu humbly requested His mother to fast from grains on Ekadasi, which as a result of smarta prejudice was not the custom of married women in West Bengal at that time.

Later, in Puri, the Lord taught His followers to fast strictly on Ekadasi, but at the same time to offer proper respect to the Lord’s prasada, which according to scripture can never be refused.

Sanatana Gosvami writes that just as members of the four orders of life should observe the vow of Janmastami from the age of eight, scriptures say the same about fasting on Ekadasi.

The word for fasting is upavasa in which upa means “near to” and vasa means “to reside,” so the essence of upavasa means to reside near Krsna, which happens for some by fasting and for others by feasting.

Again, Radha-Syamasundara’s pink and white lace dress reminds me that They want us to practise the simple austerities of Krsna consciousness and become qualified to live with Them in Goloka.

In summary, both fasting and feasting are means to attain Krsna’s company, but if we presume it is our place to do one or the other, without considering what we are qualified for, we will commit sin.

The pale pink of Radha-Syamasundara’s outfit reminds me of the softness of Their romance and the sweetness of the love They share in the endlessly flowering springtime of eternal youth.

The white lace further embellishes this symbolism at the same time that it complements the soothing and calming effect pink has for the divine couple in the summer heat of New Vraja-dhama.

Like the other Ekadasi outfits, Radha and Syama wear this one with anklets, bracelets, necklaces, and chokers that have been specially designed, made of rubies and pearls set in white gold.

Especially appealing to me is the way that the pink and white of this dress match Radha’s and Syama’s glowing ruby lips and pink toenails and fingernails, as well as His reddish and Her pink palms and soles.

The soothing, flowing lines of this pink lace outfit remind me of the winding course of the divine river Ganges, which acquired a pinkish tint by washing the reddish powder from the Lord’s lotus feet.

That reddish powder is kunkuma from Radha’s breasts. Either directly seeing it in the pinkish waters of the Ganges, or being reminded of it by this pink outfit, can purify our minds of material contamination.

Because Krsna alleviates the burning desire in Radha’s heart by the touch of His feet, He is called Hari. And because His touch fills Her with divine bliss unknown to anyone but the gopis, He is called Rama.

Because the red powder from Radha’s breasts soothes Krsna’s soles as He walks the hot sands of Vraja, She is called Hara, and because the touch of that powder always gives Krsna joy, He is called Rama.

O heart! Meditate on Radha’s lover, who wears garments the colour of a pink lotus, whose car is decorated with white flowers, who plays a silver flute, and whose feet are anointed with fragrant powder.

Meditate on the aromatic dust powder of Syama’s feet, dust that even Siva, Sukadeva, and Narada arc unable to see, dust with limitless potency that constantly fills the Supreme Person with bliss.

I think of my worshipable Deities, Radha-Syamasundara, and call out, “Hare Rama!” Turning to Syama I say, “O Hari! Now that You have allowed me to hear of Your pastimes, will I also behold them one day?”

If Sri Radha were to ask, “Which of the pastimes you have heard does your heart yearn to see?” I would join my palms in prayer and answer, “O Hara! Whatever pastimes are especially dear to You.

“Those pastimes in which Your beloved shows the highest dexterity in loving affairs, for which You call him ‘Rama,’ pastimes which then become the greatest source of pleasure for You as well.”

Were Syamasundara to ask, “What makes you think you are qualified to see those pastimes?” I would reply, “O Lord! I have no qualification. Your names alone have awakened this desire in me.

“On the strength of Your cintamani names, Hare Rama, I believe that I will one day be qualified not only to see but also to serve Your pastimes, having been transformed into Your own servant.”

This aspiration stays far distant from me, but I continue to chant Hare Rama in order to awaken a resolute attachment to the Lord, His name, and service to Him, attachment embodied in our namacarya.

Once threatened with punishment for chanting Krsna’s names Haridasa Thakura declared, “Even if my body is cut into pieces and I lose my life, I will never give up chanting the Lord’s holy name.”

By such deep faith and strong attachment the Thakura attained the full mercy of Lord Caitanya, by whose grace only one can attain Radha and Krsna and Their pastimes in the groves of Vrndavana.

I chant, praying to Haridasa Thakura for an attachment to Krsna’s names as strong as his. And I keep close to my heart the treasure of spiritual success exquisitely articulated by Prabodhananda Sarasvati:

**“Only an extremely fortunate person can get the mercy of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Yet as much as one can devote his full attention to the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya, to that extent he will be able to taste —**

**“The nectarean service of the lotus feet of Radha in Vraja. And the more one engages in the service of Sri Caitanya, the more one finds oneself in Vraja, tasting the nectar of service to Sri Radha.”**

I conclude my meditation on the fifth pair of the maha-mantra’s names, Hare Rama, with words I feel are but a sampling of the infinite truths and tastes to be found therein.

When will I, chanting the siddha-mantra of very wonderful names containing Hare Rama, and serving Vraja’s divine couple day and night in New Vraja-dhama, attain the success of my life?

**\* \* \* \***

The sixth pair of names, the second Hare Rama, symbolises the beginning of transcendental emotion (bhava), as distinguished by complete detachment from maya and complete attachment to Krsna.

This attachment (bhava) differs from attachment for Krsna still tinged with the material mode of goodness (asakti). Bhava springs from the touch of a ray of the spiritual, internal potency.

Srila Prabhupada says,

**“Bhava is the almost successful stage of spiritual life.”**

Why does he say “almost”? This attachment to Krsna is not fully mature. It needs further development to become perfect.

The perfection of spiritual life is love for Krsna (prema). Bhava is the stage beyond practice (sadhana), but before perfection (sadhya). It is a stage of devotion all its own called bhava-bhakti.

Lord Caitanya refers to ecstatic devotion in terms of something He aspires for rather than something He has achieved. As His followers, we do the same in referring to our desire for higher levels of devotion.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu addresses Krsna directly,

*nayanam galad-asru-dharaya vadanam gadgada-ruddhaya gird*  
*pulakair nicitam vapuh kada tava nama-grahane bhavisyati*

**“O My Lord! When will My eyes —**

**“Be decorated with tears of love flowing constantly when I chant Your holy name? When will My voice choke up, and when will the hairs of My body stand on end at the recitation of Your name?”**

I pause for a moment to reflect. Who knows the loneliness of a long" distance runner but a runner? And who knows the intensity of the sadhaka’s struggle for bhava but another sadhaka?

Nama-bhajana in practice awakens eternal devotion by a gradual process. Rupa Gosvami thus advises us to be patient. I abide by his order, but that does not decrease the pain of separation from Krsna.

Only in bhava can one directly approach the Lord. In the absence of such ecstatic devotion my chanting of mantras, observing vows, years of preaching, or for that matter my very life remain incomplete.

The goal of my life is to love Krsna. I serve only to serve. Yet I have one request: “Radha-Syama! So that I may please You better, kindly recognise my service in practice by giving me service in ecstasy.”

We may wonder what invokes Krsna’s mercy. Sri Prabuddha told Maharaja Nimi that the secret to invoking Krsna’s mercy lies in knowing how to chant Hare Krsna in the company of devotees.

**“One should learn how to associate with the devotees of the Lord by gathering with them to chant the glories of the Lord. This process is most purifying. As devotees thus develop their loving friendship —**

**“They feel mutual happiness and satisfaction. And by thus encouraging one another they are able to give up material sense gratification, which is the cause of all suffering.**

**“The devotees of the Lord constantly discuss the glories of the Personality of Godhead amongst themselves. Thus they constantly remember the Lord and remind one another of—**

**“His qualities and pastimes. In this way, by their devotion to the principles of bhakti-yoga, the devotees please the Personality of Godhead, who takes away from them everything inauspicious.**

**“Being purified of all impediments, the devotees awaken to pure love of Godhead, and thus, even within this world, their spiritualised bodies exhibit symptoms of transcendental ecstasy...”**

By such spirited devotional life, we are able to give up sense gratification, which is the cause of our suffering and the primary obstacle to constantly talking about Krsna amongst ourselves.

Such discussions are a means for us to remember and to remind one another of Krsna’s beauty, character, and activities. In this way we can please He who is purchased only by pure devotion.

The evidence that one has received Krsna’s descending grace is that all inauspicious things then fly away from the heart. When one is worthy, Krsna gives one bhava, which opens the door to love for Him.

What’s more, if we follow Narada Muni’s example and chant Krsna’s names and glories in public for the benefit of those who are ignorant of Him, the Lord becomes especially inclined to reward us.

Such thoughts pacify my mind and I think, “Surely one day Krsna will be merciful to me. If the envious serpent Kaliya could receive the touch of His lotus feet, why not a snake-like person such as me?”

One kick from the Lord’s lotus feet and my permanent mood of ecstasy (sthayi-bhava) would manifest itself and confirm, once and for all, the validity of my aspirations for personal service at those feet.

The preliminary symptoms of sthayi-bhava — headed by an insatiable taste for nama-sankirtana — are nine in number. These perfections, called anubhavas, induce different bodily displays of ecstasy.

But these bodily displays — such as crying — despite being a result of ecstatic emotion in bhava-bhakti, are muted in the initial stages, increasing in ardour in proportion to the development of attachment.

One amazing feature of bhava is that it subsists on and nourishes itself: mild ecstasies increase attachment to Krsna, causing greater euphoria, which increases attachment, and so on, up to ecstatic bliss.

This maturation of bhava is akin to a small spark igniting a sea of highly combustible oil. The spark starts a fire that explodes and creates a rapidly spreading inferno, inextinguishable by any means.

Such spontaneous combustion of ecstasy is a result of a heart purified of material attachments. At this stage there is nothing left to obstruct the spread of ecstasy or to hamper one’s spiritual progress.

The ecstatic emotions at the stage of bhava stimulate spontaneous devotion, and thus our spiritual development is guided by the principles of raganuga described by Rupa Gosvami.

One essential characteristic of a devotee on this platform is that his or her external conduct resembles that of a regulated devotee. As Srila Prabhupada puts it, such a devotee acts “like a neophyte.”

A man with a great treasure keeps his wealth carefully guarded, sharing it only with confidants, because he knows that such wealth naturally attracts those who would cheat or exploit him.

Lord Caitanya gives another example of how advanced devotees inwardly cultivate love for Krsna and outwardly behave as if novices. Rupa and Sanatana wrote to the Lord before they first met Him.

In their letters the two saints disclosed their love for Lord Caitanya, as well as their spiritual aspirations. The Lord, knowing that they were engaged in the service of barbarians, instructed them carefully.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s response to Rupa and Sanatana included the following words of advice,

*para-vyasanini nari vyagrdpi grha-karmasu*  
*tad evasvadayaty antar nava-sanga-rasdyanam*

**“If a woman is attached to a man other than her husband, she will appear very busy in her household affairs, but within her heart she is always relishing feelings of association with her paramour.”**

The Lord instructed His associates to instruct others in turn that the nature of ecstatic devotion is to conceal itself, like a chameleon that remains invisible by blending into its surroundings.

From Lord Caitanya’s words, and from the nature of pure devotion itself, we can see that those who make a show of raganuga-bhakti, or speak freely in public on the topic, have not actually realised it.

The development of nama-bhajana in ecstasy quickly fulfils our longawaited desire — direct vision of Sri Krsna. One who can see the Lord’s smiling face considers the prospect of liberation unsavoury.

We should develop confidence that if we become qualified we will see Krsna. Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“Devotees who are always absorbed in thoughts of Krsna will soon see Krsna face-to-face without a doubt.”**

The poetic words of Bilvamangala Thakura confirm this truth:

**“If I am steadily engaged in devotional service unto You, my dear Lord, then I can easily perceive Your transcendental youthful form.”**

Because their attachment is not yet mature, however, devotees in ecstatic devotional service still cannot sec Krsna so easily, though they desire to constantly feast their eyes on His beauty.

Still, one form of Krsna — the Deity — is readily visible at almost all hours of the day, week in and week out, and so one symptom of devotees in bhava is intense attachment to the Deity of the Lord.

When an advanced devotee sees Krsna’s Deity form, he does not see a statue of Krsna, he sees Krsna Himself. To his eyes, descriptions of the Lord in sastra find their perfection in the Lord on the altar.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda cites Uddhava’s praise of Krsna’s Deity form:

**“The Lord appeared in the mortal world by His internal potency. He came in His eternal form, which is just suitable for His pastimes.**

**“These pastimes are wonderful for everyone, even for those proud of their own opulence, including the Lord Himself in His form of Narayana. Thus His divine body is the ornament of all ornaments.”**

When Uddhava says that Krsna manifests His eternal forms in this world, the forms Uddhava refers to are those in which the Lord displays His pastimes as an incarnation and as His Deity.

Attachment to Krsna is so intense for devotees in Bhava that they cannot take their eyes off Krsna’s beautiful threefold-bending form. Even the fraction of a moment it takes to blink is intolerable.

This state of mind forces them to curse Brahma for the disturbance he has caused by creating eyes that blink, while applauding him for his artistic skill, which reached perfection in crafting Krsna’s limbs.

Dear readers! Although I lack the ecstatic devotion to properly treasure Radha-Syama, I feel compelled to devote some space to Their clothes and features that remind me of the second Hare Rama.

May Radha-Syama bless me with adequate words to portray Their brightly coloured tassel-dress, as well as Their lotus faces, always surrounded by the humming bees of Their devotees’ loving glances.

**\* \* \* \***

Those who have seen Syamasundara in His tassel-dress must have smiled broadly at His tall, oversized turban, which leans over so far that it almost brushes Radharani’s cheek with its peacock feather.

Golden tassels hang from the borders of His dhoti and shirt, which are mostly burnt-red satin-silk with embroidered, palm-size flowers of golden thread that contrast with His bright green sleeves.

His chiffon shawl fades through a spectrum of bright yellow to pale red, and its edges are embroidered to form a border that brings all the colours of the ensemble together in a delicate vine and flower design.

This tassel outfit calls to mind Sri Suka’s depiction of Krsna as a dancer on stage, especially if we take into account the dramatic flare of the tall, twisting, overarched, multicoloured turban.

Because Syama’s dashing appearance stops our minds from thinking of anything other than Him, we say, “O Hari!” and because such onepointed attention on Him brings so much pleasure, we cry, “O Rama!”

With a peacock feather on the end of His turban, flowers over His ears, dazzling ornaments on His stately limbs, and a matching flower garland, Syama displays perfect poise in His form as the best dancer.

Devotees who finally find the words to express what they are seeing, declare that whosoever sees Sri Syamasundara’s beautiful dress, features, and gestures is surely most fortunate.

As He stands before His devotees, glancing lovingly upon them with the flute to His lips, Syama is truly a vision of perfection, beyond which there is nothing greater for His devotees to lay their eyes on.

But just after this thought enters their minds — a thought which is in no way false — they turn towards Radha, only to see Her wearing a matching tassel-dress, and at first they are speechless with wonder.

But after some time they ponder whether they arc offending Syama by thinking that there is no higher perfection for their eyes than to see the princess of their village just as they see Her right now.

Syama may be dressed as the king of dancers, but in Her sari and crown Sri Radha appears to be the queen before whom that king of dancers must perform in order to receive royal favour.

An honest observer will thrill at the regal, red-velvet choker tied around Sri Radha’s neck, and at Her braid — decorated with flowers — resting on Her left thigh rather than Her right, as it usually does.

And who could not help but notice the sweetness exuding from Sri Radha’s being? Just as sugar is the essence of any confection, sweetness is the essence of Srimati Radharani’s beauty.

Because Syama is like a bumblebee drawn to the sweet beauty of the Radha-flower, He calls Her Hara, and because the hovering Syama-bee showers Srimati Radharani with bliss, She calls Him Rama.

As difficult as it may be to decide which of the two is more wonderful, Radha or Syama, those fortunate enough to have seen the tassel outfit glorify Radha and thus give bliss to Syama.

Can we say which is better, the sun or the sunlight? A mango or its taste? Certainly not! Nor can we judge whether seeing Syama or seeing Radha is the highest perfection for the eyes.

Then what can we say? We can say for certain that those whose eyes arc able to see the beautiful faces, limbs, and garments of Radha-Syamasundara are fortunate. Nay, the most fortunate.

As these two divine youths cast loving glances our way, They enact many pastimes just to enchant each other in that holy place in which we have planted tender seedlings — our hearts.

Our conviction is that for those who have eyes, there are no greater objects of vision than Radha and Syama, whose daily darsana waters the creepers of our hearts, causing tasty fruit to grow and ripen.

The devotees therefore conclude, na param vidamah. They know nothing better or more fitting for the eyes than the sight of Radha and Syama in Their tassel outfit of red, green, and gold.

Because Radha diverts my attention away from Her so that I can glorify Her beloved Syama, I call Her Hara, and because She is pleased when I do so, I joyfully call out to Him, “O Rama!”

Just like the tassel-dress, the divine couple’s transcendental facial features also remind me of the second Hare Rama. I will now attempt to describe those features as far as my material conditioning permits.

Lord Brahma explains that one’s perception of Krsna’s beauty is proportionate to his or her level of Krsna consciousness. Only those who have attained love (prema), therefore, can see Krsna as He is.

Early one afternoon, the divine couple were reclining in a grove near Radha-kunda when Srimati Radharani requested two parrots to glorify the features and attributes of Her lover, Syamasundara.

The love that Radha and Her intimate girlfriends have for Krsna is superlative. Therefore, when they heard about His attributes from these two parrots, it was the same as seeing those attributes directly.

I am not one of Vraja’s parrots. Neither do I possess their wealth of attachment for the divine couple, nor do my words possess the spiritual potency or poetic beauty that their words possess.

But I have faith in my swan-like readers. May they recognise the sincerity of my intent amidst my many shortcomings and still relish my portrayal of Radha’s and Syama’s beguiling faces.

“Hare! O Hara!” Will the full moon of Radha’s face ever rise over the ocean of my heart and cause a tidal wave of emotion to surge inland from its shore and spread its waters throughout my body?

Will my limbs ever tremble, tears flood my eyes, and my speech falter? As I say “Hare Rama” will my mind and my senses ever feel they cannot get enough of Syamasundara’s ever-expanding charm?

**\* \* \* \***

By the influence of the Lord’s names I feel drawn to the thought of how the creator might have fashioned the face of New Vraja-dhama’s Srimati Radharani from the very best things in his creation.

Had Lord Brahma taken it upon himself to fashion the face of the Deity of Sri Radha, he would have no doubt relied upon the most precious items of creation, including the opulences of the demigods.

I record this meditation of our Radha’s glories to give others impetus to reflect upon Her, and to personally reflect upon the wonder devotees must feel when they see Radharani’s incomparable beauty.

Radha’s face, like Krsna’s, is a full moon that presides over the halfmoon of Her forehead, the full moons of Her cheeks, and the full moon ornament on Her forehead that proclaims Her marital fidelity.

Actually, this jewelled dot on Sri Radha’s forehead is a sign of Her eternal fidelity to Krsna, which neither the Vedic scriptural injunctions nor Vrndavana’s moral codes could ever cause to waver.

Because Krsna has always been and always will be Radha’s only husband, master, paramour, and best friend, the ornament on Radha’s forehead is an eternal full moon that neither waxes nor wanes.

We may wonder why Radha’s forehead is a half-moon. Had Brahma created Her, he must have armed Her with weapons for subduing Hari, weapons acquired perhaps from Lord Siva himself.

Had Brahma asked Siva to present his bow to Radha for Her eyebrows, Lord Siva, overjoyed, surely would have offered Radha the crescent moon from his matted locks along with his bow.

When the crescent moon happily took its place as Radha’s forehead, and Siva’s bow became Her infallible eyebrows, Parvati must have worried how delicate Radha would be able to wield that weapon.

Siva, who knows Parvati’s mind, then said, “Devi! This bow can be drawn in two ways: by the strength of ten thousand men, or by the strength of prema. Radha has both. Therefore how could She fail?”

As he left Mount Kailasa, Brahma happened upon the graceful queen of spotted does, whose exceptionally alluring eyes prompted him to ask how she had become so endowed. She replied, “Dear Lord!

“I have taken a vow to eat only lotuses that have been offered to Radha-Krsna. Thus my eyes are like lotuses.” At this, Brahma must have requested the deer to give him the image of her eyes for Radha.

Did Brahma visit the planet of fire, beg Agni for the sparkling flames from sacrificial fires, and place it in the pupils he had created from the darkness that pervades his night? He must have.

Knowing that whatever colour he would choose for the iris would be the colour reflected by Radha’s constantly gazing at Krsna, Brahma chose the colour of storm clouds reflected on the ocean.

And when Brahma asked Cupid to donate arrows for Radha’s glances, Cupid must have replied that Krsna had already taken them, and so charitable Rati donated the arrows she shoots at her husband!

Embarrassed from not having served Radha, Cupid must have given a bowstring of bumblebees that Brahma used as curls around Radha’s forehead, from which She fires the arrows of Her glance.

Brahma then combined the bashfulness of chaste ladies like Arundhati with the coyness of Apsaras like Urvasi to fashion Radha’s eyelids and embellished them with softness from the foam of nectar.

Pleased with himself, Lord Brahma must have begged green parrots for their mystic power to make mangoes sweeter by the touch of their beaks, and used it to fashion Sri Radha’s graceful nose.

Inspired by the incomparable moon, did Brahma use its reflection from a mirror to create Radha’s right and left cheeks and then beg the moon for the vines of the soma plants to decorate those cheeks?

The juice of the soma plant extends the lives of the demigods so that they can enjoy heavenly pleasures, but the sight of those plants on Radha’s cheeks gives Krsna the purpose for His eternal existence.

The ripened fruit of the Vedas, Srimad-Bhagavatam, having been prayed to by Brahma, must have become Sri Radha’s lips, and the process of sankirtana the Bhagavatam promotes, Sri Radha’s tongue.

The goddess Sarasvati, in appreciation of her husband’s unrivaled artistic skill, contributed the redness for Sri Radha’s lips, as well as her knowledge and mastery over the fine art of love.

And had the maha-mantra clamoured for more service to Radha, Brahma must have requested its thirty-two sacred syllables to become Her pearl-like teeth, thereby making the holy names very happy.

The creator must surely have thought deeply about what he could use to complete the last feature of Sri Radha’s face, Her chin, and finally decided upon the aromatic roses that grow by Praskandana-tirtha.

Lord Brahma must have requested those roses for the determination by which they always face the sun and combined it with the softness and smoothness of their petals. But he missed something.

Absorbed in ecstasy, Brahma did not notice a bumblebee biding in the roses, until it sat upon Sri Radha’s chin. Amenable to the bee’s prayers, Brahma then transformed it into a dot of musk.

As the creator saw that Radha’s face was nearing completion, he must have performed a sacrifice to invoke the two presiding deities of hearing the topics of Krsna and placed them as Sri Radha’s cars.

At that moment, if a bird alighted on Brahma’s finger and asked to reside in Srimati Radharani’s ears, Brahma must surely have asked, “Who are you to make such an impudent request?”

The bird would then reply, “I am the song of Krsna’s flute, and I live within the nest of Sri Radha’s inner ear.” At this the creator humbly said, “So be it!” and let the bird enter Radharani’s left ear.

Brahma then invoked the perfectional stage of absorption in Sri Krsna and used it to spin soft black strands of hair that hung from Srimati Radharani’s head, all the way to Her thighs.

Finally, Brahma must have gone to his treasurer Kuvera, demanded the effulgence of the demigods’ gold, and made Radha’s complexion from it, further adding the brilliance of their jewelled ornaments.

When Brahma beheld his creation, auspicious stars took their places over Radha’s eyebrows as gopi dots. And piercing the full moon, the circle of the sun’s effulgence became Her pearl-studded nose ring.

My faith is that in some wonderful way like this, all things sweet, full of wonder, and laden with beauty must have combined to offer their qualities in order to fashion Srimati Radharani’s face.

Therefore I am certain that Radha is known as Hara because She accepted the creator’s effort to glorify Her. And when he saw the result of his handiwork, he had only one thing to say, “O Radha!”

This description may be the poetic expression of my thoughts, hut these extraordinary qualities of Sri Radha did appear through the hands of a Jaipur craftsman, who thought he was carving a Deity.

In truth, whatever is beautiful, glorious, and wonderful in the material and spiritual realms is but a display of Krsna’s energy, which is ultimately embodied in Sri Radha (*mama tejo msa-sambhavam*).

As a pastime Krsna accepts His eternal cakra from Agni, so Radha too must accept the gifts of Her own potencies from those whom She empowers. Thus She fulfils Her human-like pastimes as a gopi.

I pray that one day, with Radha-Syama’s names upon my tongue, my body near Them, my mind absorbed in topics of vraja-bhakti, I may leave my body in New Vraja-dhama. Hare Rama!

**\* \* \* \***

In the absolute sense, Radha and Krsna are two aspects of the one Supreme Soul. But to fulfil Krsna’s desire for loving pastimes, They arc eternally two, the original female and male.

Radha is eternally an adolescent girl who displays love for Krsna through every part of Her limbs and face. Krsna is a slightly older adolescent boy who embodies the enjoyment of divine mellows.

The face is both the king of the body and the index of the mind. In that sense Krsna’s face reveals something about His incomparably wonderful and all-engaging bodily and mental activities.

It is said that a picture is worth a thousand words. Therefore I don’t expect to do any more than hint at the glories of Krsna’s facial features as I meditate on them while chanting Hare Rama.

The four and a half moons of Krsna’s face are similar to Radha’s, but they arc dark moons, which astrologers say indicate Krsna’s hidden nature. And devotees know it is a nature only the gopis are privy to.

For Mother Yasoda and most other residents of Vraja, Krsna is a dutiful, innocent cowherd prince who herds cows, but for the gopis He is the relentless libertine who is constantly after them.

But Krsna’s quest for the gopis is but a quest for His own feminine counterparts, of whom Radha is the fountainhead and the fair- complexioned feminine counterwhole of the Absolute Truth.

As Srila Prabhupada said, “God is male and female, both.” Sometimes He assumes a female form as Mohini-murti, but His feminine aspect is eternally manifest separately as Sri Radha.

When Krsna is beside Radha, then, we are simultaneously seeing His feminine disposition present in Her golden form and His complete personality present in His Syamasundara form as the ultimate male.

Moreover, Krsna’s dark complexion is the hue of the amorous mellow, of which He is the fountainhead and presiding Deity. He personifies this mellow. Therefore He is the transcendental Cupid.

Krsna’s face, cheeks, forehead, and dot of sandalwood all contribute in their unique ways to entice Radha and Her bodily expansions, the gopis, and draw them into Vrndavana’s secluded groves.

Because those who worship the beautiful dark-moon Krsna find their minds submerged in an ocean of supreme bliss, and because Krsna’s limbs give pleasure to the gopis, He is known by the name Rama.

Once some gopis were poking fun at Krsna. They asked, “How is it that You are black?” One gopi joked, “Because He was born in the darkness of the new moon, the eighth night in the month of Bhadra.

“Born on a moonless night, and in a prison no less, He came out black.” Before Krsna could defend Himself, another gopi added, “You would expect that after so many years His complexion would fade.

“But because His mother always feeds Him milk-sweets made from milk that comes from black cows, He stays that colour.” Of course, Krsna’s responsive, good-natured smile only encouraged them.

Another gopi said, “Actually, Krsna’s wayward behaviour tinges Him with the hue of impiety. First He kills a woman, then He steals butter, later He kills a bull — now He’s trying to steal our chastity.”

Finally Krsna replied, “These accusations are simply a ruse to cover the truth: Your wanton ways have darkened My skin.” “How can You say that we are responsible?” the gopis protested in one voice.

Krsna pointed His flute at the gopis as He declared, “You girls have had eyes for Me since I was a baby, and so the black ointment you always smear about those eyes has stained My body.”

The gopis were about to refute Krsna’s logic, but then they looked at His handsome face, twinkling eyes, and irresistible smiling lips. Overcome by bliss, they all said in unison, “O Rama!”

New Vraja-dhama’s Syamasundara possesses this dark-moon charm, but in His attractiveness we find an enhanced feature we generally don’t read about in sastra: His arched golden eyebrows.

Since Krsna’s hair is black we may wonder why His eyebrows are not the same colour. Could it be that His eyebrows and eyelashes have become golden like Radha because He constantly gazes at Her?

My conviction is that New Vraja-dhama fulfils not only our desires for direct service to the divine couple but also Krsna’s desire not to be separated from Radha in the way He is in His unmanifest abode.

In Their manifest pastime as the presiding Deities of New Vraja-dhama, Srimati Radharani and Syamasundara are never more than one cubit away from each other, at any time of the day or night.

Because the gravitational pull of Radha’s charm draws the Syama moon into a close orbit around Her, He calls Her Hara, and because, His close proximity gives Her unending bliss, She calls Him Rama.

Radha’s influence over Krsna is also an astrological phenomenon, as Nandimukhi once explained to Candravali, who was despondent over always taking second place to Srimati Radharani. Nandimukhi said:

“My dear Candra! Please do not be unhappy to see Radharani’s good fortune. Even wise astrologers know that the Radha star has an unmatched influence over the dark moon Krsna.”

Just as the moon called Candra reigns as king over all the planetary moons in the portion of the sky we can see, Syama’s face is the undisputed monarch of the other moons on His face and body.

We often hear Krsna called “moon-faced,” but rarely “moon-cheeked.” The reason is that the other moons of His body pay tribute to His face with a loyalty tax: the essence of their own attributes.

Just as chanting “Jaya Radhe-Syama” glorifies all other Deities associated with Them, such as Govardhana Lala, praising Krsna’s “moon- face” extols all the other moons of His body, like His toenails.

Syama perpetually burns in the fire of divine lust for Radha, but the aura of His face is so cooling that its radiance extinguishes any fires of material lust that may blaze in the hearts of His devotees.

In this world Syama removes the lust from His devotees’ hearts. When they arc perfectly pure He gives them the rare privilege of beholding His pastimes with His beloved, and so He is called Hari.

But for the gopis in the spiritual world — especially for their leaders, Radha and Candra — the radiance of Krsna’s face is not cooling; rather, it inflames the divine lust that forever burns in their hearts.

This highlights one of the differences between material lust and spiritual love: That which reduces the former increases the latter, and that which increases the former reduces the latter.

As we are gradually purified of material desires, our divine love for the Lord grows day by day. But if we allow our material desires to steadily increase, we can be sure that our love for the Lord will suffer.

Therefore, until one is more or less free of material lust through regulative practice, one should not hear of Krsna’s intimate pastimes with the gopis, for it may inflame rather than extinguish lusty desires.

Krsna personally told Tungavidya how His divine lust for the gopis inspires them, whereas they are repelled by the material lust of their husbands:

**“This girl Radha is as beautiful as a lotus flower.**

**“Her breasts are like two lovely round fruits, Her hands and feet like four red lotus flowers, Her lips are like two bandhuka flowers, and Her form is adorned with twenty-three and a half moons.**

**“This lotus girl blossoms with happiness only in the rays of the dark moon of Her paramour, but when She sees the glaring sun of Her husband rising on the horizon, She wilts with disappointment.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Dense but thin and wavy, shiny like a black bee, with an aroma like blue lotuses anointed with musk, and as willowy as a black camara, soft silky hair frames Syama’s moon-face. Thus He is called Kesava.

Srila Prabhupada once spoke to a disciple in a way that gave her the impression he was seeing Krsna before him. “Just see how beautifully Lord Krsna’s hair is resting on His shoulders,” Prabhupada said.

After receiving the order from Mother Yasoda, servant boys bathe Krsna, wash His hair, dry it with smoke from aloe or aguru, comb it, and then arrange it with fragrant amalaki paste.

Sometimes they tie His hair into a braid along with a decorative rope and jasmine flowers. Sometimes they gather all of His hair together and tie it in a knot decorated with flowers on top of His head.
