I pray to Krsna’s servants — Snigdha, Karpura, Kumuda, and others — to bless the pujaris of New Vraja-dhama with devotional expertise so that Radha’s and Syama’s hair will always be nicely done.

Radha is also skilled at decorating Sri Krsna’s hair, especially at tying it into a topknot. After She and Krsna bathe in Radha-kunda, She takes Him to a temple where They first change into fresh clothes.

Radha then sits Krsna on a golden dais and directs a few gopis to assist Her in drying and scenting His hair with aguru smoke, combing it, and then braiding it with different aromatic flowers.

Srimati Radharani also braids peacock feathers into Krsna’s hair. She then winds Krsna’s braid up into a topknot and decorates its crest with a peacock feather and twigs laden with berries.

Moving in front of Sri Krsna, Radharani then takes two strands of beads — one gunja and one pearl — and drapes them in either direction from the part in His hair to a spot just behind His ears.

The end result resembles a beehive, which attracts both the bees of the forest and the bees of the gopis’ eyes. These bees then greedily compete with one another for the right to take up residence there.

At those times when Srimati Radharani adds other floral ornaments such as a crown to Sri Krsna’s hair, even He is attracted to that beehive when She shows Him His reflection in a mirror.

Recalling Radha’s expertise in decorating Krsna’s hair, one calls out, “Hare!” Voicing the pleasure we feel in seeing Her served and the pleasure Krsna derives from serving Her, we also murmur, “Rama!”

Dear readers! Please hear about one last feature of Sri Krsna’s hair. In the opinion of many, including the Vraja-vasis, it is most attractive and especially prominent when Krsna returns home each afternoon.

At that time His hair is delicately powdered white with the dust raised by the cows’ hooves. As that cintamani dust sparkles in the setting sun, it creates an ineffable shimmering aura around Krsna.

The gopis in particular appreciate the spectacle of Krsna’s powdered hair as He passes through village after village, glancing and smiling charmingly and playing on His flute as His friends sing His glories.

The cowherd girls of Vrndavana eagerly come forward to see Krsna and to be seen by Him. At that time the sparkle from His hair increases as it is reflected in their tear-filled eyes.

The most prominent feature of Krsna’s face is His noble forehead. One of Vraja’s parrots once said, “I glorify Hari’s forehead, framed by His curling locks of hair and the two vines of His eyebrows —

“Splendid as the Krsnastami moon, decorated with colourful designs drawn in Govardhana’s pigments, and bearing splendid kunkuma tilaka, it is Kamadeva’s trap to catch the deer of Radha’s heart.”

The tilaka marking on Krsna’s high forehead is sometimes yellow and sometimes red. Similar marks decorate other parts of His body, such as His neck, chest, abdomen, and upper and lower back.

From the time Krsna was a little baby, Mother Yasoda would mark His forehead with the symbol of Lord Visnu. She would use auspicious gorocana, uttering om kesavaya namah as she appliedit.

When He was just a baby lying on His back, Krsna overturned a heavily loaded cart with a kick. His mother was convinced that He had been unharmed because of His yellow gorocana tilaka.

Most descriptions of the tilaka on Krsna’s face tell that it is only on His forehead, but some authorities say it extends to His nose, matching the tilaka worn by Gaudiya Vaisnavas today.

Krsna’s servants generally grind goracana together with sandalwood for applying two vertical lines that resemble a tamala leaf, and then they fill the space in between with black aromatic musk.

Under Mother Yasoda’s supervision, the servant boy Makaranda is most expert at applying tilaka; still, other boys also do this service, sometimes using kunkuma instead of gorocana.

The gopis like to paint Krsna’s forehead crimson with kunkuma. To them this reveals His passionate nature and also points to His subservience to Sri Radha, whose feet are smeared with red lac.

Whenever Krsna’s tilaka fades due to exerting Himself while playing various games with the gopas and gopis, His companions reapply it using natural pigments like manahsila from Govardhana Hill.

Along with tilaka, Krsna’s forehead sports a dot of sandalwood paste at its centre, sandalwood pulp at its edges, curly locks of hair along its border, and designs drawn in minerals, all embellishing it further.

The spot of sandalwood in between the two vertical lines of tilaka just above Krsna’s eyebrows serves as a mystical charm that hypnotises the gopis, who become attracted to gazing at their paramour’s stately face.

To keep Him cool during the summer, Krsna’s loving cowherd boyfriends apply sandalwood paste to the two outer portions of His brow, which makes His forehead resemble a mystical gemstone.

Visakha once warned Radha of three things that have the inconceivable power to attract people to Krsna: His flower garland, His name, and the mysterious sandalwood paste on His forehead.

From a distance one could easily mistake the curly locks along Krsna’s hairline for a swarm of bees that might have taken up residence under His turban to drink the nectar of His thoughts.

Indeed, the locks on Radha’s and Krsna’s foreheads lead one to think that great sages have taken birth as two swarms of bees in order to compete with one another in constantly praising the divine couple.

Both the gopis and gopas are fond of drawing designs on the canvas between Krsna’s eyebrows and His curly locks. The boys draw calves or birds, the girls prefer Cupid’s marks, like dolphins or vines.

In New Vraja-dhama, Syamasundara’s servants draw similar designs, vanquishing their material desires. They then whisper, “O Hari!” Their work complete, they feel happy and clap and sing, “O Rama!”

Another mark on Sri Krsna’s forehead, albeit rarely seen, appears to some like nectar and to others like poison. It is the smudge of red lacquer from the sole of a fortunate cowherd girl’s foot.

If that smudge is from the sole of Srimati Radharani’s foot, then Her girlfriends feel as if nectar is pouring into their eyes, for it proclaims Sri Krsna’s complete submission to His one true beloved.

But if that smudge is from the feet of someone other than Radha, then Her friends see it as poison, for it reminds them of the lonely night-long vigils Radha spends waiting for Her unfaithful lover.

Seeing the signs of a tryst with another gopi on Krsna’s body, and after spending the whole night alone waiting for Him, Radha cuts Krsna off before He can finish His litany of excuses.

“Why do You insist on lying to Me?” She says. “Go hack to the girl who decorated Your body with those beauty marks! Don’t contaminate Me or My reputation with Your presence.”

Perhaps the most wonderful mark on Sri Krsna’s forehead is from the dust of Sri Radha’s feet, made as He bows before Her for forgiveness. Only those who chant Hare Rama in ecstasy can hope to see it.

Bilvamangala Thakura says,

**“All glories to Krsna, benefactor of the three worlds, whose forehead is marked with musk tilaka and whose love and joy increase with the love sports of Vraja’s milkmaids!”**

**\* \* \* \***

O Hara! Please remove any obstacles that prevent me from praising Syama’s beautiful eyes. Make my portrait so pleasing to Your ears that You say the name Rama. And allow me to one day hear You say it.

Krsna’s face is a full moon and His eyes are two moon-lakes filled with the nectar of His devotees’ loving glances and with the effects that Srimati Radharani’s form and qualities have made upon them.

The reflections made by the faces of associates like Yasoda, devotees like Narada, and the sights of Vraja are the elegant lotuses and graceful fish that decorate the nectar-filled lakes of Krsna’s eyes.

Streams feed these lakes in the form of Krsna’s tears of divine love for those who love Him, and the hanks of these lakes are the black kajjala stains of compassion for those who have forgotten to love Him.

The bushes on the southern banks are the lower lashes of practising devotees’ immature attachment, and the lush trees on the northern hanks are the full upper lashes of perfected devotees’ mature love.

Within each lake is an island — the pupils of Krsna’s eyes. The sphere on the left is the paradise wherein He meets Radha. On the right is the kingdom wherein separation from Radha reigns supreme.

The combined function of these two islands gives Krsna His sight, which represents His eightfold daily pastimes. And the times He rests within these periods of day and night are the blinking of His eyes.

Because Krsna removes all obstacles to loving devotion with the twinkle of His eyes, He is called Hari, and because pure Vaisnavas enjoy endless bliss by looking into His eyes, they call Him Rama.

Krsna is unlimited, as is the admiration His devotees feel for Him, admiration especially apparent in their descriptions of His eyes, which they compare to lotuses. Thus it is said that He has lotus eyes.

Not unlike a petal or the closed bud of a lotus, which are rounded near the stem and taper at their ends, Krsna’s eyes are full and round by His nose and then stretch to elegant points near His ears.

Lotuses come in many colours, depending on where they grow and when they open. Comparing Krsna’s eyes to lotuses, then, may suggest the many features He displays at different times throughout the day.

The name Pundarikaksa, for example, suggests that Krsna has eyes like red lotuses due to their being bloodshot from His having stayed up all night enjoying amorous festivities like the rasa dance.

As Lord Jagannatha, Krsna is said to have eyes like blooming lotuses. This comparison to the open petals of a lotus, easy for all to see, implies the great ecstasy He feels as He remembers the Vraja-vasis.

And, of course, comparing the Lord’s eyes to the lotus also points out that His eternal transcendental vision is unaffected by the modes of nature; in other words, He can see everything, everywhere.

Krsna’s eyes are said to surpass the beauty of white lotuses, to resemble the mature lotus of the autumn season, and to radiate a kind of softness that reminds one of the petals of a newly blossomed lotus.

What’s more, just as the heat of the sun and the rays of the moon nourish the lotus, so the gopis’ glowing faces, Radha’s cooling form, and the delightful groves of Vraja sustain Krsna’s lotus eyes.

Krsna’s eyes are compared to other things as well: saphari fish for churning the waters of His youth, cakora birds for drinking the moonshine of Radha’s face, and wagtail birds for being restless.

Krsna’s eyes are restless due to the constant ecstasies that dwell in His heart, ecstasies He feels moderately when with His friends, intensely when with His parents, and excessively when near the gopis.

Krsna’s eyes are also compared to a pair of moonstones studded with sapphires moving restlessly about, and to a pair of most exquisite fully bloomed lotuses, upon which two black bees wander.

In New Vraja-dhama, Syamasundara’s lotus eyes remind me of great actors who adopt a variety of roles in order to relish, in as many ways as possible, His close proximity to Srimati Radharani.

In the evening, Syama’s eyes become like cakora birds anxious to drink the moonlight of Radha’s face. During the day they turn into busy bees that buzz around the golden lotus of Her impeccable beauty.

During kirtana, Syama’s eyes dance like birds playing on the riverbank of Radha’s form. And when She is freshly dressed, His eyes dart about like fish swimming in the cool, clear lake of Her sweetness.

Because Krsna’s eyes assume so many forms to steal glances at Radha, He is called Hari, and because His constant gaze gives Radha a forest of happiness in which His eyes frolic like deer, He is also called Rama.

The glint in Syama’s eyes reflects His mischievous smile, yet that light is as peaceful as a vast ocean. It showers mercy upon Syama’s guests and divine love upon His devotees, shining with its own special glory.

Rupa Gosvami writes,

**“May Lord Hari’s eyes, which lovingly gaze upon His devotees, which rival the splendour of blue lotuses upon which the yogis meditate to attain auspiciousness —**

**“Which are two great oceans of handsomeness, and which fill Radha’s eyes with the nectar of love, quell the sufferings of material life within you.”**

May these eyes always reside in my heart.

I meditate upon the Lord’s eyes, two beggars who seek alms in the form of the joy they feel from seeing Radha beautifully dressed and ornamented by devotees whose very life is in bringing them this joy.

In New Vraja-dhama, Sri Radha appears to be a beautiful dance tutor whose students arc Syama’s eyes. Those two students dance with the graceful movements of sidelong glances, pleasing their guru to no end.

When Radha’s cakori eyes move to their right corners in order to reward Her students, the students become like a swarm of greedy bees that try to aggressively plunder the nectar of Her lotus face.

Then Srimati Radharani’s eyes briefly become like female bees to pacify the male bees of Syamasundara’s eyes, but quickly return to their own hive and enact their pastime of showing Him neglect.

As day turns to night, Radha’s spotless face changes, taking on the look of the moon that once rose from the ocean of nectar, a moon that in every way puts to shame the ordinary moon of this universe.

As Syama continuously drinks, through the cakora birds of His eyes, the flood of radiant, sweet, ever-fresh moonlight of Sri Radha’s face, for reasons known only to Her, She continues to ignore Him.

The two jewels Hare Rama remind me of how Krsna once responded to Radha’s neglect, disguising Himself as a gopi and falling at the feet of one of Her girlfriends to gain entrance into Sri Radha’s home.

In disguise Krsna approached Srimati Radharani, who lay on Her bed in Her home at Yavata, lamenting that She had treated Her beloved so badly. Krsna at once began to massage Sri Radha’s lotus feet.

Somehow reminded of Krsna by this new gopi’s touch, Radha said, “You too must be unhappy at being forsaken by Krsna.” She then sat up, looked into Krsna’s eyes, recognised Him, and fell into His arms.

Because Krsna removed Radha’s sorrow by the laughing glance of His unmistakable eyes, Radha called out, “O Hari!” Then, as Her heart filled with the bliss of loving pastimes, She called out, “O Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna’s cheeks are like two smaller moons in steady orbit around the larger moon of His face, and like the night that caresses the moon, His soft, curly hair caresses His moon-like cheeks.

Sastra often compares Krsna’s cheeks to mirrors; indeed, I have witnessed, as have many other devotees, that Syamasundara’s shiny cheeks appear to have received a special polish, though they have not.

The golden lustre Syama’s earrings cast upon those shiny cheeks amplifies the natural radiance of His face, and when those ornaments swing to and fro, His cheeks appear to vibrate with light.

Once, as I ornamented Syamasundara with gold shark-shaped earrings set with valuable stones, it appeared as if Kamadeva was reflected in those two glistening mirror-like cheeks.

Syama’s cheeks make a perfect canvas for drawing various pictures and designs. Pujaris in New Vraja-dhama use their artistic skills to serve His swarthy complexion, as do devotees in Goloka Vrndavana.

I always travel with a picture of Radha and Syama in which Syamasundara’s forehead and cheeks are decorated with the names of the maha-mantra. What better ornament could there be?

In Vraja, the paintings on Krsna’s cheeks are invariably washed away in the course of His pastimes. Sometimes baby Krsna cries in fear of His mother, and His tears smudge His cheeks with mascara.

At other times, as Krsna exerts Himself during the rasa dance or becomes very hot while bringing the cows back at day’s end, perspiration streams down His cheeks and washes away the designs.

Rupa Gosvami paints the following picture of Krsna’s cheeks, an account upon which we can meditate while chanting Hare Rama:

**“I worship Lord Kesava, coming back from the forest of Vraja.**

**“A stream of perspiration licks His cheeks, pictures drawn in mineral colours from the hill decorate them, and curling locks of hair surround them, deriding the splendour of a swarm of black bees.”**

Varieties of other wonderful marks — such as the kisses of His mother, father, and the elderly gopis of Vrndavana, who leave the marks of their lipstick on His dark skin — also decorate Krsna’s cheeks.

Krsna chews betel nuts, and so the betel’s reddish colour sometimes stains His face. The gopis also chew betel, so again its red stain, along with their lipstick, graces His cheeks when they kiss Him.

But painted or not, and with or without the marks left by kisses or other adornments, Sri Krsna’s cheeks become most strikingly beautiful simply by the effect of His irresistible smile.

Whenever Krsna smiles, the sweetness of His lips flows into the reservoir of His cheeks, creating a special glow that elevates His cheeks to a position above all His other facial features.

And when Krsna breaks out into laughter His cheeks blossom, spreading the fragrance of nectar accumulated from His smiles. At such times, His full cheeks are irresistibly attractive.

Mother Yasoda once saw her beautiful child laughing at bulls fighting in rut and could not help but embrace Him. By kissing His cheeks she felt giddy from the intoxicating effect of His touch.

Mother Yasoda dreads the sight of Krsna’s cheeks becoming thin when she thinks that He is not eating enough, and so she rejoices to see the movements of her son’s cheeks as He eats His meals.

In humble service to Mother Yasoda I request all the leaders of New Vraja-dhama to stay alert so that Syamasundara’s cheeks are not only shiny and nicely painted but also full from being well fed and happy.

May Lord Syamasundara, who enchants our hearts with cheeks kissed by the splendour of His smile, the dancing of His earrings, and the reflection of nearby Radha, be my shelter, forever.

Let me now briefly describe Krsna’s shapely and graceful nose, which separates His two perfectly rounded cheeks. Vrnda-devi likens Lord Krsna’s nose to a village at the foot of a mountain.

When we decorate Syamasundara’s effulgent face with earrings, the pleasure of our eyes stems from the dazzling redness of His shapely lips and the beautiful forms of His stately nose and curved eyebrows.

We rarely compare Krsna’s features to mountains or villages, but if the mountain is Nandisvara or Govardhana, and the village Nandagrama or Aniyora, our minds can accommodate the metaphor.

Rupa Gosvami writes that of the thirty-two auspicious characteristics of Krsna’s transcendental body and face, His nose represents one of the five parts where there is height.

A highly raised, prominent nose is a sign of aristocracy, and of course, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the origin of all earthly and heavenly kings, Krsna is the purest and most sophisticated aristocrat.

Unlike His incarnation Prthu, whose nose is said to be straight, Krsna’s nose is graceful, charming, and curved like a parrot’s beak, or “more handsome than the beak of a handsome young parrot.”

This conception of beauty may challenge the stereotypical idea of what makes a man handsome. The modern western standard of beauty holds that an ideal handsome man’s nose is not curved but straight.

But Krsna does not pamper to our whims or expectations; rather, His own beauty sets the standard of what is truly beautiful, just as His opinions set the standards for what is right and wrong.

The reader may wonder why some illustrations in Nava-vraja-mahima depict Krsna’s nose as curved and others as straight. Why picture Him with a straight nose at all, if it is actually curved?

The answer is that some pictures approved by Srila Prabhupada for his books show Krsna with a straight nose, as do most Deities and many other traditional paintings. In short, it doesn’t matter much.

How could it not matter, if we are in fact concerned with presenting the Absolute Truth as He is? Because such matters of contradictory detail are all resolved in the absolute person of Lord Krsna.

An example might help us to understand. In 1976 I was in Srila Prabhupada’s room when a temple president asked permission to instal Radha-Krsna Deities, permission Srila Prabhupada granted.

But when the devotee asked whether the Deity of Krsna should be white marble, or black like Krsna, Srila Prabhupada replied that it didn’t matter because “Krsna can be white and He can be black.”

The devotee repeatedly pressed Srila Prabhupada to say black, but His Divine Grace refused to commit and continued to give the same answer. Finally the devotee got the message and stopped asking.

I understood Srila Prabhupada’s words to mean that although Krsna is black, He also displays other colours in His incarnations, and thus it matters little whether the Deity is white or black. He is Krsna.

Similarly, Krsna’s nose may be curved like a parrot’s or straight, as it is in incarnations like Prthu and Deities like Syamasundara in New Vraja-dhama, but it doesn’t matter because He is always Krsna.

Scripture often compares Sri Krsna’s nose to a sesame flower because when in blossom the flower has a curved protuberance that juts out from its bottom, and that resembles a parrot’s beak.

From childhood, Krsna wears a pearl nose-ring. Saksi-gopala once appeared in a dream to the wife of the king of Puri, Purusottama-deva. She wanted to give her most cherished pearl to the Deity.

Gopala said,

**“During My childhood My mother made a hole in My nose and with great endeavour set a pearl there. That very hole is still there, and you can use it to set the pearl you desired to give Me.”**

Srila Prabhupada mentions the pearl hanging from the septum of Krsna’s nose as one of the Lord’s childhood ornaments. Other acaryas mention that Krsna continues to wear the pearl in His later years.

Various acaryas describe that the tip of Krsna’s nose is decorated with a valuable pearl hanging on a gold ring, either alone or set between two jewels. In New-Vraja-dhama, Syama also has such an ornament.

Lord Krsna’s nose is most attractive when He is feeling great ecstasy. In Dvaraka, for example, when Krsna feels far from Vraja, streams of tears flow along His nose like a slender string of pearls.

Krsna’s nose smells like a lotus flower anointed with camphor — as do His mouth, hands, and feet — and it seems to bend down from a desire to smell the aroma of His own breath and bimba-fruit lips.

As one parrot summarised, “Glorious as a sapphire sesame flower or as Cupid’s sapphire arrow, its glory rebuking a sapphire parrot’s beak, the handsome tip of Lord Krsna’s nose is gloriously manifest.”

Certainly, the fragrant flowers of New Vraja-dhama are pleasing to Syamasundara’s nose, just as its singing birds please His ears, its produce His tongue, its beauty His eyes, and its breezes His skin.

But the fragrance of Radharani pleases Krsna more than any floral or sylvan scent possibly could. May the vision of Syamasundara intoxicated by the aroma of Sri Radha’s form bless our eyes.

Syama once teased a gopi by saying, “Now that a golden lotus rests on the top of your braid and a blue flower sits on your left ear, what flower shall I place over your right ear?” May that Hari bless us all!

As He posed this question with a smile, on the pretext of smelling these flower decorations with His handsome nose, He kissed the blossoming cheek of that gopi. May that Rama protect us all!

**\* \* \* \***

Now let us hear more about Sri Krsna s face. The many glories of His lips, chin, and ears remove all miseries and bestow complete happiness. Therefore His names are Hari and Rama.

A parrot once praised Krsna’s lips,

*sarvasva-ratna-pitako vraja-sundarinam jivatu-sidhu-casakam vrsabhanujayah*  
*tac-chri-lasad-dasana-laksana-laksitarh sri-krsnadharaustham anisam hrdi me cakdstu*

**“Krsna’s lips, a treasure trove of all things desirable for the beautiful damsels of Vraja, give the nectar of life to Vrsabhanu’s daughter. May those lips, adorned by Her teeth-marks, shine in my heart!”**

When Krsna enters boyhood His copper-coloured lips take on a reddish lustre, a lustre found in six other places on His body: His eyes, palate, and tongue, and His nails, palms, and soles.

Some poets compare this reddish colour to the bimba fruit, others to the bandhujlva flower, and still others to the roseapple. I liken Syama’s lips to the firethorn berry that thrives in New Vraja-dhama.

It is said that Krsna’s upper lip is His modesty. But His fuller lower lip reminds me of His flamboyant side. These two opposing waves in the river of sweetness unite to display His matchless charm.

These two waves meet and create whirlpools in the corners of Krsna’s mouth, whose eddies draw the boat-like eyes of anyone adventurous enough to meditate on them into their mysterious depths.

Krsna’s outgoing breath, which the wise know to be the sublime source of all Vedic literature, causes a slight indentation on the centre portion of His upper lip whenever He plays the flute.

Because that small indentation makes one forget all material attachments, the Vedas call Him Hari, and because His flute playing is irresistibly pleasing, the Puranas call Him Rama.

Overall, Krsna’s lips are moderately full, neither thick nor thin. A gorgeous, soft-red glow defines His lips at their edge, a glow further embellished by the sparkling rays of His teeth as He speaks.

Krsna’s lips are famous for their taste and their fragrance, both of which are likened to enchanting nectar, indescribable sweetness, and honey drawn from the beehives of the gardens in Vaikuntha.

Only Yasoda, Radha, and a few other fortunate gopis taste Krsna’s lips directly. They testify that the taste of those lips, defying description, is relishable to the degree one’s relationship with Him permits.

As if the taste of that divine elixir were not nectarean enough, Krsna further enhances it with the sound of His flute to create a unique sweetness unattainable even by the goddess of fortune.

In addition to this unparalleled sweetness, Krsna’s lips have medicinal properties that have repeatedly saved the lives of many a love-struck gopi at death’s door. And for the conditioned souls who see them —

Krsna’s lips neutralise the poison of material existence, exerting a healing power over their audience. And by cutting the hard knots in the heart, they liberate those who hear them play the flute.

Krsna’s sparkling teeth are like hidden treasures concealed by His lips. Poets liken those treasures to pomegranate seeds, jasmine buds, diamonds, or pearls that gopi-pirates are greedy to plunder.

The reddish effulgence that emanates from Sri Krsna’s lips shines on His earrings and from there reflect onto His cheeks, making them appear flushed, like rubies reflecting onto a sapphire.

This red effulgence was once especially visible when, upon approaching Dvaraka, Krsna announced His arrival by sounding His white conch, which was reddened by the touch of His lips.

Sometimes Krsna’s lips proudly display black smudges, which are stains of collyrium acquired when He kisses Sri Radha’s eyes. The new taste of Sri Krsna’s lips then becomes a delicacy for Radharani.

In every way Syamasundara’s lips reflect the exquisite characteristics just mentioned, and every day I wonder at the fortune of the flute, whose holes fill up with the elixir that flows from those lips.

The Lord’s musical skill surely moves hearts, but the real reason His flute-song is able to enchant and entrance can be found in the effect that the nectar of His lips has when it enters the ears.

We residents of New Vraja-dhama may not hear the sound of Krsna’s flute as His eternal associates do, but we sing Radha-Syama’s glories, begging for the day that Krsna’s flute-song will enter our ears as well.

When that day comes we will also savour His lips’ sweetness, for He makes that sweetness available to all qualified devotees by transforming the nectar of His lips into sounds palpable to them.

Pure loving devotion empowers the auditory sense with the sense of taste. When we ascend to that stage of pure love we will also taste the sweetness of Krsna’s lips through the medium of our ears.

By this inconceivable potency of pure devotion, perfected devotees relish the highest taste, and scriptures reveal these topics so that by hearing, our desire to directly perceive such things will awaken.

Some readers may object, saying that accepting the remnants of the flute is not fitting for us, but, as the gopis say, “Even great devotees drink the nectar of Krsna’s lips after the flute has done so.”

But there is a way that everyone can taste the nectar of Sri Krsna’s lips, by hearing about their sweetness. The gopis explain how this is possible in the verse beginning with *tava kathamrtam*:

**“The nectar of Your words and the descriptions of Your activities are the life and soul of those suffering in this material world. These narrations, transmitted by learned sages —**

**“Eradicate one’s sinful reactions and bestow good fortune upon whoever hears them. These narrations are broadcast all over the world and are filled with spiritual power.”**

Topics of Krsna are full of complete spiritual power. Thus, to realised souls they can give full and direct perception of what they describe. And to others they give tastes in proportion to their advancement.

Therefore we hear that the gopis, who rarely enjoy Krsna’s lips directly, constantly speak about them, not only because they yearn for them but also because they actually taste them by hearing.

What’s more, all devotees can savour the nectar of Lord Krsna’s lips by seeing the constant and alluring smile of His Deity, and by tasting the food His lips have touched, His maha-prasada.

The Lord is so kind! He imparts the qualities of His lips not only to His flute playing, but also to the food we offer to Him. In this way, He blesses even practising devotees with the sweet potency of His lips.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu tells us to honour the remnants of food eaten by Krsna, food that has been turned into nectar by His lips, for even demigods like Lord Brahma find this treasure difficult to obtain.

Someone may be bold enough, or foolish enough, to suggest that since we can all see Krsna’s Deity form with our material eyes, Krsna must also be making His lips available for us conditioned souls to taste.

But Jiva Gosvami and his followers condemn such pseudo devotion. No one should even think to imitate the activities of Krsna and His eternal companions by trying to kiss or embrace Krsna’s Deity form.

Even one who has attained an intimate relationship with the Lord acts externally as a neophyte and worships the Deity with reverence, following all scriptural injunctions. That is proper behaviour.

To taste the nectar of Krsna’s lips we can also bathe in and drink the water of the Ganges or the Yamuna, where Krsna bathed and drank and in so doing imparted His sweetness to their waters.

The gopis praise the trees on the hanks of these rivers for being able to drink the nectar of Krsna’s lips through their roots because in that way one of their kin was fortunate enough to become Krsna’s flute.

If a bamboo rod became Krsna’s associate simply by drinking the nectar of His lips, what perfection can we not achieve by hearing of those lips, seeing His smile, or tasting His remnants?

**\* \* \* \***

Only Krsna’s parents, wives, paramours, and the flute have direct access to His lips. All His other eternal associates taste that nectar indirectly, in the ways mentioned above. Still, everyone is pleased.

As Mother Yasoda kisses her son, she overflows with maternal love, and as He returns her kisses, His heart melts with affection. But when she breastfeeds Him, she attains His lips in a way unique to her.

Pariksit Maharaja, after hearing about such perfections, was struck with wonder. In ecstatic love he enquired, “What auspicious activities did Yasoda perform to have the Supreme Lord suckle her breast?”

The lawful access Krsna’s wives have to His lips is a source of divine envy for Vrndavana’s milkmaids and also a wonder to Hastinapura’s ladies, who praise it thus: “O friends! Just think of His wives.

“How they must have undergone vows, baths, fire sacrifices, and perfect worship of the Lord to constantly relish now the nectar from His lips. The gopis would often faint expecting such favours.”

And although the beauty of Krsna’s wives could bewilder the mind of Brahma, because their devotion could never completely conquer their husband’s mind they could not fully enjoy His nectarean lips.

The love felt by Krsna’s queens is not completely selfless, for they want to enjoy Him for themselves; thus, even with their aristocracy, devotion, and love, they cannot agitate Krsna’s mind as the gopis do.

The Pancajanya conch is also a close associate of Krsna’s lips, but it does not share the same degree of intimacy the flute enjoys with Krsna. It cannot even be counted in the same category as the flute.

The conch enjoys the formal role of declaring Krsna’s arrival or His challenge to an enemy, roles inferior to the flute’s intimate service of conveying messages to the Vraja-vasis, especially to the gopis.

And because the flute does not communicate with anyone the way conscious beings do, it is universally accepted that the actual experts in knowing and tasting Krsna’s lips are the gopis of Vraja.

But the gopis’ amorous relationships with Krsna are clandestine, and so opportunities to kiss Him are rare. Thus they are always obsessing over the flute’s unrestricted access to Krsna’s lips. A gopi once said:

**“My dear gopis! What auspicious activities must the flute have performed to enjoy the nectar of Krsna’s lips independently and leave only a taste for us gopis, for whom that nectar is actually meant!”**

In transcendental madness the gopis taste Krsna’s lips by talking of the audacity of the flute, thereby giving practising devotees a drop of what they taste and a deeper understanding of their love for Krsna.

After much waiting, the gopis do get the company of their beloved and relish the taste of His lips. But they think it is happening for the first time, and after enjoying it, they forget that they ever tasted it.

The gopis thus always hanker for something that they think they have yet to achieve, and the flute’s constant canvassing increases that hankering more and more. And of all gopis, Radha hankers the most.

They do meet Krsna in Vrndavana forest and enjoy with Him for some time. But after He leaves them, the gopis sit with Sri Radha and appeal to Him by singing songs that beg Him to return.

On one such occasion after Krsna left them the gopis sang this song,

*surata-vardhanam soka-nasanam svarita-venuna susthu-cumbitam*  
*itara-raga-vismaranam nrnam vitara vira nas te ’dhardmrtam*

**“O hero! Kindly distribute to us the nectar of Your lips, which enhances romantic pleasure, vanquishes grief, is thoroughly relished by Your flute, and makes people forget any other attachment.”**

The gopis waited for a response, but the silent forest was all they could hear, an obvious sign that Krsna had either not heard them or was ignoring them, so the gopis begged Radha to intercede.

Addressing Her friends first and then Krsna, Radha described at length the gopis’ attraction to Sri Krsna’s lips, their rivalry with the flute, and their plight at being upstaged by that male competitor.

In great anxiety Srimati Radharani said, “My dear friends! Only after many, many pious activities can one obtain the all-surpassing nectar from the lips of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna.

“For the beautiful gopis of Vraja, that nectar vanquishes the desire for all other tastes. Madana-mohana always chews pan that surpasses the nectar of heaven and increases the desires of My tongue.”

Overwhelmed by ecstatic love, Radha drew stares from Her friends as She addressed Krsna in the way of a madwoman, “My dear lover! Let Me tell You of a few essential qualities of Your transcendental lips.

“They agitate the mind and body everyone, they increase *lusty* desires for enjoyment, they destroy the burden *of* material happiness and lamentation, and they make one forget *all* material tastes.

“The whole world falls under the control of Your nectarean *lips.* They vanquish shame, religion, and patience, *especially in* women. Indeed, they inspire madness in the minds *of all* women in creation.

“Your lips increase the greed of the tongue and thus attract it. All things considered, to us and to the rest of the world, the *activities* of Your transcendental lips appear *paradoxical."*

Krsna’s lips affect others in ways seemingly inconsistent, causing a type of confusion that culminates in madness. The mere desire for Krsna’s lips, for example, extinguishes material attachments.

Yet that spiritual awakening escalates into an intense divine lust, making its victims appear shamelessly irreligious, though in *reality* they have become pure, fully self-realised, *and free* from *duality.*

Radha also implied that although it might seem natural for handsome Krsna to attract women, the truth is that He attracts everyone, even men, who then desire to be born as women to join His pastimes.

The great heroes on the battlefield of Kuruksetra were so attracted by Krsna’s beauty as He drove Arjuna’s chariot that they also yearned for a fortunate position as wives or lovers of the Lord.

In fact, Krsna attracts even Himself! Upon seeing His own reflection, the Lord once admitted,

**“Alas! I Myself, My mind bewildered upon seeing this beauty, impetuously desire to enjoy it like Sri Radha.”**

We should note, however, that the flute — unlike other males, Krsna included — does not wait to attain a woman’s body to fulfil his desire. He tastes the nectar of Sri Krsna’s lips while still in male form.

In a voice laced with sarcasm, Srimati Radharani observed, “My dear Krsna! Since You are a man, it is not very extraordinary that the attraction of Your lips disturbs the minds of women.

“But I am ashamed to say that Your impudent lips sometimes attract even Your flute, which is also considered male. It likes to drink the nectar of Your lips, and thus it also forgets all other tastes.”

Radha laid bare this paradox by pointing out the indiscriminate and whimsical nature of Sri Krsna’s lips, which places Krsna in this socially compromised situation — kissing and being kissed by a male.

But Radha was not done. She continued to humiliate Krsna and the thoughtlessness of His lips. After all, hadn’t those lips breathed a masculine life force into the inanimate flute in the first place/

In hushed tones, Radha explained to the gopis that originally the flute was a piece of bamboo. Separated from its roots, it was no longer even alive. But after being fashioned into a flute, something changed.

By the mystic power of Sri Krsna’s lips, the flute came to life. Having attained a mind and senses of its own, it then tasted transcendental bliss and quickly became a greedy enjoyer of those divine lips.

Had Krsna’s lips made the flute humble and sympathetic to the gopis’ plight, despite this enjoying spirit forgiveness might have been called for. But no, His lips had created an arrogant, cunning competitor.

Urged on by the sorrow of Her friends, Srimati Radharani lodged a complaint on their behalf. There were already too many obstacles to the gopis’ love for Krsna in conservative Bhauma Vrndavana.

But in this case Krsna Himself had created the most formidable obstacle to the gopis’ service to Him.

**“That flute is a very cunning male who drinks again and again the taste of another male’s lips.**

**“It advertises its qualities and says to the gopis, ‘O gopis, if you are so proud of being women, come forward and enjoy your property—the nectar of the lips of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.’”**

**\* \* \* \***

Day or night, whenever Krsna played His flute to call His cows, entertain His friends, or entice the gopis, the flute would berate the cowherd girls, flaunting his own privileged place on Krsna’s lips.

Sri Radha goes on to say that the flute dismisses the other gopis, considering only Her to have some right to Krsna’s lips, and then it haughtily challenges, “Give up Your shame, fear, and religion.

“Come drink the lips of Krsna. On that condition only will I give up my attachment for them. If You don’t give up Your shame and fear, however, I will continue to drink the nectar of Krsna’s lips.

‘“\[O Radha! Because You are so dear to Krsna, I admit that\] I am slightly fearful because You also have the right to drink that nectar, but as for the others, I consider them like straw.’”

The other gopis, incensed at hearing evidence of the flute’s impudence, promised to break it into three pieces and throw it into the Yamuna the next time they managed to get hold of it.

But Radha calmed Her friends by pointing out one good quality in the flute: at least it didn’t care for the worldly opinion and religious principles that would stop it from tasting the nectar of Krsna’s lips.

Still, the male flute may be criticised for plundering the property of the fairer sex. Radha imagined the flute’s reply, “Then the gopis — especially Radha — should step forward and stake their claim.”

As a male, the flute had abandoned all shame to taste Krsna’s lips. Now he challenged the gopis to do the same. “Give up your shame, fear, and religion and come drink the lips of Krsna,” he taunted.

As women, the gopis had a natural right to Krsna’s lips, a right acknowledged by the flute. But if the gopis were not willing to make the same sacrifice as he was, then why should he step aside?

The gopis recognised the flute’s courage and nodded to each other. Meanwhile, Krsna, who was watching and listening, asked Radha from within, “If You admire the flute’s quality, then why complain?”

Radha heard Krsna’s question and responded, “Just as the gopis and I were considering the flute’s challenge, the nectar of Your lips and the vibration of the flute colluded against us.

“Out of respect for religious principles, we gopis had decided to be patient and to depend on the kindness of fate, but these two conspirators forcibly dragged us to You and shamed us.”

Radha then disclosed more details: “The nectar of Your lips and the vibration of Your flute conspire to loosen our belts and induce us to give up shame and religion, even in front of our superiors.

“O Krsna! Consider this: These two culprits forcibly take us away, as if catching us by the hair, and deliver us to You to become Your maidservants. Hearing of these things, people ridicule us.”

Radha paused and then pointed out that by breathing life into the flute, Krsna had not only created a competitor but also a cruel taskmaster: “Can’t You see how we have become the flute’s slaves?”

At this Krsna smiled and said, “If My lips and the flute have been so cruel to You, then why don’t You lodge a complaint with Maharaja Nanda? Ask him to take both Me and My flute to task.”

Radha’s eyes flared with indignation as She peered into the darkness around Her and spoke: “This flute is nothing but a dry stick of bamboo. Should it be allowed to become our master and insult us?

“We have been forced into a predicament we can do nothing about. All we can do is tolerate. The mother of a thief will not cry out for justice when the thief is punished. Thus we are forced into silence.”

And it was true. The gopis were always meditating on and talking about the nectar of Krsna’s lips, so how could they complain when the flute was relishing what they were longing for?

The gopis nodded their heads in agreement as Radha continued, “We were forcibly dragged into this deep forest. Now we have neither our reputations nor that which brought shame upon us — Your lips.”

Radharani paused for a moment to think. Wouldn’t it be wiser to place the blame where it really belonged? The flute was but an instrument. It had simply carried out the policies of Sri Krsna’s lips.

As She turned to the gopis, Radha raised Her index finger, pointed to Her own lips as if She were Krsna, and said in a trembling voice, “Such is the policy of these lips. Just consider its other injustices.

“Everything these lips touch — including food, drink, or betel — transforms into nectar, the remnants left by Krsna (krsna-phela). The demigods, even after much prayer, cannot obtain that nectar.”

By this statement Radha exposed a plot hatched by Krsna’s lips, a conspiracy by which whatever they touched — be it the flute, food, or whatever else — would acquire its own power to hypnotise others.

Thus empowered, these things could then mesmerise anyone who had contact with them, and their victim would then proceed in a state of captivity into Sri Krsna’s presence to become His plaything.

The gopis’ exchange of words and glances created a buzz. They all realised at the same moment that the flute was merely a puppet in the hands of the ultimate cause of their suffering, Krsna’s lips.

Humility softened Radha’s pride as She said, “O friends! It is said that only a person who has acted piously for many, many births and has thus become a devotee can obtain the remnants of Krsna’s food.

“The same is said about those who can taste His betel remnants,

*krsna ye khaya tambula, kahe tara nahi mula, tahe ara dambha-paripati*  
*tara yeba udgara, tare kaya ‘amrta-sara,’ gopira mukha kare ‘alabati’*

**“The betel chewed by Krsna is priceless, and the remnants of such chewed betel are said to be the essence of nectar. When the gopis accept these remnants, their mouths become His spittoons.”**

Radha paused again before going on, “The same may be said for hearing the sound of Sri Krsna’s flute. It appears that our past good fortune has enabled us to relish these things with our senses.

“But it also appears that we are neither pious nor devoted enough to taste the lips of Krsna directly. Why else would we he sitting here now in this dark forest even though our beloved is somewhere else?”

Radha’s conclusion submerged both Her and the gopis in an ocean of despair. But just as it seemed as though they would surely drown in that ocean, Krsna appeared in Radha’s heart to give them hope.

Radharani saw Krsna in the way He had looked as He stood beneath the Vamsivata, playing His flute and showering welcoming glances upon Her and the gopis as they arrived at the shelter of His lotus feet.

Thinking aloud, Srimati Radharani said, “He called us here with His flute! Was it just a trick? Is He just playing with us? How many more births must we take before we can directly taste His lips?”

Radha looked around at Her friends. Even if She was not qualified for Krsna’s grace, they must be. Surely they had achieved the pinnacle of perfection. Why would Krsna not give His mercy to them?

Krsna’s lips, and whatever those lips touch, are nectar-sweet. Doesn’t He say so Himself? Why, then, would He withhold that sweet nectar from those who answered His call and so rightly deserved it?

And above all, Krsna was the aggressor. He had tempted them. Could He then brutally deny the gopis access to even the slightest drop of nectar? If so, He must be trying to kill them. But would He do that?

As if in answer to Her questions, the wind blew, rustling the leaves on the surrounding trees. To Radha, it sounded like Krsna laughing. Was He watching? Was their suffering His entertainment?

Convinced that Krsna must be listening from somewhere nearby, Radha called out into the forest. She prayed on behalf of Her friends, hoping that Krsna would consider Her arguments reasonable.

“My dear Krsna!” Radha said. “Please give up all Your tricks. Don’t try to take the lives of these innocent gopis with Your flute-song.” The gopis scanned the forest, half-expecting to see Krsna.

“In Your frivolity, You will be responsible for killing women. It would be better for You to give us the nectar of Your lips in charity instead. That would satisfy You and spare our lives.”

The gopis had asserted that a bamboo stick has no inherent connection with Krsna’s lips, and so it must have performed some austerities in this or in previous lives to have such good fortune.

They had also said that Krsna needed no other reason than His own charitable disposition for giving them the nectar of His lips and thus let the gift itself qualify the recipients — the gopis themselves.

This principle, that Krsna’s lips themselves qualify devotees to receive nectar, also applies to us today. By Lord Caitanya’s grace, coming to us through Srila Prabhupada, we receive the touch of Krsna’s lips.

That touch permeates the taste of prasada, the sound of the holy names, the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita, and the chapters of Srimad-Bhagavatam, especially the one titled “The Song of the Flute.”

By contact with these things, Krsna’s lips enable us to increasingly appreciate their sweetness and finally become qualified to taste it in a suitable spiritual body, as do the cowherd girls of Vrndavana.

But as followers of Rupa Gosvami we do not desire direct contact with Krsna’s lips; rather, we want to serve those who have such contact. In this way, we will taste everything that they taste.

Although a bee collects honey from the flowers of a creeper, the leaves of the creeper also hear the bee’s humming and feel its touch. So it is for the servants of the direct servants of Sri Krsna.

The servant who most intently desires the divine treasure of Krsna’s lips is Srimati Radharani, who prays, “O flute, expert at drinking the nectar of the breath from Mukunda’s smiling lotus mouth-

“I offer My respectful obeisances unto you. I beg you, whenever you touch the charming bimba fruit of Krsna’s lips, please whisper in His ear and tell Him how I burn with the desire to attain Him.”

This desire of Radha’s is always fulfilled, and so the followers of Mahaprabhu pray, “When will Vrndavana’s queen, who, deep in Her forest, always enjoys a festival of transcendental amorous pastimes —

“Who becomes intoxicated by drinking the madhavika nectar of Krsna’s lips, and who always surrounds Herself with gopis dear to Krsna, be merciful to me and make me Her maidservant?”

In the mood of never directly serving Krsna’s lips, I remember the words of great souls who pray to the flute in Syamasundara’s hands,

*sunyatvam hrdaye sa-laghavam idam suskatvam — angesu me maukharyam vraja-natha-nama-kathane dattam bhavatya nijam*  
*tatkimno murali prayacchasi punar govinda-vaktrasavam yam pitva bhuvanam vase vidadhati nirlajjam udgayasi*

**“O flute! You have blessed me by giving me your heart’s emptiness, your form’s lightness, your body’s dryness, and your voice’s eloquence in constantly chanting the holy name of Krsna, Vraja’s prince.**

**“Why not give me the nectar of Syamasundara’s lips, which you constantly drink, expertly turn into song, and shamelessly use to enchant the entire world and bring it under your control?”**

**\* \* \* \***

My favourite flower is a purple rose called the “Blue Moon.” To me, Syamasundara’s face is like this aromade and stately flower, the prince of roses. Thus I call His face “the blue-moon rose.”

I offer my obeisances to Syama’s blue-moon-rose face, in which His nose, cheeks, lips, chin, and ears are petals, His eyes hovering bees, His smile its fragrance, His teeth its stamen, and His tongue its whorl.

The truth is that Syama’s face is more handsome than millions of any sort of flower, especially when He playfully jokes with Srimati Radharani, showing off His exquisite, captivating chin.

The chin naturally facilitates the movements of the lips as a person speaks. Lord Krsna’s chin and its movements are therefore equally as enchanting as the movements of His lips.

Sukadeva Gosvami says that the Lord’s chin is the transcendental hankering for victory. Thus His chin is prominent in such pastimes as stealing butter, wrestling with friends, and flirting with the gopis.

Syama’s chin, buffed to a mirror finish, increases the beauty of His mild smile and competes with the reflection of His earrings upon His cheeks. Together, His chin and cheeks make His face effulgent.

The Lord’s elders in Vraja, along with performing auspicious rituals for His benefit and showering their blessings upon Him, pinch His chin as a gesture of affection in parental love (vatsalya-rati).

Every morning, as the cowherd boys leave the village of Nandagrama with their cows, Mother Yasoda heaps blessings upon her son by placing her left hand on His back and her right hand on His chin.

In a similar gesture of affection, Mother Yasoda once caught Krsna tying the sikha of a cowherd boy to the tail of a calf, lifted up His chin, and lovingly said, “Govinda! Damodara! Madhava!”

I worship that lower part of Syama’s face, His chin, which constantly competes with His beautiful ears, whose swaying, shark-shaped earrings and dangling flower ornaments constantly caress it.

Krsna’s ears generate the ten directions and receive the transcendental vibrations of the Vedas. They facilitate His sense of hearing, which is also the source of physical sound and of the sky.

Krsna’s ears are a source of pleasure for Him, *krsna-karnamrta*, which is a chorus of the combined voices of His devotees and personal associates under the direction of their conductor, Sri Radha.

The tenors in this choir are the devotees who glorify Him to others and, by Krsna’s own admission, these preachers are also His dearmost confidants, their voices being the most attractive to Him.

The alto singers are those pure-hearted devotees who raise their voices in sankirtana of His names, drawing Him out of His own abode of Vaikuntha to hear their singing and to sometimes join with them.

The bass singers are the voices of practising and perfected devotees whose prayers, mantras, and hymns are saturated with devotion and filled with the Lord’s names. They cause His body to tremble in bliss.

The baritone voices are the lowing of cows, the sounds of Vrndavana forest, the harsh words of Jatila, and the gossip of villagers, all of which are more attractive to Him than Vedic hymns.

The sopranos of this choir are the cowherd girls of Vraja and their haughty jokes, humorous criticism, and crooked words, all of which Krsna appears to ignore, but whose every syllable is like a jewel.

The conductor is Sri Radha, Krsna consciousness personified, who directs the performance of all five sections of the choir, all the while embellishing their chorus with Her own angelic voice.

About Sri Radha’s contribution to pleasing Krsna’s ears, it is said,

**“Sri Radhika’s words, whose syllables are as beautiful as waves in an ocean of nectar, which are full of clever jokes and speech —**

**“Which resound with double meanings and metaphors, and which teach the male and female bees and all manners of birds how to sing, are like nectar to Sri Krsna’s ears (*****krsna-sravasoh rasayanam*****).”**

If one were to ask how to best portray this sublime concert, I would say, “By chanting Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.”

This rendition of Radha’s and Krsna’s moon-like faces began as an elaboration on the second Hare Rama, but turned into a lengthy meditation that, sadly, like all things must come to an end.

But who can blame me for becoming immersed in the captivating faces of Radha and Krsna? They appeared in New Vraja-dhama as Radha and Syama to remove our suffering and bring us true joy.

What I have written here, then, reflects but a tiny portion of the most beautiful features — the faces — of Radha and Krsna, the origins of all beautiful things. I have said but a fraction of what could be said.

**\* \* \* \***

I conclude my praise of the second Hare Rama by delineating the symptoms in the final stages of ecstatic devotion, and by narrating Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes at dusk, which both epitomise this pair.

A devotee at the stage of bhava-bhakti is so attracted to seeing the Deity of Krsna that he curses his eyes for blinking, for that split second interrupts his vision of the Lord, his heart’s only pleasure.

When one possesses spontaneous attraction for the Deity, hearing of Krsna’s loving exchanges with the gopis increases attachment for those pastimes until it becomes a rite of passage into krsna-lila.

A devotee who chants “Hare Rama” in ecstasy is begging Radha and Krsna for the privilege to see Their confidential pastimes at Radha-kunda, on Govardhana, and on the banks of the Yamuna.

At the previous stage of attachment, one inclined to gopi-bhava identifies strongly with what he or she has heard, but that link is merely a spiritual aspiration, not an actual transcendental emotion.

When ecstatic devotion awakens, however, one glimpses his sthayi- bhava, a transcendental though immature identity that impels the devotee to earnestly pray for full-fledged love like that of the gopis.

The absorption corresponding to this desire draws one into deep meditative trance; still, for want of the eleven elements that constitute a full spiritual identity, one remains a passive observer.

Because at this stage one calls out to Radha, saying, “Please remove the miseries I feel without direct service to You,” and because She appears to reassure Her servant, “Soon!” She is known as Hara.

To confirm Radha’s promise, Krsna suddenly appears by Her side and embraces His beloved, giving Their devotee, as well as Themselves, great pleasure. Therefore we know Him as Rama!

Radha then feigns displeasure and frees Herself from Krsna’s grasp. But He protests, “Hara! Your presence steals away My self-control. Don’t blame Me!” At this, the devotee chants, “Hare! Rama!”

Speaking to Krsna over Her shoulder, Radha replies, “O really! I thought it was because You steal away the last trace of the gopis’ determination to resist You that they call You Hari or Hare.”

Krsna then replies, with cheek, “No dearest! Your girlfriends now call Me Rama because they know that My loving ways arouse in You a divine passion to take the dominant role in Our pastimes.”

Radha strikes Krsna with Her toy lotus, and the devotee calls out “Rama! Rama!” in the hopes of seeing the confidential pastimes Krsna alludes to. But alas, the vision of the divine couple disappears.

In bliss from having seen Radha and Krsna, but distraught at having lost Them, the devotee in bhava then displays contradictory emotions that make him laugh and cry while he wildly dances and sings.

After some time has passed — perhaps minutes, perhaps hours — the devotee regains composure and, with enlivened spiritual senses, abandons all bodily demands, chanting the maha-mantra in bliss.

Like a traveller who mounts a speedy chariot for his destination, the devotee greedily ascends the vehicle of nama-sankirtana to almost instantly enter Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes at dusk.

When Rati and her friends arrive at Nandagrama, they hand the rice, sweets, and other items prepared by Radha to Dhanistha. They fall at Yasoda’s feet and then into her warm, loving embrace.

Krsna’s mother lovingly enquires about Radha’s welfare, and when she sees the neat rows of tasty laddus, she glorifies Srimati Radharani’s cooking, beauty, and chastity to all the women present.

Meanwhile, Krsna and Balarama are approaching Nandagrama surrounded by Their friends and the massive herd of surabhi cows, looking like two moons surrounded by the stars of the Milky Way.

The boys are blanketed with dust from the cows’ hooves, sacred dust that billows higher and higher as the cows’ eagerness increases more and more to return to their own villages, calves, and barns.

Gradually the sound of the cows’ lowing, mixed with the boys’ flutes, horns, and voices, reaches the homes of the Vraja-vasis and brings them pouring excitedly outside to catch the first glimpse of Krsna.

The women put aside their chores and gather on rooftops, stand in doorways, and even join the men along the road outside the village, where the houses and the pasturing grounds meet.

Nanda and his brothers, along with Yasoda and Rohini, go up to the palace rooftop, but in their eagerness to see Krsna and Balarama their eyes fill with tears, so they can hardly see anything at all.

Added to the intensifying sounds of hooves, instruments, and shouting gopas, come calls of “Here they are!” from the villagers greeting the first wave of boys, who carry flags and banners.

Behind this first wave, in the midst of Their confidential friends, Krsna and Balarama walk with the gait of baby elephants, making playful gestures and poses to show off for the young girls.

In response to the appearance of their children, the men shout, “Jaya! Jaya!” and the women ululate wildly; the combined vibration clashes joyfully with the tumult of the approaching herd.

The procession stops at the Nandagrama-Varsana junction while boys like Sridama and Sudama lovingly embrace Krsna and say goodbye, shedding tears as they sadly lead their own herds home to Varsana.

In spite of being visibly disturbed at the departure of His friends, Krsna enters Nandagrama, even as other boys withdraw their cows from the herd in order to return to their homes and parents.

At the foot of Nandisvara Hill, as the ten directions resound with felicitous sounds of greetings and good will, Krsna leaves His cows with the cowherd men and heads towards His father’s palace.

Mother Yasoda hurries out of the palace and meets her sons halfway down the hill. As she embraces Krsna, waves of loving ecstasy make milk flow as profusely from her breasts as do the tears from her eyes.

Mother Yasoda repeatedly embraces Krsna, then she holds Him at arm’s length and gazes at Him as she sobs, “My son! My son!” Then, holding Krsna’s left hand, she covers Balarama’s face with kisses.

Satisfied that her sons are safe and in good health, she offers Them cool water to drink, performs auspicious rituals, and holds Their hands as she walks Them up the winding stairs and into the palace.

Inside the palace compound, Mother Yasoda sits Krsna and Balarama next to each other on a golden lion-throne, covering Them with royal robes and wiping Their faces with the end of her sari.

Seeing the boys’ faces drawn and Their lips parched from exposure to the sun, Mother Yasoda lovingly scolds Balarama, “Haladhara! This is the last time I let either of You go out into the forest.”

At that moment servants arrive to wash the princes’ feet and wipe Their limbs. Others fan Them from either side with whisks as still others set up arati trays in front of the queen of Vrndavana.

Mother Yasoda and Rohini-devi struggle to overcome their ecstasy, somehow managing to offer arati to their sons as the assembly of gopis and gopas sing songs of Krsna’s deeds, sound gongs, and shout, “Jaya!”

After the arati, Mother Yasoda feeds the boys capatis with sugar and milk mixed with cream, as well as fruit, curd, and other sweets. She then offers Them cool water to drink and betel nuts to chew.

Having received and fed Krsna and Balarama, Mother Yasoda lovingly ushers Them into Their respective quarters, where servant boys and girls are waiting to bathe and dress the two princes.

In the summer months the boys don’t bathe at home but frolic with Their friends in Pavana-sarovara, where Srimati Radharani and Her friends also come to bathe on the women’s side of the lake.

But on this evening, in the privacy of Their own bathrooms, Krsna and Balarama sit while Their servants remove Their worn clothes, dress Them in bathing clothes, and massage Them with oils.

With all kinds of aromatic oils and unguents, the affectionate servants remove the dust from the boys’ bodies, bathe Them with an abundance of cool water, and then dry Them with soft silken towels.

They dress Sri Krsna in yellow clothes, Balarama in blue, handsomely ornament and garland Them, and finally anoint Them with sandalwood paste and tie colourful turbans on Their heads.

Following Mother Yasoda’s order, Dhanistha sets up a table in Krsna’s quarters, upon which she places the food sent by Radha and a lightly spiced dahl soup expertly prepared by Mother Rohini.

After His bath, Balarama leaves to drink varuni and so He does not share this meal with Krsna. At this time Mother Yasoda personally feeds Krsna while Rati fans Him with a peacock-feather fan.

Yasoda sits in front of her son and says, “Princess Radha has personally cooked these delicacies and sent them through maidservants like Rati, who are here to see that You eat everything.

“If Srimati Radharani hears that You have not eaten, She will feel hurt, hut if You give up Your weak appetite and honour Her service to You, She will no doubt be very happy. Is that not so, Rati?”

Rati barely whispers, “Yes, Mother,” nodding in agreement. And Krsna, hearing who has cooked for Him, eats heartily, pleasing both His mother and Srimati Radharani’s maidservant-witnesses.

After Krsna has finished His meal and washed His hands and feet, Dhanistha offers Him the garland and sandalwood paste Radha prepared. He in turn gives Dhanistha His campaka garland.

In a silent exchange of glances, Krsna tells Dhanistha where He will meet Srimati Radharani that night, and Dhanistha conveys the same message to Rati in the same mysterious language without words.

Rati happily places Krsna’s garland and the remnants of His meal on the trays she brought and then quickly returns to Yavata, where she delivers Krsna’s remnants and message to Radharani.

Radha’s spirits rise upon receiving these treasures from Rati but soar upon hearing about the rendezvous. Finally, as if celebrating a great festival, She distributes pan to Her amused and happy friends.

Eager to nurture Her festive spirit, the gopis share Krsna’s remnants with Radha, place Her on a throne, and offer Her arati, singing joyful songs for the success of the imminent meeting.

The arati complete, Radha’s friends leave Her in the care of Her maidservants. Returning to their homes, they attend to household duties, serve their husbands, bathe, and dress in fresh clothes.

Exhilarated by the news of Her scheduled meeting with Krsna, Radha is restless, but Her manjaris persuade Her to prepare for the night of festivities by resting and accepting a light massage.

**\* \* \* \***

Meanwhile Krsna, after enjoying the snack sent by Radha, chews on betel nuts as He proceeds to the meadows to milk His cows, who are eager to see Him and to receive His tender, loving touch.

Balarama, a bit unsteady and His eyes bloodshot from drinking varuni wine, then joins Krsna and Krsna’s servants, all of whom are always eager to help their master in any way they can.

Friends like Sridama and Subala, who have already bathed and milked their own cows, meet Krsna at the city gates, and together all the boys enter the pastures, dancing and singing in a festive mood.

The cows bellow loudly when they see Krsna and kick their hind legs to show their eagerness to be milked by Him. But first Krsna releases the calves so that they can drink from their mothers.

As the meadows fill up with calves scampering after their mothers and drinking happily, and cows mooing in joy and licking their offspring, all the cowherd boys feel great happiness.

One by one, Krsna approaches His favourite cows, like Pisangi. With a gold bucket between His knees He expertly milks them while His friends, happily chatting amongst themselves, milk other cows.

It is not possible for Krsna to milk the entire herd Himself, but to fulfil the desire of every cow He engages His pastime potency to make each cow think that He is the gopa milking her.

Just as Krsna’s friends thought that He was looking at them or sitting beside them as they all ate lunch together, now the cows feel the gopas’ hands and see the gopas’ forms as if they are Krsna’s.

As the reservoir of love, Krsna reciprocates equally with cows, gopas, parents, and gopis. Srila Prabhupada says,

**"... Krsna is embracing the calf and embracing Radharani also. That is perfection."**

As soon as Srimati Radharani receives the news that Krsna is milking the cows, She climbs the moon-tower at Pavana-sarovara. By divine arrangement, even though far from Him, She can see Him clearly.

With the milking complete, Krsna and His friends carry countless pails of milk to Mother Yasoda’s kitchen. The boys then go to sit outside, where they are joined by another group of Krsna’s friends.

Mother Yasoda only cooks for Krsna with milk from cows that graze on very special, succulent grasses, and when Krsna milks those cows Himself, by His touch their milk becomes extra special.

The milk Srimati Radharani uses when She cooks in Yavata or Varsana is equally special due to the loving devotion She infuses into the milk as She cooks Her beloved Krsna’s favourite dishes.

Krsna’s all-powerful transcendental body does not require nourishment from food. It thrives instead upon the love cooked into His daily meals by Yasoda, Rohini, Radha, or other gopis.

By eating, Krsna displays an unlimited appetite for loving exchanges, just as He does when He accepts service, plays games, suckles Mother Yasoda’s breast, or dances with the cowherd girls of Vraja.

When Krsna hears Mother Yasoda call, “O Krsna! O Rama! Bring Your friends and come for supper,” He at once obeys her, even though He is joking and laughing with His cowherd boyfriends.

Followed by Balarama and the others, Krsna holds the hand of a gopa in each of His own, enters the palace, and skips all the way to the dining hall, where Nanda Maharaja is eagerly waiting for Him.

Upon seeing His father, Krsna humbly bows down and takes the dust from His own devotee’s feet upon His head. Nandaraja, his eyes brimming with tears, embraces his son and lovingly smells His head.

Balarama follows Krsna’s lead and also bows to His father, who affectionately embraces Him as well. Nanda offers his blessings to the many boys who have come to eat, and has them all sit at a large table.

Nanda Maharaja’s brothers, along with the village elders, also join the meal. They wash their feet, hands, and mouths and then sit at their appointed seats as the king sits at the head, between his two sons.

Rohini first serves the brahmana dependents of Nanda Maharaja and then she feeds the gopas, who are there primarily to he with Krsna and only incidentally to honour the delicious feast she has cooked.

As usual, Madhumangala creates a jovial atmosphere with his jokes and riddles, while some of the other boys appear shy in the presence of the king and other elders, neither speaking nor laughing.

Nanda Maharaja is fully satisfied to have his son sitting next to him at the dinner table, and Mother Yasoda is happy at heart to feed Krsna and all His friends until they are full up to the neck.

After the meal, the boys escort Krsna to His quarters, chatting excitedly about the evening’s upcoming entertainment. Then Krsna and His friends take a short nap to help digest their hearty supper.

Laying His head on soft pillows, and unlike His friends who think of the evening’s entertainment, Krsna thinks of how, when everyone falls asleep, He will melt into the darkness to join Radha.

As if in obedience to Krsna’s desire, the goddess of night casts her spell over Vraja, withdrawing the last rays of sunlight, darkening all directions, and heralding the arrival of the moon and stars.

Birds settle into their nests for the night, singing of Krsna’s exploits, and the last cows to be milked low gratefully, filling Vrndavana with the felicitous sounds that accompany cow protection.

One by one, ghee lamps appear in the homes of the Vraja-vasis, as if Vraja itself is offering arati to the upcoming pastimes of the Supreme Lord, whose original identity is that of a young cowherd.

This concludes Krsna’s pastimes at dusk, after which Radha’s and Krsna’s transcendental anxiety to meet one another steadily increases throughout the six agonising dandas of the evening.

Because a glimpse of each other at dusk removes the divine couple’s distress, Krsna calls Radha Hara, just as She calls Him Hari. And because the gopis live for Radha’s happiness, they call Him Rama.

In New Vraja-dhama, this early evening begins with Radha-Syama’s gaura-arati. Then They are dressed, served a snack, and offered a final arati, after which the curtains on the altar close for the night.

I perpetually worship Hara’s beloved Hari, whose eternal youthfulness radiates divine passion and splendour, and whose dark-moon face causes high tides in the ocean of bliss, for which we call Him Rama.

May that beautiful young maiden — at the mere mention of whose name, Hare, the prince of cowherd boys, Rama, comes running to shower blessings — bless me with eternal service to Her.

*O Saragrahi Vaisnava soul, Thou art an angel fair, lead, lead me on to Vrindabana and spirit's power declare. There rests my soul from matter free upon my Lover's arms, eternal peace and spirits love are all my chanting charms. (Bhaktivinoda Thakura)*

## Chapter 41 - The Maha-mantra. Part IV

The maha-mantra's seventh pair of names, Rama Rama, represents the awakening of feelings of separation, of attachment for the amorous mellow, and for the desire to take shelter of Sri Radha.

All this takes place as the devotee in whom rati has awakened (*jata-rati-bhakta*) progresses in love for Sri Krsna, finally to become qualified to assist the gopis and taste the bliss of mahabhava.

For such a fortunate devotee, Rama Rama also corresponds to Krsna’s late-evening pastimes and to His beauteous smile, which both lead to the perfectional stage — going back home, back to Godhead.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu puts into plaintive words this ultimate in spiritual awakening,

*yugayitam nimesena caksusa pravrsayitam*  
*sunyayitam jagat sarvam govinda-virahena me*

**“My Lord Govinda! Because of separation from You, I consider even a moment a great millennium. Tears flow from My eyes like torrents of rain, and I see the entire world as void.”**

The development of priti from ecstasy to fully matured love takes place as existential ecstasy (sthayi-bhava) combines with increasingly ripened stages of the four other forms of bhava, like vyabhicari.

Caitanya Mahaprahhu’s teachings and personal example both emphasise that the maturation of rati can take place only in one who performs nama-sankirtana in the mood of separation.

Whether in the midst of public sankirtana with His many associates or in the seclusion of the Gambhira with Svarupa Damodara and Ramananda Raya, He was the embodiment of separation from Krsna.

In addition to the physical symptoms of ecstasy, such as intense crying or horripilation, a distinct characteristic of separation from Krsna (vipralambha-bhava) is to have a distorted perception of time.

Separation from Krsna makes each moment seem to stretch into infinity — days, for instance, seem never-ending—but when Krsna is present, the longest period of time passes as if it were only an instant.

The mood of separation manifests itself under two conditions: before having ever met Krsna directly (purva-raga), and during physical separation from Him after having met (pravasa).

It may seem natural that advanced devotees feel separation from Krsna after having met Him. But the thoughtful reader might question how one can feel separation before ever having met Krsna.

The answer is by hearing about Him. Many devotees became attached to Krsna before they met Him simply by hearing about Him. Feelings of separation, and then love for Him, naturally followed attachment.

The women of Mathura, the wives of the sacrificial brahmanas, and even Rukmini-devi herself, all attained love for Krsna in this way, merely by hearing about Him from others. This is purva-raga.

Princess Rukmini was the daughter of Maharaja Bhismaka, the powerful ruler of Vidarbha, and it was not uncommon for saintly persons to visit the court of that pious king and openly praise Krsna.

Simply by hearing about Krsna’s beauty, strength, and personality, Rukmini developed a love so mature that she fully dedicated herself to Him as only a wife could, and decided she must marry Him.

But her brother adamantly opposed their union. Thinking she had no choice, Rukmini wrote to Krsna and revealed how She had come to love Him. She wrote,

**“O Krsna! O beauty of the worlds!**

**“Having heard of Your qualities, which...remove all bodily distress, and having also heard of Your beauty, which fulfils all the desires of those who see, I have fixed my shameless mind upon You.”**

We can also feel separation from Krsna by hearing about Him. And by performing nama-sankirtana we can cultivate those feelings to ever higher stages of intensity and to more advanced stages of love.

The most fitting topics to hear are those spoken in the mood of purva- raga, for they perfectly transmit the three components of spiritual experience: ecstasy, impetus, and the subject of love itself

An exceptional example of purva-raga is found in the Venu-gita chapter of the Bhagavatam, in which the ecstasy is vipralambha, the impetus for ecstasy is the flute, and the subject of love is Lord Krsna.

There a gopi says, “My dear friends! As Krsna and Balarama pass through the forest with Their cowherd friends, leading Their cows, They carry ropes to bind the cows’ rear legs at the time of milking.

“When Lord Krsna plays on His flute, the sweet music causes the moving living entities to become stunned and the non-moving trees to tremble with ecstasy. These things are certainly very wonderful.”

Verses such as this, remembered while performing nama-sankirtana, transmit some degree of the Vraja gopis' ecstasy, depending on whether the chanter is a practising or a perfected devotee.

At the stage of bhava, a devotee may have had a vision of Krsna and then lost it. Such a fortunate soul easily feels pravasa separation while performing nama-sankirtana based on authoritative descriptions.

Pravasa separation is of two kinds. In the first, Krsna leaves for a short and fixed period of time, such as when He takes the cows out for pasture in the morning and returns again at dusk.

In the second, Krsna leaves to a distant place and there is no clear time when He is expected to return. In such cases, the devotee feels a greater sense of hopelessness and even deeper ecstasies.

According to Kaviraja Gosvami, Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s feelings of separation from Krsna were mostly of this second sort. His lamentation was similar to Radha’s when Uddhava visited Vraja.

“When Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu felt separation from Krsna,” writes Kaviraja Gosvami, “His condition exactly corresponded to that of the gopis in Vrndavana after Krsna’s departure for Mathura.”

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami further encourages us to faithfully hear about the Lord’s meditations and ecstatic emotions, as a result of which full knowledge and love of God will be our rewards.

We should note carefully that there are two ways of hearing about emotions and pastimes in separation: directly from the Vraja-vasis themselves, or through the medium of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

Both kinds of hearing yield equal results, but hearing Krsna’s pastimes from the all-magnanimous Lord Caitanya yields those results faster and easier, as the phrase krsna-prema-pradaya te confirms.

If we are serious, then, about entering the spirit of the gopis’ pravasa separation as portrayed in upcoming verses, we should do so through Lord Caitanya’s poetic elucidations. The gopis said, “O Providence!
