“You have no mercy! You bring embodied souls together through friendship and affection, but before their desires are fulfilled, you separate them. Your activities are like the pranks of children.”

Caitanya Mahaprabhu tasted and mercifully explained this verse, and Kaviraja Gosvami recorded it. Mature devotees take advantage of this mercy and meditate on these ecstasies while chanting Hare Krsna.

In the mood of Srimati Radharani, Lord Caitanya continued, “Providence, you do not know the purport of loving affairs, and therefore you baffle all our endeavours. This is very childish of you.

“If we could catch you, we would give you such a lesson that you would never again make such arrangements. Cruel Providence! You bring together in love people who are rarely in touch with each other.

“Then, after you have made them meet but before they are fulfilled, you again separate them. Providence! You are so unkind! You reveal the beautiful face of Krsna and make the mind and eyes greedy.

“But after they have drunk that nectar for only a moment, you whisk Krsna away to another place. This is a great sin because you thus take away what you have given as charity. O misbehaved Providence!

“If you reply, ‘Akrura is actually at fault; why are You angry with me?’ then I say to you, ‘Providence, you have taken the form of Akrura and have stolen Krsna away. No one else would behave like this.’

“But this is the fault of My own destiny. Why should I needlessly accuse you? There is no intimate relationship between you and Me. Krsna, however, is My life and soul.

“It is We who live together, and it is He who has become so cruel. He for whom I have left everything is personally killing Me with His own hands. Krsna has no fear of killing women.

“Indeed, I am dying for Him, but He doesn’t even turn back to look at Me. Within a moment He has broken off Our loving affairs. Yet why should I be angry with Krsna? It is the fault of My own misfortune.

“The fruit of My sinful activities has ripened, and therefore Krsna, who has always been dependent on My love, is now indifferent. This means that My misfortune is very strong.”

These are the expression of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s lamentation in the mood of separation. We can taste these ecstatic emotions according to our relative capacities by discussing them together.

Sri Caitanya-caritamrta contains many elaborations by Lord Caitanya on the gopis’ expressions of love for Krsna. Devotees everywhere would do well to sing or recite these beautiful songs.

**\* \* \* \***

Because chanting Krsna’s names eases the pain of separation and brings a sense of connection to Him, practising devotees and personal associates call Him Rama. Following their lead, I say, “Rama! Rama!”

Learned authorities describe separation in ten stages of intensity: anxiety, wakefulness, mental agitation, thinness, uncleanliness, talking like a madman, disease, madness, illusion, and death.

One of Srimati Radharani’s dearest friends once reprimanded Her, “Be patient! Why are You so anxious? What is the benefit of this anxiety? Your beloved, the best of heroes, will come soon.”

Radha's reply epitomises the anxiety of separation: “O friend! I don’t see any way that He will come! Our Krsna does not realise what We have suffered from injuries inflicted in the course of loving affairs.

“Love has actually misused Us because love does not know where to strike and where not to strike. Even Cupid does not know of Our greatly weakened condition. What should I tell anyone?

“No one can understand another’s difficulties. Our life is actually not under Our control, for youth will remain for a few days and soon be gone. In this condition, O creator, what will be Our destination?”

As the ecstatic devotee chants Hare Krsna, the stages of separation awaken in his heart, first as reflections of Lord Caitanya’s or the Vraja-vasis’ emotions, and later as direct displays from his own heart.

The separation of pravasa can absorb one in the Vraja-vasis’ journey to Kuruksetra, where one can savour the unique spirit of the Ratha-yatra festival — the spirit of taking Krsna back to Vrndavana.

Sri Radha articulates this mood in one of my favourite verses, wherein She says, “Still, please grant this one benediction: To those persons who reside in the profoundly sweet land of Vrndavana —

“And who for a long time yearn with a steady heart to someday attain You, please, O master of Gokula, appear before their eyes as their youthful friend and engage in Your pastimes with them.”

Srila Prabhupada brought the Ratha-yatra festival to the western world, precipitating our quest for Vraja, a quest that transforms even the Lord Himself, making Him assume the form of Lord Jagannatha.

The extraordinary bodily features that the Lord and His two divine siblings display arise for the two brothers due to Their remembrance of Vraja and for Their sister as a result of her association with Them.

Like Subhadra, who had never visited Vrndavana, we can also experience the deepest symptoms of separation by hearing of Vraja and by keeping company with those who feel that same separation.

Krsna and Vraja are not different from each other, and so feelings of separation from one or the other are also the same. Such feelings bring out the best of both and make Vraja as attractive as Krsna.

Srimati Radharani personally compares the attractiveness of Vrndavana to Krsna:

**“O son of Nanda! O Krsna! Within Mathura- mandala is the most fortunate forest of Vrndavana.**

**“Vrndavana is surrounded by many other forests ornamented with the fragrance of the sweet mellows of Your pastimes, which You enact with the help of Your inconceivable potencies.**

**“In the congenial atmosphere of that transcendental abode, You once enjoyed sports with us gopis, who gave our hearts to You in love. May we again enjoy those pastimes and the songs of Your flute.”**

The effect of cultivating feelings of separation through chanting the maha-mantra is that the chanter’s heart is purified and gradually transformed into Vraja. He or she then yearns to be there with Krsna.

As Vrndavana gradually manifests within the devotee’s heart, pravasa separation gives rise to another kind of Ratha-yatra, that in which the chanter desires Krsna to manifest pastimes within his heart.

Only when Vraja is fully manifest in the heart does Krsna appear there, and only when Krsna appears in the heart is the devotee admitted into pastimes that are available to perfected devotees.

We should always remember that Krsna’s company, the forests of Vraja, and the pastimes therein are not attained by any material adjustment within time or space, but by purification of consciousness.

And that state of consciousness wherein fully developed love for Krsna qualifies the devotee to enter the Lord’s entourage and enjoy the sublime benefits that it offers is called Krsna consciousness.

The true follower of Lord Caitanya thus prays to Krsna, “I have dedicated all my activities to You and made my heart one with Vrndavana, therefore please place Your lotus feet there.”

Will such devotees attain their goal? Will they meet Krsna and gain admittance into His pastimes? Yes! To Arjuna, Krsna repeatedly says, mam evaisyasi satyam: “You will come to Me without fail.”

Krsna spoke similar words of assurance to the *gopis* when they met Him in Kuruksetra,

*mayi bhaktir hi bhutanam amrtatvaya kalpate*  
*distya yad asin mat-sneho bhavatinam mad-apanah*

**“Rendering devotional service to Me qualifies any living being for eternal life. But by your good fortune you have developed a special loving attitude towards Me, by which you have obtained Me.”**

If I had to select one of the Supreme Lord’s instructions that has most inspired me in my lifelong pursuit of Krsna consciousness, it would be this inviolable promise that Krsna made to His dear friend Arjuna.

Service in separation is the most intense form of devotion and the source of the greatest bliss. Such service culminates in meeting Krsna, therefore Srila Prabhupada says, “Back home, back to Godhead.”

The descriptions of Lord Caitanya’s ecstasies are full of meetings with Krsna, as are the portrayals of the Vraja-vasis’ eternal attempts to quench their senses with the nectar of Krsna’s qualities.

Always in search of Her beloved, Sri Radha once saw Him nearby. Not believing Her eyes, She said to Her friends, “Has Cupid himself come? Is this an array of sweet splendours? Is it sweetness itself?

“What am I seeing? Is it an elixir for the mind and the eyes? Is it the releaser of My braids? O friends! It is the beloved of My life, the fresh youth who has appeared to give bliss to My eyes!”

Srimati Radharani and Her gopi friends had been in pain due to separation from Krsna, so they were lamenting the misfortune of being unable to see His features, which are so soothing to the eyes.

Suddenly Krsna appeared before them as He had during the autumnal rasa dance. This favourable turn of events so confused Srimati Radharani that She was unable to believe Her senses.

Now face-to-face with Him, She still feared that She would suffer further if He again left. Because of that fear She mistook Him for Cupid, guessing, “Has Cupid, invisible until now, come in person?”

But as soon as Radha perceived Krsna’s sweetness, a kind of sweetness even Cupid does not possess in such abundance, She wondered whether She was actually perceiving the sweetness of a person at all.

Perhaps sweetness had transformed itself into an apparition to tempt Her eyes and senses. Such are the devotee’s reactions during the time of transition between separation from and meeting with Krsna.

Because bewilderment and other ecstasies can only be mitigated by Krsna’s personal touch, Krsna embraces His devotee to confirm that He is truly present, as He then embraced Srimati Radharani.

In this pastime, Krsna not only embraced Radha but also mischievously opened Her braid, which brought Her to full awareness, “Yes! This indeed is Krsna, the beloved of My life.”

Upon recognising Krsna, Radha was able to fully appreciate Him. She then enthusiastically told the gopis, “O My friends! Look! This fresh youth, the beloved of My life, has now come to give My eyes bliss.”

Radha’s meeting with Krsna, by which She had regained Her lost treasure, brought the ecstasies She had called misery to an end and inaugurated a new sequence of ecstasies She then called happiness.

In a similar way, the ordeal of separation refines the attachment (rati)devotees in ecstasy feel for Krsna, until finally they attain the stage of love (prema), which qualifies them to enter Krsna’s pastimes.

Because the sorrow of being away from Krsna imparts to devotees a pleasure as immeasurable as the joy they feel from finally meeting Him, in both states they call out to Him, “Rama! Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

Having described how nama-sankirtana at the stage of ecstasy awakens spiritual feelings of separation, let us now briefly examine how the transition from bhava to prema takes place.

The constitutional symptom of ecstasy is purity of heart, and its marginal symptoms are the tastes of ecstasy that awaken one’s innate desire to render spontaneous devotional service.

As long as our hearts retain the slightest desire to enjoy sense gratification or liberation from bondage, both of which haunt us like ghosts, any bliss we might feel remains a shadow of the real thing.

Lord Caitanya warns that even though we may render devotional service according to the regulative principles, as long as these ghosts pursue us, we cannot rise to the platform of loving service.

As mentioned earlier, tastes of ecstasy are the result of one’s permanent ecstasy (sthayi-bhava) mixing with a variety of spiritual ecstasies, including the impetus for tasting love (vibhava).

As the interaction of spiritual ecstasies dynamically increases, permanent ecstasy evolves to states ever more relishable, bringing about a softening of the heart and a sense of possession over Krsna.

Rupa Gosvami describes this transition from bhava to the preliminary stage of love for Krsna (prema) in the following way:

**“When that bhava \[which\] softens the heart completely —**

**“Becomes endowed with a great feeling of possessiveness in relation to the Lord and becomes very much condensed and intensified, it is called prema \[love of Godhead\] by learned scholars.”**

This prema has seven additional stages of development. Which of these stages we can taste in our relationship with Krsna is determined by the very nature of that permanent relationship (sthayi-bhava).

Now let us hear a brief outline of the qualities of those stages of love, and how they are tasted in the five permanent mellows of devotion — neutrality, servitorship, friendship, parenthood, and amorous love.

From rati, which is known for bringing great bliss, the first stage (prema) develops, characterised by a sense of possessiveness in which the devotee thinks, “Krsna is mine. I have nothing else but Him.”

Although self-realised sages who meditate on the Supersoul are situated in neutrality, they do not attain this sense of possessing Krsna until, like Sukadeva Gosvami, they serve Him in some way.

At the second stage (sneha), the lover cannot be for a moment without the beloved: “That aspect of prema in which the melting of the heart for the lover is concentrated is called sneha, or affection.”

At the third stage of love a more intimate sense of proprietorship brings about a surprisingly devious mood in the form of anger towards Krsna (mana), in the same way the gopis are often cross with Him.

Fourth, when love awakens a kind of faith in one’s relationship with Krsna that can best be likened to a feeling of exceptional intimacy, particularly visible in Krsna’s friends, love is called pranaya.

The fifth stage of love is a sort of passionate attachment (raga) in which one cannot tolerate even a moment’s separation from Krsna, and which is said to be the limit of love for devotees in servitude.

At the sixth stage (anuraga), that passionate attachment becomes so intense that one sees Krsna in newer and newer ways at every moment. Krsna’s friends and parents taste this exalted state.

But some of Krsna’s friends, such as Subala, are exceptional. Their love matures to the next stage, bhava, wherein all the symptoms of ecstasy occur simultaneously and are equally prominent.

At this seventh stage, the tastes from relishing Krsna’s sweetness in anuraga intensify and combine to make the devotee forget everything — himself and Krsna included — except the bliss he feels.

Only Krsna’s consorts, the gopis and queens, relish the eighth and final stage of love (mahabhava). Srila Prabhupada calls this “highly advanced ecstasy.” At this stage the gopis go wild with wonder.

Because sthayi-bhava is the very essence of a devotee’s constitution, whichever of the five mellows he or she tastes is considered to be the best and most rewarding mellow of all.

Each devotee thus feels, “My service is best.” Still, each sees that objectively, based on the lesser to greater expressions of love described above, “The gopis love Krsna the most.”

Lord Caitanya compares the development of rati — from the stages of prema to mahabhava — to the changes sugarcane undergoes as it is processed, until reaching its tastiest and purest form, rock candy.

Thus it is said,

**“On the platform of amorous love, attachment for Krsna, rendering service unto Him, the relaxed feelings of fraternity, and the feelings of maintenance all increase in intimacy.**

**“On the platform of amorous love, the perfected devotee offers her spiritual body in the service of the Lord. The transcendental qualities of all five rasas are fully present at this stage of love.”**

The gopis' love, then, is the highest and most relishable form of love for Krsna; He is brought under the devotee’s control at all the stages of prema, but the gopis’ love gives Krsna the most intense pleasure.

Various levels of attainment exist even in amorous love. The queens of Dvaraka reach the stage of “advanced ecstasy” (rudha), and the gopis of Vraja achieve “highly advanced ecstasy” (adhirudha).

Highly advanced ecstasy in the state of meeting is called madana. In the state of separation it is called mohana. Of the two, the latter— called *mohana-adhirudha-mahabhava*— is most intense.

That state of highly advanced ecstasy in separation has two features: unsteadiness (udghurna), in which the gopis think themselves to be Krsna, and various types of emotional mad talks (citra-jalpa).

The gopis displayed this unsteadiness when Krsna abandoned them in the forest. Thinking themselves to be Krsna, the gopis enacted His pastimes of childhood and youth, amazing even the Lord Himself.

And the various types of mad emotional talks are encapsulated best in the ten verses spoken by Srimati Radharani to a bumblebee. That song of separation is famous as the Bhramara-gita.

Krsna’s queens also prominently display the grief of separation even while in Krsna’s presence (prema-vaicittya). These displays — albeit less intense than those of the gopis — are famous as kurari-vilapa.

Because Krsna is the source of bliss for the five kinds of devotees who love Him, they call Him Rama, and because He gives the highest bliss to the gopis, there is a special resonance when they call out, “Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

I pray, “O Rama! Please allow me to remember Your form, qualities, and pastimes as I chant Your holy name. O Rama! Make me worthy to enter Your sports and to serve You there in Vraja.”

Amongst all kinds of devotees, those in amorous love are highest, amongst Krsna’s consorts, the gopis reign supreme, and amongst the gopis, Srimati Radharani is foremost in giving Krsna joy.

Lord Caitanya and Rupa Gosvami both teach that to serve Krsna’s servants is the best way to serve Krsna, and most of their followers consider service to Sri Radha the perfection of these teachings.

For this reason, one whose sthayi-bhava is in amorous love aspires to become a maidservant of Srimati Radharani's girlfriends (manjari) and thus become a servant of those who serve Sri Radha.

Srila Prabhupada translated part of Lord Caitanya’s final instruction to Sanatana Gosvami (*vrndavane krsna-seva...kariha pracara*) as “Establish devotional service to Krsna and Radha in Vrndavana.”

Cultivating devotional service to the divine couple ultimately leads to loving devotional service to Them, the upper limit of the goal of life, an attainment beyond which there is nothing further to attain.

Furthermore, Ramananda Raya remarks,

**“The pastimes of Radha and Krsna are very confidential. They cannot be understood through the mellows of servitude, fraternity, or parental affection.”**

The pastimes of Radha and Krsna can be fully appreciated only by one who has the sthayi-bhava of a gopi. Indeed only the gopis, and no one else, can nourish, taste, expand, and broadcast these pastimes.

One cannot attain the confidential service of Radha and Krsna without worshipping Them in the gopis' mood. One must follow in the footsteps of the gopis, and receive their affectionate mercy.

Only by serving Radha’s and Krsna’s girlfriends can one serve the divine couple. Although those two divine lovers are self-sufficient, They require the gopis to complement the moods of Their pastimes.

One may wonder what makes Radha’s and Krsna’s love dependent upon the gopis. The answer is that despite their own love for Krsna, the gopis never want to personally enjoy with Him.

This selfless purity of the gopis’ love so endears them to the divine couple that Radha and Krsna feel incomplete without the presence of Their girlfriends and the affectionate service those girls offer.

Since all the gopis are attracted to Krsna, one may also wonder why all of them do not offer themselves to Him. The answer is that indirect service gives far greater ecstasy than does direct service.

In other words, the gopis enjoy a pleasure ten million times greater when they help Radha please Krsna with Her own loving ways, than if they were to directly enjoy with Him through their lesser devotion.

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains this wonder by comparing Srimati Radharani to a creeper of love for Krsna and the sakhis and manjaris to the twigs, flowers, and leaves of that creeper.

Water sprinkled on the roots of a creeper gives full benefit to the twigs, flowers, and leaves of the creeper. In contrast, water sprinkled directly on the twigs, flowers, and leaves gives very little benefit.

The Thakura concludes,

**“The gopis are not as pleased when they directly mix with Krsna as when they serve to unite Sri Radha with Him. Their transcendental pleasure lies in uniting Them.”**

Obviously the nectar of Krsna’s pastimes, when poured on the Radha creeper, gives a far greater happiness to the gopi twigs, leaves, and flowers than if that nectar were poured on them directly.

Still, Srimati Radharani wants the gopis’ and Krsna’s love to be complete by their direct, mutual exchange, so She makes various arrangements for Krsna to enjoy Himself with Her girlfriends.

On some pretext or another She sends Her friends to Krsna so that they can be with Him directly. She then enjoys happiness ten million times greater than She does when She unites with Krsna Herself.

These are some of the transcendental wonders of the gopis’ divine love for Krsna, which appears similar to the lust of conditioned souls but is, in reality, completely distinct due to its pure, selfless nature.

Under the sway of material lust, conditioned souls are concerned only with their own sensual gratification, but the spiritual lust of the gopis desires only to satisfy Krsna’s senses and give Him pleasure.

The gopis personally reveal their selflessness and absorption in Krsna’s happiness in the following song:

**“Dear Krsna, we carefully hold Your delicate lotus feet upon our hard breasts.**

**“When You walk in the forest, Your soft lotus feet are pricked by small bits of stone causing You pain. Since You are our life and soul, our minds are greatly disturbed when Your lotus feet are pained.”**

Considering all of the above, liberated persons attracted to serving Krsna in the mood of the gopis adopt the gopis’ transcendental mood and always think of the pastimes of Radha and Krsna.

By chanting ñama-sankirtana in such a mood for a long time, after being freed from the material body such devotees are transferred to Goloka Vrndavana, where they may serve Radha and Krsna as gopis.

Should one wonder, “Can I achieve such perfection?” Lord Caitanya assures us that it is possible for anyone and everyone,

*bhavite bhavite krsna sphuraye antare*  
*krsna-krpaya ajna paya rasa-sindhu-pare*

**“When one thinks of Krsna constantly, love for Him manifests within the heart. Even though one may be ignorant, one can reach the far shore of the ocean of transcendental love by Lord Krsna’s mercy.”**

In this way, as devotees chant and chant the holy names, gradually their meditation on the Lord qualifies them for direct entrance into Radha’s and Krsna’s late-evening pastimes (pradosa-lila).

In the form of a beautiful young gopi, such a devotee helps Radha dress Herself for Krsna’s pleasure and then guides Her to the appointed meeting place, a secluded bower on Yamuna’s bank.

Meanwhile, after the evening’s entertainment, Krsna’s mother brings Him home and puts Him to bed, unaware that Her son will soon slip out of bed and leave for a rendezvous with His beloved.

Because Krsna gives His devotees entrance to His pastimes and gives them the greatest pleasure, He is known as Rama, and because He then assigns blissful services to those devotees, they call Him Rama.

Because Krsna is the cause of all kinds of bliss in devotional service, from ecstasy to the greatest love, He is known as Rama. And because I feel great happiness in describing all these things, I shout, “O Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

By always standing next to Her beloved Syamasundara, Srimati Radharani feels unbounded bliss. Her happiness is apparent to all who see Her face — radiant, eyes glistening, overflowing with ecstatic love.

In Vrndavana, great ecstasy has a way of nurturing and expanding itself by making Radha think that Krsna has in fact gone to some other place, even though He remains faithfully by Her side.

Radha’s subsequent ecstasies of separation echo Lord Caitanya’s words: “Even the most learned man cannot understand the words, activities, and symptoms of a person situated in love of Krsna.”

This anguished state, which arises from deep feelings of separation in spite of the fact that Krsna is still present, and which is caused by an exceptional sort of love for the Lord, is called prema-vaicittya.

This extraordinary feature of prema absorbs the mind in one of Krsna’s qualities to the exclusion of all others — including Krsna Himself—and makes one think Krsna is not present when He is.

Sometimes Sri Radha becomes so absorbed in one feature of Krsna, like His singing, dancing, or flute playing, that She cannot see Him in front of Her. As the proverb says, “not seeing the forest for the trees.”

After some time, love makes Radha remember that Krsna is present before Her, but because at first She cannot see Him, the distress of separation overwhelms Her, further obstructing Her vision of Him.

This condition of prema-vaicittya can also arise when, out of intense love for Krsna, Radharani thinks that Her good fortune to always be with Her beloved is too good to be true and He will leave.

In this state Radha’s mind is so absorbed in the possibility of Krsna’s departure that again She actually loses sight of Him, and She sees only Her eternal adversary — separation from Krsna.

Once, under the influence of prema-vaicittya, Radha placed straw between Her teeth and begged one of Her friends, “O sakhi! Please show Krsna to Me!” But He was standing right in front of Her!

Krsna was speechless to see Radha in this state. On another occasion, Radha pleaded with Madhumangala, “Where is that Krsna who answered the cries of the gopas trapped in the forest fire?

“O learned brahmana, have I offended your friend in some way, or has some other attractive gopi called Him to a secluded place, to make lotus-eyed Krsna so quickly abandon Me in this forest?”

As I remember this pastime, it calls to mind another incident in which prema-vaicittya made Radha call out into the forest, as Her lover stood there right next to Her, amazed, “O Rama! O Rama!”

While on the topic of prema-vaicittya, let us hear about another one of Radha-Syama’s outfits, one suited for late-evening pastimes, whose colours and texture could easily awaken such ecstasy in Sri Radha.

Radha’s dress is blue and green, and Syama’s is green and yellow. Whoever proposed that “blue and green should never be seen,” surely never saw this outfit on Radha and Syamasundara.

Had he seen it, I have no doubt he would have amended his dictum with the words, “...except on Radha-Syama!” I prefer the divine couple in these clothes over many, if not all, of Their other outfits.

The pleats of Radha’s skirt alternate between grass-green and navy- blue. The green pleats are embroidered with blue desire-vines, and the blue pleats feature diamond patterns stitched in golden thread.

Her belt is green, and Her blouse is blue on the left side and green on the right. A delicate, dark-blue chiffon cloth, draped from Radharani’s right shoulder to Her left hip, covers Radha’s chest.

The veil covering Radha’s head is blue organza criss-crossed with gold thread and features a green embroidered border. Her beautiful braid is set with green silk ribbons, and a blue tassel bangs at the end.

A blue velvet choker graces Radha’s neck, matching coloured necklaces and a garland of blue flowers rest on Her shoulders, and the rings adorning Her fingers match the tiara on Her head.

As I chant, “Rama! Rama!” the green and blue colours of this outfit remind me of the beautiful green form of Krsna’s expansion, Lord Ramacandra, so dear to Sita-devi and the residents of Ayodhya.

Syamasundara wears a short, knee-length dhoti. In contrast to Radha’s blue and green skirt, Syama’s dhoti is yellow with light green pleats that flare out at the end between His lotus feet.

His upper cloth is a similar yellow colour, pleated and flared at both ends. Like His dhoti, each pleat is embroidered with alternating yellow and green thread, accentuating His threefold-bending form.

Like Radha’s dress and blouse, Syama’s outfit is of fine shiny silk, and like Her veil, His shirt is see-through organza. Though light green, over His dark form that shirt mysteriously appears golden to the eye.

It is for this reason that I suggested Syamasundara’s dress could invoke prema-vaicittya in Sri Radha. In admiring Syama’s handsome dress, Radha could easily lose the sight and sense of Her beloved.

If She did, the sound of devotees’ kirtana would quickly make Radha realise that the rainbow to Her right is Syama’s multicoloured turban, and the flashing sunbeams the sparkling of His eyes and earrings.

She would see that the mass of darkness is not a cloud from which demigods are showering flowers, but Syamasundara’s hair, full of small jasmine flowers from His own garden, set there by His devotees.

Revived from such loving delusion, Srimati Radharani, who rarely looks directly at Syamasundara, would cast all bashfulness aside and stare at Him, feasting Her eyes on His features as She thought:

“O Rama! O crest-jewel of charming cowherds! How lucky I am that without interference I can now relish with both My eyes the beauty of Your youthful face, indeed the beauty of Your very soul.

“O Rama! Although at times You are the dominant lover and at other times You make Me dominate You, somehow it appears as if You always incarnate in the acts of love as their very essence.”

Dear readers! Earlier I mentioned that Rama Rama represents the winsome smiles of Radha-Syama. Writing of Radha’s happiness in seeing Syama reminds me that now it is time to praise those smiles.

If Syama’s dark form is like the glossy ocean and His face the moon above that ocean, then His smile is like the moonshine. May the beams of that moonlight empower me to praise that smile.

The reflection of moonlight off the silky surface of the ocean is more attractive and mysterious than the moonrays themselves, but these two aspects of moonlight are inseparable and complementary.

I cannot fully describe Syama’s smile, but if a description of Radha’s smile accompanies it, I may be able to capture them both. As with the dual aspect of moonlight, Their smiles are inseparable.

**\* \* \* \***

Bilvamangala writes,

*madhuram madhuram vapur asya vibhor madhuram madhuram vadanam madhuram*  
*madhu-gandhi mrdu-smitam etad aho madhuram madhuram madhuram madhuram*

**“O my friend! The transcendental body of Krsna is very sweet, and His face is even sweeter than His body. But His soft smile, which has the fragrance of honey, is sweeter still.”**

Caitanya Mahaprabhu would recite verses such as this, tasting their contents and meanings by explaining them Himself. Absorbed in the mood of Srimati Radharani, the Lord would say:

"Of all His features, the beauty of Krsna’s smile is the sweetest, for it is like a full moon distributing its rays in all ten directions throughout the material world, Vaikuntha, and beyond in Goloka.

“The fragrant illumination of Krsna’s smile is like camphor. It permeates the sweetness of His lips, which He then blows into His flute and transforms into divine vibrations that enter into space.”

“Krsna’s camphor-like smile also mixes with His pleasing speech to produce a mysterious, deeply meaningful sound that awakens all kinds of divine mellows in the hearts of those who hear it.”

A gopi once said, “How can I describe the charm of Krsna’s smile?”Sweetened by the words of our previous acaryas, blended with the beverage of my own observations of Syama’s smile, allow me to try.

Praying at the lotus feet of the divine couple, Radha and Syama, and to the foremost authority on Their lips, the flute, I humbly request my readers to happily drink this praise through greedy ears.

Our lives are perfect if Krsna smiles at us, either personally or in the form of His Deity. Srila Prabhupada writes, “If you can get Krsna to smile upon you just once, your life’s goal is fulfilled.”

But how can a Deity smile? Isn’t His smile limited to the form given by the sculptor? Srila Prabhupada says that a devotee’s conviction is that the Deity cannot only smile, but can also talk and walk.

We repeatedly hear such things from the histories of Deities like Saksi-gopala. And why should we doubt them? Those who doubt should at least accept that the Deity’s sculpted smile is Krsna’s smile.

Krsna has appeared to us in Deity form so that, amongst other things, we will he easily attracted to His smile. If not, we will he attracted to the reflection of His smile — the alluring, illusory energy.

It is said that this material nature, from which we seek deliverance, resides in Krsna’s smile, and that those obstinate fools who do not worship Him remain forever entangled in the network of illusion.

But for those who bow down before Him, Krsna’s smile and laughter are most merciful. For devotees, the Lord’s smile and laughter dry up the ocean of tears caused by the suffering of this world.

Lord Kapiladeva therefore teaches us to practise this meditation:

**“With devotion steeped in love and affection, the yogi can easily meditate in his heart upon the captivating laughter of Lord Visnu.**

**“The yogi will then see the Lord’s small teeth, which resemble jasmine buds made rosy by the splendour of His lips. The yogi should devote his mind to this and no longer desire to see anything else.”**

Syama’s smile is gentle, pleasing, and full of abundant grace. Decorated with the splendour of His teeth, it defeats the kunda jasmine. Dancing upon His ruby lips, it is the guru of all dancers.

Advanced Vaisnavas all agree that Krsna’s smile is nectarean. Some say it is filled with drops of nectar, others say it showers nectar, and yet others say that it is gazed at by nectar personified.

Exalted and poetic Vaisnavas also liken Krsna’s smile to moonshine. They say it glistens like the autumn moon, or that its effulgence is like moonlight, or that it shames the light of countless moons.

The gopis liken Krsna’s smile to a jewelled necklace because it casts its effulgence on His chest or reflects glittering light onto His jewelled necklace as He bends His head down to play His flute.

Along with His abode, flute-song, bodily fragrance, eternal companions, and tinkling ankle bells, Krsna’s enchanting smile is an impetus (uddipana) that precipitates symptoms of ecstatic love.

In addition to relieving us from the grief of material suffering, Krsna’s loving smile frees us from all kinds of sinful reactions, thus making us increasingly susceptible to its own captivating magic.

Krsna’s lips glisten like rubies when He smiles, filling the directions with a radiance that sustains all living things with light and enchants plants, animals, humans, and demigods with sweetness.

Although His smile is ever His supreme opulence, when Krsna reaches adolescence, youth itself combines with His smile and proudly enthrones itself upon the pearl-set ruby throne of His bimba lips.

At that age, amorous desire is the crown upon the emperor that is Krsna’s smile. The recklessness of youth is its sceptre, Kamadeva its insignificant footman, and the rasa dance its daily banquet.

The sweetness of Krsna’s smile is like a camphor-scented intoxicant that first inebriates women’s minds, then addicts them to its effects, and finally forces them to abandon everything else.

But when women, especially the gopis, are unable to obtain the sweetness of Krsna’s smile, they suffer an anguish so intense that they lament as if they had attained everything and then lost it.

Lord Siva once said that the humorous dealings of youthful Krsna — enhanced by the beauty of His sidelong glance and open, merciful smile — increase the amorous feelings in the gopis’ hearts.

In fact, the gopis are the women most affected by Krsna’s smile because they love Him most, even more than do earthly beauties, the wives of the demigods, or even the goddess of fortune.

Krsna’s smile ignites an amorous obsession within the gopis’ hearts, a craving so contagious that it spreads not only throughout their own bodies, but to those of the other girls with whom they speak.

Just as moonlight creates in vegetables the juice of life that makes them palatable, Krsna’s smile induces amorous longings in the gopis, longings that sweeten His amorous dealings with Them.

In Vraja it is well known that the glory of Krsna’s smile excites desire in the saintly village girls. But in Radha, amongst all the other gopis, the desire for amorous pastimes is most intense and most perfect.

Krsna uses His smile as a mantra to charm Sri Radha’s heart, as a messenger to signal Their rendezvous, as a beacon to direct Her to a grove, and as the most persuasive argument needed to win Her over.

Radha is like a cakora bird, living by the moonlight of Krsna’s smile. In that smile’s absence, Her senses, body, and mind burn in anguish, the pain of which can only be extinguished by that moon-like smile.

May the radiance of Krsna’s enticing smile, which welcomes Radharani to a forest grove, entices His friends to a wrestling match, and soothes Mother Yasoda’s eyes, protect and bless us all.

**\* \* \* \***

Rupa Gosvami describes six kinds of smiling: *smita, hasita, vihasita, avahasita, apahasita,* and *atihasita*. He classifies these six into two groups; the first three as major, the second three as minor.

When Krsna’s teeth are not visible but there are definite changes to His eyes and cheeks, that smile is called smita. It is common to Deities’ faces and is easily recognisable in both Radha and Syama.

The next two kinds of smiling are defined by the extent to which Krsna’s teeth are visible. The smile in which His teeth are slightly visible is called hasita, and when fully visible, vihasita.

This major classification of smiling is followed by its minor counterpart, in which the symptoms of smiles and laughter relate to transformations of the body and other gestures.

If the nose puffs up and the eyes squint as a result of extensive smiling, such smiling is called avahasita, and if the eyes fill with tears and the shoulders shake, such smiling is called apahasita.

And finally, when smiling becomes extreme and is expressed by laughter, the clapping of hands, and leaping into the air, it is called atihasita or overwhelming laughter, as exemplified in this pastime:

Krsna once told Jarati, “My dear woman! The skin of your face is now slackened; in fact, your face exactly resembles a monkey’s. As such, the monkey king, Balimukha, has selected you as a worthy wife.”

Although Jarati was Krsna’s aged nurse, He was teasing her. The old lady replied, “My dear boy! I know well that the king of the monkeys wants to marry me. But it’s too late for him!

“I have already taken shelter of Krsna, the killer of many powerful demons. I have carefully considered my options and have decided to marry Him instead of the monkey king. What do You think of that?”

Upon hearing talkative Jarati’s sarcastic reply, all the cowherd girls present began to laugh very loudly, jump up and down, and clap their hands, making a perfect display of atihasita smiling.

Because Krsna’s various kinds of smiling give pleasure to everyone, He is called Rama. And because these smiles indicate the various levels of pleasure He Himself enjoys, He is also called Rama.

Syamasundara’s smile can be classified as smita. However, devotees sometimes comment that in a blissful kirtana His smile appears to widen and His eyes glisten. Such an enhanced smile is called hasita.

Srila Prabhupada makes an interesting observation of how Krsna’s different belts, all very colourful, combine with His enchanting smile to expand the transcendental bliss of His companions.

Amongst Krsna’s companions, the cowherd boys and the gopis are especially expert at making Krsna smile by their jokes, riddles, and games. Thus they are also blessed to witness His many responses.

And of all His personal companions, Madhumangala is the chief jokester, who provides Krsna with comic relief at all times and enhances all the rasas, including the amorous mellow.

The Vraja-vasis adore Krsna’s smiling according to their relationship with Him and the depth of their love for Him. In this way, each of them tastes the rays of His smile differently.

Krsna’s servants relish His smile as a reward for their services, His parents as a sign of His well-being, His friends as confirmation of their intimacy, and His lovers as fuel for their amorous desires.

The Vraja-vasis want to bathe their eyes in the smile that dances on Krsna’s dust-covered face as He places the flute to His lips, His eyes flashing on His way home at dusk with His friends and cows.

Krsna’s smile is not only the nourishment by which the cakora-like Vraja-vasis subsist but also the salve with which He anoints their eyes to help them realise the ultimate purpose of His divine pastimes.

As a child, Krsna would sometimes release the calves just before milking time, allowing them to drink most, if not all, of the cows’ milk. Infuriated, the cowherd men would then chase after Him.

Krsna would run from the elder gopas as they pursued Him through the streets, houses, and courtyards in the village, calling out, “Catch that rascal!” until He was finally cornered with nowhere to hide.

At that time Krsna would smile at the cowherd men, attracting them just as a snake charmer hypnotises a serpent, and the charmed gopas would then totally forget why they were chasing Him.

Krsna would also use His smile to hypnotise the women of Vraja, and then He would sneak into their homes, pinch their babies to make them cry, and cat and distribute their freshly churned yogurt.

But if the elder gopas and gopis were somehow able to resist Krsna’s mystique, capture Him, and bring Him before Yasoda for punishment, Krsna would easily dissipate His mother’s anger with another smile.

Only on rare occasions was Yasoda so angry that she could break through the protective magic of her son’s smile and follow through with punishing Him in some way, like binding His belly with ropes.

Krsna’s smile acts not only as a hypnotic charm but also as a signal, revealing His thoughts and hinting at what He is about to do, as shown in His conversation with His friend Sudama in Dvaraka.

The brahmana had brought some chipped rice for Krsna, but even though the two were intimately reminiscing about their childhood, Sudama was too shy to offer the Lord such a paltry gift.

Smiling as He looked upon Sudama with great affection, Krsna, who knows the hearts of everyone, laughed out loud to indicate that He knew about the gift hidden in His friend’s shawl.

Visvanatha says that Krsna’s smile initiated His plan to make Sudama reveal the gift, and that Krsna’s laugh was His way of asking,

**“For how long will you be able to hide this precious gift in your cloth?”**

The Lord’s wives and lovers know the hidden meanings and ecstatic effects of the smiles Krsna showers upon one and all, but Krsna’s wives relish the Lord’s smile in ways no one else can.

Krsna’s wives perceive His smiles as arrows — Cupid’s arrows — that pierce their hearts. And in states of prema-vaicittya, they think that everyone else must also be pierced like them.

The osprey’s lonely cry for its mate prompts Krsna’s wives to ask,

**“Our friend! Have you also been pierced by Krsna’s smile? His smile is very sweet. One who is pierced by such an arrow is very fortunate.”**

But the gopis, whose love for Krsna is deeper than that of His queens in Dvaraka, feel the Lord’s smile more intensely and in ways known to but not personally enjoyed by Krsna’s wives.

Vrnda once said, “My dear Madhava, Your newly invented smile has so captivated the hearts of the gopis that they are simply unable to express themselves! As such, they have become bewildered —

**“And will not talk with others. All of these gopis have become so affected that it is as if they had offered three sprinkles of water upon their lives. In other words, they have given up all hope of living.”**

Radha’s incomparable love, of all the other gopis', extracts the most from Krsna’s qualities. And yet, paradoxically, His smile alone cannot satisfy Her because it makes Radha so intensely eager for His touch.

Radha once disclosed to a friend Her dissatisfaction at having Krsna’s smile without any further contact with Him: “Friend! Although I have drunk the coconut nectar of Krsna’s talks —

“Conversation that is nectar mixed with the camphor of His smile, because I have not also drunk the nectar of the touch of His body, I am now broken and withered, as if I had drunk poison.”

I could discuss the topic of Krsna’s smile for as long as the moon shines, but I will conclude my praise with one of my favourite meditations on that charming and peerless countenance.

Late one evening in Gokula, as Mother Yasoda sat on Krsna’s bed stroking His face and waiting for Him to fall asleep, she asked, “O my rising dark moon! My child! Why are You not asleep?”

Child Krsna replied with a voice slightly drowsy, “I do not know mother. I suppose sleep has not yet come.” Yasoda lovingly said, “Then I will tell You a bedtime story to make You fall asleep.”

Krsna snuggled up closer to Yasoda’s body, who was the very form of motherly love and parental care, and asked, “Mother, what is this new story that I have never heard before? Please tell me.”

Yasoda described the appearance of Lord Nrsimhadeva, and when she said, “The Lord then appeared from the pillar, very eager to rip the demon to shreds,” a smile appeared on child Krsna’s lips.

May that smile on the lips of a beautiful gopi’s son, a smile that remains on His lips even as He drifts off to sleep thinking of His pastime as Lord Nrsimha, be etched forever within my heart.

I find that thoughts of Syama’s smile replace distress with joy, as Nandaraja himself once said to Uddhava,

*smaratam krsna-viryani lilapanga-niriksitam*  
*hasitam bhasitam canga sarva nah sithilah kriyah*

**“As we remember the wonderful deeds Krsna performed, His playful sidelong glances, His smiles, and His words, O Uddhava, we forget all our material engagements.”**

May we all attain such forgetfulness.

O Syama! When I leave New Vraja-dhama, I weep from not being able to see Your smile, and when I return, similar tears flow, but from the happiness of being able to see that smile once again.

In between leaving and returning, only the remembrance of Your lotus face, bumblebee eyes, and mild smile keeps the unhappiness of separation at bay and allows me to perform my duties in Your service.

By executing the services Radha-Syama allot me, I try to please Them and secure my reward in the form of Their smiles. “If you can get Krsna to smile upon you just once, your life’s goal is fulfilled.”

Upon hearing the cries of the Vraja-vasis, who were about to be consumed by a forest fire, Krsna quickly swallowed it up, and then smiled at them as they cried out to Him in joy, “O Rama! O Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

Allow me to continue praising the pair of names Rama Rama by discussing the smile of Srimati Radharani, a smile that is not only the life of Her followers but also that of Syamasundara Himself.

Because Krsna brings Radha to the summit of loving affairs and then provokes Her to take the dominant role in Their exchanges, devotees amazed by His dexterity in bestowing bliss call out to Him, “O Rama! ”

When Radha first arrived in New Vraja-dhama, we noticed that Her entire body was suspiciously uniform in colour and lacked the translucence of marble. We discovered She had been painted.

Once the white paint that covered Her from head to toe had been removed, one devotee remarked, “She looks more stern now than before.” I disagreed. We had uncovered Her mild, enigmatic smile.

The mystery of Srimati Radharani’s smile and the secret that She shares with Her followers eclipses the famous and supposedly mysterious smile of the Mona Lisa, favoured by mundane people.

They speculate endlessly on the Mona Lisa’s inconsequential secret, but we need not speculate at all about Radha’s momentous secret, *santatasrava-kesava*:

**“She always keeps Krsna under Her control.”**

Indeed, everyone can clearly see on New Vraja-dhama’s altar how Syama is subordinate to Radha. As one devotee commented after Their installation, “It’s certainly clear who’s in charge here.”

Srimati Radharani’s smile is like a night-blooming lotus. It expands and contracts according to the shining phases of Syamasundara’s autumn-moon face as He stands beside Her.

As Syama’s pleasure increases in response to the services rendered by the residents of New Vraja-dhama, His beaming face and glistening smile broaden the range of smiles Sri Radha Herself displays.

The festivals, kirtanas, harvests, and newborn children and calves all offered to the divine couple are endlessly pleasing to Syamasundara, and in turn Radharani’s smile waxes more and more.

Can a Deity’s smile change? Srila Prabhupada answered that very question:

**“Regarding Radha’s smiling, that is not imagination — so She must smile. Let this be an impetus to your increased service.”**

So let us not argue over what some say is a river of nectar in which the swan of Syama’s mind takes shelter, others assert to be rays of ambrosial moonlight sustaining His thirsty cakora eyes —

And yet others see as a bank of clear-white ambrosial clouds that quench the cataka-Syama’s thirst. In truth, all these devotees have mistaken the nectarean wave of Radha’s smile for something else.

Poets, gopis, and Krsna Himself have attempted to portray Radha’s smile. None of them have fully succeeded. But the attempt alone — like defining nectar by constantly tasting it — is infinitely rewarding.

The joy of Radha’s smile is compared to camphor, which, when combined with the sandalwood paste of Her affection for Her friends and the kunkuma of Her beauty, is smeared over Her body.

The sweetness of Radha’s smile is most commonly compared to camphor’s mysterious aroma, but that smile has other qualities in common with camphor — it is also cooling and highly combustible.

When smeared over the eyes, camphor is quite cooling. But it ignites quickly and burns very hot. Similarly, Srimati Radharani’s smile cools the Vraja-vasis’ eyes and mind — especially Krsna’s.

But when the flames of êama ignite Radha’s smile, it causes such combustion in Her loving affairs with Krsna that He feels His limbs aflame in the fire of amorous desire, a fire only She can extinguish.

Sri Radha’s smile is of six kinds, like Krsna’s. She is also fond of joking, because the secondary mellow of humour (hasya-rasa) suits Her friendship with the gopis and Her loving sports with Krsna.

Chaste girl that She is, Radha sometimes covers Her face with Her veil when Krsna sees Her in public. But even then She cannot help but smile at Her beloved, who cannot help but smile at Her in return.

On one such occasion Krsna remarked,

**“Radha is very beautiful when She covers Her face with Her sari; the little I see of Her smile is like liquid camphor filtered through a finely woven cloth.”**

Ever-fresh nectarean loving sentiments flow from Srimati Radharani’s smile. Naturally, then, Her smile is compared to a white lotus, to celestial streams of nectar, and to a lotus-filled lake.

Her face is like the moon, and so it is only natural that Her smile be compared to moonlight. But, unlike Krsna’s smile, which is like moonlight from the dark moon, Hers is the light of the silvery moon.

In praising her princess, a gopi once described Radha’s smile in this way:

**“The desire-vine of Hari’s qualities grows in the garden of Radha’s heart and flowers in the form of Her smile.”**

These beautiful metaphors exalting Srimati Radharani’s smile are more than just poetic ingenuity. They are born from the effect Her smile has on Vrndavana, on the Vraja-vasis, and on Krsna Himself.

It is a well-known fact that the effulgence of Srimati Radharani’s smile makes Vrndavana’s creepers grow, its flowers blossom, its stones melt, and all manner of birds and beasts sing Her praises in joy.

The budding of Sri Radha’s gentle smile lights up the ten directions and nourishes Her swan-like friends, who blossom with love for Her and sing of Her unlimited glories with angelic voices.

The soothing effect of Her cooling smile — the moonlight of Her face — shames the material moon in this universe and transforms Krsna, day by day, into an increasingly thirsty cakora bird.

As this shower of unique sweetness descends upon Krsna, His heart’s thirst grows until, unable to contain Himself any longer, He stops Her in a secluded place and begs Her to save Him, lest He die of thirst.

Just as Krsna’s breath transmits the sweetness and radiance of His smile into the vibration of the flute, Radha’s smile infiltrates and then emerges from Krsna’s flute as Her own song.

When She steals His flute, when He gives it to Her, or while They are rasa-dancing, Radha pours the nectar of Her smile into the flute, which is the ultimate authority on Radha’s and Syama’s smiles.

According to Srila Prabhupada, Radharani’s smile is one of the sixty- four arts, which also include dancing and cooking. The purpose and effect of any or all of those arts are to make Krsna happy.

Does Radha succeed in Her purpose? His Divine Grace answers,

**“Krsna is captivated by Radharani. Therefore the devotee says Krsna is Madana-mohana...but Radharani is Madana-mohana-mohini.”**

How does Radha enchant the enchanter of Cupid? Sitting with Radha, Krsna once saw His own reflection on Her breasts. Confused, Krsna said,

**“Two youths are now reflected upon Your breasts.**

**“I don’t know how these twins acquired such charming elegance, which flows in waves of blue splendour, but You should accept Them as friends and embrace Them firmly with love.”**

The chronicler of this pastime, Prabodhananda Sarasvati Thakura, blesses us,

**“May Sri Radha’s smile, which appears when Krsna sees His own reflection and speaks these bewildered words, protect us all.”**

Because Krsna, His attributes, and His many ways — such as playing the flute — give unlimited pleasure to Sri Radha, and because Her smile makes this evident to everyone, Krsna is called Rama.

Radha remembers Krsna’s charming ways even in the presence of Her husband and Her seniors. At such times She restrains Her smiling with great difficulty only by silently chanting, “Rama, Rama.”

Sri Radha once related a similar situation to an intimate gopi friend: “O sakhi! What shall I say to you? I have fallen in love with Krsna. My body and heart, careless of dharma, are wild after Him.

“Since His handsome form filled My eyes, I haven’t been able to see anything else. My bodily hairs stand on end. And since I first heard His flute-song, I haven’t been able to hear anything else.

“My nose is wild after the fragrance of His body, My tongue will speak nothing but His name, and My heart simply searches after more of His virtuous qualities, causing disturbances throughout My body.

“My husband and elders see all these symptoms and rebuke me. I pray to the sun god to conceal the meaning of My irrepressible smile, and I count the moments to the next meeting with My lover.”

Krsna is just as obsessed with Radha as She is with Him. The splendour of Her mysterious smile, magnified by Her beauty and youth, always plays in His mind like a bumblebee around a flower.

Radha’s smile also signals the lowering of the drawbridge of Her anger towards Krsna, whether as a result of Krsna’s own wily schemes or the persuasive arguments of some gopis. Vrnda once told Krsna:

“Angry Radharani’s mood changed when She heard a gopi-messenger say, ‘Dear Princess! On the shore of the Yamuna, the charming, nectar autumn moon now bathes the forest with splendid moonlight.’

“Suddenly, Srimati Radharani's heart was pacified by the prospect of pastimes offered by such a romantic atmosphere, and so Her smile assumed a lustre that signalled She was pleased with You.”

As previously mentioned, Srila Prabhupada says that if Krsna smiles at us our life is a success. The same can be said for Radha’s smile. And until that time comes, it should be our constant meditation.

Now let us hear how Radha’s suppressed smile erupted into laughter as She played a joke upon the gopis. Once, after amorous pastimes with Krsna, Radha asked Him to give the same bliss to Her friends.

As Krsna was courting Lalita and the other gopis, Radha’s maidservants freshly adorned Her, carefully removing all signs that She had been with the lion-king of the groves, Kunja-bihari.

Radha decided to play a trick on Her friends. First, She pretended to be waiting in vain for Her lover, and as the gopis’ entered Her bower, She shed crocodile tears and openly sobbed as She lamented:

“Where is My dearest? Bring Him here at once. Of what use are My body and My ornaments now?” Pretending to be shocked at the sight of love marks on Her girlfriends, Radha knitted Her eyebrows angrily.

But just as She was about to admonish Her friends, She lost Her composure and broke into a naughty smile. Hastily covering Her face with Her veil, She went on to taunt the gopis:

“O My friends! I am so sad to see cuts on your bimba-fruit lips and scratches on your breasts. Did you perchance run into a cave to chase after a snake or some other creature that then bit you?”

The gopis replied with one voice, “The snake that bit us is under Your control, and it was You who sent Him to us! O fair-faced girl! Aren’t You the one who is famous for these kinds of tricks?”

Unable to contain Herself, Radha dropped Her veil, and Her smile changed to laughter as Her friends threatened, “Laugh now! But when we reveal Your schemes, Hridevi will stifle Your laugh.”

Because Krsna gives pleasure to Radharani by pleasing Her friends, She calls Him Rama, and because He derives great pleasure from the gopis’ quarrel with Radha, I call out to Him, “O Rama!”

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna’s pastimes of love are a source of pleasure for His associates, who call him Rama. These pastimes give both practising and perfected devotees great joy, and so they call out to Him, “O Rama!”

In this world of turmoil and distress, my service to the Lord and the chanting of His holy names are my two unshakable sources of spiritual pleasure, a truth I celebrate by calling out, “Rama! Rama!”

I conclude my praise of the seventh pair of names in the maha-mantra by narrating some evening pastimes of Krsna. These pastimes bring joy to those who hear them, making them chant, “Rama! Rama!”

The cowherd boys rise from their after-dinner nap and quickly wake their friend Krsna, saying, “Hari! Just listen to the tumult below! The performers are waiting for Your arrival. Let’s go, quickly.”

Mother Yasoda has servants dress her son in regal attire before allowing Him to join His friends and the audience waiting downstairs. Krsna will, after all, be sitting at the centre of the royal assembly.

Servants dress Krsna in elegant royal robes, tuck a jewelled dagger in the sash around His waist, smear sandalwood paste on His limbs, and place the prince regent’s sceptre in His hand.

They tie Krsna’s hair in a topknot, bind it with a red and golden string, and crown it with a handsome peacock feather. Finally, they place a delicate wreath woven from tiny flowers on His head.

The servant boys adorn Sri Krsna with flashing earrings, a precious pearl nose ring, diamond choker, jewelled locket, and assorted strings of giant pearls, all from the royal treasure chest.

Krsna is now restless to meet His friends and join the fun below, so Mother Yasoda opens the door of His apartment and invites the gopas to escort their dear friend to the festively decorated courtyard.

Flanked by friends, with servants to the front and the rear, Krsna holds Balarama’s hand as He enters the assembly, looking like the moon rising in the sky alongside its influential planets.

Nanda Maharaja, also dressed in royal finery, sits on a large throne, with his two divine sons on either side of him. The two brothers, with joined palms, humbly offer respects to Their elders.

The throne is surrounded by silk carpets, upon which Krsna’s friends take their scats in two groups. Subala, Arjuna, and their friends sit in front, while Sridama, Sudama, and their friends sit to the left.

Stout servants hold lamps aloft, brahmanas recite auspicious invocations to inaugurate the evening’s entertainment, and row upon row of expert musicians play instruments and beat drums.

Townspeople quickly fill the royal courtyard, but no matter how many guests arrive, there is space to accommodate them all. And every guest, from his or her particular vantage point, can see Krsna.

With so many devotees gathered together in such a close space, and all lovingly uttering Sri Krsna’s names, so much bliss is generated that they wonder if entertainment is necessary to add to their enjoyment.

Still, the performance begins. Bards sing their own compositions devoted to Krsna’s exploits, accompany themselves with musical instruments, and bring their songs to life with exuberant dancing.

The audience is quite pleased with this presentation, so Nanda Maharaja rewards the performers with gold coins and requests that they return on another night. A dance performance follows.

Talented singers call out the dance steps to the accompaniment of drums, and dancing girls charm the audience by depicting Krsna’s pastimes killing asuras like Arista and Vyoma, and chastising Kaliya.

As before, Nanda rewards the performers. Then a pot-bellied comedian makes everyone laugh by singing and playing instruments as he impersonates foolish villains like Kamsa and Jarasandha.

In the middle of the comedian’s act, a mute clown suddenly appears at the far end of the stage, where he begins a second show that leads to a staged argument and then a mock fight between the two jokers.

When not rolling on the ground laughing, the boys throw coins on the stage, and the clown and comedian fight over the money, sometimes pulling each other’s noses or slapping each other’s cheeks.

At the peak of the hilarity, when the audience is laughing as if with one voice, Madhumangala unexpectedly appears onstage, pushes the two clowns into the wings, and then takes centre stage himself.

The boys jeer Madhu and pelt him with flowers, but the great brahmana has his own act prepared. Unruffled, he starts his routine by cutting indelicate jokes that immediately have everyone laughing.

After picking arguments with members of the audience and drawing them into his act, Madhu disappears from the stage, only to return in one disguise after another, each with its own corresponding scenario.

First he comes out dressed as an outcaste and ridicules the foolish ways smartas treat those of low birth, then he dresses as a prostitute and struts across the stage, casting seductive glances at Krsna.

For his next act Madhu appears as a dacoit and threatens members of the audience, scaring little children into their parents’ arms. He finally discards his costume to again become lovable Madhumangala.

For his finale, Madhu sings the glories of the six kinds of foods as he contorts his body in various postures and makes outlandish faces. Finally he leaves the stage to an overwhelming round of applause.

Krsna and His friends hold their stomachs and laugh, but before the next act can begin, Raktaka comes and whispers to Nanda, “Mother says you must stop the show. Rama and Krsna must sleep.”

Nandaraja dutifully rises to his feet and addresses his subjects. Thus bringing the evening to a close, he rewards the performers and separates his sons from Their friends so the two boys can take rest.

Nanda takes Krsna and Balarama by the hand, bids farewell to his subjects, and enters the palace. The spectators, abuzz and aglow with the bliss of enjoyment, gradually return to their own homes.

Once the two boys are inside, servants remove Krsna’s and Balarama’s royal jewels, unbind Their hair, dress Them in light sleeping clothes, wash and dry Their feet, and offer them cozy slippers.

Overwhelmed by exhaustion, Balarama offers respect to His father, embraces Krsna, and retires to His room, where He quickly falls asleep as His dedicated servants massage His weary body.

Krsna also says goodnight to His father. With Maharaja Nanda’s blessings, Krsna enters His own room, which has just been freshly washed, dried, and scented with aguru incense, Krsna’s favourite.

The moonlight streaming through the open window and balcony door illuminate Krsna’s jewel-studded bed, whose moonstone posts, golden canopy, white sheets, and soft pillows beckon Him to sleep.

Most of the furniture in the bedroom is carved ivory. Perched in a corner, a pair of green parrots spread their wings to greet Krsna and then huddle together to sleep, as they expect Him to do as well.

But Krsna does not lie down. He walks out onto the balcony with His servants to appreciate the sweetness of the Vrndavana night, concluding that it is the most fitting atmosphere for His pastimes.

Returning to His room, Krsna sees that His mother and a few maids have brought Him a bowl of condensed milk. Smiling, Yasoda says, “The night is long. Don’t go to bed hungry. This will help You sleep.”

Krsna looks at the beautiful face of His mother, her eyes full of tears of love and her dress wet from the milk of affection that flows from her breasts. How can He refuse anything she asks of Him?

Sitting down to eat, Krsna says, “I’m not hungry. But because you have requested Me to eat, I must do so. But only when I see that you have gone to your own room to rest after your long day of work.”

Yasoda sits on a chair opposite Krsna and replies, “I will go. But first I want the pleasure of seeing You eat.” To satisfy His mother, Krsna relishes every drop of condensed milk and then washes His mouth.

Mother Yasoda warmly embraces her son, repeatedly kisses His forehead, and with great difficulty leaves Him, retiring to her own quarters, followed by maidservants sincerely dedicated to her feet.

One of my godsisters, in the months before she left this world, came to the realisation that her svarupa was that of Mother Yasoda’s maidservant, and that her service was packing Krsna’s lunch.

Though she spoke about this only to her husband, she revealed a deep affection for Krsna’s divine mother, a transcendental blessing that must surely have been the special mercy of Srila Prabhupada.

In His bedroom in Nandagrama, Krsna climbs into His foam-soft bed, rests His left arm against a large bolster, and basks in the rays of moonlight that stream through His window in brilliant, silver shafts.

The two pet parrots open their eyes and mistake one such shaft of moonlight for a crystal rod. But when they repeatedly try to land on it, they are left flapping their wings frantically in the air.

The young servant boys attending Krsna giggle at this amusing scene. And although Krsna tries to keep His composure, eventually He can no longer contain Himself and He too laughs aloud.

Finally Krsna leans back against a pillow and fixes His mind on Srimati Radharani’s smiling face, gradually drifting off to sleep as some intimate servants massage His feet and others fan Him.

Soon the goddess of sleep also overcomes the servant boys, who lay down right there in Krsna’s room and quickly fall into a deep, sound sleep just as Krsna is waking up to pursue His nocturnal pastimes.

Krsna rises from bed without disturbing the boys who are scattered about the room like tossed flower petals and, stepping out on to the balcony, He plays His flute in a way that only young gopis can hear.

The flute’s message is an affectionate plea to Srimati Radharani and Her friends, “Leave your houses now and set out on the path to the meeting place. I am on My way there. Soon we will be together.”

Tucking the flute in His belt, Krsna leaps onto the balustrade. With the help of a thick creeper, He slides to the ground and stealthily makes His way down the rear, uninhabited part of the hill.

Once Krsna reaches the forest of Domila, rarely visited by travellers due to its wilderness, He moves more freely and quickly on the familiar path that will lead Him to the bank of the Yamuna.

Because Krsna’s charming ways give pleasure to His friends, parents, and beloveds, they all call Him Rama, and because the pleasure Krsna bestows is fully transcendental, scriptures also call Him Rama.

Radha’s heart skips for joy as She hears the flute’s message, so She says to Herself, “O Rama!” and as soon as She can, She follows His call, running ever faster, driven by the strength of His name, Rama.

**\* \* \* \***

As Nanda’s subjects were starting their evening entertainment, in Yavata Jatila continued to show kindness to Radha, but born out of fear of Surya’s wrath, not genuine affection for her daughter-in-law.

How could anyone be unfavourably disposed to such a kind, gentle, and loving person as Radharani? Certainly Abhimanyu, Jatila, and Kutila can feel the way they do only by Krsna’s divine arrangement.

Radha has detractors amongst the Vraja-vasis and harsh critics within Her own family, just as She has competitors amongst the gopis. All this just serves to enrich Krsna’s pastimes and give Him greater joy.

But we may ask why Radha has to suffer this injustice. Will we share the same fate in the spiritual world? In short, the answer is that Krsna’s will is never unjust. It is always completely perfect.

Such doubts arise in the hearts of those controlled by the laws of material nature. In the spiritual realm, the term injustice has no meaning, nay, no existence, because there only love moves us to act.

In other words, at the stage of perfection we do not accept Krsna’s will out of duty, but out of love. We equally embrace anything that He wants of us, be it a source of our personal happiness or distress.

The very nature of spiritual life is that any distress accepted in Krsna’s service becomes spiritual bliss. How that can be true is only completely understood at the stage of full realisation, not before.

With the following words Radha not only makes a philosophical statement but also reveals the heart of a true Vraja-vasi:

**“Let Krsna tightly embrace this maidservant who has fallen at His lotus feet —**

**“Or let Him trample Me or break My heart by never being visible to Me. He is a debauchee, after all, and can do whatever He likes, but He is still no one other than the worshipable Lord of My heart.”**

Justice and injustice are based on the relative considerations of dharma. But in Vraja the only consideration is Krsna’s happiness, which Vraja-vasis embrace whether its cause is just or otherwise.

This is the inner meaning of Krsna’s final teaching in the Gita, wherein He says,

**“Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do not fear.”**

The residents of Vrndavana are completely surrendered to making Krsna happy, and so what may appear unjust to conditioned souls is, by His grace, a source of bliss for the residents of Vrndavana.

Radha tastes Abhimanyu’s anger, Jatila’s meanness, and Kutila’s censure just like a boy enjoying the pains of mock-wrestling, a mother cleaning her baby’s waste, or a bride bearing her husband’s weight.

There can never be injustice in surrendering to Krsna. Nonetheless, there is a limit to how much the conditioned mind can value absolute surrender and for this reason a devotee’s faith must be strong.

The faith of practising devotees will be tested in myriad ways, and, as they advance in Krsna consciousness, one of those ways may well be that they are made to endure circumstances that appear to be unjust.

If we learn to accept seemingly unjust circumstances as readily as we do those easily justified by the rational mind, we will be ornamented with the deep faith that qualifies us for loving devotion.

Jatila encourages Radha to eat Her dinner, saying, “O daughter! Since Your husband has already eaten and my daughter has gone to bed, You should eat Your supper along with Your friends.

“You must forgive me for listening to village gossip and insulting You. I promise that it will not happen again. Indeed, I have arranged that tomorrow quarrelsome Kutila will stay at another’s home.”

Radha is happy to hear these words, but covers Her face with Her veil and just looks down submissively at Jatila’s feet. The old woman rubs her own head and says, “I can’t even remember what I was saying.

“O dear! I fear that I may not be alive for much longer. My hopes rest with my son, and with You. O my girl! I think Your mother and father must be demigods to have given birth to such a daughter.”

For some time, Jatila carries on like this, smiling at Radharani and holding Her hand. Then they go to the kitchen, where the old woman sits Radha down and serves Her puris, milk, and sweet rice.

But Radha’s heart is racing from the thought of soon meeting Krsna. She doesn’t fancy sharing a meal with Jatila, and so She says, “Mother! You must be tired. Please go to bed. I will cat upstairs.”

The old woman seems pleased to be relieved of her duty. The two embrace and retire to their respective quarters, and Radharani breathes a sigh of relief as She closes the door to Her apartment.

Perhaps Jatila’s apologetic attitude is a sign that fate has finally decided to smile upon Radharani. Seeing that Her maidservants have set a table for Her with Krsna’s remnants, Radha sits down to eat.

Radha sets Jatila’s dishes aside to make room for the laddus and milk brought from Nandagrama that Lavanga-manjari has placed in front of Her. Just by looking at His remnants, Radha sees Krsna.

As soon as Radha touches Krsna’s prasada with Her hands, Her body erupts in goosebumps, and when She tastes it, Her lips tremble and She becomes so excited that She forgets about eating.

The touch, smell, and taste of Krsna’s remnants make Radha appear mindless for some time. Tears trickle onto Her plate as She mechanically places a few morsels into Her mouth, as if out of habit.

Suddenly Radha is stunned. Unable to move Her hands, She cannot eat. Concerned that Radha might be late for Her meeting, a maidservant speaks softly into Her ear, “O beautiful girl!

“You should eat quickly if You want to arrive at the meeting place on time. Lalita-devi is here now and Visakha-devi is on her way. And they are both eager to go with You into the dark night.”

These clever words have the desired effect. Radharani gradually withdraws from Her trance and begins to eat again, though Her throat is still choked with love, making it difficult for Her to swallow.

And yet, somehow She finishes Krsna’s remnants, wipes Her mouth with the edge of Her sari, and lies down on Her bed, chewing pan. Quickly She falls asleep and dreams of meeting with Krsna.

Meanwhile, in a grove within a campaka forest along the bank of the Yamuna, Vrnda-devi and her assistants are busy making arrangements for the divine couple’s imminent meeting.

The forest goddesses hang plenty of flower garlands around the grove and petal garlands around the bedstead. They hang golden lamps that burn with a soothing glow and set a table with refreshments.

On another table, Vrnda’s servants place other items such as aguru, betel nuts, and sandalwood paste. Vrnda lights incense and repeatedly washes the floor inside and outside the grove with rosewater.

The pastime grove within the campaka forest glows with a soothing blue hue, inspiring the bees to drink honey from the flowers, the peacocks to dance, and the songbirds to serenade everyone.

Indeed, to bring pleasure to Krsna’s senses, Vrndavana dresses itself in all its sylvan sweetness and, just to serve the Lord, keeps the forest creatures, birds, flowers, breezes, and all its opulences awake and alert.

As the waves of the Yamuna quietly sing of Krsna’s victories within her groves, the gopis in Yavata make preparations to further add to Krsna’s glories as the lion of the groves, Kunja-bihari.

**\* \* \* \***

The darkness of night has sprinkled the residents of Yavata with the potion of sleep. Only the effulgent gopis are left to be targets for Cupid as he wanders around town, letting loose his flower arrows.

Having lulled their husbands and in-laws into deep sleep, girls like Citra and Visakha quietly dress and ornament themselves by lamplight and, at just the right time, tiptoe out of their homes.

The gopis assemble in Radha’s sitting room as She rises from bed, washes Her face, and, with Her maidservants’ help, dresses to blend in with the darkness of the forest caused by the dark moon in the sky.

Attired in dark clothes and ornaments, Radha will surely be invisible to the world, but at the same time She will instantly attract the eyes of a certain dark Lord making His own way to the campaka forest.

Radha puts on a dark blue sari and blouse, decorates Her braid with a black tassel, smears musk on Her body, and, from anklets to tiara, dons a variety of dark-blue ornaments to match Her dress.

Radha, a blue lotus in Her hand, joins Her friends for a few moments to exchange embraces and hushed words of assurance. Then they all look through the window out onto the courtyard below.

Peering into the darkness, one gopi asks, “Do you see anyone?” Another answers, “No. Everyone is asleep.” And with that they all tiptoe down the stairs and leave the house like thieves.

The gopis' bodies burn with longing, but their minds are agitated with fear as they slowly, silently move through the shadows of Yavata village until they reach the edge of the outlying forest.

As the gopis enter the forest, which will shelter them during their journey to the Yamuna, they let out a collective sigh that resembles a sandalwood-scented breeze blowing in from the Malaya Hills.

Carrying the burden of their youthful beauty, the gopis walk as fast as their full hips, heavy breasts, and thin waists allow, stopping at times to catch their breath, holding each other’s hands for comfort.

In time Sri Radha’s entourage reaches the campaka forest. Radharani enters the appointed grove with a few friends, while most of the girls wait outside, all hoping that Krsna is already there. But He’s not.

And yet, Radha is pleased to see the beautifully decorated grove. Visakha places a wreath of flowers on Radha’s head as She sits down, another gopi straightens Her clothes, and another garlands Her.

But it isn’t long before Krsna’s absence starts to weigh on Sri Radha’s mind, pouring fuel on the fire of love that rages in Her heart. She begins to cry, and tears streak Her cheeks with mascara.

Radha’s friends at once come in to console Her. A glance and gesture from Lalita prompts one maidservant to say, “Princess! Do not fear! I will go just now to find Your lover and bring Him to You.”

Krsna has not been held up by anyone on the way, but the lotus of Vrndavana conspires to increase Srimati Radharani’s desire for Her beloved by making His journey a little longer than expected.

Sri Krsna knows that Radha is anxiously waiting for Him and so, in spite of all danger, He fearlessly rushes through the night over secret paths. Such are the austerities of loving others’ wives.
